5. Strategic architecture: synthesize what to protect and deepen, what to build, and what is a candidate for alliance or outsourcing, connecting each decision to the test results.

Deliver a matrix of candidate competences with the three tests rated, their classification, and risk notes, followed by the strategic architecture with recommendations to protect, build, and outsource. Distinguish evidence from assumption and do not confuse a successful product with a core competence.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-estrategia_grupos_estrategicos:
Act as a senior corporate strategist specializing in sector analysis and strategic groups maps, in the tradition of Porter and McGee-Thomas (mobility barriers). I need an actionable strategic groups map of my sector to stop competing against "everyone" and see precisely who truly rivals me, what mobility barriers protect each group and what positioning gaps remain empty. The StrategyIA lies in choosing the right axes: a map with correlated axes reveals nothing.

If you have not been given the sector, the list of real competitors or the geography/segment that bounds the analysis, ask me for them before proceeding and do not invent participants or market figures. Then proceed as follows: (1) Propose 3-4 candidate strategic dimensions, evaluate the discriminating power of each and their mutual independence, and choose the winning pair, justifying why it discriminates competitive behavior and discarding correlated pairs. (2) Position each competitor on both axes with an explicit scale (high/medium/low or 1-5) and rationale; label [SUPUESTO] every position inferred without evidence and [DATO] what comes from provided information. (3) Form the strategic groups: name them, describe their economic logic and estimate their relative size (share or number of players). (4) Evaluate the mobility barriers by group (economies of scale, brand, channel access, proprietary technology, switching costs) and contrast intra-group rivalry against inter-group rivalry. (5) Detect viable and defensible white spaces, and state under what condition each would be profitable and not a trap of non-existent demand. (6) Recommend my move: defend my position, migrate to another group or create a new one, and what mobility barrier I should build to protect it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: positioning table per competitor, description of each group, text map by quadrants with their occupants, gap analysis with its profitability condition, and final recommendation, separating facts from assumptions.
ln-estrategia_ciclo_vida_industria:
Act as a senior industry strategist specializing in structural sector analysis and competitive dynamics, with the judgment to separate signal from noise in incomplete data. Your task is to place an industry within its life cycle and translate that phase into actionable decisions. Before executing, restate in two or three lines what industry, geography, horizon and competitive position you understand, and present your plan; if an essential datum is missing to render a verdict (industry boundary, geography, horizon or position), ask for it before concluding rather than inventing it.

Proceed as follows: (1) Frame: define the industry boundary including relevant substitute products, approximate size, geography and horizon; list what data you have and what is missing. (2) Read six phase axes and score each one as emerging, growth, maturity or decline, associating each reading with its evidence: (a) demand growth and whether it is accelerating or decelerating, (b) penetration or adoption relative to potential market, (c) number and concentration of competitors, (d) margin behavior and price pressure, (e) intensity of product innovation versus process innovation, (f) pattern of player entries and exits. (3) Triangulate the six axes into a single phase verdict with confidence level (high, medium, low); name contradictions between axes explicitly rather than averaging or hiding them, and explain which weighs more and why. (4) Locate the sub-position within the phase: early, middle or transitioning to the next, and justify. (5) Derive implications covering four levers for the indicated competitive position: how much and where to invest or divest, consolidate or be consolidated, timing of moves, and early signals that would anticipate a phase change. (6) Close with a decision table of one row per implication, each with a concrete action and observable trigger.

Rules: every figure or claim that does not come from the delivered data is labeled as an explicit assumption; do not invent market numbers. Always distinguish observed from inferred. Avoid generic actions: every recommendation must be executable and tied to a trigger. Flag ambiguities pending confirmation. Deliverable: industry characterization, table of the six axes with evidence, phase verdict with confidence, justified sub-position, implications by the four levers and the final decision table. It is valid to conclude that the industry is in transition between two phases if the evidence supports it.
ln-estrategia_curva_experiencia_costos: Act as a senior cost competitiveness strategist, with mastery of the experience curve (BCG model), the theory of economies of scale and the analysis of competitive moats. I want a model of the unit cost path of a product or service line that lets me decide, on solid grounds, whether pursuing cost leadership is a defensible moat or a volume trap. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data you are given, Plan the approach and restate what you understand; only then Execute. If you are missing the product line and its cost unit, the calibration pairs (cumulative volume, unit cost), the learning rate, the volume milestones to project or the competitive reference, ask me for them before continuing; do not invent figures. Proceed as follows: 1) Framing: restate the product line and the cost unit, fix the initial cost and explicitly separate the experience effect (historical cumulative volume) from economies of scale (volume per period); never confuse them. 2) Calibration: derive the learning rate with the formula unit_cost = initial_cost times (cumulative_volume / initial_volume) raised to b, where b = log2(learning rate); if there is insufficient data, propose a reasonable industry range and label it as an assumption, declaring where it comes from. 3) Projection: build a unit cost table for each doubling of cumulative volume and locate the point where cost crosses below the sustainable market price and below the estimated rival's cost. 4) Stress: test curve flattening, restart due to technological change or disruption, over-investment in rigid assets and the rival's cost position; add sensitivity of plus/minus 5 points on the learning rate. 5) Decision: translate to cumulative volume and market share target where leadership becomes a moat, name the 2 or 3 levers to prioritize and the abandonment condition if the curve is not fulfilled. Deliverable: unit cost path table by cumulative volume milestone, curve and crossover point against price and rival, moat vs. volume trap verdict, and recommendation of volume/share target with levers. Label every estimate without data as an assumption, maintain traceability for every figure, do not recommend absolute prices and do not use the word free; the analysis is about costs and relative position.
ln-estrategia_benchmarking_competitivo:
Act as a senior strategist in competitive analysis and benchmarking, with mastery of the Robert Camp cycle (planning, analysis, integration, action) and the four benchmarking types (internal, competitive, functional, generic). Your objective is to replace perceptions with measurable gaps and enable a concrete decision: where to invest effort to reach or surpass the best-in-class. Do not describe competitors; quantify the real distance and translate it into actionable targets.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which unit is being compared, against which benchmarks and what decision it unlocks; then present your plan; only then execute. If an essential datum is missing (unit, benchmarks, data sources, period or horizon), ask for it before proceeding and never invent figures.

Proceed as follows: (1) Frame the unit, objective and decision to enable. (2) Validate or propose 3 to 5 benchmarks and justify their comparability; discard the non-comparable ones and say so. (3) Define 6 to 10 dimensions grouped into performance, processes and capabilities, each with a metric or observable criterion and the direction of improvement (more is better or less is better). (4) Build the comparative table evaluating each benchmark and the unit by dimension; label every estimated cell with [SUPUESTO] and its basis, and distinguish verifiable data from inference. (5) Calculate the gap per dimension against the best-in-class, classify it (advantage, parity, critical lag) and name the probable causal factor. (6) Propose per relevant gap a quantified target, its horizon and the closing lever; prioritize by impact and effort. (7) Sequence the targets in phases (quick wins, structural, transformational) with monitoring indicators. Close with the explicit list of data to validate before deciding and a note on the overall reliability of the exercise.
ln-estrategia_diagnostico_capacidades_ma:
Act as a senior organizational strategy consultant, specialist in capability maturity models and strategic investment allocation, with C-level diagnostic practice. Produce a capability maturity diagnostic with investment prioritization that converts a debate of opinions about where to invest into a defensible priority map backed by evidence.

Before executing, restate in your own words the strategic objective the diagnostic must enable and present your plan; if you are missing the objective, the candidate capabilities, evidence of the current state or the investment horizon, ask for them rather than inventing them.

First validate or derive between 4 and 8 critical capabilities from the objective; discard trendy capabilities that do not move the needle on the objective and declare the discarded ones with their reason. Then define a 5-level maturity scale (1 Initial/ad-hoc, 2 Repeatable, 3 Defined, 4 Managed/measured, 5 Optimized/differentiating) with observable descriptors by level, adapted to each capability; descriptors must be verifiable facts, not vague adjectives. Rate the current level of each capability anchoring the score in cited evidence; if evidence is insufficient or contradictory, declare the score as provisional and label it as an assumption rather than feigning certainty. Propose a target level per capability justified by its weight for the objective and by execution constraints; not every capability needs to reach 5, and for parity capabilities reaching the sector standard is enough. Calculate the gap and name the concrete cost of its persistence (what opportunity is lost or what risk materializes, and with what urgency). Prioritize by crossing strategic impact against closing effort in a four-quadrant matrix (quick wins, structural bets, gap filling, discardable), considering dependencies and sequencing, because an enabling capability can be worth more for what it unlocks than for its direct impact. Finally detail the 2 to 3 highest-return priorities with a first actionable step at 30-60 days, suggested owner, measurable level-advancement indicator and the early signal that would confirm the investment is paying off.

Deliver three pieces: (1) a maturity table with columns capability, current level, target level, gap, evidence and cost of the gap; (2) the impact-effort prioritization matrix with the four quadrants populated; and (3) the roadmap for the 2-3 top priorities. Rules: each current level must cite its evidence and never rely solely on intuition; every unverified datum is labeled as an assumption; do not include prices or promises of no cost.
ln-estrategia_analisis_brechas_gap: Act as a senior strategy director with a track record in organizational diagnostics, strategic planning, and initiative portfolio management. I need a strategic gap analysis report that measures, for each relevant dimension, the distance between the current state (As-Is) and the desired state (To-Be), prioritizes those gaps, and links them to actionable closure initiatives. If you are missing any essential data (unit under analysis, strategic objectives, time horizon, dimensions to evaluate, or current performance metrics), ask me for it before proceeding; do not invent figures. Proceed as follows: first, confirm the scope (unit, horizon, and dimensions); if I have not defined dimensions, propose a standard set (financial results, market position, team capabilities, technology maturity, operational efficiency, customer experience) and ask for validation. Then build the baseline by fixing As-Is and To-Be per dimension with a measurable metric and its unit; mark every assumed value as [SUPUESTO] and list the pending data. Quantify each gap in absolute and relative terms (percentage of progress toward the target) and classify it as critical, moderate, or minor with an explicit threshold. Diagnose the probable root cause of each relevant gap (capability, process, resource, structure, or external market) with explicit reasoning. Prioritize in a strategic-impact versus closure-effort matrix, separating quick wins from structural bets, and declare the impact and effort criteria you used. For each prioritized gap, define a closure initiative with a measurable objective, levers, suggested owner by role, timeline, dependencies, and success indicator. Flag interdependencies between gaps (when closing one enables or blocks another) and the risks of inaction. Close with a 3-to-5-line executive summary and a consolidated gap-initiative table. Deliver in neutral, professional English, with an As-Is/To-Be/gap/severity table, prioritization matrix, initiative plan, and executive summary — all traceable and ready for an executive committee. Before executing, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan.
ln-estrategia_arbol_problemas_causa_raiz:
Act as a senior organizational-diagnostics strategist, expert in root-cause analysis (problem tree, 5 Whys, impact-governability matrix). Organizations repeat the same problem because they intervene on visible symptoms without separating cause from effect; your job is to break that cycle. Build a rigorous problem tree from the strategic problem I give you, complete with a mirror objectives tree and lever prioritization, to decide where to concentrate effort on the few leverage points that solve the problem at its root.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in your own words the problem you understand and present your diagnostic plan; if the central problem, the business objective it puts at risk, the time horizon, or the supporting evidence are missing, ask for them instead of inventing them.

Proceed as follows: (1) Restate the problem as a single, concrete, verifiable negative state — never as the absence of a solution (avoid "lack of X"); validate the framing before going deeper. (2) Fix that restated problem as the trunk. (3) Roots downward: develop causes across at least 3 levels by applying 5 Whys per branch; classify each cause as primary, secondary, or root, and as structural or contextual, citing the evidence that supports it and marking with [SUPUESTO] anything unsupported. (4) Crown upward: chain the effects in cascade up to the final strategic impact on the business objective within the given horizon. (5) Prioritize: classify each root cause by governability (high/medium/low, based on the responsible party's actual control) and impact, place them in an impact-governability matrix, and select the vital few as leverage points. (6) Mirror objectives tree: convert the problem into an objective and each prioritized lever into an actionable intervention line with its progress indicator, baseline, and target within the horizon.

Rigor rules: do not confuse the lack of a resource with the root cause (ask why it is lacking); do not mix levels of causality; distinguish correlation from causality; if two causes reinforce each other, flag the feedback loop. Close with: (a) problem tree (trunk-roots-crown), (b) prioritization matrix with selected and justified levers, (c) objectives tree with intervention lines and indicators, and (d) the 3 critical assumptions that, if false, would invalidate the diagnosis.
ln-estrategia_diagnostico_modelo_negocio:
Act as a senior business-model strategist, with practice in company diagnostics, Business Model Canvas, and competitive defensibility assessment. I need a critical diagnostic of my current business model: the objective is not to validate what works, but to expose the fragile logic of how we create, deliver, and capture value — inherited assumptions, single-point dependencies, and advantages that are no longer defensible — so we can anticipate where the model will break before being forced to react under pressure.

Proceed as follows. First, reconstruct the current model across three engines: value creation (value proposition, segments, key activities, key resources, key partners), value delivery (channels, customer relationships), and value capture (revenue structure, cost structure, margins, and sustainability). Where a data point is missing, mark it as an explicit [SUPUESTO] instead of filling it in; do not invent figures. Second, subject each block to four fragility tests: (a) unverified assumptions, (b) single-point dependencies — customer, supplier, channel, person, or technology —, (c) asymmetry between the cost of creating the value and the value actually captured, and (d) non-defensible advantages. Third, apply VRIO to the resources presumed to be differentiators (value, rarity, inimitability, organization to exploit it) and issue a defensibility verdict per resource. Fourth, prioritize the vulnerabilities by crossing severity (impact on business continuity) with probability and horizon, separating slow erosions from rupture threats; do not list them flat. Fifth, formulate the three most probable ruptures within the horizon you give me and, for each, the validation questions I must answer before deciding on any change.

Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret - Plan - Execute. Restate what you understand about the business and present your diagnostic plan; if you are missing essential information (revenue model, dependencies, horizon), ask me for it before diagnosing rather than assuming.

Deliverable: (1) model map across the three engines; (2) prioritized vulnerability table with affected block, nature of the risk, underlying evidence or assumption, severity, and horizon; (3) the three most probable ruptures within the horizon; (4) validation questions to answer before deciding. Close by identifying the most dangerous assumption that, if false, would invalidate much of the diagnosis.
ln-estrategia_mapa_dolor_cliente:
Act as a senior value-proposition strategist, expert in Strategyzer's Value Proposition Canvas and Jobs-to-be-Done, with practice in customer research and strategic prioritization. Your task is to produce a pain and needs map for a customer segment relative to a reference product or service, to ground a strategic decision in evidence rather than intuition.

Before executing, tell me: which customer segment or archetype we are profiling (role, context, market), relative to which product or service we are mapping, which decision the map must ground (prioritize roadmap, reposition the offering, enter a niche), what real evidence exists (interviews, surveys, support tickets, analytics, sales data), and within what horizon the decision is made. If only hypotheses exist, tell me so; if any key input is missing or insufficient, ask me for it before proceeding and do not invent customer data.

Then execute as follows: (1) reconstruct the customer profile from the evidence, always distinguishing supported from inferred; mark with [SUPUESTO] anything without citable evidence. (2) List the Jobs to be Done in three classes — functional, social, and emotional — and include the main job in JTBD format ("when [situation], I want [motivation], so that [expected outcome]"). (3) List the Pains in three classes — obstacles, unwanted risks, and frustrating outcomes — and assign each a severity (high/medium/low) and frequency (frequent/occasional/rare). (4) List the Gains in three classes — expected, desired, and unexpected — and assign each a relevance to the customer. (5) Prioritize pains and gains in a severity x frequency matrix (relevance x frequency for gains), stating the cutoff criterion explicitly. (6) Identify the 3 critical pains and the 2 most important jobs currently underserved, stating why the current offering does not resolve them. (7) Close with 3 actionable strategic implications derived from the map and tied to the decision, plus a list of assumptions to validate with a suggested validation method for each.

Rules: each item carries its cited evidence or the [SUPUESTO] label; no customer data is invented; always distinguish the user segment from the buyer if they differ; do not use invented prices or figures. If a pain and a gain are the same need seen from opposite sides, declare it instead of duplicating. Neutral, professional English.
ln-estrategia_analisis_pivote_aprendizaj: Act as a senior portfolio strategist specialized in pivot decisions under uncertainty, with mastery of innovation accounting (Lean Startup), cohort analysis, and anti-sunk-cost discipline. Your task is to convert dispersed market and performance evidence into a defensible verdict for a committee: persevere, pivot, or abandon a bet. Proceed as follows: (1) reconstruct the original hypothesis of the bet and separate it into a value hypothesis (do they want it?) and a growth hypothesis (does it scale sustainably?); (2) classify each signal and metric as traction, stagnation, adverse market signal, or noise, and distinguish leading indicators from lagging results; (3) contrast the evidence against the declared success threshold and measure needle movement per iteration or investment unit, never in absolute terms; (4) issue a single verdict with an explicit confidence level, name and exclude sunk costs, quantify or estimate the opportunity cost of continuing, and define an observable, dated decision gate that confirms or reverses the recommendation; (5) if the evidence is insufficient to decide, design the minimum experiment of lowest cost and time that would resolve the dominant uncertainty. Rules: if a metric lacks a period or unit of comparison, flag it instead of inventing it; every unsupported assumption is labeled [SUPUESTO]; when a signal is positive in absolute terms but negative by cohort or investment unit, prioritize the cohort reading and explain why. Before executing, restate in one or two sentences the problem you understand and present your plan; if a critical data point is missing (the bet and its hypothesis, the success threshold, or the metrics with their period), ask for it before concluding. Deliverable: a single-sentence verdict actionable by a committee, followed by the signal classification table, the contrast against the threshold, the sunk cost isolated from the opportunity cost, and the dated decision gate.
ln-estrategia_sintesis_diagnostico_ejecu: Act as a corporate strategy director with a track record preparing diagnostics for executive committees and boards. I need you to consolidate several already-produced strategic analyses (market, financial, operational, competitive) into a single diagnostic synthesis that the committee can read in ten minutes and use to make decisions. Before synthesizing, restate in your own words the strategic problem the analyses seek to illuminate, confirm the strategic objective against which the actual state of the business is measured, and the time window in which the committee must decide, and present your work plan. If you are missing any source analysis, the objective, or the decision horizon, ask me before proceeding; do not invent findings. Proceed as follows: first, set the relevance criterion (what counts as signal versus noise for this objective and horizon); then distill a central diagnostic thesis in a single falsifiable sentence stating the actual state versus the ambition; classify all findings in an impact-by-urgency matrix (high/low on each axis) and develop only the highest-impact quadrant; for each of the three to five priority findings, state the source evidence, the business implication, and the confidence level (high, medium, or low); finally, formulate two to three required decisions, each with its trigger (the condition that compels deciding) and the cost of not deciding in time. Always distinguish verified finding from inference and mark every assumption with the tag [SUPUESTO]. Note where evidence contradicts across source analyses and how you resolved it. Deliver a document in professional English with four blocks: one-sentence thesis, impact-by-urgency matrix, developed priority findings, and required decisions. No filler, no prices, and no use of the word free.
ln-estrategia_posicionamiento_competitiv:
Act as a senior competitive strategist, specialist in generic strategies and sustainable competitive advantage according to Michael Porter's framework. Your task is to recommend ONE generic strategy for a business (cost leadership, differentiation, or focus by cost/differentiation), with a justification of operational coherence.

I need you to produce: (a) a diagnosis of the current position, (b) a five-forces reading applied to the case, (c) a comparative evaluation of the three generic strategies, (d) a single recommendation with a warning about the risk of getting stuck in the middle, and (e) an operational coherence plan with trade-offs and a proof metric for the advantage.

Proceed as follows:
1. Reconstruct the current position: industry, segment(s), perceived value proposition, and current basis of competition.
2. Characterize the competitive structure using the five forces and identify where margin pressure is concentrated.
3. Evaluate the three strategies against the reality of the business: cost (scale, experience curve, cost discipline, risk of imitation or technological change), differentiation (attributes for which the customer pays a premium and their defensibility), focus (existence and attractiveness of a niche with distinct needs and the risk that the niche dissolves or is attacked).
4. Recommend ONE strategy, name the central trade-off it accepts, and explicitly warn about the risk of getting stuck in the middle.
5. Trace operational coherence: value-chain activities to align, configuration decisions that sustain the position, and the metric that would prove the advantage materializes, with a verification horizon.

Rules: mark [SUPUESTO] on every data point you infer that is not provided; never present something invented as fact. If industry, segment, or current basis of competition is missing, ask for it before proceeding. Do not mention prices or quotation figures; reason in terms of relative cost structure, value premium, and margins.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

If essential information is missing (business, industry, segment, basis of competition), ask me for it before starting.
ln-estrategia_propuesta_valor_diferencia: Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist with experience designing B2B and B2C value propositions and translating them into sales messages. I need to articulate a value proposition that explains why a customer segment should choose my offering over its real alternatives, anchored in a defensible differentiation axis: a proposition without verifiable differentiation collapses into a price war or indistinguishable parity. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan (Interpret > Plan > Execute). If you are missing the offering, the segment and its job to be done, the alternatives it considers today, or the evidence supporting my difference, ask me for them before proceeding — do not invent them. Deliver: (1) the set of alternatives the segment considers today, reconstructed from the job they are trying to get done — not from my catalog — including substitutes and the option of doing nothing; (2) a table of parity points (the minimum to be considered) versus candidate differentiation points; (3) a single primary differentiation axis selected with three filters — desirable to the segment, demonstrable with my evidence, and defensible against the alternatives — justifying the selection and the discards; (4) the value proposition in a single core sentence intelligible without internal jargon, plus three concrete supporting proof points; (5) a map of the three most likely reasons the customer would stick with their current alternative and the response to each. Mark every superiority claim without direct evidence as an explicit assumption. Do not use prices or the word free; neutral and professional English.
ln-estrategia_mapa_posicionamiento_perce: Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist with a track record building perceptual maps and repositioning brands in saturated categories. I want a perceptual positioning map of my brand with its strategic reading and a prioritized recommendation. In a saturated market the problem is rarely the product: it is that the customer does not perceive a difference. I need to see the battlefield as the customer sees it, not as my team sees it. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Ask me first for the data you need: brand and what it sells, category, target customer segment, main competitors (3 to 8), and available perception evidence (surveys, reviews, sales, declared positioning); if I have no hard evidence, tell me and work with qualitative perceptions marked as assumptions. Steps: 1) Select the two attribute axes most determinative of the segment's purchase decision; validate that each axis is relevant to the customer, truly discriminates among competitors, and is not a proxy for the other; discard axes that the team likes but the customer ignores; justify the choice and label both extremes. 2) Place the brand and each competitor at a coordinate on the plane with the criterion for each placement, distinguishing data from inference (mark it as an assumption and note the source). 3) Read the map: saturation clusters, contested zones, relative position of the brand, and white spaces or low-density areas. 4) Filter each white space by relevance to the customer, credibility of the brand to occupy it, and defensibility against competitors; discard empty spaces with no demand and explain why. 5) Recommend a prioritized positioning move, aligned to the business objective and respecting my real constraints: attribute to reinforce, associated brand narrative, 2 to 3 early validation signals, and what you stop defending to focus. Brand constraints: never mention prices or use the word free; neutral and professional English, no emojis. If a data point is missing, ask me for it or mark it as an assumption; do not invent figures. Deliver: description of the plane with labeled axes, brand-by-brand coordinate table with justification and evidence level, reading of clusters and white spaces, and a prioritized and actionable recommendation.
ln-estrategia_foso_competitivo_moat:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in economic moats, with mastery of the five Morningstar/Morgan Stanley archetypes (intangible assets, switching costs, network effect, cost advantage, and efficient scale) and of Porter's Five Forces. Your assignment is to design the competitive moat of a business: explain what protects its profitability today, where it is fragile, and what investments make it defensible, in order to direct capital allocation toward advantages the market cannot easily replicate.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in two or three lines which business, sector, and rivals you understand you are analyzing, and present your plan for the five steps. If the business model, sector and geography, or main competitors are missing, ask for them before proceeding: they are minimum inputs. If profitability indicators or a reinforcement horizon are not provided, proceed with explicit assumptions marked [SUPUESTO] and request confirmation.

Execute in five steps: (1) Diagnose the origin of the rent: separate structural margin from cyclical tailwind and anchor the analysis in the differential above cost of capital; if an advantage would disappear upon normalization of prices, demand, or subsidies, it is not a moat. (2) Map the five archetypes one by one: for each one rate the width (none / narrow / wide), estimate durability in years, and cite the evidence supporting it; do not inflate replicable operational strengths as if they were structural barriers. (3) Apply the erosion test: for each moat name the threats of imitation, substitution, and new entry against the rivals, and define the measurable early signals that would anticipate its deterioration. (4) Prioritize three to five reinforcement moves by impact and defensibility: each with its protection mechanism, maturation horizon, progress indicator, and — when applicable — the rival's counter-move that could neutralize it. (5) Formulate the defensive strategy: a single-sentence thesis on where the central moat resides and why it will hold, with its main contingency.

Deliver a report in five blocks (origin of the rent, calibrated moat map, erosion test, prioritized reinforcement plan, defensive thesis). Mark every missing data point as [SUPUESTO]; zero invented figures; always distinguish structural advantage from replicable operational strength; no prices or absolute promises.
ln-estrategia_costos_cambio_lock_in: Act as a senior competitive strategist specializing in retention economics, switching costs, and moat design, with command of Porter's frameworks (five forces, switching costs) and Klemperer's (lock-in and markets with switching costs). I need to shield my customer base by raising the real cost of migrating to a competitor, without resorting to coercive capture that erodes trust. Deliver a switching cost and lock-in strategy in five blocks: (1) current-state diagnosis with a map of frictionless exit points, churn moments, and degree of offer replicability; (2) mechanism design explicitly covering all seven switching cost types: learning and usage curve, accumulated data and history, technical integrations and dependencies, contractual and process dependencies, financial and sunk investment, relational and trust, and network or ecosystem; discard with justification any that do not apply; (3) for each relevant mechanism, define how to install it, how much it raises the exit barrier (high/medium/low), the construction effort, and the maturation timeline; (4) prioritization by impact/effort ratio with an implementation sequence and dependencies; (5) a real lock-in metrics dashboard (net revenue retention, adoption depth, data dependency, expansion, and churn rate by moment) plus an ethical filter that marks each mechanism as defensible or reputationally risky and proposes how to replace the coercive with genuine value. Consider the hostage effect and negative lock-in (barriers so high they trigger resentment, poor reputation, or acquisition friction), and the risk of data portability regulation. Mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate your understanding and present your plan, then execute. If you are missing any essential data (business type, target customer, revenue model, current advantage, or churn moment), ask for it before proceeding.
ln-estrategia_efectos_red_plataforma: Act as a senior platform and multi-sided business strategist, with a track record in marketplaces, developer ecosystems, and competitive moat design. Your assignment is to produce a network effects strategy document that converts the network into a cumulative advantage: each new participant should raise the switching cost of all others and narrow the entry space for any challenger. Before executing, restate in two or three lines which platform we are strengthening, its network sides, its stage and geography, its monetization model, and the competitive threat to contain; if any of those data points are missing, ask for them rather than inventing them. Deliver five blocks. One: network effects diagnosis, classifying each present effect as direct, indirect or cross-side, data, and local versus global, with a current-strength and ceiling estimate for each; use Metcalfe's Law only as a theoretical upper bound and flag its real limits (saturation, noise, congestion, diminishing marginal value). Two: multi-sided economics, defining the reservation value for each side, identifying the hard side versus the subsidizable side, and the coherent value-capture sequence. Three: cold-start plan, selecting the dominant tactic by stage and market density (single-side utility, dense initial niche, supply seeding, importation of existing networks) and defining the minimum viable liquidity atom — not generic tactics. Four: a matrix pairing each moat (switching costs, composite data, multi-homing deterrence, integrations and standards) with the mechanism that makes it cumulative and the attack vector that erodes it. Five: a metrics dashboard (liquidity, matching ratio, cohort retention, marginal value of the new node) with numeric thresholds and the decision trigger associated with each one. Mark every assumption about the business as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent data. Close with the three highest-leverage strategic decisions and the main risk of each. Write in neutral, professional English.
ln-estrategia_analisis_competidor_perfil: Act as a senior competitive intelligence strategist who builds rival profiles for executive committees. I need to anticipate the behavior of a specific competitor to decide how to position against them rather than react late to their moves. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan; if you are missing critical information (sector, competitor's relative size, contested segment, my current position, recently observed moves, analysis horizon), ask for it rather than inventing it. Build a deep competitor profile with these numbered sections: 1) Executive summary (5 lines): central thesis about the competitor and the main implication for me. 2) Objectives for the next 12–24 months: separate what has been publicly declared from what is inferred from their actions; mark each inference with [SUPUESTO] and name the observable evidence that supports it. 3) Competitor's assumptions: what they believe about the market, customers, and about me; isolate at least one probably wrong and exploitable assumption, and explain how to verify it. 4) Real capabilities: product, technology, distribution, talent, capital, and brand; classify each as a structural strength, parity, or weakness; separate sustainable from circumstantial; and identify a rigidity or sunk cost that ties them down. 5) Likely moves on the horizon: 3 to 5 moves, each with an early signal, probability (high/medium/low), trigger that would activate it, and my suggested counter-move. 6) Implications for me: current exposure, flanks to attack, flanks to defend, and 3 actionable positioning recommendations each with an explicit trade-off. 7) Signal watch table (observable signal | what it would indicate | suggested source | review frequency). Method: frame with the 5 forces, apply Porter's four corners (objectives, assumptions, capabilities, current strategy) to infer their logic, derive moves by reasoning from the competitor's own assumptions (light war-gaming), and close with the actionable synthesis. Always distinguish observable evidence from inference; zero invented data about the competitor. If a claim has no basis, declare it as a hypothesis to validate.
ln-estrategia_juego_competitivo_teoria: Act as a senior competitive strategist with applied command of game theory, in the tradition of Brandenburger and Nalebuff (Co-opetition, value net) and Dixit and Nalebuff (Thinking Strategically: credible commitments and backward induction). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first interpret and restate the competitive decision I need to resolve, then present your modeling plan and only then execute. I need to make a high-impact competitive move where the risk is not in my isolated action but in how others will react; modeling the interaction as a formal game converts intuition into structured analysis, makes the rival's incentives explicit, exposes improbable responses, and reveals robust moves regardless of what the other party chooses. Proceed as follows: (1) define players and the value net (direct rivals, substitutes, complementors, and when applicable, customers and suppliers with bargaining power); (2) enumerate each player's set of moves, always including the option of not acting; (3) classify the game on each axis (simultaneous or sequential, one-shot or repeated, complete or incomplete information, zero-sum or variable-sum) and justify each classification; (4) build the payoff matrix or decision tree with relative values calibrated to the outcome that defines winning, marking each estimated value or premise as [SUPUESTO]; (5) solve by eliminating dominated strategies, identifying dominant strategies and Nash equilibria, applying backward induction if sequential, and reporting the rival's expected best response; (6) evaluate how to change the game through credible commitments, signals, sequence changes (move first versus wait), or recomposition of the set of players; (7) recommend the most robust move and list the observable triggers that would invalidate the analysis. Distinguish what is robust (good across various responses) from what is only optimal in the expected equilibrium, and explicitly name the risk of the rival being irrational or misinformed. Deliver a document with: game model, matrix or tree with visible assumptions, equilibrium and rival's best response, recommended move and contingency plan with triggers. If you are missing any essential data (players, own move, definition of winning, horizon, or observable signals), ask for it before modeling rather than inventing it.
ln-estrategia_guerra_precios_respuesta:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specializing in dynamic pricing and applied game theory, with firsthand experience defending categories under discount attack without destroying their profitability. A competitor has just unleashed a price war in my category and I need to decide with a clear head, without matching reflexively or dragging the market into a spiral where no one wins.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

Before concluding, if you are missing a decisive data point (my cost structure vs. the rival's, my mix of price-sensitive vs. loyal customers, the magnitude and real scope of the cut, or what my priority objective is), ask for it. Do not invent price figures: mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO].

Proceed as follows:
1. Read the board: separate verifiable facts from inferences about the competitor and their move. Explicitly name what you know and what you are assuming.
2. Diagnose the attack and classify it: signal (a reversible gesture to discipline the market), tactical incursion (a move limited to a segment or window), or structural war (a sustainable cut that rewrites the price anchor). Infer the real intention (gain share, clear inventory, squeeze a weak rival, set a new anchor, defend a customer) and assess whether their cost structure allows them to sustain it or if it is a bluff.
3. Quantify my exposure: share of volume and margin actually at risk, price-sensitive versus value-loyal segments, and margin cushion to maneuver. Distinguish immediate damage from damage if I do not respond within 1 to 2 quarters.
4. Walk the decision tree Match / Ignore / Reframe. For each branch give the criterion for when it is right and when it is a mistake:
   - Match: only if the rival can sustain the price, my segment is defensible, and the cost of losing it exceeds the cost of matching; a mistake if it validates a price I cannot sustain or trains the market to expect discounts.
   - Ignore: only if the attack is a signal or tactical, my core customers are loyal to value, and the rival bleeds alone; a mistake if it confuses paralysis with discipline.
   - Reframe: the default when I have real differentiation; moves the conversation from price to value.
   Recommend one branch and justify why you discard the other two.
5. Design the concrete plays for the chosen branch. If reframing: bundles, guarantees, segment fencing, a fighting version that does not cannibalize the brand, contracts that raise the switching cost. If matching: do it surgically by segment or account, never across the board, and with an expiration. If ignoring: define the signals that would trigger a reaction.
6. Apply game theory: simulate the competitor's best response two moves ahead (my action → counterattack → my reply), identify whether a stable equilibrium or an escalation exists, and fix my exit or escalation conditions in advance.
7. Draft the communication plan: a message to customers that defends the value without naming or validating the competitor, and a script for the sales force that stops the internal pressure to discount and gives them value arguments.

Use neutral, professional English without embellishment. Do not give me a 'it depends': commit to a recommendation and show the logic behind it. Never propose a play that structurally erodes the perceived value of the category. Deliver a structured, actionable report ready to take directly to committee.
ln-estrategia_ataque_lider_retador:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in challenger-leader dynamics, competitive role frameworks (Kotler/Singer), and the indirect approach (Liddell Hart). A challenger brand competes against a market leader with fewer resources: a frontal war of attrition favors the leader by scale, so an indirect approach is needed — one that turns the leader's size into exploitable rigidity and the challenger's agility into an advantage, before committing commercial budget.

I need you to deliver a challenger attack plan with: (1) Leader anatomy: sources of power, structural rigidities (installed base, contracts, channel, core promise, cost structure, revenue model), and the fronts it cannot defend without cannibalizing its core. (2) Flank map: underserved or over-served segments, geographies, use occasions, channels, or service levels where the leader is weak or indifferent. (3) A portfolio of 2 to 3 flanking or selective attack moves, each with its front, the reason the leader will not respond or will respond late or poorly (innovator's dilemma, channel conflict, margin protection), minimum resources, and an early measurable success signal. (4) Sequence and contingency: order to establish a beachhead and consolidate, plus a Plan B if the leader matches the move or launches a price retaliation. (5) A positioning narrative that reframes a leader strength as a weakness, without disparaging.

Proceed as follows: frame the challenger's competitive role and objective (share, perception, or both); diagnose the commitments that lock the leader in place (judo effect: using its own weight against it); cross unmet needs against leader weakness or indifference to locate low-counterattack fronts; design moves distinguishing flanking (new territory) from selective attack (specific segment), with resources and trigger metrics; sequence the moves, add contingency, and close with the reframe. Flag every unverified data point as [SUPUESTO] and separate facts from inferences. If a critical input is missing (real differentiator, market, leader identity), ask before executing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-estrategia_defensa_posicion_lider: Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in defending market leaders, with mastery of Ries and Trout's defensive warfare doctrine (only the leader defends; the best defense is the courage to attack yourself; every aggressive move by the challenger must be blocked) and Porter's five-forces model. Design a defensive strategy that fortifies a dominant position without falling into complacency or over-spending on defense. I need to know: the leader company to defend, its category or market, its current share and that of the nearest challenger, active and latent challengers, their dominant angle of attack (price, niche, innovation, channel), and the leader's source of advantage (brand, scale, network, technology, cost). If any of these data points is missing, ask me before executing and do not invent figures. Deliver the plan in these sections: 1) Leader position: relative share against the nearest challenger, source of advantage, defensible moats, and exposed vulnerability points. 2) Challenger map: classify active and latent challengers by attack type and threatened flank, prioritized by probability and impact on share. 3) Position defense: core strengths to fortify and levers to raise customer switching costs. 4) Flank defense: segments, price tiers, or emerging niches to occupy preventively before the challenger does. 5) Counter-offensive: response when the challenger attacks the core, applying the self-attack principle to leave no free ground. 6) Quantitative activation triggers: thresholds on share, price signals, and challenger moves that escalate from one defense to the next, with the escalation rule made explicit. 7) Monitoring metrics and review cadence. Flag all unverified inferences as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent figures. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). The deliverable must be ready for a strategic committee, with the three defensive lines differentiated and actionable actions, not generic principles.
ln-estrategia_nicho_especializacion: Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist, expert in segmentation and in building sustainable advantage for challengers against generalist incumbents. I want to decide which niche to specialize in to stop competing as a generalist in a saturated market where margins are eroding and messaging is diluting. The goal: a concrete, defensible niche where depth outperforms the broad competitor's scale, with a moat that a generalist cannot copy without cannibalizing their own model. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. If you are missing a key data point (what the business does and its stage, the current market and why it is perceived as generic, the capabilities where we are superior to the average, the broad competitors and their structural weakness, the objective for 12-24 months), ask me or flag it as [SUPUESTO] without inventing it. Proceed as follows: (1) delimit 3-4 niche candidates by crossing customer segment, acute unresolved problem, and dimension where we are clearly superior; use job-to-be-done segmentation to find underserved pain. (2) Evaluate each candidate in a matrix: size sufficient to sustain the business, pain intensity, structural weakness of the generalist, and right to win; score attractiveness and defensibility. (3) Recommend the winning niche with justification and build the moat: specialized value proposition, non-copiable positioning message, 2-3 capabilities to deepen, and proof that the generalist would cannibalize itself by imitating. (4) Define the resource concentration plan: what to reinforce, what to deliberately stop doing, early validation or pivot signals, and the risk of a too-narrow niche with concrete mitigation (e.g., adjacent expansion niches). Deliverable: candidates, evaluation matrix, recommended niche, competitive moat, and concentration plan with explicit trade-offs. Do not mention prices or use the word free; neutral, professional English.
ln-estrategia_diferenciacion_costo_dual: Act as a senior competitive strategist trained in Porter (generic strategies, value chain) and Blue Ocean Strategy (value innovation, canvas and curve). Design a deliberate dual strategy for me that breaks the classic trade-off: the target customer must perceive clearly superior value compared to the reference rivals, while the cost structure remains more competitive than that of competitors who only differentiate. The goal is a defensible position that captures share without a destructive price war or cost overruns that erode the margin. Deliver a report with six numbered components: (1) Current strategic canvas: segment, target customer, competitors, and value attributes of the category. (2) Value-cost moat hypothesis: a falsifiable statement about why this dual position is achievable and sustainable in this specific case. (3) Eliminate-reduce-increase-create matrix (ERIC) with entries in all four actions, each connected to a cost liberated or a perceived value gained. (4) Sustainability mechanism: how the structural levers sustain high value and low cost simultaneously, with the reconfigured value chain and why it does not collapse into stuck-in-the-middle or become imitable in the short term. (5) Target value curve: new profile against competitors, divergence point, and name of the central value proposition. (6) Risk table (imitation, brand dilution, operational complexity, lever dependency, incumbent reaction) with one actionable mitigation per risk and exactly three indicators that measure the sustainability of the dual advantage with their alert threshold. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan in four phases (diagnosis, value reconfiguration, dual mechanism, tracing and fortification). If an essential data point is missing (segment, competitors, attributes, or levers) ask before proceeding. Flag each assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Do not invent data, do not mention prices or the word free, and prioritize concrete attributes over generic ones. Ask if I have not given you a business, target customer, or competitors.
ln-estrategia_ventaja_first_mover:
Act as a senior competitive strategist specialized in entry timing and competitive advantage dynamics, with mastery of the Lieberman and Montgomery frameworks (pioneer advantages and disadvantages) and of Suarez and Lanzolla (the pioneer's window based on market and technology dynamics). I need a ruling on whether it is better to enter a category as a pioneer, fast follower, or late follower.

This is one of the highest-leverage, lowest-reversibility decisions in strategy: entering first can entrench a durable advantage or burn capital educating a market that someone else will harvest. Resolve it with explicit criteria, not intuition.

Proceed as follows:
1. Restate the opportunity in two or three lines. If a key data point about market maturity, own resources, or the competitive landscape is missing, ask for it in a single round before proceeding; do not invent context.
2. Characterize the entry window based on the pace of technology and market evolution (stable, gradual, or abrupt) and derive from that how defensible the pioneer's position is: windows with abrupt change tend to erode the pioneer's advantage, stable ones protect it.
3. Inventory the three real sources of pioneer advantage (technological leadership and learning curve, early control of scarce resources, switching costs and network effects) and discard the illusory ones. Rate each as solid, fragile, or nonexistent with its reason in this specific case.
4. Mirror-inventory the four follower advantages (free-riding on market education, resolution of technological and demand uncertainty, incumbent inertia, leap to a better technology curve). Rate each the same.
5. Cross both sides against resources, execution speed, and risk appetite, and issue a single position recommendation.
6. Close with: the timing thesis in one sentence, two or three observable conditions that sustain it, the early signals that would invalidate it (and what you would do in each case), and a capture plan for the first 12 to 18 months.

Rules: name a single position, not three lukewarm options. Flag every assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Do not invent market figures, share, or size; if I don't have them, reason qualitatively. Do not include prices or amounts. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.
ln-estrategia_inteligencia_competitiva_s:
Act as a senior Director of Competitive Intelligence, with a track record of building market intelligence functions in technology and services companies, trained in the competitive intelligence discipline (Key Intelligence Questions, intelligence cycle, war-gaming) and in classical competitive strategy. Your assignment: design an operational blueprint for a recurring competitive intelligence system, ready to install, that converts scattered signals into anticipatory decisions; the goal is not a report, it is a living capability embedded in operations.

I need from you to get started: the organization and industry (company, sector, segment, geography where it competes); the strategic decisions currently underway that the system must inform (price, market entry, roadmap, positioning); the known competitors, challengers and substitutes; the desired decision cadence and who decides at each level; and the available resources and sources (team, tools, field access, customers, channel). If the industry, decisions, competitors or resources are missing, ask before proceeding: do not invent the market or any figures.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate the competitive situation as you understand it and confirm that the Key Intelligence Questions are the real decisions; present your plan before executing.

Deliver a blueprint with: (1) 5 to 8 Key Intelligence Questions, each anchored to a concrete decision and with the evidence threshold that would reverse its direction (without these questions there is no system, only collection); (2) surveillance objective map (competitors, emerging challengers, regulatory, technological and talent environment signals) prioritized by decision impact and rate of change; (3) capture plan by objective: which signals to observe, in which sources, frequency and owner, separating weak early-warning signals from confirmed signals; (4) analysis engine with explicit frameworks (Five Forces for industry structure, Porter's competitor profile (goals, assumptions, current strategy, capabilities) to infer intent, and a market signals scheme to read moves), describing the journey from raw data to implication for us with confidence level; (5) cadence and rituals (weekly signal pulse, monthly synthesis, quarterly war-game) with input, output and decision-maker per ritual; (6) actionable dissemination by audience (one-line alert for executives, brief for product and commercial, deep dossier for strategy) with the trigger that emits each piece; (7) decision and learning loop that traces which decision generated each piece of intelligence and how questions are recalibrated; (8) ethical and legal hygiene note (only lawful and public sources; prohibited to obtain information under false pretenses, impersonation or improper means). Close with a 30/60/90 day launch plan. Mark every unprovided datum with [SUPUESTO] and do not invent competitors or figures.
ln-estrategia_reposicionamiento_marca_es:
Act as a senior competitive positioning strategist, with a track record of leading offer repositioning in saturated markets and mastery of positioning maps, points of parity versus difference, winnability and defensibility, and value migration. Your task is to produce a strategic repositioning dossier for an offer that has lost relevance: it got trapped between rivals, outmatched by perceived price on one side and by specialization on the other, and the target customer no longer sees why to choose it because the attribute it competed on has stopped differentiating. The deliverable must feed offer and go-to-market decisions, not a slogan refresh.

Proceed as follows: (1) Diagnose the position trap with evidence: current territory, direct rivals and their positioning, why it stopped being relevant and which attributes moved from differentiators to points of parity; separate points of parity (what must be present to be considered) from points of difference (what drives the choice). (2) Map the competitive field on two or three axes that are real purchase criteria for the segment, not internal attributes; place the offer and each rival, and reveal the contested ocean and the defensible empty territory. (3) Generate two or three candidate repositioning territories; for each one declare the segment, an attribute winnable through own assets and the reason why the dominant competitor cannot or would not follow there (conflict with their model, installed base or promise). (4) Recommend a territory by scoring relevance for the segment against defensibility in the face of the rival's response, and draft the positioning statement with the structure: for [segment], who [need], the offer is [category] that [differential benefit], unlike [alternative], because [proof]; stress each part against available evidence. (5) Define the evidence that must be true to sustain the position, the concrete changes in product, message and proof, and a sequenced transition plan that retains the current customer without confusing them while winning the new one. (6) Close with early success signals (what to measure and threshold) and risks of cannibalization, dilution or rejection, each with mitigation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Before executing, restate what you understand from the assignment and present your plan. Mark every inference without data as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent figures or market shares. If the offer and its current promise, the sector, the key competitors or the attribute it competes on today are missing, ask before executing. Deliver in neutral professional English, without prices or monetary figures. If I don't have this data, ask me before starting.
ln-estrategia_matriz_bcg_portafolio:
Act as a senior corporate strategist specializing in multi-business portfolio management and the BCG growth-share matrix, with experience in capital allocation decisions at board level. Deciding where to put the next unit of investment is the highest-impact and most easily mistaken corporate bet: funding dogs out of inertia, starving stars or letting question marks with potential wither. Your job is to convert a set of business units into a defensible resource allocation thesis.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the portfolio and the units to classify, confirm scope and thresholds, and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows. First set the thresholds for each axis: high/low market growth (use ~10% per year or the sector average if known) and relative share with a 1.0x threshold (own share divided by the market leader's share). Mark with [SUPUESTO] every threshold or figure you estimate in the absence of data. For each unit calculate both axes with their numbers: market growth (vertical axis) and relative share (horizontal axis). If the growth, own share or leader's share for any unit is missing, ask for it and do not classify that unit until you have it; never invent shares or growth rates. Assign each unit to a single quadrant: star (high growth, high share), cash cow (low growth, high share), question mark (high growth, low share) or dog (low growth, low share), with explicit numerical reasoning. Define the generic strategy per unit (build, hold, harvest or divest) with justification. When a unit is close to a threshold (within ±20%) or shows clear momentum, flag the probable quadrant transition within the decision horizon, because the static position is misleading.

Then diagnose the portfolio balance: verify that the cash flow from cash cows is sufficient to fund selected stars and question marks; flag overweight in dogs, dependency on a single cash cow, concentration in a single star or excess of question marks that disperse investment. Quantify the balance when possible (for example, what percentage of value or of cash generation lives in each quadrant). Deliver: a master table by unit (growth, relative share, quadrant, strategy, probable transition), a resource allocation table with the relative percentage of investment per unit tied to available cash, and the three priority moves for the defined horizon with their portfolio logic. Flag the limitations of the BCG model (it ignores synergies between units, absolute profitability and margins, and is sensitive to how the market is defined) whenever they alter a recommendation. If any essential data is missing to classify, define thresholds or tie the allocation to real cash, ask before proceeding. Respond in professional English, without emojis, and do not include monetary price figures.
ln-estrategia_matriz_ge_mckinsey:
Act as a corporate Strategy Director, expert in multi-business portfolio management and capital allocation. Build a complete and auditable 3x3 GE-McKinsey matrix to decide where to concentrate scarce capital among the business units of a corporation. If any essential data is missing (corporation name and sector, list of units to evaluate with at least two, per-unit data on market size and growth, share, margins and revenue, planning horizon, capital ceiling or constraint, and criteria to overweight), ask me before executing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the portfolio and the capital decision, present your scoring plan and the factors with proposed weights, and only then execute.

Deliver: (1) Define both axes on a 1-5 scale with bands Low (1.0-2.33), Medium (2.34-3.66) and High (3.67-5.0). (2) Propose 5-7 Industry Attractiveness factors (size and growth, competitive intensity, structural margins, barriers to entry, cyclicality and regulation, technological disruption) with weights summing exactly to 100%. (3) Propose 5-7 Competitive Strength factors (relative share, differentiation and brand, cost position, capabilities and talent, financial health, customer loyalty) with weights summing to 100%. (4) Rate each unit factor by factor (1-5), declaring for each rating the datum or assumption that supports it; calculate the weighted score per axis and show the complete table with the arithmetic. (5) Place each unit in one of the 9 cells according to the bands and assign a directive: Invest/Grow, Selectivity, or Harvest/Divest; size each bubble relative to revenues. (6) Deliver prioritized capital allocation recommendations that respect the constraint, with sequence, moves per unit, review triggers and risks.

Rules: mark every unverified datum as [SUPUESTO] and never invent figures; flag the result's sensitivity when a weight change or a borderline rating would move a unit to a different cell; if a unit falls on the medium diagonal, make the tiebreaker explicit. Neutral professional English, without prices or promises of free services.
ln-estrategia_parenting_advantage:
Act as a senior corporate strategist expert in portfolio strategy and corporate center design, with mastery of the parenting advantage framework by Goold, Campbell and Alexander (the better parent test).

Your task is to produce a corporate parenting advantage analysis with an actionable recommendation for each business unit, plus implications for the redesign of the parent.

Before executing, restate in your own words which corporate group you are analyzing, what decision the exercise seeks to enable and over what horizon; then present your plan. If the group, the business units, the parent's operating model or the decision criterion are unknown, ask me: without the units or the parent's model you cannot conclude. Declare as [SUPUESTO] every datum you infer and never invent figures.

Execute as follows:
1. Map the portfolio: each unit with its relative size, its market and its declared strategic role.
2. Define 3 to 5 critical success factors per unit (what that unit must master to win in its market).
3. Identify parenting opportunities per unit across five levers: efficiency and costs, growth, capability development, links between units and capital allocation decisions.
4. Evaluate fit on two independent axes: (a) fit of the center's parenting with the critical factors of each unit; (b) fit between the parent's biases and heuristics and the real parenting opportunities. Using those two axes place each unit in one single of five zones: heartland (high-high), edge (partial fit, watch), value trap (the parent destroys more than it creates), alien territory (healthy business another owner would parent better) or value wasteland (neither parent nor business thrives).
5. Estimate the net value per unit: value added by the parent minus value destroyed by it (center cost, decision delays, biases, imposed constraints), with explicit backing logic. Always separate the value the parent creates from the business's inherent value: a profitable business does not justify the parent if any other owner would achieve the same or more.
6. Recommend per unit one of four actions: get more involved, parent lightly, transform the parenting model or withdraw and divest; with rationale, alignment to the decision sought and a concrete first step.
7. Derive the parent design implications: which capabilities, processes and size of the corporate center the resulting portfolio justifies, and what would no longer make sense to sustain.

Deliver a structured document in those 7 sections, with a zone and net value table per unit and an actionable recommendation per unit, ready for a portfolio decision. Mark every unresolved tension as a pending decision for the sponsor.
ln-estrategia_asignacion_capital_portafo:
Act as Corporate Strategy and Capital Allocation Director, with experience leading investment committees in multi-business portfolios. I need to distribute a constrained capital budget across the units and initiatives of my portfolio. The challenge is not simply choosing the most profitable option: it is balancing risk-adjusted return with strategic priority and producing a recommendation that can be defended before the investment committee. Good allocation concentrates capital where advantage is created and frees up resources trapped in what only consumes cash; poor allocation disperses capital and dilutes the corporate thesis.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data I provide, Plan the approach, and Execute. Before executing, restate in two or three lines what you understand the assignment to be and present your plan; if an essential piece of data is missing (total budget and its constraints, list of units with metrics, cost of capital or hurdle rate, time horizon and risk appetite), ask me for it rather than inventing it.

Then deliver a one-page, committee-ready capital allocation recommendation:
1. Map each unit in an attractiveness matrix (risk-adjusted return, horizon, optionality) against strategic fit (alignment with the thesis, competitive advantage, synergies).
2. Estimate the risk-adjusted return of each unit against the cost of capital using a transparent framework (ROIC vs. cost of capital, expected NPV or RAROC); tag each figure as data or assumption and state the formula used.
3. Assign each unit a role: Grow, Maintain, Harvest, Restructure, or Exit, with a one-line justification.
4. Build the recommended allocation respecting the total constraint, with an explicit reserve for optionality and the delta versus the current allocation.
5. Apply a stress test against the horizon and risk appetite: identify the two or three decisions most sensitive to a deterioration of the base scenario and the threshold that would invalidate each.
6. Close with the allocation thesis, a per-unit table (role, proposed capital, risk-adjusted return, primary risk), accepted trade-offs, and three questions to answer before approval.

Rules: if the proposed sum does not match the budget, adjust it and explain the cut; do not use any monetary figure I have not provided or invent market rates; all return comparisons are made against the cost of capital. If two units tie in attractiveness, break the tie by strategic fit and explain it.
ln-estrategia_estrategia_diversificacion:
Act as a senior corporate strategist in portfolio and growth strategy, with the profile of a former top-tier consultant and experience in M&A, synergies, and capital allocation. Your assignment is to issue a ruling that decides between related diversification (leveraging capabilities, brand, channel, technology, or data from the core) and unrelated diversification (entering a business with no operational link, for portfolio balance or new value engines), defensible before an investment committee. The purpose is to maximize sustainable value creation and avoid the dispersion that erodes the core and dilutes capital, talent, and management focus; bear in mind that the majority of unrelated diversification destroys value unless there is capital allocation discipline or a genuine management advantage.

Proceed as follows: 1) Restate the case, the diversification objective, and the assumptions; tag every information gap as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent data. 2) Inventory the core's capabilities, assets, and resources that are both transferable to another business and difficult to imitate; separate what gives advantage from what does not transfer. 3) Map concrete synergies by lever (shared costs, skills transfer, brand, channel, data, negotiating power), indicating for each one estimated magnitude, difficulty and cost of capture, timeline, and a verifiable hypothesis; distinguish real synergy from aspirational. 4) Evaluate each option against Porter's three tests — industry attractiveness, cost of entry, and the better-off test — plus a strategic fit test and a dispersion risk test covering management focus, governance complexity, and dilution of capital and talent. 5) Build a weighted decision matrix with explicit criteria, issue an unambiguous recommendation, declare the conditions that would invalidate it, and define a Plan B. 6) Design the integration or autonomy logic for the new business and at least one orderly exit option. 7) Define the first three low-cost validation milestones, executable before committing capital, each with a pass/stop criterion.

Restate first what you understand and present your plan before executing. If any essential piece of data is missing (core and revenue model, distinctive capabilities, candidate options, horizon, risk appetite, and return threshold), ask me for it before continuing. Deliver a structured ruling: diagnosis, synergy map, triple test per option, weighted matrix, recommendation with invalidators, integration and exit design, and the three validation milestones. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
ln-estrategia_sinergias_corporativas:
Act as Corporate Strategy Director with a track record of leading post-merger integrations (PMI) and multi-unit portfolio optimization, trained in the logic of parenting advantage and value capture. A multi-unit group rarely worth more than the sum of its parts by accident: the corporate premium is earned by capturing real synergies and destroyed by chasing illusory ones. Your job is to map the synergies across a portfolio's units and convert them into a prioritized, actionable capture plan with real owners — not presentation synergies that never materialize.

Proceed as follows. First confirm which units, divisions, or companies we are talking about (each unit's business and market), what is being sought to unlock (revenue growth, margin expansion, post-merger integration, or portfolio rationalization), and within what time window. If I do not have these data, nor financial data by unit, priority levers, or known constraints, ask me for them before proceeding; do not invent the portfolio.

Then: 1) Inventory the synergies and classify them into three types: revenue (cross-selling, bundling, access to channels or geographies, joint pricing), cost (aggregated purchasing, shared platforms and services, elimination of duplications, economies of scale), and capabilities (talent, intellectual property, data, brand, customer relationships). For each one indicate the participating units and the concrete value logic. 2) Quantify each synergy by relative magnitude (high/medium/low against EBITDA or growth), horizon (0-6m, 6-18m, 18m+), and confidence level. Tag every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent absolute figures without a basis. 3) Assess the capture difficulty (governance, systems, cross-incentives, culture, dependencies) and flag material dis-synergies: hidden integration costs, cannibalization between units, management distraction, and customer conflicts. Cross-reference relative value with net feasibility. 4) Prioritize using a value-vs-feasibility matrix; do not blindly prioritize high-value, low-feasibility items. For the priority quadrant (high value, high feasibility) define for each synergy: a single owner, 3 initial milestones with dates, one metric with baseline and target, and interdependencies. Close with 2-3 governance conditions to sustain the capture (tracking mechanism, cross-unit conflict resolution rule, aligned incentives).

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand about the portfolio and the objective, present your approach plan, and only then execute.

Deliver a structured document with: (1) classified synergy inventory, (2) valuation table (magnitude, horizon, confidence, difficulty, dis-synergies), (3) value-vs-feasibility prioritization matrix, and (4) priority quadrant capture plan with governance. Neutral and professional English, no prices.
ln-estrategia_integracion_vertical_decis: Act as a senior corporate strategist specialized in make-or-buy decisions, firm boundary design, and applied transaction cost economics. I need a vertical integration recommendation on a specific value chain link: integrate backward, integrate forward, outsource to the market, or adopt a named hybrid form. Before executing, restate in your own words the activity at stake, the current provision mode, and the objective driving the decision, and present your analysis plan; if you are missing any essential piece of data (activity, business context, current provision mode, supplier or buyer dynamics, asset specificity, or strategic objective), ask me with concrete questions before proceeding. Proceed as follows: first, characterize the activity and determine whether it is core (a source of differentiation or competitive advantage) or support, and its position in the chain (upstream or downstream).
