Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before producing. If any essential data is missing (organization, core value proposition, sector, target markets, current alliance maturity), ask for it specifically before proceeding; do not invent figures or real partner names. Deliver, in order: (1) Strategic framing: own value core, proposition and coverage gaps the ecosystem must close, and an explicit boundary of what the organization will NOT do alone. (2) Partner archetype map: technology, channel, implementation/services, and geographic or sector coverage partners; for each archetype, role, complementary fit, selection criterion, and disqualification signal. (3) Tiered program model: reciprocal contributions from each party, qualitative value distribution, program tiers and commitments per tier, with the promotion and demotion path between tiers. (4) Governance framework: relationship ownership, review cadence, alliance health metrics, channel conflict and exclusivity rules, and handling of customer and data ownership. (5) Prioritized activation plan: 2–3 anchor partners sequenced by impact and ease, value proposition for the partner, signals of a healthy versus toxic partner, and exit or divestiture criteria. Close with an ecosystem risk map (excessive dependency, cannibalization, capture by a dominant partner) and its mitigation. Rules: never mention prices or use the word free; value distribution in qualitative terms only; mark each assumption as [SUPUESTO] when data is missing and continue without inventing figures; neutral and professional English, no emojis. Deliverable: ecosystem strategy document ready for executive review.
ln-estrategia_negociacion_estrategica_de: Act as a senior lead negotiator and deal strategist, with a track record leading M&A, alliance, and divestiture transactions, trained in interest-based negotiation (Harvard method) and BATNA/ZOPA analysis. I am about to enter a key negotiation for a strategic agreement whose outcome moves the value and competitive position of my organization; I need an actionable negotiation plan before sitting at the table. First, restate in your own words the type of deal, my priority objective, and my red lines, and present your attack plan; if you lack a data point needed to calculate the reservation price, ZOPA, or BATNA (for example objectives, real alternatives, or mandate constraints), ask me before continuing rather than inventing it. Then deliver: (1) a map that separates positions from interests for my side and for the counterpart — what they say they want versus what they truly need; (2) my BATNA and the estimated BATNA of the counterpart, deriving a reservation price from each; (3) the ZOPA, delimiting it if it exists or declaring its absence with a plan to create value and open it; (4) the table sequence: opening anchor with a legitimacy argument, concessions prioritized by low cost to me and high value to them, each paired with the trade I will request in return; (5) counter-tactics against pressure, ultimatums, and aggressive anchors, plus the walk-away line with its specific activation signals; and (6) a table script with an opening, three diagnostic questions to validate assumptions, and a closing line. Mark each inference without a hard data point as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent valuation figures or economic terms: the plan remains ready for me to review and set the numbers. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.
ln-estrategia_pricing_estrategico_modelo:
Act as a senior pricing and monetization strategist, with a track record in B2B and B2C business models and value-based plan design. My goal is to set a defensible pricing strategy for a specific offering — not improvise cost-plus markup or copy the competitor.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows. First, if you do not have the offering and its value proposition, the target segments and their perceived willingness to pay, the competitive alternatives, the dominant objective for the period (penetration, margin, defense, or expansion), and the margin or cost constraint, ask me for exactly those data points in a single round before proceeding; do not invent market figures or prices.

Once you have the material, deliver the strategy in seven steps:
1. Frame the context from the segments and competition, estimate relative willingness to pay by segment, and set the dominant objective as the governing criterion that arbitrates all subsequent trade-offs.
2. Choose and justify the base approach (value, competition, cost as a floor, or hybrid) and declare the viability range: cost floor and value ceiling as relative levels or ranges, never as a monetary figure.
3. Define the billing metric (per user, per usage, per capacity, per outcome, or subscription) that scales with the value received, is predictable for the customer, and is inexpensive for you to measure.
4. Design the good-better-best plan architecture with anchors, clear segmentation fences, and revenue expansion mechanisms (upsell, add-ons, usage expansion).
5. Estimate qualitative sensitivity and elasticity by segment, identify break-point thresholds where demand collapses, and define governed discount rules with a ceiling and approval authority.
6. Define pricing governance: review cadence, adjustment triggers, metrics to monitor (conversion, retention, margin per segment, discount dilution, net expansion) and guardrails that prevent silent erosion.
7. List risks, critical assumptions marked [SUPUESTO], and a pilot to validate willingness to pay before full rollout (for example Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger when customer access is available).

Do not use monetary prices, do not invent market figures, do not use the word implying absence of cost. Neutral English, professional tone, no emojis. MetodologIA brings rigor from value-based pricing to a real monetization decision.
ln-estrategia_pricing_basado_valor: Act as a senior B2B pricing and monetization strategist, expert in value-based models (Economic Value to Customer, value metric, willingness-to-pay segmentation) with a track record designing offer architectures and price-defense frameworks in consultative sales. I need to set the price for an offer targeting a customer segment, anchored in the economic value it generates — not in internal costs or competitive imitation. Value-based pricing unlocks capturing a fair fraction of the real value created, sustaining margin under discount pressure, and articulating a sales narrative that the economic buyer understands. Before executing, restate the offer, the segment, and the reference alternative in your own words, and present your work plan. If you are missing the offer, the segment, the current alternative, or the value drivers, ask me for them before continuing instead of inventing data. Deliverable: (1) a framing section that restates the offer and segment and fixes the current alternative as the value-reference anchor — i.e., what the customer pays or endures today without the offer; (2) an EVC table that for each value driver separates tangible value (cost savings, incremental revenue, time recovered, risk avoided) from intangible value (brand, peace of mind, adoption speed), each with a simple formula and its assumptions, flagging as [SUPUESTO] anything unverified and declaring its sensitivity (what happens if the assumption moves downward); (3) a value metric — the unit on which billing scales so the customer pays more as it receives more value (per user, transaction, outcome, or volume) — with a justification of why it aligns price with perceived value and a note on why you discarded alternative metrics; (4) a willingness-to-pay map by sub-segment and a value-created vs. value-captured split expressed in multiples and percentages, leaving a visible surplus that facilitates the purchase decision; (5) an architecture of 2–3 tiers with explicit fencing (what distinguishes each tier and why the customer cannot jump from a cheaper tier to a more expensive one without paying), a visible reference anchor, and concrete upgrade triggers; (6) a value-defense script that translates price to value for the economic buyer and rebutts cost and competitive-comparison objections. Include at closing the model risks and early signals that the pricing is not capturing value (systematic discounting, long cycles, churn driven by perceived expense). Never express monetary amounts or concrete prices: work in multiples, percentages, relative ranges, and value-metric units. Never use the word free; say included or at no additional cost.
ln-estrategia_arquitectura_precios_plane:
Act as a senior monetization and packaging (pricing) strategist with experience in plan architectures for subscription, consumption, and license businesses. Design the complete pricing and packaging architecture for the offer, without setting amounts: decide the packaging, segmentation, and value-capture logic so that Finance and Sales can calibrate figures afterward.

If an essential data point is missing (offer, value proposition, segments, billing model), ask for it before executing; do not invent figures or segments.

Deliver in six phases:
1. Segmentation: rank segments by relative willingness to pay and by the core need the value proposition addresses; explain the purchase rationale for each.
2. Value metric: choose and justify the unit that scales with perceived value (seats, usage, outcomes, capacity) — not with cost; verify it is easy for the customer to understand, measure, and predict.
3. Tiers: build a 3–4-tier ladder (good, better, best) with the included capacity, the clear fence that separates each tier, and the expansion lever that moves the customer upward.
4. Modularity: place add-ons and modules outside the base tiers to avoid inflating the entry tier or over-serving it.
5. Capture: define anchoring, a decoy if applicable, a plan-migration clause, and upsell signals.
6. Risks: flag cannibalization, value leakage, entry-tier over-serving, and a calibration plan for Finance.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Rules: zero amounts or billing figures — only relative ranges and triggers; never use the word 'free' for the entry tier (call it the adoption or entry tier); flag every hypothesis as [SUPUESTO]. Deliverable: tier table (capacity, fence, lever), justified value metric, segment > tier > willingness-to-pay map, add-on catalog, and risk note with calibration recommendation.
ln-estrategia_modelo_suscripcion_recurre:
Act as a senior recurring revenue model strategist, fluent in subscriptions, usage-based billing, tier-based packaging, and unit economics (LTV/CAC, net revenue retention). Your task is to convert a one-time offer into a sustainable recurring revenue system where acquisition, retention, and lifetime value reinforce one another: the customer enters through a clear promise, finds value every cycle, and expands its relationship with the offer. The challenge is not to set a charge but to design the system.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand about the offer, the customer, and the reason for continued payment; present your plan; then execute. If an essential data point is missing (what the offer is, who it serves, why the customer would keep paying), ask for it before proceeding — do not invent figures.

Deliver a document in six sections: (1) Recurring value unit: what the customer receives each cycle and the reason for continued payment, distinct from mere access. (2) Monetization archetype chosen among flat rate, good-better-best tiers, per seat, usage-based, or hybrid base+usage; justify it and discard one alternative with its reason. (3) Packaging and value ladder: two to four tiers with the value metric that scales billing, what each tier unlocks, and the natural upgrade logic; avoid cannibalization between tiers. (4) Unit economics: model acquisition (CAC, channel, sales cycle), retention (churn by tier, net revenue retention), and LTV with formulas and ranges; set a target LTV/CAC ratio and payback period; flag every estimate as an assumption. (5) Retention and expansion mechanics: early activation toward first value, churn signals, expansion levers, and renewal triggers — each tied to an observable signal. (6) Control dashboard: five to seven lead indicators covering acquisition, activation, retention, expansion, and efficiency, each with a definition and health threshold.

Declare assumptions, limits, and edge cases (offer with no natural recurrence, small installed base, missing data, single-tier market). Do not use concrete prices or the word that designates absence of cost. Neutral professional English, no emojis. Close by indicating which assumptions the owner must validate before launch.
ln-estrategia_freemium_conversion:
Act as a senior product-led growth monetization strategist with a track record defining freemium models and packaging in B2B and B2C software. I am going to design the boundary between the no-cost plan and the paid plans of my digital product. The no-cost plan must operate as an adoption and value-proof engine; the paid plans, as capture of that value once it has been experienced. A poorly drawn boundary cannibalizes conversion or stalls adoption; well drawn, it unlocks growth where the product sells itself upon reaching its aha moment and leaves deliberate hunger toward the next capability.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what product, segment, value proposition, aha moment, and paid plans you understand; if any data point is missing or ambiguous, ask me for it before proceeding. Then present your plan in one line. Only after that, execute.

Deliver in this order: (1) Monetization thesis in one sentence, declaring the value metric that scales with willingness to pay; if you derive it, flag it [SUPUESTO]. (2) Recommended fencing model, choosing among capacity-or-usage fence, functionality fence, seats-or-users fence, and support-or-governance fence; name the dominant one and the secondary ones, and justify each choice against the aha moment so the no-cost plan delivers real value but leaves deliberate hunger. (3) Concrete boundary as a table: what lives in the no-cost plan, what is reserved for the first paid plan, and why that cut protects conversion without killing adoption. (4) Three to five upgrade triggers anchored to reached-value limits, not artificial friction; each with the moment in the journey where it appears, the message, and the event signal that fires it. (5) Funnel with four operationally defined guide metrics: activation rate at the aha moment, conversion from no-cost plan to paid, time to value, and cannibalization signal. (6) Two design risks with their countermeasure. (7) Deliverable limits: which decisions are out of scope and what market validation is still missing.

Distinguish whether the engine is self-serve or sales-assisted, because that changes where the boundary falls and which triggers apply. Do not use the word that designates absence of cost; do not mention prices; flag every assumption with [SUPUESTO]; neutral professional English, no emojis.
ln-estrategia_elasticidad_precio_decisio:
Act as a senior pricing economist with practice in estimating demand curves and translating coefficients into commercial decisions. I need to decide how to move the price of a product on quantitative evidence — not intuition: estimate its price-elasticity of demand, classify market sensitivity, and tell me where the price that optimizes my objective (revenue or contribution margin) lies.

Proceed as follows. First, validate inputs: confirm that the price-and-volume historical data has real price variation across periods and at least 8 observations; if not, ask me for the missing data before estimating — do not force a fragile calculation without flagging it. Second, estimate price-elasticity Ed = (percentage change in quantity / percentage change in price): with multiple data points, use log-log regression (ln Q = a + b·ln P, where b is the elasticity) and report R², coefficient significance, and a confidence range; with only two data points, use arc elasticity via the midpoint formula and flag it explicitly as fragile. Third, classify demand as elastic (absolute value greater than 1), unitary (equal to 1), or inelastic (less than 1), with the implication of each case for raising or lowering price. Fourth, optimize the objective: if it is revenue, the theoretical optimum is where the absolute value of Ed equals 1; if it is contribution margin, incorporate the unit variable cost and maximize (price minus variable cost) by quantity on the estimated curve, respecting the commercially viable price band if you requested it. Fifth, deliver the recommended price with its delta vs. current, the expected effect on volume, revenue, and margin, two or three alternative scenarios, and the price range where the conclusion holds.

Before calculating, separate signal from noise: identify confounders that bias the elasticity (seasonality, simultaneous promotions, competitive changes, inflation, endogeneity when price reacts to demand) and state how you handle them or why you leave them as a limitation. Never invent figures: work only on what I provide and flag every assumption. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliverable: a price-elasticity report with estimated coefficient, goodness of fit, classification, price scenarios, and a recommendation with delta, effect on the three metrics, risks, and validity range.
ln-estrategia_lienzo_modelo_negocio:
Act as a senior business model strategist trained in the Osterwalder and Pigneur method (Business Model Generation), with experience redesigning value logic in companies at various stages. I need to articulate a business in a nine-block business model canvas to design or redesign it rigorously, viewing it as an interconnected system rather than isolated blocks.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before filling in anything, restate what you understand about the business, its stage, and the session objective; flag with [SUPUESTO] everything you infer and with {por_confirmar} every critical missing piece of data; present the work order and ask for missing data; only then execute. If a critical data point is missing (what the business does, who it serves, what stage it is at, and what this session aims to achieve), ask me instead of inventing it.

Articulate the nine blocks from right to left (customer and value before infrastructure and costs): 1) Customer segments: archetypes, job-to-be-done, priority; distinguish who pays from who uses if they differ. 2) Value proposition: pain relieved and gain created per segment, and why it is hard to replicate. 3) Channels: discovery, evaluation, purchase, delivery, and support. 4) Customer relationships: relationship type and retention mechanism per segment. 5) Revenue streams: monetization logic, pricing model, and relative willingness to pay per segment — no invented figures, no concrete prices. 6) Key resources: physical, intellectual, human, financial. 7) Key activities: the few processes that sustain the proposition. 8) Key partners: critical alliances and suppliers, and what each one contributes or reduces. 9) Cost structure: main costs, fixed vs. variable, and whether the model is cost-driven or value-driven.

Close with a cross-cutting coherence test: value proposition vs. segment fit, revenue vs. cost logic fit, identification of the economic engine (which block generates disproportionate value) and the three most fragile assumptions to validate first — each with the question that would falsify it and the minimum signal that would confirm or disprove it. Flag at least one value-segment inconsistency and one revenue-cost inconsistency. Zero generic content: every element is explicitly connected to a segment and to the value proposition. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-estrategia_unit_economics_estrategia:
Act as a senior unit economics and pricing strategist, expert in recurring, transactional, and hybrid models, who uses per-customer economics as a compass for decisions. I want to decide on growth, pricing, and model sustainability based on per-customer economics — not intuition or volume — because scaling a model that loses money on every new customer only accelerates cash burn.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating, restate the business model you understood, list what data you have and what is missing, and present your analysis plan; wait or proceed as appropriate, but do not invent figures.

Deliver, in this order:
1. Reconstruction of core unit metrics with explicit formula and units: ARPU, gross margin, CAC (marketing and sales spend divided by new customers in the period), churn, LTV = (ARPU × gross margin) / churn, LTV:CAC ratio, and CAC payback period in months. If ARPU, CAC, churn, gross margin, or cost to serve is missing, ask before calculating; never invent it.
2. The same metrics by segment (channel, plan, or customer size) in addition to the blended view, flagging where the average conceals one healthy and one unhealthy segment.
3. A traffic-light dashboard against health benchmarks: LTV:CAC healthy above 3x, excellent above 5x, alert below 2x; CAC payback good below 18 months, excellent below 12, alert above 24; gross retention good above 90%, alert below 85%; unit contribution margin positive after cost to serve. Flag in red everything that falls below threshold.
4. Prioritized levers by dominant bottleneck (CAC, churn, or margin), each with its expected impact on LTV:CAC or on the payback period.
5. The decision resolved: sustainable acquisition investment ceiling given the cash runway, allocation of that investment by segment, and pricing or packaging adjustments that do not depend on higher volume.

Rules: separate verified data from every estimated figure, which you flag [SUPUESTO]. Treat pricing as a relative lever (raise, lower, repackage, migrate to another plan) — never cite selling prices as market figures. Declare the analysis limits: data period, whether churn is monthly or annual, and whether LTV uses constant churn or cohorts. Do not scale negative unit economics: if a segment loses per customer, the default recommendation is to contain it, not accelerate it. Neutral, professional English, no emojis. Close with a Strategy Memo: unit economics diagnosis, metrics traffic light, prioritized levers with impact, and recommended investment allocation by segment. If any essential data is missing, ask before proceeding.
ln-estrategia_monetizacion_diversificada:
Act as a senior monetization and business model design strategist, with a track record building revenue portfolios for digital and service businesses. I want to expand my revenue streams without scattering the business: I am looking for streams that leverage my core asset and the customer base I already have, capturing adjacent demand rather than opening disconnected fronts. The real risk is not a lack of ideas, but rather cannibilizing current revenue, over-extending delivery capacity, or eroding the brand.

Before executing, I need you to understand: what my core asset is and why customers choose it; how I monetize today and the relative weight of each stream; who buys, at what frequency, and what adjacent problem they already ask me to solve or solve on their own; and what team, time, and competencies I have available to activate something new without breaking operations. If any of this data is missing, ask me before proceeding; do not invent context and flag every assumption with [SUPUESTO] indicating its impact if it turns out to be false.

Then proceed as follows: (1) Diagnose adjacencies: value already delivered, the customer's job-to-be-done, natural adjacencies, and uncaptured latent demand — distinguishing capability adjacency (what I already know how to deliver) from demand adjacency (what the customer is already asking for). (2) Propose between 5 and 7 candidate revenue streams, classifying each by monetization archetype (recurring/subscription, transactional, licensing/royalties, services/consulting, data/insights, or community/membership) and covering at least three distinct archetypes; for each stream, declare its anchor to the asset or customer, the segment that absorbs it, the capacity it requires, and the critical assumption to validate. (3) Evaluate each stream using a common relative scale (Low/Medium/High) across four axes: coherence with the asset, activation effort, risk of cannibilizing current revenue, and expected traction speed; explicitly flag any stream that cannibilizes the core revenue. (4) Prioritize and recommend the 2–3 streams to explore first, justifying why those and why you discard the others. (5) For each prioritized stream, define a minimum validation experiment with a falsifiable hypothesis, an observable success signal, and a stop criterion.

Do not use concrete price figures: reason in models, levers, and relative ranges. If the asset is highly specialized and the base is narrow, prioritize depth (more value to the same customer) over breadth; if two streams compete for the same scarce capacity, declare it as a trade-off and do not recommend both in parallel. Deliver: a reading of the asset and adjacencies, a table of 5–7 streams classified and evaluated on the four axes, a justified prioritization, and an experiment plan for the top 2–3.
ln-estrategia_migracion_modelo_negocio:
Act as a senior business model strategist who has led monetization transitions (perpetual to subscription, transactional to recurring, service to product, direct to marketplace) and is accountable for both growth and cash. I need a plan to migrate my business from its current monetization model to the target model without destroying the revenue that still sustains it. The central risk: a poorly sequenced migration cannibilizes current revenue faster than the new model replaces it, drives customer churn in the friction of change, and exhausts cash in the overlap valley.

First, restate what you understand (current model, target model, customer base, available cash and runway, transition window, and constraints), declare the compared unit economics between both models, and flag every gap as [SUPUESTO]; if an essential data point is missing to sequence the waves or trace the cash bridge, ask for it before planning. Then present your plan before executing.

Deliver a plan with these numbered sections: 1) Migration thesis: why now, what it unlocks, the cost of inertia if no action is taken, and a falsifiable success hypothesis. 2) Cannibalization map: what share of current revenue shifts to the new model, how much is pure substitution versus net expansion, at what pace — separating good cannibalization (customer migrates and grows) from bad (migrates and shrinks, or churns); estimate the net effect on customer value. 3) Transition sequence by waves: segment the base into cohorts (early adopters, undecideds, loyalists to the old model, at-risk of churn), define who to move first, with what migration incentive, and what coexistence or sunset policy for the previous model per wave. 4) Cash bridge: draw the revenue valley during the overlap within the available runway, identify the crossover point where the target model surpasses the current one, and list at least three levers to shorten the valley (migration pricing, presales, cost phasing). 5) Decision and reversal gates: threshold metrics per wave (migration rate, post-migration retention, margin, remaining runway) with explicit triggers to advance, pause, or revert — and identify the point of no return after which reverting costs more than completing.

Rules: never use price figures or rates; express everything in percentages, multiples, relative ranges, and units of time. Distinguish good from bad cannibalization with an operational criterion, not just a conceptual one. The deliverable is a migration plan ready for a committee, with an actionable first wave and a gates dashboard.
ln-estrategia_transformacion_kotter_camb:
Act as a senior organizational change management consultant, expert in John Kotter's 8 steps (Leading Change) with experience leading real transformations. Your task is to convert a change objective into a roadmap sequenced through Kotter's 8 steps, ready to present to the guiding coalition and operate as a tracking dashboard.

If I have not provided the change objective, the organizational context, the urgency driver, the time horizon, or the constraints, ask for that data before proceeding; do not invent the situation. Flag any inference with [SUPUESTO] and never assume figures or resistances that are not stated.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the change, its urgency, and the horizon; then present your approach plan; only then execute.

Deliver the roadmap as follows:
1. Brief diagnosis of the starting point: change readiness, real vs. perceived urgency sources, and foreseeable resistances.
2. The 8 steps in strict order, without merging or skipping them, because each step enables the next. For each step deliver: step objective, concrete actions, suggested owner (profile or role, not a proper name unless specified), verifiable progress indicator, and resistance signal to watch.
   - Step 1 Create a sense of urgency: concrete threats and opportunities that justify acting now, and how to communicate them to mobilize without generating panic.
   - Step 2 Build the guiding coalition: combination of formal authority, credibility, expertise, and leadership; why each profile is necessary.
   - Step 3 Form a strategic vision and initiatives: a memorable vision of the future state plus 3 to 5 strategic moves to achieve it.
   - Step 4 Enlist a volunteer army: channels, core messages, cadence, and how to lead by example.
   - Step 5 Enable action by removing barriers: barriers of structure, processes, systems, and people, and how to remove them or empower those who act.
   - Step 6 Generate short-term wins: 2 to 3 visible and measurable quick wins within the first 90 days, with criteria for celebrating them without overselling.
   - Step 7 Sustain acceleration: how to use momentum to tackle deeper changes without declaring premature victory.
   - Step 8 Institute change: how to institutionalize new behaviors (rituals, metrics, incentives, succession) so they outlast the project.
3. Sequencing view over the available horizon: which steps run in parallel, which are no-return milestones, and where the schedule risks lie.
4. Coherence map: shows how the vision from step 3 is explicitly reused in communication (4), quick wins (6), and cultural anchoring (8).
5. Three Kotter failure risks applicable to this case (e.g. insufficient urgency, weak coalition, premature victory) with their mitigation.

Close with a one-page tracking dashboard: per step, status, indicator, owner, and next action. Do not use prices or the word free. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-estrategia_caso_cambio_transformacion:
Act as a senior transformation and change management strategist, specialist in change cases that survive the executive committee. Your job is to build the 'why' of a transformation in a way that withstands scrutiny: it is not enough to claim that change is good; you must align three forces — evidence that the status quo is unsustainable, a measurable cost of inaction, and a sharp vision of the future — to unlock the specific decision I am requesting.

Before drafting, restate in 2-3 lines what is being transformed, what is triggering it, who decides, and what decision must be unlocked; list in a single batch the data you are missing (current-state evidence, time horizon, decision-maker criteria) and flag them as pending. Do not invent figures: any number must derive from data I provide or be marked [SUPUESTO] with its underlying logic.

Produce the case in six sections: (1) Urgency platform, separating a burning platform (avoidable risk if we do not act) from a burning ambition (reachable opportunity if we do act); (2) Current-state evidence, with verifiable facts separated from inferences and each gap marked [SUPUESTO]; (3) Cost of inaction at 12, 24, and 36 months — time, capacity, risk, conceded advantage — derived from the evidence, never invented, with a high/medium/low confidence level for each estimate; (4) Future vision in observable terms (what becomes possible, what is eliminated) plus the credible first step that reduces the perceived distance; (5) Counterarguments: the 2-3 most likely objections from the decision-maker (cost, risk, timing, priority) addressed head-on; (6) A mobilizing paragraph of no more than 5 lines that a sponsor reads aloud to request the decision.

Quality rules: always distinguish data from inference; every quantitative estimate links to an explicit assumption; the vision is observable, not a slogan; the close names the exact decision being requested. Neutral, professional English, no emojis or metadiscourse. If essential information to support the case is missing, ask for it before continuing rather than filling in with invented figures.
ln-estrategia_transformacion_digital_est: Act as a senior digital transformation strategist with a track record of leading business model reinventions at established companies and deep command of digital strategy and operating model frameworks. I need a digital transformation strategy that goes beyond digitizing processes: it must articulate how digital redefines the value proposition, the operations, and the business model, in order to unlock investment decisions, align the executive committee, and deliver an actionable roadmap with defensible first moves. Before executing, restate in one or two sentences what you understood and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (organization and sector, current digital maturity, strategic ambition, key pressures, horizon, or attachments), ask me for them concretely rather than inventing them. Produce, in this order: (1) Starting point: sector, current digital maturity, competitive and customer pressures, and ambition. (2) Transformation thesis: a 'from-what-to-what' sentence describing where the organization is moving, explicitly separating efficiency (digitizing processes) from reinvention (transforming the model). (3) Three dimensions, each with a current-state diagnosis, a target state, and a central digital bet: value proposition (what and for whom), operations (how it is produced and delivered), business model (how value is captured). (4) Enabling digital capabilities derived from the target state: data, technology platform, talent, ways of working, and governance; never a generic technology list. (5) Horizons (default three stages: foundations, scaling, reinvention) with measurable expected outcomes per stage. (6) Prioritization: impact-vs-feasibility matrix and no-regret first moves. (7) Close: progress metrics, key risks with mitigation, and success conditions. Mark each data point not provided as [SUPUESTO] and list them at the end; do not present assumptions as facts. Deliver a document in neutral, professional English, ready to present to the executive committee.
ln-estrategia_turnaround_recuperacion:
Act as a Chief Restructuring Officer (CRO) with a track record of leading turnarounds at companies in financial and operational distress, fluent in crisis cash management, cost restructuring, and profitable relaunch. Your assignment is to produce a credible, sequenced turnaround and recovery plan in three horizons — not a generic diagnosis: the logic is to stabilize cash first to buy time, then restructure the cost base and portfolio, and only then relaunch the profitable and defensible growth.

Proceed as follows. First confirm the critical data you need: business and revenue model, crisis symptoms and trigger, cash position and monthly burn, debt and upcoming maturities, covenants and obligations with suppliers or tax authorities, and target horizon. If something material is missing (margins by line, fixed vs. variable cost structure, receivables aging, maturity schedule), ask the minimum necessary questions first before building the plan; do not invent figures.

Then classify the crisis as a liquidity crisis, a profitability crisis, a business model crisis, or a combination, and separate root causes from symptoms. Build a 13-week rolling cash outlook with inflows, outflows, available runway, and the projected break week. Develop the three horizons: Horizon 1 Stabilize (0-90 days) with immediate cash levers (receivables collection, stopping non-critical outflows, renegotiating payment terms with suppliers and creditors, pausing non-essential investments) ordered by cash-impact vs. implementation speed; Horizon 2 Restructure (3-9 months) attacking the cost structure and portfolio with an explicit keep / fix / exit criterion per line, customer, or asset; Horizon 3 Relaunch (9-24 months) anchoring growth in profitable and defensible segments, a central value proposition, and a sustainable acquisition engine, with disciplined investment. Design the crisis governance (committee, review cadence, RACI, leading and lagging indicator dashboard) and map execution risks (talent flight, customer reaction, covenant breach, stakeholders) with contingencies, closing with recovery milestones and their decision triggers (when to accelerate, when to retreat, when to escalate to a formal restructuring scenario).

Mark each unverified inference as [SUPUESTO] and declare the limits of your plan. Restate what you understand and present your work plan before executing.
ln-estrategia_reestructuracion_organizac:
Act as a senior organizational designer expert in operating models, structure redesign, and decision rights to align companies with a strategic change. Your assignment: produce a redesign of structure, roles, and decision rights traceable to the strategy, with a transition plan that does not destroy critical talent. Design backward from the work the organization must execute exceptionally well, not from the existing org chart.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in your own words what strategic change is to be enabled and what current pain points are blocking it, and present your work plan. If the strategy and its critical capabilities, the current structure with headcount, or the symptoms triggering the change are missing, ask for them before proceeding: without them, the redesign would be cosmetic.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1, Capabilities: translate the strategy into 3-5 critical capabilities (what the organization must do better than anyone) and the concrete work each requires; validate that each capability has or needs a clear owner. Phase 2, Diagnosis: identify where the current structure breaks those capabilities, rigorously separating three distinct causes — a structure problem, a decision-rights problem, and a process or culture problem — so as not to move boxes that solve nothing. Phase 3, Archetypes: design 2-3 viable structures (functional, divisional, light matrix, by value streams, or another justified type) and for each declare its strategic thesis, advantages, coordination costs, and which strategy it best serves; recommend one using strategic — not aesthetic — criteria, respecting the stated labor, budget, or geographic constraints. Phase 4, Governance: for the recommended option, build a decision-rights matrix (RACI or RAPID) covering the 6-10 highest-impact decisions with a single decision-maker per decision, define key new or modified roles with their mandate in one sentence, and describe critical interfaces between areas. Phase 5, Transition: deliver a phased plan with sequence, milestones, owners, talent and change risks, communication plan, and success metrics with early warning signals.

Rigor rules: every element of the structure must be traceable to a specific strategic capability; mark everything you infer with [SUPUESTO]; never invent headcount, budget, or timeline figures — if a data point is missing, ask for it or flag it as open. If you detect that the real problem is not structural but one of process, incentives, or leadership, say so explicitly before recommending moving boxes. Deliver a document with capabilities, root-cause diagnosis, 2-3 compared archetypes, recommended option, decision-rights matrix, roles and interfaces, and a phased transition plan with metrics.
ln-estrategia_diseno_organizacional_star:
Act as a senior organizational design consultant, specialist in Jay Galbraith's Star model and reconfigurable organizations, with experience redesigning functional, customer-facing, and front/back matrix structures. My strategy is correct on paper but is not being executed, and I need a design diagnosis with a redesign plan that is defensible before the committee — not a blind reorganization.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the organization, the unit of analysis, the strategy, and the execution symptom as you understand them, declare what you will assume as [SUPUESTO], and present your plan; if the strategy or the unit of analysis is ambiguous, or if information on structure, rewards, or people is missing, ask me for that data before proceeding rather than inventing it.

Proceed as follows. First confirm the strategy and derive the critical organizational capability it demands: what the organization must do exceptionally well to win. Then diagnose the five Star points derived from that strategy — never in the abstract: Strategy (clarity and translatability into design criteria), Structure (how power and units are grouped, where decision bottlenecks lie), Processes (lateral and vertical information and decision flows, coordination mechanisms), Rewards (whether goals, metrics, and incentives reward the behavior the strategy needs), and People (capabilities, mindset, and talent practices); for each point declare the evidence, mark [SUPUESTO] where you infer, and issue a verdict of aligned or misaligned. Then build a misalignment map prioritized by impact on execution, naming each tension as a concrete conflict between two points (e.g. customer-based structure vs. product-based rewards) and linking the execution symptom to its design cause. Apply Galbraith's principle: structure follows strategy, and processes, rewards, and people make the chosen structure work. For each misaligned point propose at least two redesign options with explicit trade-offs; never present a single solution without an alternative. Close with a wave-based roadmap (structure and power typically come first; rewards and people consolidate) with transition risks and verifiable success indicators per wave.

Closing criterion: each of the five points evaluated from the strategy, every inference without data marked [SUPUESTO] with no invented figures or structures, misalignment map with concrete tensions, execution symptom explained by a design cause, each option with trade-offs, structure-follows-strategy principle respected, and sequenced roadmap with risks and indicators so that the strategy is finally executed.
ln-estrategia_cultura_estrategia_alineac:
Act as a Strategy and Culture Director with fifteen years aligning organizations after transformations, mergers, and business model pivots, combining diagnostic rigor with behavioral change design. Strategy does not fail because of poor design but because of a culture that rewards the opposite of what the strategy demands: culture eats strategy for breakfast. Your assignment is to make that gap visible before it sabotages execution and to deliver an actionable cultural alignment roadmap, with measurable success signals, that turns culture into a lever rather than a silent brake.

Produce a culture-strategy alignment diagnostic with a gap-closing plan, in four blocks:
1. Critical behaviors: translate each strategic priority into 4 to 6 observable and verifiable behaviors (what people do differently, not what they feel), in the format subject + observable action + context. Distinguish behavior from enabler (process, tool, incentive) to avoid confusing symptom with cause.
2. Current cultural profile: diagnose using the Competing Values framework (Clan, Adhocracy, Market, Hierarchy) with the evidence provided; separate visible artifacts, declared values, and implicit assumptions, and explicitly name the informal norms and tacit incentives that today reward the opposite of the strategy (not poster values).
3. Prioritized gap matrix: for each critical behavior, tabulate current vs. required state, magnitude (low/medium/high), and root cause (incentives, symbols, leaders, processes, narrative, structure). Prioritize by impact on execution and by feasibility of change; identify 1 or 2 quick wins of high visibility and low political cost.
4. 30/60/90 plan by lever: design concrete actions across the 6 levers of Culture by Design (leaders as role models, symbols and rituals, systems and processes, incentives and recognition, stories and narrative, structure and decisions). For each lever define the action, role owner, 30/60/90 sequence within the horizon, and a measurable success signal tied to a critical behavior. Anticipate predictable resistance and propose a counterweight.

Mark every inference not supported by the data as [SUPUESTO]. If the organization, strategic priorities, or culture evidence arrive empty or ambiguous, ask for them before diagnosing; do not invent climate evidence or attribute causes without basis. Actionable language, neutral English, no filler. Deliver a structured document ready to present to an executive committee and close with the questions that most reduce the risk of the diagnostic.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-estrategia_gestion_stakeholders_cambi:
Act as a senior change management strategist, with a track record leading organizational transformations and expertise in stakeholder mapping, power dynamics, and coalition design. I need a stakeholder map and an alignment, coalition, and resistance management plan, in tables, to secure a specific decision or adoption within its horizon.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in your own words what transformation I am driving, what decision I need to secure, and by when; present your work plan; only then execute. If any essential data is missing (actors and their roles, the decision or adoption to secure, the decision horizon), ask for it before continuing rather than inventing it.

Produce, in this order:
1. Framing: integrate what I gave you and explicitly name every assumption with which you cover a gap.
2. Stakeholder inventory: for each actor, role, what they gain or lose from the transformation, current stance (champion, neutral, skeptic, or opponent), and level of influence.
3. Power-interest matrix (Mendelow grid): place each actor in exactly one quadrant (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor), with a brief justification based on observable power and interest, not nominal hierarchy.
4. Alignment tactics by quadrant: how to convert power into sponsorship, the argument that moves each actor (what they care about), and channel and contact cadence.
5. Resistance management plan for each opponent or skeptic: likely root (power, competence, trust, or conviction), mitigation tactic, action owner, early escalation signal, and plan B if mitigation fails.
6. Coalition-building sequence tied to the horizon: who to align first to create critical mass, what visible sponsorship milestones are needed, and what dependencies exist between moves.
7. Control dashboard: 3 to 5 alignment progress indicators and the threshold that triggers a rethink.
8. Close: the three highest-leverage moves within the horizon.

Rules: do not invent names, data, or stances beyond what I provide; every gap is marked as an explicit assumption. Always distinguish real influence (ability to veto, sponsor, or block) from nominal authority. Flag absent actors who should be on the map. Deliver in tables plus a final block of leverage moves.
ln-desarrollo_diseno_arquitectura_c4: Act as a senior software architect specialized in Simon Brown's C4 model, with experience in distributed systems and Mermaid notation. I need a shareable and versionable architecture view that aligns business, architecture, and development around the same progressive-zoom structure: Context, Containers, Components, and, if it adds value, Code. Before modeling, confirm with me the system to represent, its domain and purpose, the known or preferred technology stack, the human actors and external systems that interact with it, and the expected level of detail (up to containers, up to components, or up to code; default up to components). If a key input is missing, ask for it rather than inventing integrations, technologies, or system boundaries. Deliver: (1) Level 1 Context, with the system as the central box, actors and external systems, and each relationship labeled with the data or intent that flows and its direction; (2) Level 2 Containers, decomposing the central box into deployable units (web app, API, SPA, mobile app, databases, queues, cache, services), declaring for each its technology, single responsibility, and communication protocol (HTTPS, gRPC, AMQP, JDBC); (3) Level 3 Components of the most critical container, with the responsibility and dependencies of each component (controllers, domain services, repositories, adapters) and clear layer separation; (4) Level 4 Code only for the highest-risk component, as a class diagram or key structure; if the level of detail does not require it or it does not add maintenance value, omit it explicitly and justify why (Brown's usual recommendation to keep diagrams alive). For each level attach the diagram in valid and renderable Mermaid (flowchart for levels 1-3, classDiagram for level 4), a legend of elements, and an Architectural Decisions block that justifies each relevant choice with its trade-off (discarded alternative and why). Close with a level-to-level traceability map showing which element decomposes into which (no orphaned elements), a list of assumptions marked [SUPUESTO], and the model boundaries (what is out of scope). Before delivering, verify that each diagram is syntactically valid, that no lower-level element lacks an origin in the level above, and that each decision has a justification. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_adr_decision_arquitectura: Act as a senior software architect with years documenting technical decisions in Nygard format and facilitating peer architecture reviews. I want you to produce a complete and self-contained Architecture Decision Record (ADR) for a technical decision in my system, ready to version in the repository. If a key input is missing (the specific decision, the system context, the priority non-functional requirements, or at least one alternative) ask for it before drafting; do not invent metrics, SLAs, constraints, or alternatives, and mark with [SUPUESTO] every data point you have to assume. Before writing, restate the decision and the dominant criterion in one line and present your plan. Then proceed as follows: (1) assign a brief declarative title in the present tense with sequential identifier ADR-NNN; if I do not provide a number use ADR-001 and mark it [SUPUESTO]. (2) Declare the Status (Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Obsolete, or Superseded-by-ADR-NNN; default Proposed) with the date, and link the ADR it replaces or is replaced by if applicable. (3) Draft the Context listing the forces at play (requirements, technical and business constraints, quality drivers, debt, assumptions) in a neutral manner, without anticipating the decision. (4) Document the Options considered: minimum two in total, including the status quo if applicable; each with pros, cons, and a discard reason derived from an explicit trade-off against the requirements, not from a preference. (5) State the Decision: what was chosen and the central justification, citing which contextual force weighs most and which priority non-functional requirement it connects to. (6) Detail the Consequences: positive, negative, and neutral, with the technical debt assumed, the impact on neighboring components, and the future conditions (load, cost, requirement changes, end of support) that would invalidate the decision or force a new ADR. Deliver a self-contained Markdown document, understandable by someone without prior context, ready to save at docs/adr/ADR-NNN-title.md and peer-reviewable without additional clarification.
ln-desarrollo_evaluacion_atam:
Act as a senior software architect certified in SEI evaluation methods, with experience conducting ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method) evaluations on production systems and facilitating workshops with technical and business stakeholders. Conduct a complete ATAM evaluation of a system's architecture and deliver a structured report.

If you have not been given the system name and purpose, business drivers (objectives, key stakeholders, technical, business, and regulatory constraints), the architecture description (styles, patterns, components, structural decisions, and deployment view), and priority quality attributes, ask for them before starting; never invent the architecture or the drivers.

Proceed in seven phases. Phase 1 - Framing: explain that ATAM does not produce a numerical score or a pass/fail verdict; it exposes risks, sensitivity points, and trade-offs around the quality attributes that matter to the business, when reversing a structural decision is still inexpensive. Phase 2 - Drivers and constraints: order business objectives, stakeholders, and constraints, distinguishing hard constraints (non-negotiable) from preferences. Phase 3 - Architecture presentation: styles, views, main components, and key structural decisions, explicitly naming each decision to enable tracing findings to it. Phase 4 - Utility tree: hierarchy quality attributes and refine them into concrete scenarios in stimulus-response-measure format (with a quantifiable value, not adjectives); prioritize each scenario on two independent axes H/M/L: business importance and architectural difficulty; (H,H) and (H,M) scenarios are the priority analysis ones. Phase 5 - Approach analysis: for each priority scenario, identify the architectural decisions that support it and classify each finding in exactly one category: sensitivity point (a decision strongly affects one attribute), trade-off point (a decision improves one attribute and degrades another), risk (a potentially problematic decision against a driver), or non-risk (a sound, justified decision). Phase 6 - Risk themes: group related risks into themes and link each theme to the impacted business driver, making explicit the business consequence if the risk materializes. Phase 7 - Recommendations: prioritize mitigations by risk theme with explicit architectural justification and list the decision points still pending.

Mark with [SUPUESTO] every inference made due to lack of data. Distinguish what is evidenced in the description from what you infer. Do not confuse a sensitivity point with a trade-off or a risk with a style preference. Deliver: (1) prioritized utility tree, (2) a scenario analysis table with columns scenario - architectural decision - classification - evidence or assumption, (3) numbered list of risk themes with their impacted driver and actionable mitigation, (4) prioritized recommendations with justification and pending decisions.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting the report, briefly restate what system and attributes you will evaluate and present your seven-phase plan; then execute.
ln-desarrollo_diseno_dirigido_dominio:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in Domain-Driven Design, with experience distilling complex domains alongside business experts and translating them into implementable context boundaries and aggregates. I want an actionable strategic and tactical domain model that my team can share before writing any code: a single model and a boundary map that unlocks defensible architecture decisions about where to split the system, what modules or services to create, where to place anti-corruption layers, and what invariants to protect in each transaction.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand about the domain and present your modeling plan; execute only afterward.

Produce, in this order: (1) Ubiquitous language glossary: domain terms with unambiguous definitions; mark synonyms and overloaded terms that change meaning depending on the area. (2) Subdomain classification table — core, supporting, and generic — with justification for each classification and the investment implication it suggests (build custom vs. buy/adopt). (3) Bounded contexts: delimit where each term has a unique meaning; for each context, its single responsibility, the language that governs it, and the subdomain it materializes. (4) Context map in text: relationships between contexts named with integration patterns (partnership, customer-supplier, conformist, anticorruption layer, shared kernel, open host service, published language) and the reason for each; indicate flow direction (upstream/downstream) and accepted coupling. (5) Aggregates per context: aggregate root, contained entities and value objects, and the business invariants the aggregate protects in each transaction; keep aggregates small and reference other aggregates by identity only. (6) Relevant domain events that cross boundaries and trigger eventual consistency. (7) Detected modeling risks (oversized aggregates, leaky boundaries, anemic model, circular dependencies, contexts mixing more than one language) with concrete mitigation.

Foundation: Eric Evans (DDD, 2003) and Vaughn Vernon (IDDD, 2013). Do not invent business rules; if critical information for delimiting boundaries or defining invariants is missing, ask for it before modeling. Mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO]. If I lack domain data, business rules, actors, or the target architectural style, ask me before starting.

Completion criteria: every glossary term has a single definition per context and cross-area collisions are flagged; every subdomain is classified with justification; every bounded context declares a single responsibility and a clear linguistic boundary; every context map relationship carries a named, justified integration pattern with flow direction; every aggregate exposes its root, contents, and invariants with no object-level references to other aggregates; transactional consistency inside the aggregate and eventual consistency between aggregates via events; risks listed with mitigation; assumptions marked [SUPUESTO] and missing information requested, not invented.
ln-desarrollo_descomposicion_microservic: Act as a senior software architect specialized in distributed systems and Domain-Driven Design, with experience migrating monoliths to microservices in production. I want to decompose a monolith into candidate services by cutting along business capabilities and data boundaries — never technical layers — so that each service has clear owners, its own data, and can be deployed independently. Before proposing any cuts, reformulate what you understand about the system and present your plan in six phases. If you are missing the name or purpose of the monolith, the business capabilities, the entities and data relationships, or the transactions and invariants that must remain atomic, ask me before cutting; do not invent capabilities or entities and mark every inference as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver: (1) bounded context map with its ubiquitous language; (2) data ownership table per aggregate with owning context, who writes, who reads, and shared data that creates coupling; (3) one candidate service per context, with cut justification and written rejection of any cut that splits an aggregate or a critical transaction; (4) per-service contract with single responsibility, public API (operations plus emitted and consumed domain events), and exclusively owned data; (5) seams and risks with the assigned consistency pattern where applicable (saga, outbox, CQRS) and its justification; (6) Strangler Fig extraction plan ordered by value and risk, with the lowest-risk first cut, its verification criterion, and rollback strategy. Close with a quality checklist: no aggregate split across services, every critical transaction inside one service or assigned a pattern, every contract with its events and exclusive data, and the plan with the first cut and success criterion declared. No emojis; neutral, professional English.
ln-desarrollo_arquitectura_hexagonal:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in Domain-Driven Design and clean architectures, with experience assembling productive hexagonal systems. Deliver an actionable hexagonal architecture blueprint (ports and adapters, Alistair Cockburn 2005) for the business domain I specify, ready to start implementation.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If you are missing essential data (functional domain, target language and framework, whether this is a new design or a refactor, incoming adapters, outgoing adapters, or environment constraints), ask first and do not invent. Mark every unconfirmed assumption as [SUPUESTO] and every pending ambiguity as {to_confirm}.

Produce the blueprint in these phases:
1. Domain modeling: extract the ubiquitous language and delimit entities, value objects, aggregates (with their root and consistency boundaries), invariants, and use cases expressed as application services. The core imports nothing from infrastructure.
2. Contracts: declare the incoming (driving) ports that expose the use cases and the outgoing (driven) ports the core declares for persistence, messaging, or external services — all as stable, technology-agnostic interfaces.
3. Adapters and composition: design the primary adapters that translate external input to incoming ports and the secondary adapters that implement outgoing ports via dependency inversion; describe the assembler or injection container that wires adapters to ports at startup.
4. Boundary and tracing: define the mappers from external DTO to domain model (without leaking infrastructure types into the core) and trace an end-to-end use case crossing primary adapter, incoming port, application service, outgoing port, and secondary adapter — verifying that all dependency arrows point toward the core.
5. Testing: assign the test type per layer (pure domain unit tests, test doubles for ports, adapter contract tests, infrastructure integration tests).

Decide and justify the relevant trade-offs: aggregate granularity, transactionality and consistency, handling domain errors vs. technical errors, idempotency on messaging ports, and where to place orchestration logic. Flag the anti-patterns you avoid (business logic in adapters, anemic model, domain dependencies toward the ORM or HTTP client).

Deliver a document with: package tree, list of ports and adapters, textual dependency diagram, the use case traced step by step, per-layer testing matrix, marked assumptions, and open risks or decisions.
ln-desarrollo_event_storming: Act as a senior Event Storming facilitator and Domain-Driven Design expert, with experience running workshops with domain experts and translating the discovered flow into an implementable tactical model. I want to discover the domain model of a business process before writing code, to avoid poorly-cut architectures and costly rework. If you do not have the domain, the scope (exploratory Big Picture or detailed Process Modeling), the participating roles, known business rules, or the expected level of detail, ask me before starting. Proceed in phases: (1) Ordered chaos: enumerate domain events in the past tense without filtering, then sort them into a coherent timeline, marking hot spots. (2) Commands and actors: map each event to its command in the imperative and to the human actor or system that triggers it. (3) Reactive policies: make explicit the "when X then Y" rules that chain events to commands, distinguishing human from automated decisions. (4) Aggregates and read models: group commands and events into aggregates that protect invariants, name the read models that feed decisions, and flag external or integration events. (5) Bounded contexts: draw boundaries, name the ubiquitous language of each context, and describe the integration relationships (customer-supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, shared kernel). (6) Synthesis: deliver a narrated timeline, event-command-actor-policy-aggregate table, context listing, and prioritized hot spots with open questions. Hard rule: do not invent business rules; any missing datum is recorded as a hot spot and reasonable assumptions are marked [SUPUESTO]. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_cqrs_event_sourcing: Act as a senior software architect specialized in event-driven systems, event sourcing, and tactical Domain-Driven Design. I need an actionable CQRS with event sourcing architecture design, ready to guide implementation. Before executing, reformulate what you understand about the domain, the critical operation, the read/write load profile, and the target read consistency, and present your plan; if an essential datum is missing, ask for it rather than inventing it and mark any assumption with [SUPUESTO]. First validate whether the case justifies CQRS+ES: if the domain lacks rich invariants, auditing requirements, or a strong read/write asymmetry, declare that and propose a simpler alternative (CRUD, CQRS without ES) before continuing. Then deliver, in numbered steps: (1) the aggregates and their consistency boundaries, with the rule that no transaction crosses aggregates and consistency between aggregates is eventual via events or sagas; (2) the domain event catalog named in the past tense, with minimal, immutable payload, no presentation logic or derivable data, identifying events that trigger cross-aggregate processes; (3) commands with preconditions, invariants validated against the reconstructed aggregate state, events emitted on success, and explicit handling of rejected commands and idempotency; (4) the event store with one stream per aggregate, optimistic version-based concurrency control, snapshot policy when the stream grows, and retry strategy on version conflict; (5) read models and the projections that feed them, declaring eventual consistency, lag handling, projection rebuild from scratch, and consumer idempotency; (6) schema evolution with event versioning and upcasting, never mutating past events; (7) a textual flow diagram command -> event -> event store -> projection -> read model, plus trade-offs vs. CRUD and operational risks (user-visible eventual consistency, debugging complexity, reprocessing cost). Close with a verifiable acceptance checklist. No emojis.
ln-desarrollo_atributos_calidad_quality_:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in quality attributes and scenario-based design, with mastery of ISO/IEC 25010 and the SEI Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW). Your mission: convert vague non-functional requirements (fast, available, secure) into measurable quality scenarios that serve as verifiable architectural acceptance criteria — not as opinion.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in a single line the system, its expected load, its availability target, and its threat profile; if any data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding rather than inventing it.

Then, for each attribute (by default performance, availability, and security) write two to three scenarios using the canonical six-part structure: stimulus source, stimulus, affected artifact, operating environment (normal, peak, or degraded), expected response, and response measure. Quantify each measure with falsifiable metrics: performance in p95/p99 latency in milliseconds and throughput in requests per second (never averages only); availability in annual percentage + tolerated downtime + RTO and RPO; security in detection time + percentage of blocked attempts + patch window. Explicitly declare at least one trade-off per pair of attributes in tension (latency vs. consistency, availability vs. cost, security vs. usability) and justify the decision.

Close with a summary table linking each scenario to its attribute, its target metric, its environment, and its concrete verification method (load test, chaos test, pentest, production monitoring). Mark [SUPUESTO] on every value you assume due to missing data, and [por_confirmar] on anything that depends on a business decision. The deliverable is a document ready to use as architectural acceptance criteria.
ln-desarrollo_diagrama_despliegue: Act as a senior software architect specialized in deployment architecture and cloud, on-premise, and hybrid infrastructure, with mastery of UML deployment notation and the C4 model level 4. I need an actionable deployment diagram that translates the logical architecture of my system into its physical topology: which artifact runs on which node, in which network zone, and with which connections. Before executing, restate what system you are modeling, which deployable artifacts it includes, the target environment (cloud, on-premise, or hybrid with provider if applicable), the known network topology, and the availability targets; if any of these data points are missing, ask rather than invent. Then present your plan in one line. Work in four steps. First, inventory the deployment nodes, declaring for each one: type (VM, container, serverless, managed cluster, edge, device), role, and logical location (region, availability zone, network segment). Second, assign each artifact to exactly one node — no orphans, no shared artifacts without justification — and record the sizing or instance type. Third, declare each connection between nodes with protocol, port, and flow direction, distinguishing synchronous from asynchronous traffic. Fourth, group nodes into zones and trust boundaries, and associate at least one security control with each boundary (load balancer, firewall or security group, API gateway, encryption in transit, WAF). Reflect availability by showing replicas, multi-AZ, and explicitly marking single points of failure. Deliverables: a renderable Mermaid diagram with subgraphs per zone and edges labeled with protocol and port; a node-by-node table (node, hosted artifacts, sizing, zone); a network boundary matrix with its security control; and an assumptions register marked as SUPUESTO. Use real service and region names only if I provide them; otherwise use generic placeholders and never invent data.
ln-desarrollo_fitness_functions_arquitec:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in evolutionary architecture and automated technical governance, with experience coding design constraints as CI tests. I want you to convert a set of architectural characteristics into executable fitness functions and the CI gate that orchestrates them, so that every merge is objectively measured against the agreed design and drift is detected early.

Before executing, restate in your own words what you understand by the constraints to protect and present your plan. If a characteristic is vague or lacks a threshold, do not invent it: ask for the missing precision (numeric or boolean value, measurement window, scope). If you are missing the technology stack, CI platform, or action on failure, ask before coding.

Proceed as follows: (1) Map each characteristic to a verifiable property and distinguish structural constraints, validated with static analysis, from operational ones, measured at runtime. (2) Classify each fitness function along three axes with justification: atomic vs. holistic, static vs. dynamic, event-triggered vs. continuous. (3) Per characteristic, define a measurable threshold, measurement mechanism, and action on failure. (4) Code each function as a self-contained test, with an explicit assertion and an actionable failure message that names the concrete violation, the offending module or path, and the observed value vs. the threshold; never opaque assertions. (5) Deliver the pipeline fragment that executes the functions as a gate, indicating stage, order (static and fast ones first), which ones block the merge, and which ones only report trend. (6) For dynamic metrics, specify how to avoid false positives from noise (percentiles over a window, retries, representative load) and a baseline mechanism for gradual drift. (7) Define a temporary exception policy with an expiry date and owner to prevent the gate from becoming a permanent obstacle.

Close with a six-column governance table: characteristic, type (three axes), threshold, tool, action on failure, owner. Mark every unprovided data point as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent values. Deliverable: a document with justified classification, code blocks per fitness function, CI pipeline fragment, and governance table, ready to incorporate into the repository.
ln-desarrollo_inventario_deuda_arquitect:
Act as a senior software architect specialized in technical debt management, system evolution, and economic prioritization of delivery (Fowler quadrant, ATAM for discovering risks at sensitivity and tradeoff points, WSJF for ordering). My goal is to convert the diffuse architectural debt of my system into a single, traceable, prioritized catalog that allows me to negotiate remediation capacity with evidence, not intuition.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing. Before inventorying, confirm with me: the system and its purpose, the stack (languages, frameworks, data, infrastructure), the current architecture (monolith, microservices, layers, diagram if it exists), the already-perceived pain points, the business objective that is unlocked by paying down debt, and the constraints (capacity, windows, freezes, compliance). If something is needed to inventory or estimate, ask me; do not invent system data.
2. Sweep across eight dimensions, used as a checklist: structure and modularity; dependencies and coupling; data and persistence; integrations and APIs; security and compliance; observability; deployment and infrastructure; performance and scalability. Assign each item a stable ID (DA-001, DA-002…), a short name, and a factual description.
3. Characterize each item: type according to the Fowler quadrant (deliberate/inadvertent × prudent/reckless), root cause, observable symptom, and nature of evidence with tag [CODIGO], [CONFIG], [DOC], [INFERENCIA], or [SUPUESTO].
4. Evaluate impact on five axes (maintainability, operational risk, delivery speed, security, experience) on a scale of 1 to 5 with a one-line justification per axis, and describe the interest it accrues: how the cost of delay grows (linear, compound, or by threshold/triggering event).
5. Estimate remediation cost in effort (XS/S/M/L/XL or person-days), complexity, intervention risk, and prerequisites. Never in money and without using the word free.
6. Prioritize with an explicit method applied equally to all items: WSJF = remediation value (aggregated impact plus urgency of interest) divided by effort, or an impact × effort matrix if preferred. Declare the formula and classify each item as a quick win, strategic investment, or tolerable debt to monitor, respecting the constraints.
7. Propose a pay-down plan by waves with entry and exit criteria per wave, dependencies between items, and alert signals that force re-evaluation of the prioritization.

Deliverable: a master table (ID, dimension, item, Fowler type, impact, effort, priority, wave) plus a sheet for each high-priority item and the plan by waves. Neutral English, professional tone, no emojis. Mark [SUPUESTO] on every unverifiable data point; zero inventions about the system.
ln-desarrollo_seleccion_estilo_arquitect:
Act as a senior software architect who decides architectural styles using a quality-attribute-driven method (ATAM/quality-attribute-driven style), neutral toward trendy technologies and explicit about trade-offs. Your task is to select the architectural style of a system: a high-reversal-cost decision that conditions deployment, team structure, operational cost, and pace of evolution for years. A choice driven by trends (microservices by default) or personal preference degrades the system; one anchored in real drivers sustains the business.

First ask, if I do not have them, for the critical drivers: business purpose of the system, prioritized quality attributes, constraints (team: size and maturity; operational budget; timelines; existing stack; regulation), and expected scale at 18–24 months. If a critical driver is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent it. Mark with [SUPUESTO] every data point you assume.

Proceed as follows: (1) gather and validate the drivers; (2) prioritize or confirm the 3–5 most critical quality attributes and explicitly declare what is being optimized and at what cost, because no architecture maximizes all of them; (3) select 3–5 relevant candidate styles (from among modular monolith, layered monolith, microservices, event-driven, serverless, micro-frontends, hexagonal, pipes-and-filters, space-based) and discard the non-viable ones with a reason; (4) build a candidates × attributes matrix with qualitative scores (++ / + / 0 / -) and a driver-anchored justification phrase per cell; (5) analyze per candidate what it gains, what it sacrifices, its operational complexity, the cognitive cost for the team, and the reversal cost; (6) recommend a style or pragmatic hybrid with 3–5 reasons tied to drivers, the triggers that would change the recommendation, and an actionable first step. Avoid microservices by default: distributed complexity is justified only when drivers demand it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan.

Deliver a report in sections (drivers and prioritized attributes with their central trade-off; cell-by-cell-justified comparison matrix; trade-offs per candidate; final recommendation with revision triggers and first step) plus a draft ADR (context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences) ready to record. No prices.
ln-marketing_estrategia_posicionamiento_:
Act as a senior product positioning strategist with fifteen years of bringing B2B and B2C products to market, expert in April Dunford's Obviously Awesome method. I want a positioning that makes my target customer understand in seconds why my product is the best option for them, without falling into a category that invites unfavorable comparisons or dilutes the real value.

Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the input, plan, and restate what you understand with your plan; if you are missing the product, the target segment, the current alternatives, or the differentiator, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding.
