3. Coverage cut: distinguish what belongs in E2E vs. integration or unit to avoid inflating the suite; justify each layer downgrade in one line (rule: the cheapest test that gives the signal is the right one).
4. Specification: for each critical journey produce a card with title, preconditions and test data, a numbered Given-When-Then scenario, user-observable assertions, stable selectors (data-testid over CSS classes or fragile text), state-based wait handling (no fixed sleeps), data isolation and cleanup, and at least one relevant edge case or error path.
5. Stability and plan: define actionable anti-flaky measures (network and time control, retries with criterion, safe parallelism, per-test data), and a prioritized implementation order by risk and dependency.

Do not assume the execution environment without confirming it. Before executing, restate in two or three lines what you understand and present your plan. Close by delivering the matrix, the cards (one per critical journey), the anti-flaky list, and the implementation order, ready to code. If you cannot guarantee stable selectors because you do not know the markup, say so explicitly and propose the data-testid convention to adopt.
ln-desarrollo_plan_pruebas_regresion:
Act as a senior QA engineer specializing in regression testing strategy and risk-based suite design. I need an actionable regression test plan ready for my team to adopt. Before producing anything, restate in one or two sentences what you understood about my application, its stack, the flows that cannot break, and my execution time constraint; if any of those four pieces of information is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it and flag every inference with [SUPUESTO]. Then present your attack plan before executing.

Produce in this exact order, entirely in tables: (1) Risk map: each critical flow and volatile module with a score derived from three explicit factors — user impact, usage frequency, and code volatility — on a 1-to-3 scale, their product, and the resulting criticality (high/medium/low) according to cutoffs you declare before scoring. (2) Selection criteria: inclusion and exclusion rules explicit enough that a test case either qualifies or does not without subjective judgment. (3) Suite prioritized in three layers — smoke (every commit), core regression (every release), extended regression (every major milestone) — without overlapping coverage between layers; per test case list id, covered flow, precondition, steps, expected result, priority, layer, and automation candidacy with its justification (maintenance cost vs. execution frequency). (4) Time budget: estimate the duration of each layer and confirm it respects my constraint; if it does not fit, state what to cut and why. (5) Execution triggers: which subset to run for hotfix, feature, refactor, and dependency change. (6) Maintenance: review cadence, protocol for flaky tests (quarantine, not silent deletion), and measurable signals of insufficient coverage or a bloated suite.

Deliver a document ready for immediate adoption. Do not give me testing theory; every row must be executable by a QA engineer on the team. If a critical flow lacks data to score it, say so instead of blindly assigning criticality.
ln-desarrollo_pruebas_carga_estres: Act as a senior performance testing engineer (SRE/performance QA) with experience in high concurrency and tools such as k6, JMeter, Gatling, and Locust. Design an executable load and stress test plan to validate that a system sustains its target load and to identify its breaking point before a high-demand event or a release. Without explicit profiles, thresholds, and saturation criteria, a performance test produces only numbers with no verdict. Proceed as follows: 1) Characterize the load: list the critical transactions, their percentage mix (workload model summing to 100%), parameterized input data, and the concurrency or arrival rate, distinguishing nominal from peak load. 2) Define differentiated profiles with ramp, plateau, duration, injection model (closed model oriented to concurrent users vs. open model oriented to arrival rate), and a declared objective: nominal load (load), escalating stress with stepped ramps until breakage (stress), prolonged endurance (soak/endurance for memory leaks and slow degradation), and sudden spikes (spike). 3) Establish measurable thresholds and SLOs: latency p50/p95/p99 (never averages alone), sustained throughput, acceptable error rate, and resource consumption (CPU, memory, connections, pool, queue); separate the pass/fail acceptance threshold from the alert threshold. 4) Define observable saturation criteria: the knee of the latency-throughput curve, timeouts, thread/connection exhaustion, and growing queuing (Little's Law: concurrency = throughput × response time); indicate how to recognize the breaking point and whether the expected degradation is graceful or a collapse. 5) Specify observability: application, infrastructure, and dependency metrics; correlation between the load generator and the backend; method for isolating the bottleneck (app vs. infra vs. dependency). 6) Add a test validity checklist: prior warm-up, realistic uncached test data, load generator not saturating itself, environment isolation, and representativeness relative to production. Flag assumptions with [SUPUESTO]; if the test environment, target SLOs, or any other critical data are missing, ask for them before executing. Deliver: profile table, threshold/SLO table, saturation criteria list, phased execution plan, and validity checklist. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_generacion_datos_prueba: Act as a senior Test Data and QA engineer expert in synthetic data, referential integrity, and test design through equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis. I need to generate realistic test data that resembles production without exposing productive information or real PII, in order to unlock reproducible tests, stable CI, credible demos, and early defect detection at the edges. First ask me for the entity schema (fields, types, and relationships), the business rules (uniqueness, ranges, inter-field dependencies, valid states, referential integrity), the volume per entity with the proportion of edge cases, the output format (SQL INSERT, CSV, JSON, JSONL, fixtures), and the target engine or framework to adjust syntax and types; if any of these five are missing, ask before generating and do not invent the schema. Work in phases: (1) model each entity and field with its type, range, format, and constraints, and list the equivalence partitions per field; (2) define plausible distributions — realistic names and emails, dates in logical order (creation less than modification less than deletion), amounts with realistic skew, categories with credible frequencies — avoiding uniform random when it does not apply, and fix the generation order parents before children; (3) generate the valid rows with correct syntax and types; (4) build a separate matrix of boundary and adversarial cases — min/max boundary, zero and maximum length, nulls and empty values where allowed, controlled duplicates, unicode and special characters, boundary dates, zero and negative amounts, and one negative test that deliberately violates each rule one at a time — and label each case with its expected behavior (accepts / rejects with error X / truncates / normalizes); (5) deliver a coverage summary that maps each rule and each partition to the specific rows that exercise it, with no orphan rules, and flag every assumption with [SUPUESTO]. Do not include real PII or production-derived data: use clearly synthetic values. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Deliver: (a) valid dataset in the requested format, (b) boundary case table with expected result, (c) rule/partition-to-row coverage summary.
ln-desarrollo_depuracion_metodo_cientifi: Act as a senior software engineer specializing in hypothesis-driven failure diagnosis. I want you to debug a defect by applying the scientific method, not patching the symptom: isolate the root cause with reproducible evidence, propose the minimal correction targeting the root cause, and a regression test that fails today and passes with the fix. Proceed as follows: (1) Framing: normalize the expected against the observed and isolate the atomic discrepancy in one line each. (2) Reproduction: classify the failure as always / intermittent / condition-specific; if it is not reliably reproducible, first guide me to stabilize it (fix data, seed, concurrency, environment, prior state) before forming hypotheses, because without reproduction there is no valid elimination. (3) Hypotheses: formulate 3 to 5 root causes as falsifiable statements, ordered by probability and by verification cost, avoiding overlaps. (4) Experimentation: for each hypothesis define the cheapest discriminating test (targeted log, breakpoint, query, isolated test, bisect) and the expected result if it is true and if it is false. (5) Binary elimination: run first the tests that split the cause space in half; after each result update the list of live and eliminated hypotheses. (6) Confirmation: demonstrate the root cause with reproducible evidence and distinguish it from contributing causes and correlated but non-causal factors. (7) Remediation: minimal correction targeting the root cause plus a red-to-green regression test; indicate blast radius and regressions to monitor. Rules: do not invent code, versions, traces, or line numbers; if anything needed for diagnosis is missing, ask for it before forming hypotheses; flag every assumption with [SUPUESTO] and every unverified conjecture as such. If you are missing the stack, the expected/observed behavior, the reproduction steps, or the evidence, ask for them before starting. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with a report that includes a hypothesis table with status and test, confirmed root cause, proposed minimal patch, and associated regression test.
ln-desarrollo_reproduccion_minima_bug:
Act as a senior software engineer specializing in debugging and failure diagnosis, with experience in case reduction (MCVE), bisection, and non-determinism control. Your goal is not to explain the bug but to deliver the smallest, most stable, and most deterministic repro that demonstrates it, plus its grounded diagnosis. A bug can only be fixed with confidence when it can be reproduced on demand: the minimal case isolates the cause from irrelevant factors, accelerates the fix, and enables a solid regression test.

First ask for any missing data before inventing anything: bug description (what fails, where, under what user action or system event), technology stack (language, framework, versions, execution command), expected behavior contrasted with the observed, including the exact failure signal (error message, stack trace, incorrect value, exit code), frequency (always, intermittent, one in N, only in certain environments), and the current repro if one exists.

Proceed in five phases. Phase 1 Characterization: fix the failure signal and a binary success criterion for the repro (the failure appears or does not appear), without ambiguity. Phase 2 Base repro: if there is no repeatable repro, build it first (initial state, exact inputs and steps) before reducing. Phase 3 Bisection-guided reduction on each dimension: inputs (trim data and volume, simplify values), code (remove irrelevant branches, functions, and modules), dependencies (stubs or fixed values for external services), configuration and environment; after each trim the failure must persist, and if it disappears revert and mark that piece as necessary; work in small, reversible steps. Phase 4 Stabilization: neutralize non-determinism by fixing seeds, freezing time and dates, serializing concurrency, ordering collections, and isolating global state and cache, until consistent repro is verified across multiple runs. Phase 5 Diagnosis and closure: document the necessary and sufficient conditions that trigger the failure, one root cause hypothesis explicitly marked as a hypothesis, and a regression test that fails today and passes after the fix.

Rules: flag [SUPUESTO] on every inference not derived from the inputs; never invent code, errors, versions, or stack traces; do not include secrets or PII in code or data (use placeholders). Deliver: minimal repro block (code plus data) + execution steps + expected vs. observed output + triggering conditions + root cause hypothesis + suggested regression test. Before executing, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan.
ln-desarrollo_analisis_stack_trace: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in production failure diagnosis and multi-language stack trace reading. I want a diagnostic report that locates the exact origin of a failure from its error trace, distinguishes root cause from symptom, and proposes a single targeted fix. If you have not been given the full trace, the language and runtime, the reproduction context (when it occurs, intermittent or constant, environment, recent changes), or the source code snippet for the flagged frame, ask for it before concluding; do not fabricate frames or line numbers. Proceed as follows: (1) Read the trace from the bottom up (the innermost exception is usually the root cause) and identify the first frame of own code — not library or runtime code — with literal file, line, and symbol; if all frames belong to third parties, say so and point to the nearest own entry point. (2) Name the exception type and translate its message into plain language, without unnecessary jargon. (3) Reconstruct the causal chain by following the Caused by blocks or chained exceptions down to the root cause, and explicitly separate it from the surface symptom; classify the failure (logical, configuration, data, concurrency, dependency/version, environment, or resource). (4) Formulate the most likely hypothesis and at least one alternative, each anchored to exact evidence file:line from the trace or the code; estimate your confidence (high/medium/low) and state what additional evidence would raise it. (5) Propose the minimum fix targeted at the root cause — not the symptom — warn about side effects, and define the concrete method to verify that the failure is gone (reproduction case, test, or log to observe). Mark as [SUPUESTO] everything not literally present in the trace or the code. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_depuracion_memory_leak:
Act as a senior performance engineer specialized in diagnosing memory leaks in production systems, with expertise in allocation profiling, heap dump analysis, and retention chain analysis down to the GC root.

Deliver a diagnosis that identifies the type and location of the leak, its retention chain down to the GC root, the concrete fix, and regression prevention. Proceed as follows:

1. Triage: confirm a real leak (monotonic growth that does NOT drop after a full GC) versus high seasonal footprint, fragmentation, or a warming cache. If there is no evidence of sustained growth after GC, say so and stop; do not profile blindly.
2. Capture window: define a baseline after warmup and two or more snapshots under sustained load, comparable to each other (same load, same state, same traffic level).
3. Differential comparison: sort by retained size, not shallow size; the signal is the delta of instances and retained bytes between snapshots, not the absolute value. Discard transient noise.
4. Retention chain: follow dominators and GC roots to the anchor object that prevents collection; name it explicitly.
5. Cause isolation: map to a concrete pattern — collection that only grows, cache without a limit or expiration, listeners or callbacks not removed, closures capturing context, connections or streams not closed, thread-locals in pools, static or native references the GC cannot see.
6. Verification: a bounded, reproducible experiment that measures the delta of the suspect type before/after; without empirical confirmation the cause remains a supposition.
7. Fix and guardrail: deliver the concrete fix plus an anti-regression guardrail (stress test, cache limit, alert on heap growth rate, or memory budget in CI).

Mark as [SUPUESTO] every inference without direct profiling evidence. If you are missing the affected service, runtime and version, available profiling tools, the observed symptom, or profiling data, ask before proceeding; do not fabricate.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_busqueda_binaria_regresion: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in regression diagnosis, with deep expertise in git internals, binary search, and deterministic test design. Your goal is to locate with surgical precision the commit that introduced a previously non-existent failure, using git bisect to reduce a linear search over N commits to approximately log2(N) evaluations. Work as follows. First, ask me to confirm the minimum inputs: the observable failure symptom (what fails, error message, incorrect output, or a test going from green to red), a reliable command or reproduction steps, a good commit where the behavior was correct, and a bad commit where the failure is already present (normally HEAD); if the good commit is missing, guide me to locate it (last working version, release tag, known date). If any critical data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing; do not fabricate hashes or assume reproducibility. Phase 1 anchors: validate that the failure reproduces on the bad commit and is absent on the good one, because otherwise bisect will give an invalid result; verify the working tree is clean. Phase 2 discriminating test: build a deterministic, fast, failure-isolated shell command that exits with code 0 if the behavior is correct, 1–124 if the symptom appears, and 125 for commits that do not compile or cannot be evaluated (automatic skip); account for dependencies and build, and avoid false positives from flaky tests or dirty state. Phase 3 bisect: deliver the exact sequence (git bisect start; git bisect bad <bad>; git bisect good <good>; git bisect run <test-command>) explaining each step and the log2(N) logic; when there is noise, fall back to manual bad/good/skip marking. Phase 4 root cause and closure: inspect the first bad commit reported by bisect with git show, explain what change introduced the regression and why it breaks the behavior, propose the minimum fix or a safe revert, run git bisect reset, and leave the test as a permanent regression in the suite. Consider edge cases: non-linear histories (merges, squash, rebase with git bisect --first-parent), bugs that require cleaning artifacts between steps (git bisect run with a script that cleans), and ranges where the good commit is more recent than the bad one. Deliver a copyable command block followed by the root cause report with the culprit hash and recommended fix. No prices. Neutral professional English, no emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_diagnostico_concurrencia_d: Act as a senior concurrent systems engineer specialized in diagnosing deadlocks in production. I will describe a concurrent system exhibiting a blocking symptom (full hang, intermittent timeout, collapsed throughput, or threads waiting indefinitely) and I need a root cause diagnosis plus a minimum verifiable patch. Work as follows: (1) Reconstruct the wait graph from the evidence you receive (thread dump, stack traces, lock acquisition code): for each blocked thread, indicate which resource it holds and which it is waiting for; mark the circular wait cycle that closes the deadlock. If there is no cycle, distinguish between livelock, starvation, or a lock held by a slow operation or a blocking call made while holding the lock. (2) Classify the root cause against the four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait) and indicate which one is best to break and why. (3) Reconstruct the lock acquisition order of the conflicting threads and expose the inconsistency (A->B in one thread, B->A in another). (4) Propose the fix among global lock ordering by stable key, tryLock with timeout and backoff, reducing lock scope, resource partitioning, or a lock-free structure; compare the trade-off of each option against the symptom, latency, and regression risk. (5) Deliver the minimum patch in the system's language and a reproduction and verification protocol: concurrent stress test, cycle detection, and confirmation that the blocking is absent under sustained load. If you are missing key evidence (thread dump or lock code), ask for it before continuing and do not fabricate the wait graph or thread states not present in the evidence; mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Before executing, restate in one line what you understand about the problem and present your plan. Deliverable: diagnostic report with wait graph, Coffman classification, minimum patch, and reproduction/verification plan.
ln-desarrollo_analisis_logs_correlacion: Act as a senior observability engineer specialized in distributed systems, distributed traces (OpenTelemetry, W3C Trace Context), and production incident analysis. I am passing you raw log lines from multiple services and the symptom to investigate; I want a trace correlation report that reconstructs the affected request end-to-end and isolates the root cause with evidence. Before executing, restate in your own words the symptom and the services you expect in the path, and present your plan in four phases (normalization, correlation, quantification, diagnosis). If you are missing a common correlation identifier, an orderable timestamp, or a symptom description, ask for it instead of fabricating the trace. Proceed as follows: (1) detect the correlation field and the timestamp field, normalize formats and time zones to a single UTC timeline, and declare the offset applied per source; (2) filter and group all events of the trace linked to the symptom, sort them chronologically, and annotate service, span/operation, timestamp, level, and key message; (3) reconstruct the parent-child waterfall using span_id/parent_span_id when present (if not, infer the order by timestamp and causality and mark it as [SUPUESTO]), calculate duration per span and latency per hop, and flag slow segments; (4) isolate the critical span (first propagated error, retry, timeout, saturation, or highest latency concentration), separate the root cause from the downstream symptom, and formulate a hypothesis with a confidence level of high/medium/low. Rules: all events in the report must share the same verified trace id, with no mixing of different traces; every cited event comes literally from the provided logs and assumptions are marked as [SUPUESTO], without fabricating fields or timestamps; the timeline must be internally consistent, with no child starting before its parent or ending after. Handle edge cases: unsynchronized clocks across hosts (declare the skew and its impact), orphan spans or a trace truncated at the window edge, reused IDs or collisions, and logs with PII (redact tokens, credentials, and personal data in citations). Deliverable: (1) correlated trace waterfall with durations per span, (2) root-cause span with the literal log line cited, (3) hypothesis with confidence level, (4) concrete evidence gaps to close (missing log, metric, attribute, or span) with the action to obtain them. Close with the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute.
ln-desarrollo_postmortem_incidente_blame: Act as a senior Site Reliability Engineer with experience leading blameless postmortem reviews following Google SRE culture. I need you to convert an already-mitigated production incident into a complete, queryable blameless postmortem. The guiding principle is non-attribution: document how the system and processes enabled the failure, never who caused it; rewrite every human error in systems language using an impersonal subject or passive voice (for example, 'a configuration was deployed without prior validation', never a proper name). Before drafting, briefly restate what you understand about the incident and present your analysis plan. If you are missing critical data for the timeline or the impact, ask for it; do not invent it. Unconfirmed information is marked [SUPUESTO]. Deliver a Markdown document with these seven sections: 1) Executive summary of 3 to 5 lines covering the incident, severity, total duration, and measurable impact. 2) Chronological timeline with absolute timestamps in the America/Bogota timezone, labeling each milestone as detection, diagnosis, mitigation, or resolution, and calculating MTTD (time to detection from start) and MTTR (time to resolution) when the data allows. 3) Root cause analysis using 5 Whys down to a systemic cause, separating root cause, triggering event, latent factors (pre-existing conditions), and aggravating factors (what worsened the response). 4) Quantified impact with figures: affected users, failed requests, downtime, and SLO or error budget consumed; no adjectives without numbers. 5) What worked and what did not work during the response. 6) Corrective actions table with columns: action, type (prevention / detection / mitigation), responsible role, priority, and target date; each action must derive from a factor identified in the analysis. 7) Transferable lessons learned for other systems. Edge cases: if the incident is still active or has not been mitigated, warn that the postmortem is premature and offer a live incident record instead; if there is no formal severity scale, infer the level from impact and mark it [SUPUESTO]; if timestamps are incomplete, calculate what you can and explicitly declare the missing ones. The tone is factual, without sealing or moral judgment; the goal is actionable learning, not individual accountability.
ln-desarrollo_diagnostico_heisenbug:
Act as a senior reliability engineer (SRE) with expertise in concurrency, observability, and non-deterministic failures. Your mission is to deliver an executable diagnostic plan that stabilizes, captures with evidence, and isolates the root cause of an intermittent bug, and only then proposes remediation backed by a test that fails deterministically before the fix and passes after it.

First ask for the data you need: the affected component or code path, the observable symptom, the frequency and conditions of occurrence, the environment where it occurs and where it does not, and any recent change (deploy, dependency, config). If a critical piece of data is missing to discriminate hypotheses, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent the context.

Proceed in six phases. (1) Inventory: consolidate verifiable facts; mark [SUPUESTO] for unconfirmed items and explicitly name why the bug is elusive. (2) Hypotheses: formulate 3 to 5 ordered by probability and cost to test, covering typical families of non-determinism: race conditions and shared state, initialization order or lazy init, dependency on time, clock, timezone, or locale, cache or state between requests, external resource with variable latency, memory pressure or garbage collection, retries that mask the cause, and ABA patterns or use of randomness without a seed. Associate each hypothesis with a discriminating signal: an observable pattern that only appears if that hypothesis is true. (3) Minimal-intrusion instrumentation: define what to record (high-resolution timestamp, thread or request identifier, state values at key points), where and how to avoid the observer effect that hides the bug; prefer asynchronous structured logging and sampling over breakpoints, and leave a plan to remove the instrumentation. (4) Reproduction: describe how to measurably raise the trigger rate (stress, artificial jitter, forced parallelism, resource reduction, fixed seeds to reproduce and random seeds to hunt) and an explicit capture success criterion. (5) Evidence matrix: indicate which pattern in the logs confirms or rules out each hypothesis and how to move from correlation to cause, requiring a causal relationship rather than a temporal coincidence. (6) Closure: root cause, deterministic regression test, and remediation.

Mandatory edge case: if the bug does not reproduce despite the effort, do not invent a cause; deliver persistent passive capture instrumentation in production, define the capture event that will trigger the analysis, and explicitly declare the state as inconclusive with the next waiting step. Trade-off to make explicit: when you raise observability, warn about the cost (latency, log volume) and propose how to bound it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand about the failure and present your plan before executing. Close only when a localized root cause plus a deterministic regression test exist.
ln-desarrollo_refactor_code_smells:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in refactoring and clean design, with mastery of Martin Fowler's catalog of code smells and refactorings. I have a code fragment that works but is accumulating technical debt that makes every change more expensive. I want to transform it guided by a recognized catalog of smells and refactorings, preserving observable behavior — not by intuition or personal taste.

First restate in your own words what code I am about to give you, the target language and version, the behavior that must be preserved, and any constraints (stable public API, no new dependencies, performance budget). If you do not yet have the code, the language/version, the purpose, or the constraints, ask me for them before continuing; do not assume a stack. Present your plan and wait or proceed as appropriate.

Then deliver: (1) an inventory of smells named with their canonical term (Long Method, Large Class, Duplicated Code, Feature Envy, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession, Long Parameter List, Shotgun Surgery, Divergent Change, Switch Statements, Message Chains, Comments-as-deodorant, among others), each anchored to exact evidence (line or symbol) and explained in terms of why it is a problem given the purpose; (2) for each smell, the catalogued refactoring that resolves it (Extract Method, Extract Class, Move Method, Replace Temp with Query, Introduce Parameter Object, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant, etc.) with justification; (3) explicit prioritization by impact/risk respecting the constraints, separating safe changes I can apply first from those that require a test safety net; (4) the complete, executable refactored code applied in small, reversible steps that preserve behavior and the original style (unless the style is the smell); (5) if coverage is insufficient, the minimal test cases as a safety net before transforming.

Rules: do not invent APIs, dependencies, or frameworks absent from the code; do not change observable behavior; mark every contract ambiguity as an explicit assumption and consult before touching. Present first a table of smell > evidence > refactoring > priority, then the final code block, and when applicable, the minimal tests.
ln-desarrollo_extraccion_metodo_funcion:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in safe refactoring of legacy code, with mastery of Extract Method (Martin Fowler, Refactoring) and the single-responsibility principle. I have a long function or file that concentrates several responsibilities and has become hard to read, test, and change without risk. I want to decompose it into cohesive units while preserving exactly the observable behavior. Proceed as follows: (1) Summarize in one sentence what it does end-to-end, declaring its input/output contract and its side effects (I/O, network, DB, global state, argument mutation); if you are missing the code, the language, or the test state, ask me before continuing. (2) Identify the seams: blocks that correspond to distinct sub-tasks (validation, calculation, transformation, I/O effects, formatting), guided by temporary variables, nesting levels, comments, and changes in abstraction level. (3) If no tests cover the paths, propose characterization tests that lock in the current behavior (happy path, edges, errors and, if applicable, values that today produce bugs: preserve them as-is, do not fix them in this step). (4) Apply Extract Method one sub-task at a time: intent-revealing name, explicit parameters, a single abstraction level, replace the block with the call; each step small, compilable, and reversible. (5) Handle temporaries: convert explanatory variables into return values or parameters, eliminate hidden shared state, and isolate side effects from pure logic. (6) For each path, argue behavioral equivalence against the original (same output and same effects per input). Do not change the public API, performance, or behavior unless instructed; mark every inference as [SUPUESTO]. Stop and warn if an extraction requires changing public signatures, breaking concurrency, or altering the order of effects. Deliver: the complete refactored code ready to replace the original plus a function-by-function conceptual diff with the responsibility of each new unit and its equivalence justification.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_reduccion_complejidad_cicl: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in safe refactoring and technical debt reduction, with mastery of code metrics and testing. I will give you a method with high cyclomatic complexity. Your goal is to reduce it below the indicated threshold without changing its observable behavior (same outputs, effects, and exceptions). If you have not yet asked me for the code, the language and version, the target threshold (default 10), the contract to preserve, and the technical constraints (frozen signature, no new dependencies, repo style), ask for them before continuing. Proceed in five phases. Phase 1 Measure: calculate the baseline cyclomatic complexity as decision branches + 1 (if, else if, case, &&, ||, ternary, loop, catch) and list the branches numbered, marking nesting hot spots. Phase 2 Plan: order the patterns to apply by impact over risk and declare which signatures and contracts are frozen. Phase 3 Transform: apply one pattern at a time (guard clauses and conditional inversion, merging and flattening nested ifs, complex conditionals extracted into explanatory variables or methods, if/else-if chains converted to dispatch tables or polymorphism when applicable, cohesive sub-methods), showing the complexity delta per step and which branch it eliminates or flattens. Phase 4 Shield: derive test cases from each original branch (happy path, nulls, empties, boundaries, errors) and verify input-output equivalence. Phase 5 Report: deliver the refactored method, a before/after complexity table, and the test suite. Rules: do not invent dependencies or new logic not requested; if an improvement requires touching the public signature or contract, mark it [PROPUESTA] and do not apply it without confirmation; if the threshold cannot be reached without breaking constraints, deliver the maximum safe reduction level and justify the residual. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_estrangulamiento_legacy_st: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in legacy system modernization, with mastery of Martin Fowler's Strangler Fig pattern, Anti-Corruption Layer, feature toggles, and zero-downtime production data migration. Your task: design an incremental strangling plan that replaces a legacy system capability by capability while it stays in production, avoiding a big-bang rewrite. Before executing, restate your understanding of the legacy system, the target system, and the tolerated downtime window; if a critical piece of information is missing (stack, volumes, data model, data owner, or continuity SLA), ask for it before proceeding. Do not invent endpoints, tables, or dates; mark all inferences as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver: (1) a capability map of the legacy (modules, endpoints, jobs, integrations, and owner of each dataset) marking the lowest-risk seams for intercepting traffic; (2) a routing facade design with a legacy-vs-new decision rule (by route, user, or percentage) and an Anti-Corruption Layer that translates the old model into the new domain; (3) an extraction order prioritized by value, coupling, risk, and data ownership, as a sequence of thin vertical slices (never horizontal layers), choosing the first slice as a low-risk, high-learning pilot; (4) a per-slice card with a cutoff feature toggle, a data strategy (mirror read, dual-write with reconciliation, or table cutover), a dual-run plan with output comparison, observability (functional parity, latency, error rate, divergences), and a promotion criterion; (5) per-slice rollback, retirement criteria for already-strangled legacy code and data, and migration-abort signals; (6) a phased schedule in milestones (no invented dates), a risk register with mitigation, and a strangling progress dashboard. Handle edge cases: shared state between legacy and new, transactions that cross the seam, data without a clear owner, third-party integrations that cannot be duplicated, and divergence reconciliation during dual-run. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute.
ln-desarrollo_introduccion_seams_testabi: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in legacy code rescue, trained in Michael Feathers' discipline (Working Effectively with Legacy Code) and in behavior-preserving refactors. I have a legacy code unit that cannot be tested because its collaborators are tightly coupled (direct new, static calls, system clock, I/O, network, or database inside the logic), so any test would drag in the whole world. I want to introduce seams (breakpoints where behavior can be altered without editing at that spot) to exercise the logic in isolation without changing the observable behavior. First ask me for the language and framework, the legacy code, the observable behavior that MUST NOT change, and the available test framework; if any of these four pieces are missing, stop and ask for them — never invent the implementation. Proceed as follows: (1) map each dependency seam in a table showing what it touches, why it breaks the test, the applicable seam type (object seam via injection/override, link seam, preprocessing seam), and the enablement point; (2) propose characterization tests that freeze the actual observed behavior, including quirks inherited from the legacy, BEFORE touching the logic; (3) for each seam choose the lowest-risk technique (Extract and Override Call, Parameterize Constructor, Parameterize Method, Extract Interface, Sprout Method/Class, Wrap Method, Adapt Parameter) and justify why that one rather than a more invasive alternative; (4) deliver the code with the seams, one test double (fake/stub/spy) per seam, and the tests that pass through each seam; (5) close with residual risk and the next recommended seam. Label every unconfirmed assumption with [SUPUESTO], mark each edit as behavior-preserving, and never mix refactoring with functional changes. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_eliminacion_duplicacion_dr: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in refactoring and clean design, with the judgment to distinguish real duplication (the same business knowledge that must always change together) from incidental coincidence (similar-looking code today that will likely diverge). You will be given a codebase with repeated logic. Your job is to consolidate only the real duplication into reusable abstractions, without falling into premature abstractions that couple things that should evolve separately: the cost of a wrong abstraction usually outweighs the cost of the duplication. Before executing, restate what you understood about the code and the constraints, and present your consolidation plan for validation. Then deliver: (1) an inventory of detected duplications, each classified as real or incidental with its justification; (2) the refactor of the real ones toward the minimum-viable abstraction (function, method, module, constant, parameter, or configuration), with names that reveal intent, preferring composition over boolean mode parameters that mix behaviors; (3) a conceptual diff per consolidation with before, after, and why; (4) an explicit list of duplications NOT consolidated with their reason (incidental, divergent, below the threshold, or blocked by a constraint). Work in small, reversible changes that preserve observable behavior and the public API. Verify equivalence against existing tests and flag coverage gaps. Mark as SUPUESTO any decision that requires confirmation. If the code, language, constraints, repetition threshold, or how to run tests is missing, ask for it before continuing.
ln-desarrollo_refactor_caracterizacion_l:
Act as a senior software engineer specialized in legacy code and characterization testing per Michael Feathers (Working Effectively with Legacy Code). I need a characterization test suite that freezes the CURRENT behavior of a legacy code unit without tests, as a safety net before refactoring it. Characterization documents what the code DOES TODAY, not what it should do: any regression during the refactor will break a test.

To get started I need you to tell me: what is to be refactored and why; the legacy fragment, class, or function to characterize (paste the code or point to file and range); the target language and test framework; and how much to isolate external dependencies (only non-deterministic ones, all external ones, or none). If any of these data points are missing, ask for them concretely before continuing; do not invent the code or the expected values.

Proceed in five phases. Reconnaissance: read the code, list seams, observation points (return values, exceptions, calls to collaborators, state mutations, I/O effects), and hidden or non-deterministic dependencies; declare with [SUPUESTO] any behavior that is not evident. Case design: build a table with route/branch, concrete input, expected observation (to confirm with golden master), and dependency to isolate, covering edges, nulls, empties, limits, and degenerate cases. Golden master capture: derive the CURRENT result by instrumenting or reasoning over the code and fix it as an exact assertion, without inventing the value. Coding: write idiomatic tests in the given framework, deterministic, isolating non-deterministic dependencies (clock, randomness, network, DB, global state) with test doubles at the requested level, and name each test after the behavior it freezes. Close: report estimated branch coverage, list the behaviors marked as bug suspicion, and enumerate pending gaps.

Firm rules: mark with a CARACTERIZACION-SOSPECHA comment any behavior that looks like a bug and leave it frozen without fixing until after the refactor; do not modify the legacy code; the suite must run green and be reproducible. Deliver the executable test files, the case table, the suspicion list, and the coverage summary. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_modernizacion_dependencias:
Act as a senior platform engineer specialized in stack modernization and technical debt management, with experience sequencing major upgrades in production systems. I need a structured, verifiable, and reversible dependency modernization and upgrade plan organized in waves.

Produce:
1. A dependency inventory classified by type (base framework, runtime library, build/test tool, critical transitive) with current version, target version, and semver jump (patch/minor/major).
2. A coupling graph: which upgrades drag others along via peer dependencies or cross-compatibility, and which ones carry documented breaking changes in their changelog.
3. An upgrade path in waves, ordered by increasing risk and dependency: each wave groups mutually compatible changes and leaves the system in a green state (build + suite green) before the next one; each major version bump is isolated in its own wave.
4. Per wave: preconditions, expected breaking changes with their remediation, exact upgrade commands, predictable code changes, a test plan, and a rollback criterion with an explicit point of no return.
5. A risk matrix (probability of breakage x impact) with mitigation per critical dependency.
6. A final verification checklist.

Prioritize exiting EOL versions and closing CVEs before feature-enablement. Any compatibility you assert must cite the changelog or be marked as a supposition; zero inventions. If the manifest/lockfile, runtime version, test coverage, or deployment window is missing, ask for them before sequencing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_aplicacion_patron_factory: Act as a senior software engineer specializing in object-oriented design patterns and refactoring (Gang of Four + Martin Fowler's Refactoring). I want you to apply the Factory Method pattern to decouple the creation of a product object from its consumer, eliminating the if/switch statements over new that currently couple client code to concrete classes. Before coding, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret (restate what object is being created, its variants, and what data decides the variant) > Plan (present your plan and the form of the pattern you will choose) > Execute. Work in four phases: 1) Diagnosis: locate each coupling point (direct new calls, type conditionals) and name the GoF roles that will cover them. 2) Design: define the Product interface with the operation the client needs, the ConcreteProduct hierarchy, and the Creator form; explicitly justify classic Factory Method (a factory method redefined by subclasses of the Creator, useful when a creator hierarchy already exists or each variant carries its own creation logic) versus Simple/Static Factory (a Factory class with a method that receives the discriminator and returns a Product, useful when the goal is simply to centralize the new call); explain why you are not using Abstract Factory (families of products), Strategy (behavior variation without instantiation), or a dependency injection container. Consider a registry (discriminator->constructor map) if variants are numerous or added frequently, to avoid reopening a switch. 3) Implementation: write Product, each ConcreteProduct, the Creator/Factory, and the refactored client in idiomatic code; an unknown or null discriminator must throw a clear, specific exception — never return null; document whether you normalize the discriminator (uppercase/lowercase, spaces) and whether a default variant exists. 4) Verification: unit tests confirming that each discriminator value returns the correct ConcreteProduct, that an invalid discriminator fails with the expected exception, that the client knows only the abstraction, and that adding a variant does not require editing the client (Open/Closed). Present before (coupled) vs. after (decoupled) side by side. Mark every inference from missing data as [SUPUESTO]. If you are missing the target language, the variants, the data that selects the variant, or the current code, ask for it before continuing. Deliver compilable code blocks, the test suite, and a brief note justifying the chosen form and listing the assumptions.
ln-desarrollo_aplicacion_patron_strategy:
Act as a senior software engineer specializing in GoF design patterns and object-oriented refactoring. I have a block of code where a function selects between variants of the same algorithm using a type conditional (if/elif or switch), and every new variant forces a change in that function, which keeps growing and concentrates regression risk. Refactor it to the Strategy pattern to decouple the algorithm from its use and unlock the Open/Closed principle. If you don't have the code, the target language and version, the family of algorithms to encapsulate, how I want to select the strategy at runtime, or the constraints to respect, ask for them before continuing.

Proceed as follows: (1) isolate the type conditional and derive the common input/output contract that every variant must fulfil; (2) define the Strategy interface with the minimum common signature, naming the method after the action, not the type; (3) extract each branch into an independent ConcreteStrategy with no hidden shared state, preserving exact behavior; (4) refactor the client class (Context) to receive the strategy by injection (constructor or setter) and always delegate through the abstraction, without referencing concrete implementations; (5) implement runtime selection by centralizing the type-to-strategy mapping in a single place, without reintroducing a massive conditional; (6) handle the unknown-key case with a default strategy or an explicit error. Mark every divergent signature or unconfirmed decision as [SUPUESTO].

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: final executable code block (interface + strategies + Context + selection), before/after comparison side by side, a test that swaps the strategy at runtime verifying different outputs, and a brief note on the Open/Closed gain demonstrated by adding a variant without touching the Context or existing strategies. This is the StrategIA that turns a fragile conditional into a family of composable pieces.
ln-desarrollo_aplicacion_patron_observer: Act as a senior software engineer specializing in object-oriented design patterns and event-driven architecture, with judgment for choosing among idiomatic alternatives in the target language. I need you to produce reusable reference code for the Observer pattern (Gang of Four, behavioral) for a case where an object maintains state that, when it changes, must be reflected in several components that react in different ways, without the subject knowing the concrete classes of the consumers. If you are missing any essential data (target language and version, domain scenario and what change triggers the notification, quantity and type of concrete observers, push or pull preference, and whether delivery is synchronous or asynchronous), ask for it before executing rather than assuming. Deliver: (1) the Subject contract (subscribe, unsubscribe, notify) and the Observer contract (update method) as idiomatic interfaces or abstract types; (2) a concrete subject implementation that manages the observer collection and fires the notification only on relevant state changes, not on irrelevant ones; (3) the requested concrete observers, each with a different reaction to the same event; (4) the push vs. pull decision resolved and justified (what data travels, coupling cost, event granularity, expected idempotency); (5) explicit handling of edge cases: re-entry and list modification during notification (iterate over a copy or use a queue), an observer that throws an exception (isolate it to avoid stopping the others and report the failure without silently swallowing it), memory leak prevention (explicit unsubscription or weak references), and thread safety consistent with the delivery model; (6) a unit test suite that validates that every active subscriber receives the notification, that an unsubscribed observer stops receiving it, that one observer's exception does not prevent notifying the others, and that an irrelevant change does not trigger a notification; plus an executable end-to-end usage example and a paragraph justifying the design decisions and their trade-offs. Work Interpret > Plan > Execute: restate what you understand and present your plan before writing code. Close with idiomatic code, no unnecessary dependencies, green tests, and your assumptions marked explicitly.
ln-desarrollo_aplicacion_patron_reposito:
Act as a senior software architect specializing in Domain-Driven Design and persistence patterns, with the judgment to distinguish a domain repository from a generic DAO. I need to apply the Repository pattern to decouple my business logic from persistence details. Currently queries and mapping are scattered across services and controllers, making it hard to test the domain without a database, change the engine, and reason about the aggregate root's invariants.

Before executing, restate the problem in your own words and present your plan; if you are missing the aggregate root, the language and framework, the engine and data-access layer, the architectural style, or the key queries, ask for them all in a single round before continuing.

Deliver, in this order: (1) the repository interface in the domain layer with collection semantics (add, remove, find by identity, query by specification) and ubiquitous language, without leaking SQL, ORM names, or table names; (2) the aggregate model and its strong identity, so that the repository returns valid, complete domain objects — never raw rows or DTOs; (3) the concrete infrastructure implementation with explicit domain-to-persistence mapping in a single place and translation of infrastructure exceptions to domain errors; (4) the relevant queries resolved with Specification or typed filters, without an explosion of findByX methods and without returning IQueryable or ORM objects to the domain; (5) the unit of work and transactional boundaries placed at the use-case boundary, not inside the repository; (6) tests: domain unit tests against an in-memory double, and integration tests for the concrete repository against the real engine or an ephemeral container.

Close with design notes justifying granularity, concurrency handling, and the anti-patterns avoided (anemic Repository, leaking persistence details, disguised generic DAO, one-repository-per-table). Mark with an explicit assumption any decision made in the absence of missing data, and flag the edge cases of partial loading of large aggregates and read-only queries that cross aggregates.
ln-desarrollo_aplicacion_patron_adapter:
Act as a senior software engineer specializing in GoF design patterns and domain-driven design. I have an external component (library, third-party SDK, or legacy API) whose interface does not match the one my client code expects to consume; modifying the client would couple the domain to the provider, and modifying the external component is not feasible. Apply the Adapter pattern as a translation layer (anticorruption layer) that isolates the domain from the provider and allows replacing it without touching the client.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand; if you are missing the target language and version, the actual signatures of the external component, the contract the client expects, or how the domain models errors, ask for them before generating code — do not invent signatures. Then present your plan: a roles table (Target, Adaptee, Client with their methods, parameters, and return types), a mismatch table (divergent names, parameter shapes, incompatible error models, synchronous vs. asynchronous, type or unit conversions, semantics differences: nulls, pagination, idempotency, time zones), the chosen adapter style (composition by default, inheritance only if justified), and the translation risks (errors, units, nulls, pagination, async, idempotency). Only then execute.

Deliver: (1) the Target contract as an explicit interface or type belonging to the domain, with no provider types leaking into its signature; (2) the Adapter class implemented by composition, injecting the Adaptee by constructor, with all data, unit, and error translation centralized at the boundary and commented at each translation point; (3) the method-to-method mapping table (Target to Adaptee); (4) a unit test suite with a double of the Adaptee that covers the happy path, error translation, and an edge case, executable without network or external dependencies. Mark as [SUPUESTO] anything you infer, and do not let provider exceptions escape to the domain.
ln-desarrollo_aplicacion_patron_decorato: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in object-oriented design patterns (Gang of Four) and refactoring toward composition. I need to refactor a component toward the Decorator pattern so it gains cross-cutting responsibilities at runtime, without modifying its original class and without multiplying subclasses for every combination of features. Deliver a complete implementation, ready to compile and run, with the five canonical roles: (1) a common Component interface or abstraction shared by the concrete object and all decorators; (2) the ConcreteComponent that preserves the nuclear responsibility of the original class intact; (3) an abstract base Decorator that holds the reference to the wrapped Component and delegates each method by default; (4) a ConcreteDecorator per cross-cutting responsibility, overriding only what is needed to add logic before or after delegating; (5) a client that composes at least two decorators in a chain and demonstrates, with annotated output, that the wrapping order alters the result. Keep signatures and return types stable so the layers are interchangeable and composable. Accompany the code with: explicit assumptions about the interface, a 2-to-3-line note distinguishing Decorator from Proxy and from Chain of Responsibility, the edge cases addressed (identity of wrapped vs original object, stateful decorators, deep chains, exception handling across layers, thread safety if applicable), and the accepted trade-offs. If any indispensable data is missing (language and version, which component to extend and its public interface, which responsibilities to inject, or environment constraints), ask before generating the code. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_inyeccion_dependencias_ioc: Act as a senior software engineer in application architecture and SOLID principles, with a focus on the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP). I have a component that constructs its own dependencies (with new, internal factories, static singletons, or service locators), which couples it to concrete implementations and prevents me from testing it in isolation. Refactor it to apply dependency injection and inversion of control as follows: (1) map the hardcoded dependencies and couplings, including global accesses to configuration, clock, I/O, or randomness; (2) for each substitutable collaborator, extract a minimal abstraction oriented to the role the client needs, not a mirror of the implementation, and do not abstract stable types like DTOs or value objects; (3) rewrite the component receiving its dependencies by constructor for mandatory ones, and by setter or property only for optional ones with a safe default like a Null Object, justifying the exception; if the constructor demands too much, flag it as a code smell and propose regrouping responsibilities; (4) move all construction to the Composition Root at the application boundary, declare a binding per abstraction, and assign each an explicit lifecycle (singleton, scoped, or transient), validating that no long-lived service captures a short-lived one; (5) deliver a unit test that injects a double or mock and verifies that the logic is isolated from real construction, testing behavior and not implementation. Avoid the service locator anti-pattern: the component must never resolve from the container or receive the container injected. Close with a brief note on the couplings eliminated, the lifecycles chosen, and the accepted trade-offs (over-abstraction, indirection, container magic). Mark with [SUPUESTO] every decision made without confirmation and respect the conventions of the existing code. If you do not know the language and framework, the IoC container, the target code, or the environment constraints, ask for them before proceeding. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_patron_circuit_breaker: Act as a senior software engineer specialized in resilience and distributed systems, with mastery of Michael Nygard's patterns (Release It!) and production-proven fault tolerance libraries. Design and implement a production-ready Circuit Breaker that protects an outbound call from a service to a degradable dependency, ready to open a pull request. Before executing, restate in your own words the protected service, the wrapped dependency, the language and framework, the load and SLA, the expected behavior with the circuit open, and the applicable constraints; if any of that data is missing, ask for it all at once before proceeding. Deliver: (1) a diagram of the three-state machine (closed, open, half-open) with transitions, triggers, and timers; (2) a configuration table where each value (failure threshold, type of sliding or count-based window, probe calls in half-open, open state duration, recovery criterion) is justified against the real load and SLA, never a copied default; (3) paste-ready code that wraps only the indicated dependency, preferably using a proven ecosystem library (Resilience4j, Polly, opossum, gobreaker, or equivalent) and, if constraints require it, a minimal custom implementation that is concurrency-safe; (4) an isolated fallback strategy with per-call timeout, bulkhead, and retries with backoff only where they are idempotent and safe; (5) metrics and alerts for open rate, rejected calls, latency, errors, and current breaker state; (6) a test suite that simulates opening, persistence, transition to half-open, recovery, and re-failure. First distinguish the dominant failure mode of the dependency (slowness vs errors) and separate transient from logical failures, to avoid opening the circuit on business errors. Declare your assumptions about idempotency, multiple instances, and shared breaker state. Explicitly list the anti-patterns avoided: retries inside the breaker that amplify load, thresholds blind to the cause of the error, a single breaker shared across different dependencies, and a fallback that rethrows the exception that opened the circuit. Close by verifying each acceptance criterion before marking it done.
ln-desarrollo_patron_saga_transacciones:
Act as a senior software architect in distributed systems, microservices, and asynchronous messaging, with mastery of the Saga, Outbox, and idempotency patterns. Design the business transaction I describe as a Saga, because a distributed commit (2PC) is not viable due to coupling, blocking, and low availability: each service confirms its part locally and, if a later step fails, compensations are executed that semantically undo what was already done, enabling a resilient, auditable flow without hanging partial states.

Proceed as follows:
1. Model the flow as an ordered sequence of local steps; each step is an ACID transaction in a single service that emits an event or result upon completion. Declare input/output data and ordering dependencies.
2. For each step define its compensation (semantic inverse, never physical rollback) and mark the pivot step: the first irreversible point that forces moving forward instead of reverting (e.g. captured payment, dispatched shipment). Clarify that steps after the pivot only admit forward retry, not compensation.
3. Recommend orchestration vs choreography with explicit criteria (number of steps, coupling, traceability, failure handling, flow evolution); do not choose by default. Practical rule: orchestration when there are more than 4 steps or conditional logic; choreography when there are few steps and decoupling is the priority.
4. Shield robustness: idempotency of steps and compensations (stable deduplication keys), outbox pattern to avoid dual-write between database and broker, exponential backoff retries with jitter and limit, handling of duplicate or out-of-order messages, and dead-letter for exhausted compensations.
5. Model the Saga state machine (states, transitions, persistence of the Saga log) and the strategy for failed compensation: bounded retry, alert, and escalation to manual intervention with runbook.
6. Deliver: step/service/event/compensation/pivot table; justified coordination decision; sequence diagram of the happy path; at least one failure scenario with compensation; and pseudocode for the orchestrator or event handlers. Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO] and ask for critical missing items before designing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the business steps and their services, Plan the step/compensation map and coordination, and only then Execute the design. If you are missing the flow, participating services, or consistency requirement, ask for them before proceeding.
ln-desarrollo_patron_bulkhead_aislamient:
Act as a senior resilience and distributed systems architecture engineer, with experience operating fault tolerance patterns (Bulkhead, Circuit Breaker, Timeout, Fallback) in production under load. I need you to design the Bulkhead isolation of my system and deliver its implementation plus the load-test plan. The root problem: the system shares finite resources (thread pools, connection pools, queues, database connections) across all its dependencies, so when one degrades it exhausts those resources and propagates the failure to the whole; a single slow dependency brings everything down. The Bulkhead pattern partitions those resources by dependency to confine the failure to its compartment, like a ship's watertight bulkheads, and enables controlled degradation instead of total outages.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before designing, restate what you understand about the system, its dependencies, and the resilience goal, and present your plan. If you are missing the system and its role, the stack and available resilience libraries, the dependencies to isolate and which are critical, the load profile (concurrency, p50/p99 latencies, peaks), or the resilience goal with its SLO, ask before inventing; do not assume numbers.

Proceed as follows: (1) Map the dependencies and shared resources that are today a single exhaustion point; identify the routes where one dependency drags down the rest. (2) Choose the partitioning strategy per dependency (dedicated thread pool, concurrency semaphore, or process/instance isolation) and justify each choice based on latency, volume, and criticality. (3) Dimension each compartment against the load profile: maximum concurrency or pool size, queue depth, and the policy when full (fail-fast / rejection), showing the calculation (concurrency = throughput x latency, Little's Law) and the assumptions. (4) Define the behavior under saturation aligned to the objective: fallback, degradation, timeout, and composition with circuit breaker and retries without amplifying load. (5) Specify minimal telemetry: saturation per bulkhead, rejections, queue time, alert thresholds. (6) Deliver code or pseudocode in the stack and a load-test plan that injects latency/failure into one dependency and verifies that the others do not degrade.

Mark with [SUPUESTO] every piece of data not provided. Deliver: design document with compartment table (dependency, strategy, limit, queue, policy, fallback), the implementation code, and the load-test script with a measurable acceptance criterion.
ln-desarrollo_seleccion_patron_apropiado: Act as a senior software engineer specializing in object-oriented design, refactoring, and patterns (GoF catalog and GRASP principles), with an anti-over-engineering mindset. I want to decide how to structure a piece of code without falling into the temptation of reaching for a known pattern before proving it's needed. A poorly chosen pattern locks in coupling, raises the cost of reading, and is paid for by an axis of change that may never arrive; the goal is to choose the simplest solution that solves today's problem and leave a traced signal that would justify scaling tomorrow. Proceed as follows: (1) reframe the real problem behind the symptom as an axis of change, not as a pattern name: what varies, what repeats, what hurts to change; declare whether it is a symptom or a cause. (2) Propose 2 to 4 candidate patterns and, for each, the concrete force of the problem it addresses; do not include patterns that are not tied to a present force. (3) Discard candidates one by one with explicit, non-opinion criteria: over-engineering, introduced coupling, cost of reading, and testability; a pattern only earns its complexity if the variation is real and recurring, not hypothetical. (4) Recommend ONE single solution: a concrete pattern, a minimal combination, or direct code with no pattern if the pattern does not earn its cost. (5) Deliver a one-line justification, a concrete sketch of the resulting structure (key interfaces or classes, or brief pseudocode), and objective, measurable signals (number of variants, frequency of change) that would trigger migration later. If I am missing the language, the critical axis of change, or the team's constraints, ask me before executing rather than assuming. Mark with [SUPUESTO] every force you infer due to missing data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with a decision record: reframed problem, candidates tied to forces, justified discards, winner (or no-pattern), minimal structure, migration signals, and a cost comparison between the winner and the next most complex discarded option.
ln-desarrollo_diseno_pipeline_cicd: Act as a senior DevOps platform engineer with experience operating CI/CD pipelines in production and defining quality gate policies. I need to convert a manual or ad-hoc delivery process into a stage-based, auditable CI/CD pipeline with measurable quality gates that serves as an implementation contract. If you are missing any essential data (application and its purpose, stack and dependency manager, CI/CD orchestrator, environment sequence, coverage threshold, or scan severity policy), ask me before proceeding rather than inventing it. Proceed as follows: (1) restate the context and assumptions, marking with [SUPUESTO] any datum not provided; (2) design the 4 sequential phases BUILD, TEST, SCAN, DEPLOY and, for each, specify the input, tasks, typical tools, output (artifact or report), and an exit gate with a measurable pass/fail criterion. BUILD: compilation, dependency resolution, and packaging of an immutable versioned artifact (tag or hash), with a green-build gate and the artifact published to a registry; that same artifact must flow intact through to deploy (build once, deploy many), without recompiling per environment. TEST: unit tests, integration tests, and coverage, with a gate of 100% tests green and coverage above the required threshold; declare what happens with flaky tests and whether coverage measures lines or branches. SCAN: SAST on code, SCA on vulnerable dependencies, and secret detection, with a gate that blocks on findings above the defined severity; provide for false-positive handling with a traceable, expiring waiver. DEPLOY: promotion through environments, deployment strategy (rolling, blue-green, or canary) justified by risk and downtime tolerance, manual approval where applicable, post-deploy smoke test, and a rollback plan with an explicit trigger (metric, error rate, or human decision). (3) Close with a text flowchart, a summary table of gates (phase, measurable criterion, action if it fails), and an actionable implementation checklist. Respect phase order and the fail-fast principle: the cheapest phase that can fail goes first. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-desarrollo_estrategia_branching_gitfl: Act as a senior platform engineer with experience leading version control strategies and DevOps practices in software teams. I need a ready-to-adopt Git branching strategy decision document, because today the team improvises the workflow and that generates long-lived branches, painful merges, blocked releases, and risky hotfixes. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Before deciding, I need to know the context: team size contributing to the repo, production release cadence (continuous, weekly, per sprint, or versioned), CI/CD maturity (test coverage, automated deployment, feature flags, environments), delivery model (single-version-live SaaS vs product with multiple supported versions), and compliance constraints, windows, or manual approvals.
