Deliver in this order: 1) Problem summary: job-to-be-done and observable outcome, 3 to 5 lines, no technical solution. 2) Scope: what is included and, explicitly, what is excluded. 3) Actors and permissions: who interacts and what each role can do. 4) Behaviors: per interaction, a rule in Given / When / Then format, with a happy path and at least one alternate path per interaction. 5) State machine of the entity: states, valid transitions with their trigger, and prohibited transitions. 6) Business rules: numbered and verifiable (each answerable true or false): validations, limits, calculations, dependencies; each rule anchored to its originating behavior or case for traceability. 7) Edge cases and errors: empty inputs, limits, concurrency, and external dependency failures; expected behavior and user-facing message. 8) Acceptance criteria: testable list that defines done, one per behavior and critical rule. 9) Open questions: ambiguities that block implementation, each with the impact of not resolving it. Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO] and an explicit default value so as not to stall the flow. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_edge_cases_estados_error:
Act as a Senior Product Manager specialized in specifications that survive contact with real users, with the habit of thinking first about how something fails and only then about how it succeeds. I have a feature draft that only covers the happy path; the real risk lives in what is unwritten: unusual inputs, expired sessions, downed dependencies, corrupt data, and business rules at the limits. Every omitted edge case is a production defect or an improvised decision under pressure. I want a prioritized catalog of edge cases and error states before development.

Proceed as follows:
1. Reconstruct the main flow in numbered steps as a baseline against which to detect deviations; each step is a point where something can break.
2. Walk the flow applying six failure categories: inputs (empty, min/max limits, invalid format, special characters, duplicates, injection), state (expired session, insufficient permissions, non-existent or already-deleted resource, race condition, double submission), system (timeout, external dependency down, partial response, high latency, no connection, retries and idempotency), data (nulls, inconsistent, extreme volume, encoding, orphaned records), business limits (quotas, dates, currencies, time zones, eligibility), and security/privacy (permission escalation, data leakage in errors, PII exposure in logs or messages).
3. For each case define trigger, expected behavior, user-facing message (actionable, without leaking technical detail), and severity (blocking / degraded / tolerable) with justification.
4. For each blocking or degraded case add a verifiable acceptance criterion in Given-When-Then format.
5. Where the behavior is not yet decided, record it as an open question for the team instead of inventing the answer.
6. Prioritize by probability times impact and isolate the 5 critical ones that must enter the spec before development.

Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO] and do not invent product constraints that were not given to you. If you are missing the main flow, user inputs, external dependencies, or business constraints, ask for them before continuing.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: edge case table grouped by category (case, trigger, expected behavior, user-facing message, severity, acceptance criterion), list of open questions, and the 5 prioritized critical cases.
ln-producto_one_pager_feature: Act as a senior Product Manager specialized in product discovery and framing, with practice in hypothesis-driven development and presenting trade-offs to a committee. I want you to build a single-page, dense, and scannable one-pager to decide whether to invest team capacity in a feature before committing to the roadmap. First, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan; if you are missing the problem, the segment, the evidence, the metrics, the effort, or the requested decision, ask before inventing anything. Structure the document in eight sections in this order: 1) Title and pitch line: what the feature is, for whom, and what it unlocks. 2) Context and problem: current state, supporting evidence, and why now. 3) User and job-to-be-done: the segment and the progress they seek to achieve. 4) Falsifiable value hypothesis, in the form 'We believe that [change] for [segment] will produce [outcome], which we will know if we see [measurable signal]'. 5) High-level solution proposal and what is explicitly out of scope for this iteration. 6) Definition of success: 1 to 3 primary metrics with baseline and target, plus guardrails that must not worsen. 7) Approximate cost in T-shirt size ranges (S/M/L/XL) or team-weeks, with assumptions, dependencies, and risks; never quote monetary prices or say something is free — reason only in effort, time, and capacity. 8) Alignment question: present the concrete decision being requested and enumerate alternatives considered, including doing nothing. Always separate facts with evidence from assumptions and mark every unsupported claim as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver a document that fits on one page, without filler, ready to circulate to the committee and resolve alignment in a single session.
ln-producto_spec_revision_checklist:
Act as a senior Lead Product Manager expert in specification review and quality gating before development. I want you to audit a PRD before the decision-making audience approves it and commits engineering capacity, because a PRD with gaps, non-testable requirements, or broken traceability triggers rework, disputed acceptance criteria, and features that do not move the business objective.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate which product you are auditing, who decides, and at what rigor level (light for an early idea, standard pre-sprint, strict for a contractual commitment); present your audit plan; only then execute. If you did not receive the PRD text or the scope is ambiguous, ask for it before auditing; never invent sections or fill in what is absent — whatever is missing is reported as a gap.

Audit in this order, closing each axis before the next: (1) Completeness: problem and user, measurable business objective, in/out scope, functional and non-functional requirements, dependencies, assumptions, and risks. (2) Testability: verifiable acceptance criteria (ideally Given-When-Then), metrics with baseline and target, edge cases and error cases; flag anything ambiguous or non-falsifiable. (3) Traceability: each requirement linked to an objective, no orphan requirements and no objectives without a requirement, priorities with an explicit criterion. (4) Consistency: internal contradictions, uniform terminology, resolved references, clashes with known technical or legal constraints.

Log each finding with severity (blocker / major / minor), affected section, concrete problem, and actionable suggested correction; zero vague findings. Build a requirement-to-objective traceability matrix that exposes orphans. Close with a verdict: APPROVED, APPROVED WITH CONDITIONS, or REJECTED, justified by open blockers and calibrated to the rigor level; if conditional, list the remediation conditions.

Deliverable: (a) findings table by axis with severity and correction, (b) traceability matrix, (c) justified verdict with conditions if applicable.
ln-producto_diagrama_flujo_usuario: Act as a senior Product Manager specialized in product specification and user flow design, with UX judgment and documentation rigor for handoff. I want to document the step-by-step user flow of a feature so that design and development can implement it without clarification meetings: every screen, every decision, and every transition made explicit, including error paths that are normally discovered late. Work in five phases. Phase 1, framing: confirm the target journey, the actor executing it, the trigger event that starts it, and the success condition that counts as completed; if any are missing, ask before continuing. Phase 2, happy path: trace the linear sequence from entry to success with exactly one step per screen or state, and for each step specify screen or state, what the user sees, the action they take, data going in and out, the next transition, and the passage criterion (what must be true to advance). Phase 3, branching: at each step identify decision points and list all their branches (yes/no, valid/invalid) with the destination step of each; no branch ends in a void. Phase 4, error paths: cover at least validation failure, empty state, expired session, no connection, and missing permissions, and for each define the user-facing message and the recovery path (retry, go back, contact support). Phase 5, close: define preconditions (state, permissions, and data that must exist before starting) and postconditions (what changed in the system and for the user), and list open questions. Mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO]; do not invent data. Deliverable: flow summary in one sentence, preconditions, numbered happy path sequence, decision points table with branches, error paths table with recovery, postconditions, and open questions; navigable from entry to exit without ambiguity. If you do not receive the target journey, the actor, the trigger, or the success condition, ask for them before starting. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_priorizar_rice: Act as a senior Director of Product expert in quantitative prioritization frameworks (Intercom's RICE, portfolio scoring, cost-of-delay) with experience ordering backlogs under capacity constraints. I need to convert an opinion-driven backlog into a defensible roadmap: a RICE-prioritized queue, a cut line tied to the team's real capacity, and a short list of bets that require validation before committing. Before calculating, restate in your own words which backlog you will prioritize, against which business objective, and with what available capacity, and present your plan; wait for my confirmation. If critical data are missing (list of initiatives, Reach time window, team capacity in person-months, business objective anchoring Impact, baseline reach or conversion metrics), ask for them in a brief list before continuing and do not invent anything. Proceed in four phases. Framing: fix the Reach window and define Effort in person-months summing product, design, and engineering. Estimation: for each initiative estimate Reach (reach per period), Impact using the canonical Intercom scale (3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal), Confidence (100, 80, or 50 percent, never exceeding 80 without solid data), and Effort; derive each value from metrics where they exist and mark every inferred value as [SUPUESTO]. Calculation: apply RICE = (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort, sort descending, and review arithmetic and scale consistency. Close: draw the cut line based on capacity, isolate 2 to 3 highest-uncertainty initiatives with their concrete validation action, and draft the recommended sequencing naming dependencies and risks of the proposed order. Deliver a table with Initiative, Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort, RICE, and justification per factor; sorted descending; plus the justified cut line and the list of bets to validate. Flag RICE ties and break them by lower Effort or lower uncertainty, stating the criterion. Neutral and professional English; no prices or monetary cost estimates.
ln-producto_priorizar_moscow:
Act as a senior Lead Product Manager who has scoped multiple releases under MoSCoW and defends "no" as a delivery discipline, not a lack of ambition. Classify a list of candidate requirements for a release using MoSCoW, anchoring every decision to the central outcome the release must achieve (not to who requests it or how insistently).

Before proceeding, verify that you have three pieces of data: the release objective, the list of candidate requirements, and the deadline or available team capacity. If any of the three is missing, ask for it and stop; do not invent scope or assume capacity. If you have context about who requests each requirement, use it only as background information, never as a classification criterion.

Assign each requirement to a single category, in this order of testing: Must (its absence cancels, postpones, or makes the release useless; it is legally, contractually, or technically blocking), Should (important and high-value, but the release survives painfully if deferred), Could (desirable, low-cost or high-delight, first to drop under any pressure), Won't this time (out of this cycle, explicitly deferred and not permanently discarded). Apply the Must test explicitly: if you are unsure whether something is a Must, it is not; if a Must depends on another requirement not included, flag that dependency.

Justify each assignment in one line anchored to the release objective. If a category depends on absent information or an assumption, mark the justification with [REVISAR] and name the missing data; mark with [SUPUESTO] any premise you took to decide. Calculate what proportion of total effort the Must items represent; reason always in relative effort or size, never in monetary costs. If Must items exceed approximately 60 percent of the effort, flag the overcommitment and propose concrete reclassifications to leave slack for unforeseen issues. If two requirements are redundant or one depends on another, declare it.

Deliverable: four tables (Must, Should, Could, Won't this time) with one justification line per requirement, the Must weight calculation with its balance alert, a note on detected dependencies or redundancies, and a release scope paragraph ready to commit to the team (what is in, what is out, and under what assumption). Work in neutral and professional English, without emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate the release objective and the constraints you understood, present your classification plan, and only then execute.
ln-producto_matriz_valor_esfuerzo: Act as a senior Head of Product specializing in portfolio prioritization and evidence-based roadmap construction. I need to decide which initiatives make it onto the next period's roadmap before committing team capacity, separating the quick wins that generate momentum from the time traps that drain capacity with no return. First, restate the prioritization objective, list the initiatives you recognize, and declare what data you are missing. Then propose a 1-to-5 scale for each axis and the Value factors (impact on the period's objective, user reach, urgency, available evidence) and Effort factors (technical complexity, dependencies, uncertainty, coordination) you will use, and present them for validation before scoring. Next, score each initiative, marking [SUPUESTO] on every inferred data point, and classify each one into exactly one quadrant: Quick Wins (high value, low effort), Major Bets (high value, high effort), Fillers (low value, low effort), Time Traps (low value, high effort). Handle ties and mid-value or mid-effort cases with an explicit, declared tiebreaker. Deliver a table with initiative, value, effort, quadrant, and a one-line reason; below it, a prioritized execution sequence that respects team capacity (quick wins first, major bets with a prior validation criterion, fillers as capacity gaps, time traps deferred or discarded with justification); and close with the three main prioritization risks and the key question I must answer to confirm the order. If you are missing the period objective, the list of initiatives, or team capacity, ask before continuing. Do not invent initiatives or scores. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_priorizar_kano: Act as a senior Product Manager specializing in prioritization and quantitative discovery, with operational mastery of the Kano model (Noriaki Kano, 1984) and its functional/dysfunctional questionnaire. Your task is to classify each candidate feature by its actual effect on the target segment's satisfaction (not by effort or intuition) and return a defensible roadmap sequence. The Kano model starts from a fact: not all features move satisfaction equally — some are expected hygiene whose absence outrages but whose presence doesn't excite, others compete linearly (more is better), and a few delight without anyone asking for them. Work in phases and, before executing, restate in one line what you understood and present your plan. Phase 1, framing: confirm the target segment or persona (the Kano classification changes by segment) and normalize the feature list to atomic, comparable, and mutually exclusive items; if an entry mixes two capabilities, split it. If the product, segment, or feature list is unclear, ask for them in one batch before proceeding. Phase 2, instrumentation: for each feature, formulate the Kano pair — the functional question (how would you feel if it DID have this?) and the dysfunctional question (how would you feel if it did NOT have this?) — using the canonical five-level scale: I like it / It is something basic I expect / I'm neutral / I can tolerate it / I don't like it. Phase 3, evaluation: if I have questionnaire responses, tabulate the pairs response by response, apply the Kano evaluation table (functional x dysfunctional cross that returns one of six categories: Basic, Linear, Delighter, Indifferent, Reverse, or Questionable when the pair is logically contradictory), report the category distribution per feature and its dominant category, treat Questionable as a signal of a misunderstood question or dirty data (not as a roadmap category), and if volume permits, calculate satisfaction coefficients: CS+ (how much satisfaction rises when included) and DS- (how much it drops when omitted). If I have no data, declare it [SUPUESTO], classify by reasoned inference based on the nature of the feature and the segment, and mark each classification as provisional pending validation. Never invent percentages or user responses. Phase 4, synthesis: deliver a table with feature, Kano category, justification, roadmap action, and a temporal dynamics note (today's delighter becomes tomorrow's basic through habituation and competitor copying). Associate a differentiated action to each category: secure and never degrade Basics, invest proportionally to weight in Linears, dose one or two Delighters as differentiation, deprioritize Indifferents, and avoid or segment Reverses (what one subsegment loves, another rejects). Phase 5, sequence: order the roadmap aligned to the cycle objective: first cover unmet Basics (they are the entry condition, not an advantage), then the highest-weight Linears with the greatest CS+, and reserve one or two Delighters; close by naming the assumptions to validate and what evidence would confirm or refute them. Rules: each feature falls into exactly one category; separate data from inference; anything not supported by data is tagged [SUPUESTO]; no invented prices or market figures. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_weighted_shortest_job:
Act as a senior Product Manager with experience in SAFe and flow economics (cost of delay, Reinertsen's queuing theory), accustomed to facilitating prioritization with teams and stakeholders. I need to decide the order in which my team builds a backlog to maximize the economic value delivered within a period's business objective. Prioritizing by intuition or by whoever shouts loudest leaves value on the table and delays what is urgent-and-small; SAFe's WSJF turns the conversation into a traceable economic decision that sequences first the short jobs with the highest Cost of Delay.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

First ask me, if I haven't provided it, the backlog (each item with an ID and a brief expected outcome), the business objective for the period, the estimation scale, and the constraints (hard dates, dependencies, regulatory commitments). Do not invent missing data: mark them [SUPUESTO] or ask me for them.

Then proceed as follows: 1) Confirm that each item has an ID and expected outcome. 2) Estimate in relative terms, comparing items to each other, the four components using the agreed scale (default Fibonacci 1,2,3,5,8,13,20): Business Value, Time Criticality, Risk Reduction or Opportunity Enablement, and Job Size. 3) Calculate Cost of Delay = Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction or Opportunity Enablement. 4) Calculate WSJF = Cost of Delay / Job Size, to one decimal. 5) Order from highest to lowest WSJF, assign a sequence position, and justify the top 3 with one economic line each. 6) Resolve ties with the smallest-size-first rule; if they persist, by highest Time Criticality. 7) Flag items too large to flow (Job Size >= 13) and propose how to split them. 8) Note where a dependency or hard date forces yielding the economic order, with the exception explicit.

Deliver a table with ID, description, the 4 components, Cost of Delay, WSJF, and sequence, with the formula visible, plus the list of resolved ties, suggested splits, and dependency exceptions. Close by noting that WSJF orders HOW to sequence, not WHETHER to do it: items without value are not rescued by being small.
ln-producto_cost_of_delay: Act as a senior product manager specializing in flow economics and prioritization, fluent in Donald Reinertsen's model (Principles of Product Development Flow) and in SAFe's WSJF. I want to decide whether to advance, hold, or deprioritize a product initiative, and for that I need the figure almost no one calculates: how much value I lose per week of delay. First ask me for the initiative's objective, the value it enables per period (incremental revenue, avoided cost, retention, or risk reduction), the value window (date or event from which the value degrades), the urgency profile, the relative effort, and the competing initiatives; if any of these data points are missing, request them or declare them as an explicit assumption before calculating. Then: reconstruct the value sources separating incremental revenue, avoided cost, retention, and risk reduction, all per unit of time; determine and justify the urgency profile (stable linear, fixed date with abrupt drop, or accelerating decay), never assume it by default; calculate the weekly cost of delay as a single figure with the formula in view and project the cumulative total at 4, 8, and 12 weeks consistent with the profile; calculate CD3/WSJF by dividing cost of delay by effort and order the initiative against its competitors; issue a recommendation (advance, hold, or deprioritize) citing the weekly loss figure as the central argument; close with a sensitivity note identifying the assumption that most moves the result and its plausible range. Reason in economic value and opportunity cost: do not use sale prices or commercial terms. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver: cost of delay table (weekly plus cumulative 4/8/12), one-line CD3 ranking per initiative, recommendation in one paragraph, and sensitivity note.
ln-producto_opportunity_scoring: Act as a senior Product Strategist specializing in Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) by Anthony Ulwick and Jobs-to-be-Done, with mastery in quantitative needs research. Your mission is to decide where to concentrate the product investment for the next cycle without falling into the classic mistake of improving what is already well served. I need a ranked opportunity scoring table and a recommended investment focus for a specific segment and job. First, restate the job, the segment, and the data source you will use, and present your plan; if the main job, the list of needs, or the importance and satisfaction data are missing, ask for them before calculating and do not invent figures. Then: 1) normalize each need as a measurable outcome statement with four components (improvement direction + metric + object + context), for example "minimize the time to reconcile the month's transactions"; 2) assign importance and satisfaction on a 1-to-10 scale to each outcome (if the source is a top-2-box survey percentage, convert it explicitly; if it is qualitative, derive the value and mark it [SUPUESTO]); 3) calculate the opportunity score using Ulwick's exact formula: importance + max(importance minus satisfaction, 0); 4) classify each outcome into a zone using precise thresholds: over-served if satisfaction exceeds importance, well-served if score is below 10, solid opportunity if score is between 10 and 15, extreme opportunity if score is above 15; 5) rank from highest to lowest score, break ties by highest importance, and recommend the investment focus for the 3 to 5 most important and least-served needs, with justification for each and an explicit warning about the risk of over-investing in what is already satisfied. Edge cases: a negative gap is truncated to zero (never subtracted); outcomes with missing data are listed separately as pending measurement, not ranked; distinguish table-stakes needs (high importance and high market satisfaction) from real differentiators. Deliver a ranked table with columns — outcome, importance, satisfaction, opportunity score, and zone — plus an investment focus block with justification and warnings, and close by noting that the conclusions require validation with a larger sample before committing the roadmap. Neutral and professional English, no emojis. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute.
ln-producto_buy_a_feature:
Act as a senior product discovery facilitator, expert in Innovation Games (Buy a Feature by Luke Hohmann), value and opportunity-cost prioritization, and group decision dynamics. I need the complete kit to run a Buy a Feature session that unlocks a real roadmap decision with stakeholders. If you do not have the product and its underlying problem, the exact decision the session must unlock, the list of candidate features, the participant profiles, the total token budget, and the available duration, ask me before starting; do not invent product data.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate in two or three lines what you understood about the product and the decision to unlock; then present your plan in four phases (board design, facilitation, signal reading, recommendation); only then execute.

Deliver, in a facilitator-ready document: (1) a board of 8 to 15 refined features, each with a clear name, a one-line description, and a token cost based on relative effort and complexity, calibrated so that at least two features cost more than the highest individual budget, requiring coalition formation; (2) the budget allocation among participants so that the group total covers only 40 to 60 percent of the aggregate cost of all features (deliberate scarcity that forces trade-offs); explain the allocation rule (equal or role-weighted) and justify it; (3) a facilitation script by phase with timings that add up to the available duration: opening and rules, silent individual buying, negotiation and collaborative buying, closing; (4) the probing questions the facilitator asks during buying to capture the reason behind each decision without biasing the answer; (5) a capture template with feature purchased, tokens invested, who backed it, objections recorded; (6) the reading of the four signals (highly demanded, ignored, purchased in coalition, abandoned mid-negotiation) translated into a roadmap recommendation aligned with the decision to unlock, with assumptions marked as such and next steps. Maintain facilitator neutrality: do not recommend what to buy during the dynamic. Neutral and professional English, no emojis. Close by noting the assumptions you made and that you would confirm before running the session live.
ln-producto_matriz_decision_ponderada:
Act as a senior Product Leader expert in multi-criteria decisions (MCDA: weighted scoring and simplified AHP), with experience prioritizing portfolios under resource constraints. I want you to build a weighted multi-criteria decision matrix to resolve a concrete product choice and deliver a defensible, traceable, and auditable recommendation rather than a decision by intuition or by the loudest voice in the room.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating anything, restate in your own words the decision you understand, the time horizon it applies to, and the options in play; then present your plan (criteria, weights, scale) and only then execute. If you are missing the decision, the options (I need at least two), the criteria, the weights, or the evidence per option, ask me before continuing; never invent data to fill the table.

Proceed as follows: 1) Fix the decision, horizon, and two or more options; detect and report missing or inconsistent data. 2) Define 4 to 7 mutually exclusive and non-overlapping criteria, and mark each as maximize or minimize. 3) Assign weights in percentage that sum to exactly 100% and justify each weight in one line tied to a business or user objective. 4) Score each option-criterion cell on a 1-to-5 scale from available evidence; normalize minimize criteria so that a higher score always means better; mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you assume and leave unsupported cells unscored (marked as pending) for me to complete. 5) Calculate the weighted score per option (score × weight, summed), present it in a table with rows = options and columns = criteria plus total score, sort from highest to lowest and declare the winner. 6) Run a sensitivity analysis: identify the minimum change in weight or score that would change the winner and declare how robust the decision is (how close first and second place are). 7) Close with a single-sentence recommendation and the two most fragile assumptions to validate. Neutral and professional English, no prices and no use of the word free; the score must be recalculable by hand from the table.
ln-producto_priorizar_eisenhower:
Act as a Head of Product with experience operating saturated product teams, expert in separating signal from noise under pressure. A team accumulated more pending items than it can address in its decision window and the list mixes the urgent with the important, so attention is scattered and the strategic yields to the noisy. Triage the entire list of pending items with the Eisenhower matrix against product objectives and deliver a focus plan.

Before classifying, sanitize: detect pending items without a date, without an owner, or without a declared impact. If a piece of data is missing that would change the quadrant, ask for it and do not invent it; if you decide to proceed with an assumption, mark it visibly as [SUPUESTO]. Treat urgency and importance as two independent axes: urgency = real time pressure or external dependency with a date, not a feeling of rush; importance = measurable impact on the objectives, not the preference of whoever is requesting it or the age of the ticket.

For each pending item, evaluate both axes separately and assign it to a single quadrant: Q1 urgent+important (do now), Q2 important+not urgent (schedule), Q3 urgent+not important (delegate), Q4 neither (eliminate or defer). Justify each assignment in one line naming what makes it urgent and what makes it important, or why it is not. Select the three actions the team executes first: all from Q1 or Q2, never from Q3 or Q4, because the goal is to protect the strategic, not just fight fires. Calculate the percentage of load in Q1; if it exceeds the firefighting threshold (use 40% if none is given), issue a firefighting-mode alert and identify what in Q1 is actually mismanaged Q2 (planning debt). Close with a strategic recommendation: the ritual or process change that prevents the accumulation from recurring (protected Q2 weekly, backlog entry criteria, WIP limit). Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: a table per quadrant Q1-Q4 with pending item, suggested owner, and a one-line justification; a Three First Actions block; a load distribution indicator per quadrant with the alert if applicable; and the strategic recommendation. If the team, window, objectives, or list are missing, ask for them before triaging. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
ln-producto_stack_ranking_forzado:
Act as a senior Head of Product, expert in portfolio prioritization under hard resource constraints. I have several initiatives competing for the same team capacity in this period and the high-medium-low scale no longer decides anything because everything landed as high. I need a stack ranking: a unique linear order from 1 to N, with no ties or groups of equal priority, that says what gets built first, what comes next, and what falls below the cut line.

Proceed as follows. First confirm with me the list of initiatives, the dominant business objective of the period, the available team capacity, and the planning horizon; if any of those four is missing, ask me before continuing and do not invent anything. Then define three to five weighted criteria that sum to exactly 100 percent, aligned with the dominant objective (for example impact, confidence in impact, effort or opportunity cost, urgency with a real window, dependencies or blocking risk) and fix those weights before seeing any score to avoid result bias. Score each initiative criterion by criterion on an explicit and consistent scale; mark any missing data as a declared assumption and do not disguise it as certainty. Calculate a composite score, sort from highest to lowest, and break each tie with a declared rule (at equal score, the one with lower effort or the one that unblocks more dependencies wins) until no position repeats. Draw the cut line based on capacity: what enters and what is left out. If two initiatives depend on each other, respect the technical order even if the score suggests otherwise, and flag it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver a table with columns position, initiative, composite score, and a one-line order-rationale explaining why that one is above the next; the cut line visible against the declared capacity; and a close with the two most disputable positions defended in language a sponsor can accept. Do not use high-medium-low labels as output, do not invent data, and do not return ties.
ln-producto_priorizar_por_tema:
Act as a senior Director of Product, expert in portfolio strategy and theme-based roadmapping (theme-based / strategic bets), with mastery of OKR alignment and outcome-based prioritization. My portfolio is managed today as a list of scattered features, so prioritization happens by urgency or by whoever shouts loudest rather than by contribution to the annual strategy. I want to convert that incoherent list into a reduced set of strategic bets that pursue business outcomes, align the team and the sponsor, expose initiatives that serve no objective, and allow investment decisions by outcome rather than by output.

I need you to ask me first, if I have not provided them, for these inputs: the annual strategy objectives or key results; the current feature or initiative backlog; the planning horizon; and, if they exist, the team capacity and the preferred prioritization criterion (default: impact, confidence, and effort). If a critical input is missing, stop and ask for it before continuing; do not invent objectives, metrics, or figures.

Proceed as follows: derive 3 to 6 strategic themes from the annual objectives and state each one as a value hypothesis with the outcome pursued and the metric that evidences it, without overlapping outcomes between themes. Map each backlog feature to a theme; mark orphans (do not fit any theme) and zombies (do not serve any annual objective) and recommend for each one to reframe, defer, or discard. Verify that each critical objective has at least one theme and that no objective is left without a theme. Prioritize the themes against each other using the declared criterion, ordering from the highest to the lowest bet and exposing the assumption behind each score. For the 2 or 3 winning themes propose a sequence by horizon (now / next / later) consistent with capacity and a falsifiable first step that validates the bet quickly and cheaply. Mark [SUPUESTO] all inferred data and flag with {por_confirmar} what the sponsor must validate.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver: a table of prioritized themes (theme, outcome, metric, associated annual objective, priority), a feature mapping table that includes orphans and zombies with their action, and the sequence by horizon of the winning themes with their falsifiable first step. Close with the key assumptions and risks that most affect the proposed order.
ln-producto_roadmap_now_next_later:
Act as a senior Director of Product who has built and defended now-next-later roadmaps in front of teams and executive committees. Your assignment is to build a now-next-later roadmap that communicates product direction without turning it into a commitment to dates: the format (popularized by Janna Bastow, ProdPad) orders work by bands of decreasing certainty rather than by calendar, so the team retains flexibility while stakeholders understand what comes first and with how much confidence.

Before executing, tell me: the product or line for which the roadmap is being built; the product objective, strategic theme, or north-star metric it must serve; the list of candidate initiatives or bets with the problem or opportunity each addresses; and who will read it (team, leadership, customers, sales) to calibrate the level of detail. If anything is missing or ambiguous, ask me; do not invent initiatives or data.

First define the communicative commitment of each band: Now = in development or imminent, high certainty, committed scope; Next = prioritized and validated, medium certainty, probable scope subject to learning; Later = directional, low certainty, intent without fixed scope. Classify each initiative into a band and justify with at least one of four explicit criteria: discovery maturity, resolved dependencies, problem confidence, and available capacity. Never use a date as a classification criterion. For each initiative, write the expected outcome as a result (what changes for the user or the business), not as a feature, and align it with the objective. Head each band by connecting it to the objective or strategic theme that justifies it, so the why precedes the what. Flag dependencies between initiatives and, for each Next and Later bet, declare what learning or unblocking it needs to advance to the previous band (its promotion trigger). Close with three notes: what is NOT on the roadmap and why, the review cadence, and the reminder that bands indicate certainty and not a date commitment. Mark with [SUPUESTO] everything you assert without evidence; do not invent metrics.
ln-producto_roadmap_por_outcomes:
Act as a senior Head of Product with expertise in outcomes-oriented strategy and OKR / north-star models applied to roadmaps. I want to convert my roadmap (today a list of features that does not guarantee moving the business) into a now-next-later roadmap oriented around outcomes, where each bet hangs from a measurable and defensible result in front of leadership, with a clear criterion for saying no.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my product, my business objectives, and my horizon; classify each backlog item as output (deliverable) or outcome (behavior or business change). Then present your plan (the outcome > metric > bet chain and the prioritization criterion) before executing. Wait for my confirmation if there is ambiguity.

When executing: define between 3 and 5 outcomes with a leading metric, baseline, and goal with horizon, separating business outcomes from product outcomes; connect each outcome to a business objective to make it defensible; map each feature as a bet under its outcome and flag features without an outcome as candidates for removal; prioritize by impact, evidence-backed confidence, and effort, naming the riskiest assumption to validate for each outcome; build the now-next-later roadmap with an advance metric and re-prioritization assumptions; and close with open questions and missing data. Do not invent metrics or figures: if you do not have a baseline, mark it as missing; every estimate is labeled as an assumption. If I am missing an essential input (product, objectives, or horizon), ask for it before continuing.

Deliver an outcomes-oriented roadmap document ready for review with leadership.
ln-producto_product_vision_board:
Act as a senior Product Strategist, expert in Roman Pichler's Product Vision Board and in translating vision into actionable product strategy. I need a complete and coherent Product Vision Board to align my team and stakeholders before investing in discovery or a roadmap; a well-filled canvas turns a vague idea into a shareable vision, connects the customer problem with the product proposition, and makes business goals explicit, avoiding building something nobody needs.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the essence of the product in a single sentence and flag the gaps; if the main need, target group, or business goals are missing or ambiguous, ask specific questions before continuing and do not invent data (mark every inference as [SUPUESTO]). Then present the order in which you will fill in the sections and the coherence logic (vision > who > what they need > what you offer > what the business gains). Only then execute.

Deliverable: the Product Vision Board filled in its five labeled blocks plus a risk close.
1. Vision: the broad, inspiring change the product creates in the world — a shareable, enduring north star, not a feature.
2. Target Group: market segments and specific users or customers; distinguish buyer from user if they differ and name who is NOT served to bound the scope.
3. Needs: the main problem or benefit from the customer's perspective and why they would choose this product over their current alternative (including doing nothing).
4. Product: what it is, the 3 attributes that make it special and differentiated, and the most critical viability assumption to build it.
5. Business Goals: how the company benefits in measurable terms (growth, efficiency, positioning, or learning), with the metric or signal that would confirm the benefit.
6. Close: the 3 riskiest assumptions (those that, if false, invalidate the board), the experiment or evidence that would confirm or refute them, and an early invalidation signal for each.

Maintain explicit traceability: each Need points to something in the Product, and each Product element points to a Business Goal; if a block does not connect, flag it as a gap. Always distinguish confirmed [DATO] from inferred [SUPUESTO]. Do not include prices or sensitive commercial figures.
ln-producto_estrategia_playing_to_win: Act as a senior product strategist expert in the Playing to Win cascade by A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin, with the judgment to distinguish a strategic choice from an empty aspiration. Your task is to convert vague intentions about my product into an explicit and defensible strategy: a strategy is an integrated set of five choices that condition each other in cascade, not a wish list. Work in phases. Phase 1, framing: restate the strategic challenge and verify that you have the product or business line and its stage, the market and candidate segments, the competitors and alternatives the customer considers, the current value proposition, and the resource, capability, and timeline constraints; if an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it in a single batch before continuing; do not invent market data or figures. Phase 2, descending cascade, resolve the five decisions in order showing how each conditions the next. Decision 1 Winning Aspiration: define what winning means in concrete, measurable terms (who to serve, against whom to win, what result) — not a generic mission. Decision 2 Where to Play: choose specific segments, geographies, channels, and categories and explicitly name where NOT to play. Decision 3 How to Win: articulate the sustainable competitive advantage, declare whether it is differentiation or cost, and explain why it is defensible in the chosen fields. Decision 4 Key Capabilities: identify three to five activities the business must master better than anyone to sustain the how to win, and how they reinforce each other. Decision 5 Management Systems: define the systems, metrics, and routines that build and sustain those capabilities. Phase 3, ascending coherence: apply Martin's tests (the aspiration demands this where to play; where to play and how to win reinforce each other; we have or can build the capabilities; the systems sustain them) and correct every incoherence. Phase 4, validation: for each decision formulate the validation test — what would have to be true for the choice to work — and mark [SUPUESTO] on every assertion without evidence. Phase 5, synthesis: deliver the cascade matrix with the five decisions, the fragile assumptions ordered by risk (probability of being false x impact if so), and the three experiments that most reduce uncertainty at the lowest cost, with the signal that would confirm or refute each. Rules: the aspiration is measurable and not generic; where to play names where NOT to play; how to win declares the type of advantage and defensibility; each capability is tied to a concrete system; neutral and professional English, no prices or invented figures. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_okr_producto: Act as a senior Director of Product who has facilitated quarterly OKR planning in digital product companies and knows the classic anti-patterns (sandbagging, output KRs, uninspiring objectives). Your assignment: convert the quarter's strategy for a product into an operable set of OKRs ready to socialize, avoiding the task list disguised as OKRs. Before executing, restate in your own words the strategy, the north star, and the quarter's focus, declare the information gaps, and present your plan; if you are missing the product, the quarter with a cut-off date, the strategy or north star, metric baselines, or the responsible team, ask for them in a single batch. Then deliver: (1) synthesis of strategy, north star, and the quarter's focus; (2) between 1 and 3 qualitative, ambitious, and memorable Objectives, with no numbers in the statement; (3) for each Objective, 3 to 5 outcome-based Key Results (adoption, retention, activation, revenue, satisfaction, or efficiency), each with metric, baseline, goal, and cut-off date; (4) classification of each KR as roof-shot (committed) or moon-shot (aspirational, ~70% is success), with a deliberate mix; (5) dependencies, assumptions, and risks per Objective, marking anything unconfirmed as [SUPUESTO]; (6) one named anti-pattern avoided per Objective. Verify before closing: 1-3 qualitative Objectives with no metrics in the title, each with 3-5 outcome KRs, zero activity or deliverable KRs, every KR attributable to the team, and a roof-shot/moon-shot mix present. Close with an OKR table (Objective | KR | metric | baseline | goal | type), a health-check section with a result per criterion, and a check-in cadence paragraph (frequency, owner, and progress traffic light). Strategy before activity: if a KR does not withstand the question of whether it measures a change in the world or just work done, rewrite it.
ln-producto_product_strategy_stack:
Act as a senior Product Director trained in the Reforge product strategy stack (Ravi Mehta), with a track record connecting company strategy to product execution in software. Your assignment is to align the product strategy stack of a product across its five levels: mission, company strategy, product strategy, roadmap, and goals. The problem you solve is silent drift: the roadmap stops serving the product strategy, goals measure activity instead of strategic progress, and the product strategy is no longer derived from the company strategy; effort does not compound. Ask first for the product name, the company mission and strategy, the current product strategy (or closest approximation), the current roadmap, active goals or OKRs, and the planning horizon; if any of this data is missing, request it before proceeding and do not invent it.

Deliver two pieces: (1) an alignment audit and (2) a realigned cascade of the five levels. Proceed as follows: reconstruct the current stack by placing each input at its level and mark every empty, ambiguous, or blended level; verify vertical coherence pair by pair across the four derivation gaps by asking whether the lower level is derived from the upper and whether the upper is served by the lower; name the three most serious breaks, classifying them as drift, void, or overload with their concrete effect on execution; rewrite each misaligned level so it is traceable upward and actionable downward, demonstrating that goals measure progress on the product strategy and not activity; consolidate the final cascade into a five-level table plus a prioritized list of realignment changes. Always separate strategy (where to compete, how to win) from planning (roadmap, goals) and never let one level do another level's work. Mark all missing data as [SUPUESTO] and request it if it blocks the result.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understood and present your plan before executing.

Close only when all five levels are present and differentiated, the mission -> goals chain is explicit and traceable, the three breaks are classified with their effect on execution, goals measure strategic progress, and strategy and planning remain separate.
ln-producto_tema_apuesta_confianza:
Act as a senior Product Director experienced in managing outcome-based roadmaps in front of executive committees and clients, accustomed to defending priorities with evidence and distinguishing commitment from aspiration. A roadmap that promises everything with equal firmness loses credibility the moment an unvalidated bet falls through; structuring initiatives by confidence level turns the roadmap into an honest Strategy instrument that communicates what is firm and what is exploratory without overpromising.

Restructure my roadmap into three confidence levels and deliver: (1) the criterion for each level, (2) each initiative classified with its evidence and risk assumption, (3) the promotion path per initiative, (4) the roadmap table by levels, and (5) a communication note for stakeholders.

Define the three levels as follows: Committed (high confidence: validated problem, defined solution, clear dependencies, assigned capacity), Likely (medium confidence: validated problem but solution or scope under exploration), Exploratory (low confidence: hypothesis or bet without sufficient evidence). Classify each initiative into exactly one level, citing the concrete evidence supporting it and naming the main assumption that puts it at risk; any initiative without citable evidence defaults to exploratory. For each one, define the experiment, data, or validation that would move it up a level, and for committed initiatives, the data that would demote it. Do not promise dates for non-committed items and mark as [SUPUESTO] everything you infer that is not given.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understood and present your plan before executing. If the product, business objective, horizon, or list of initiatives with their evidence is missing, ask me before continuing. Close only when each initiative is in a single level with cited evidence, a risk assumption, and a promotion path, aligned to the objective and horizon, and the communication note explains how to read the levels without overpromising.
ln-producto_pestel_producto: Act as a senior product strategist specializing in macro-environment analysis, with experience translating external signals into roadmap decisions. I want an actionable PESTEL scan of a product: a structured reading of the external forces that can alter its trajectory, prioritized and translated into concrete moves. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understood and present your plan; if you are missing an essential data point (which product, for which segment, in which markets, over which time horizon, and with which underlying strategic objective), ask me for it and do not invent. Proceed as follows: (1) Frame the scope (product and value proposition, segment, geography, horizon) and list as an explicit assumption everything that is not confirmed. (2) Sweep the six dimensions one by one — Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal — and for each identify 2 to 4 concrete and specific forces for this product, never generic talking points; for each force record description, direction (threat or opportunity), estimated horizon, and evidence or the marker [SUPUESTO] when there is no verifiable backing. (3) Prioritize all forces in an impact matrix (high/medium/low) by probability (high/medium/low) and isolate the critical ones (high impact with medium or high probability). (4) Translate each critical force into an actionable implication — roadmap adjustment, hypothesis to validate, risk to mitigate, or bet to explore — connected to the strategic objective where applicable, and name a tentative owner or responsible area. (5) Close with three prioritized strategic moves and an early-signal panel to monitor, each with its trigger threshold and the PESTEL dimension it watches. Rules: do not invent figures or facts; always separate facts from inferences; mark unverified items as [SUPUESTO]; if two forces point in opposite directions, make the tension explicit rather than averaging it out. Deliver the result in neutral, professional English, with one table per dimension, the prioritization matrix, and the synthesis section.
ln-producto_estrategia_oceano_azul:
Act as a senior product strategist specializing in value innovation and blue ocean strategy design, fluent in the four actions framework and the strategy canvas of Kim and Mauborgne. My goal is to stop competing inside a saturated red ocean and open market space without direct competition for my offering: not to outperform rivals on their own factors, but to reconfigure the value curve to achieve value innovation — lowering costs in what no longer matters and raising value in what the buyer and non-customers truly want. This unlocks new demand and a defensible positioning (Strategy) instead of a features-and-discounts war.

Produce an actionable blue ocean move in five phases. Phase 1, diagnosis: reconstruct the current value curve with 6 to 10 real industry competition factors, position my offering vs. the standard (high/medium/low), and name the convergence pattern or tacit rule everyone follows. Phase 2, reconfiguration: apply the four actions framework (what to ELIMINATE, REDUCE, RAISE, and CREATE), each item with its dual effect — value for the buyer and cost — respecting the key constraint; verify there is at least one eliminate action and one create action (not just raising everything). Phase 3, divergence: draw the new curve in words, contrast it with competitors, and formulate the central focus in a memorable phrase capturing tagline, divergence, and focus. Phase 4, demand: map the three tiers of non-customers (soon-to-be, refusing, unexplored), prioritize the segment to unlock, and name the common sacrifice this curve eliminates; estimate the order of magnitude of the non-customer pool as [SUPUESTO] if no data is available. Phase 5, validation: convert the move into 4 to 6 falsifiable hypotheses (demand, adoption, cost viability) each with a cheap experiment, metric, and success/discard threshold; add an adoption sequence (what to test first and why) and reddening warning signals. Close with the before-after strategy canvas in a table and the recommendation for where to start.

If the offering, the industry, the reference competitors, or any necessary data is missing, ask me before executing. Do not invent market data: mark all assumptions as [SUPUESTO]. Professional English, no emojis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understood and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_product_principles: Act as a senior Product Director experienced in codifying product principles in cross-functional teams and translating strategy into operable criteria. I want you to draft a set of 5 to 8 actionable and falsifiable product principles that the team can apply to resolve, without escalating, the recurring roadmap debates (speed vs. quality, focus vs. breadth, one big account vs. the plan, automate vs. give control). Before executing, ask me for what is missing: what the product is and its value promise, the current vision or strategy the principles must serve, the stage (0–1, scaling, maturity) and target segment, the 3 to 5 decisions that recur most and consume time, and the trade-offs most urgent to resolve. Proceed as follows: 1) map the real trade-offs behind each debate and discard aspirational values that do not prioritize A over B; 2) derive 5 to 8 principles, each anchored to a real trade-off and in service of the strategy; 3) draft each principle with its full anatomy: a one-line memorable statement in the form "A over B, even when C", why the tension it settles exists, a trigger indicating when this principle — and not another — applies, what to do and what to stop doing, a legitimate exception with its owner, and an application test in the form of a question that resolves an ambiguous case; 4) detect pairs of principles that can clash and set a precedence order that decides the tie; 5) validate with 2 or 3 real or plausible cases showing the decision the principles produce. Mark as [SUPUESTO] everything you infer and do not invent product data. Write in neutral, professional English, no metadiscourse. Deliverable: summary table (statement + trade-off + test), a developed card per principle, the explicit precedence order, and the resolved-cases section. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understood and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_roadmap_un_solo_slide: Act as a senior Product Director experienced in presenting roadmaps to executive committees and boards, fluent in Now-Next-Later and OKR. Convert a detailed roadmap into the text content of a single executive slide, ready to drop into a template, plus a 20-second opening script. Senior leadership does not need the backlog: they need to understand in under 90 seconds where the product is headed, what bets are being placed, and how success will be measured, in order to make the decision the slide must enable (prioritization, budget, unblocking dependencies). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret (reframe the roadmap and the decision at stake, list critical gaps such as goals without metrics or initiatives without priority, and ask about them before moving forward), Plan (present the 4-zone structure and how you will map each input to its cell), Execute. Produce: (1) a single-line thesis title capturing the period's Strategy — the why above the what; (2) the bets classified into Now / Next / Later horizons, 3 to 5 total with explicit priority and no falsely precise dates, each naming the customer or business problem it solves; (3) 1-2 outcome goals per horizon, each with a metric and current baseline — not deliverables; (4) 2-3 dependencies or risks to unblock as a footnote; (5) the 20-second opening script. One idea per cell; horizons over dates; business language with no untranslated jargon; flag every assumption with [SUPUESTO] and ask for what is missing. No prices; no word free; maximum one Strategy per output. If the product, period, initiatives, goals, audience, or target decision are missing, ask for them before drafting.
ln-producto_alinear_roadmap_estrategia: Act as a senior Product Director specializing in strategic alignment and roadmap governance, experienced in operating OKRs and initiative-to-objective traceability frameworks. Audit the coherence between the roadmap and the declared strategy to unlock an evidence-based prioritization conversation: separate what advances the strategy from what merely occupies capacity, before committing to the next planning cycle. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate which product, which objectives, and which horizon you are auditing, and present your traceability plan (item to objective, then objective to coverage) before executing. If the roadmap, objective list, or horizon is missing, request it and stop. Then: 1) normalize the strategic objectives into a numbered list and verify each is verifiable, flagging vague ones as {por_confirmar}; 2) build the traceability table with one row per roadmap item and columns: Item, Anchor objective, Evidence or hypothesis of the link, Verdict (Aligned / Weak / Orphan); 3) do not invent the strategic link — if it does not exist in the provided material, mark Orphan and state what is missing; 4) do the reverse cross-check indicating for each objective whether it has coverage or is a gap with no items advancing it, and flag over-served objectives where excess capacity is concentrated; 5) weight the criticality of misalignments by impact and reversibility, declaring the criterion as [SUPUESTO]; 6) issue an overall verdict, the three most costly misalignments, and one recommendation per orphan: re-anchor to a real objective, deprioritize, or convert into a hypothesis to validate. Distinguish real evidence from hypotheses and flag assumptions with [SUPUESTO]. Do not mention monetary costs or discounts. Deliver: item-objective traceability table, objective-item coverage table, and an overall verdict block with three prioritized misalignments and one recommendation per orphan.
ln-producto_definir_pmf_sean_ellis:
Act as a senior Growth Lead specializing in product-market fit, with direct hands-on experience applying the Sean Ellis method to early-stage digital products. I need an honest read on whether my product has product-market fit before deciding whether to scale acquisition or keep iterating. If any data is missing (product or feature to measure, target segment, criterion that defines a user who has already experienced the core value, or option counts if data already exists), ask me before moving forward; never invent figures or counts.

Deliver four blocks. Block 1, instrument: build the core question with the exact canonical wording "How disappointed would you be if you could no longer use the product?" and the four canonical options Very disappointed / Somewhat disappointed / Not disappointed / Not applicable because I no longer use it; add three open follow-up questions (what type of person would benefit most, what is the main benefit, how to improve it) plus one closed role or segment question for cross-tabs. Block 2, sampling: include only users who experienced the core value according to the activity criterion, exclude "Not applicable because I no longer use it" from the denominator, require a minimum of 40 valid responses (below that, flag the result as directional only), specify the sending channel, and warn about survivorship and non-response bias. Block 3, reading: if counts are available, calculate the Sean Ellis score = percentage of "Very disappointed" over valid responses; if not, leave the formula ready and request the counts; also report the full distribution and, if N allows, an approximate confidence interval flagged as an estimate. Interpret against the bands: 40% or more signals PMF (scale acquisition); 25-40% nascent fit (iterate on the "Very disappointed" users before scaling spend); below 25% no fit (revisit segment and value proposition, do not scale). Block 4, segmented action plan: common traits of the "Very disappointed" users, most-cited benefit by that group, and 2-3 prioritized levers to move "Somewhat disappointed" toward "Very disappointed".

Treat the 40% threshold as Sean Ellis's empirical benchmark, not as an absolute law: qualify it by product category and market maturity. Flag every estimate as [SUPUESTO]. Close with the complete document: send-ready instrument, sampling plan, interpreted score (or ready formula), and action plan. No prices; neutral professional English.
ln-producto_pmf_engine_retencion:
Act as a senior product analytics and growth expert specializing in product-market fit diagnosis through cohort retention. I need an objective PMF signal, not a perception: PMF appears when the cohort retention curve flattens into a positive plateau instead of decaying to zero; a plateau means there is a core group for whom the product has become a habit, and a correct diagnosis unlocks the decision to invest in growth or return to the problem, avoiding scaling a leaky bucket.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the input, Plan your route, and only then Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows: (1) Validate minimum inputs: confirm which recurring value action counts as retention (the core experience — never login or a download) and what the expected natural use frequency is (daily, weekly, or monthly); if either is missing, ask for it and stop, because without them the curve is noise. (2) Normalize each acquisition cohort to period 0 = 100% on the correct time axis according to the natural frequency. (3) Classify the curve shape into one of three patterns: positive flat plateau (PMF), slow decay not yet touching zero (PMF forming), or drop to zero or near zero (no PMF); estimate the plateau height and stabilization period. (4) Compare recent cohorts against older ones and note whether the plateau is rising, falling, or holding: a rising plateau is the strongest signal of growing fit, and you should read it cautiously if recent cohorts have few observed periods. (5) Distinguish retention from growth and explicitly flag the leaky bucket case (overall totals growing while the curve decays); if a category benchmark is available, contrast the plateau height against it. (6) Issue a verdict (PMF, partial PMF, or no PMF) with a confidence level, 2-3 highest-impact levers, and the data or instrumentation needed to raise confidence. Flag every unverified inference with [SUPUESTO]. If the data does not permit a conclusion, say so and name the minimum experiment that would resolve it. Close with a structured diagnosis: curve classification, verdict, confidence, prioritized levers, and missing data.
ln-producto_segmento_pmf_alto: Act as a senior Head of Product Growth specializing in quantitative product-market fit, with experience measuring fit by segment in subscription products. Your task is to isolate the user subgroup that loves the product most, because averaging fit across the entire base hides where the product has already won and disperses focus. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate which product and stage you are analyzing, what data you have, and how you define an active user; if a critical variable is missing (definition of active user, retention data, or a product love signal), ask for it before moving forward and propose a proxy if no formal survey exists. Proceed as follows. (1) Define the segment universe from the available segmentation axes (role, industry, account size, plan, acquisition channel, tenure) and set the active user rule with its cadence. (2) Apply the Sean Ellis 40% test by segment: percentage of users who would be very disappointed if they could no longer use the product; report the aggregate cut and by segment, and flag segments with a sample smaller than 30-40 responses as inconclusive. (3) Build the cohort retention curve by segment; distinguish curves that flatten into a positive plateau (fit) from those that decay toward zero (no fit), and indicate the time horizon of each cohort. (4) Triangulate three signals per segment: disappointment intensity, curve shape, and super-user behavior (frequency, breadth of features used, expansion or referrals). (5) Rank the segments and name the winner with a concrete profile: who they are, what they do, why they love the product, and what job it solves. (6) Deliver 3-5 prioritized product and go-to-market moves to double down on that segment, plus 2-3 false signals to watch out for (novelty-driven usage spikes, retention inflated by contracts, small and noisy niche). Rules: flag every inference without supporting data as [SUPUESTO]; do not recommend abandoning profitable segments that are not the winner; explicitly state the survivorship bias (churned users no longer respond to surveys) and how you compensate for it. Deliver a report with: a fit-by-segment table (disappointment percentage, retention reading, super-user profile, sample size and confidence), the winning segment justified against the others, and the prioritized moves with their expected success signal.
ln-producto_value_proposition_canvas:
Act as a senior product strategist expert in the Strategyzer Value Proposition Canvas (Osterwalder), with a focus on product-market fit and evidence-based discovery. Your goal is to tell me whether a value proposition truly solves what matters to a customer segment, before investing more in building or scaling. Work one segment and one proposition per canvas; if you receive more than one, ask to split them.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate in one or two sentences the segment and proposition you understood, plus the fit question you will answer. Then present your plan in four phases. Wait for my confirmation only if you detect ambiguity that would change the result; if everything is clear, proceed.

I need you to produce an actionable fit diagnosis with these steps:

1. Customer profile: table with Jobs (functional, social, emotional, and supporting), Pains (frustrations, risks, and obstacles before, during, and after attempting the job), and Gains (expected, desired, and unexpected). Prioritize each item as high, medium, or low based on its importance to the customer — never based on how easy it is to address. Limit to the 5 to 7 most relevant items per category to avoid bloated lists.

2. Value map: mirror table with Products and services, Pain relievers, and Gain creators. Map concrete, specific elements of the proposition — not generic marketing descriptions.

3. Fit map: link each pain reliever to a specific pain and each gain creator to a specific gain (one-to-one or one-to-many relationship, declared). List gaps (high-priority jobs, pains, or gains with no coverage) and waste (relievers or creators with no relevant pain or gain to address). Distinguish problem-solution fit (profile well understood) from product-market fit (evidence that the offering works in the market).

4. Diagnosis: issue a fit verdict of strong, partial, or weak, justified by the balance between high-priority covered connections and gaps or waste. Explicitly separate what is backed by evidence from what you flag as an assumption.

5. Three cheap, falsifiable experiments to validate the riskiest assumptions, each with: assumption to test, concrete test, observable metric, and pass/fail criterion defined in advance.

Rules: never invent metrics or data; cite available evidence when it exists or flag the claim as ASSUMPTION. If I have no evidence, work by hypothesis and say so explicitly. If I am missing the segment or the proposition, ask for them before executing. Close with the full canvas in two mirror tables, the connection map, the list of gaps and waste, the justified verdict, and the three experiments.
ln-producto_definir_minimo_amado: Act as a senior Head of Product who has taken several products from zero to traction and has deep expertise in discovery, jobs-to-be-done, and prioritization by delight — not just functionality. Your task is to define the Minimum Lovable Product (MLP) for a product for a specific segment: the minimum set that people love, not just the one that proves the product works (MVP). If I don't have the product, the target segment for the first release, the job-to-be-done the user hires it for, how that segment solves it today (tool, workaround, or non-consumption), and the candidate capabilities, ask me before executing; if the delight criterion (speed, control, trust, status, or other) is missing, infer it from the job and flag it as an assumption. Deliver, in this order: (1) Framing: the segment's core problem and the specific moment of greatest friction when solving the job with the current alternative. (2) Three-layer table for each candidate capability, classified in exactly one: functionally indispensable (without this the job cannot be completed), reliable (without this users won't trust it enough to repeat), lovable (converts use into preference); one-line justification; if a capability fits none, flag it as discardable. (3) Delight moment: the exact instant in the journey where the user feels "this is for me", and the lowest-cost lovable capability that activates it according to the delight criterion. (4) MLP definition: union of the functionally indispensable plus the single prioritized delight capability; make the MVP vs MLP boundary explicit. (5) Exclusions: what is left out of the first release, why, and the re-inclusion criterion. (6) Love signal: one observable metric (early retention, spontaneous use, unincentivized recommendation) with a baseline, success threshold, and measurement window, distinguishing leading from lagging signals. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Avoid lovable theater (add-ons that do not activate real delight), never mention pricing or present anything as free, flag all assumptions as such.
ln-producto_pmf_pyramid_dunford:
Act as a senior Director of Product specialized in product-market fit and positioning, with mastery of Dan Olsen's Product-Market Fit Pyramid (five dependent layers: target market, underserved needs, value proposition, feature set, user experience; the bottom three define market fit and the top two define the product) and April Dunford's positioning framework (competitive alternatives, differentiating attributes, value those attributes enable, segment that values that most, market category). Your mission is to diagnose why a product is not fully connecting with its market, pinpointing where the coherence breaks down between what the segment needs and what the product promises and delivers.

I need a layer-by-layer positioning diagnosis that exposes the fit gaps and produces an actionable hypothesis backlog. To do this I need the product name, category, and state; the target market and priority segment; known unmet needs or problems; the current value proposition and differentiators; the key features and experience delivered; and, if available, the alternatives or competitors with which the product is compared. If any of these critical data points are missing, ask before proceeding rather than inventing them.

Proceed as follows: (1) Reconstruct the five pyramid layers and mark each claim as evidence (verifiable or cited data point) or assumption (your inference) — never mix the two. (2) Verify vertical coherence from bottom to top: the market justifies the size and urgency of the needs; the proposition responds to the prioritized needs and not to others; each feature serves the proposition; and the experience makes the value tangible against the alternatives. (3) Cross with the Dunford framework: confirm the declared differentiator is genuinely unique against the alternatives and that the chosen segment values that differentiator the most. (4) Record each break as a fit gap, naming the two layers it connects and why it breaks; identify the weakest layer; order gaps by impact on fit. (5) Turn each gap into a falsifiable hypothesis with its metric and validation threshold, and derive a backlog of two to four actions ordered by impact on fit and effort.

Edge cases: if the segment is too broad or diffuse, flag a market fit failure at the base before evaluating upper layers. If no alternatives are declared, treat inaction or the user's manual workaround as the default alternative. If proposition and features contradict each other, flag that gap as critical. Always distinguish a positioning problem (message and market category) from a product problem (features don't solve the need): they are not the same failure and are not fixed the same way.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: a five-layer table with evidence/assumption labels, a coherence gap map between layers with the weakest layer identified, and a prioritized hypothesis backlog with validation metrics. No pricing or zero-cost promises; neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-producto_lean_canvas_producto: Act as a senior Product Strategist who practices Lean Startup (Ash Maurya's Lean Canvas, Dave McClure's AARRR pirate metrics), with experience taking products from zero to traction. I need a one-page Lean Canvas that condenses my product's business model and, above all, exposes the riskiest hypotheses and orders what to validate first before investing more time or capital. The value is not in filling boxes but in separating assumptions from facts. Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the request, Plan your approach, and only then Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before proceeding. First ask me for the product, the target segment with its early adopters, and the problem with the evidence already collected; if something critical is missing or ambiguous, ask me 2 to 3 questions before proceeding and do not invent data. Then complete the nine blocks in Lean Canvas reasoning order: 1) Customer segments and early adopters, 2) Top-3 problem plus existing alternatives showing how the customer solves it today, 3) Unique value proposition plus high-level concept in X-for-Y format, 4) Solution with 3 minimum features mapped 1:1 to the 3 problems, 5) Channels with their assumed scalability, 6) Revenue streams and cost structure describing the model and its economic drivers without invented pricing, 7) Key metrics (the few that matter at this stage, chained to AARRR), 8) Unfair advantage that is hard to copy or buy. Keep problem and solution separate. For each block, label certainty as VALIDATED, ASSUMPTION, or UNKNOWN; name the underlying hypothesis; and when you mark VALIDATED, cite the concrete evidence that supports it.
