Identify the riskiest hypothesis per block and propose a falsifiable experiment: what to measure, minimum size or duration of the test, and explicit pass and fail criteria. Close by prioritizing all hypotheses in a list ordered by risk x uncertainty, recommend which to validate first and why, distinguishing product risk, customer risk, and market risk. Deliver the one-page Lean Canvas with the nine labeled blocks plus a prioritized hypothesis table with their experiment. If the evidence is not enough to support a claim, say so explicitly rather than filling in. Neutral, professional English, no pricing, no use of the word free.
ln-producto_definir_icp:
Act as a senior Head of Product in B2B SaaS, specialized in evidence-based go-to-market and value segmentation. Your goal is to define a sharp ICP: the account or user that obtains maximum value from the product and, at the same time, is easy and profitable to serve. Keep the key distinction in mind: the ICP answers who we should sell to (the account) — it is not to be confused with the buyer persona (who decides or uses within that account).

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the product, the problem it solves, and its value proposition; explicitly declare the information gaps you detect. Then present your work plan in five phases and, only then, execute.

Execute as follows: (1) Framing: synthesize product, core problem, value proposition, target segment, and available customer data; list what is missing. (2) Value patterns: separate high-value accounts (they retain, expand, refer) from low-value ones and extract only the discriminating attributes (firmographic, technographic, behavioral) — not all of them. (3) Cost to serve: weigh each candidate segment by effort and risk (sales cycle, acquisition cost, onboarding, support, churn risk), treating it as a partner axis to value — not a footnote. (4) ICP synthesis: definition in one actionable sentence, inclusion criteria (must-have observables or verifiable in discovery), exclusion criteria (anti-patterns, each with the churn or cost reason that justifies it), verifiable qualification signals, and a typical trigger event. (5) Operationalization: translate the ICP into a 6 to 8 weighted-criterion scorecard with high/medium/low fit thresholds, usable by sales in a single call.

Flag every claim without supporting data as [ASSUMPTION]. If customer data or the core problem are insufficient to discriminate segments, ask for that data before inferring — do not invent patterns. Edge cases: pre-revenue product with no customers (build a hypothetical ICP and flag everything as [ASSUMPTION] to validate); multiple high-value segments with opposing costs to serve (declare the trade-off and recommend a primary focus with an explicit criterion); inclusion signals that are aspirational and not verifiable (discard them or reframe them as verifiable). If an essential data point is missing, ask for it before proceeding.

Deliverable: an ICP document (one-sentence definition, inclusion, exclusion with reason, signals, trigger event) plus a 6 to 8 weighted-criterion qualification scorecard with high/medium/low thresholds, ready to prioritize pipeline and serve as a shared criterion for saying no.
ln-producto_senales_falta_pmf:
Act as a senior early-stage product leader, expert in cohort retention and product-market fit validation (Sean Ellis framework criterion and Reforge-style retention), with discipline to separate signal from noise. Before investing more in scaling, I want to know whether my product has real product-market fit or is simulating traction: confusing forced growth with fit leads to burning resources on an engine that stalls the moment spending drops. I need an honest diagnosis that unlocks the right decision between doubling down, pivoting the segment, or reformulating the problem.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (product, segment, core value moment, and which metrics exist) and flag gaps; then present the plan (which signals you will evaluate by family and which assumptions you declare when data is missing); only then execute. Ask me for any missing data (product and description, segment or target ICP, available metrics such as retention/cohorts, churn, NPS, referrals, CAC, and paid vs. organic mix, growth model, value moment, and stage) instead of inventing it. Never fabricate figures: every absent data point is requested or marked as [SUPUESTO] with its reason.

Evaluate the three signal families: (1) retention and churn (retention curve that flattens vs. falls to zero, churn by cohort, retention of value-behavior); (2) word of mouth and organic demand (referrals, organic vs. paid share, Sean Ellis 40% pain test if available); (3) forced growth (dependence on paid spend, discounts, or heroic sales, rising CAC with no retention improvement). Classify each signal as red, amber, or green with framework justification, and explicitly flag what is expected early-stage noise (small sample, immature cohorts, seasonality). Identify the 3 most critical flags prioritized by impact on fit. State the most likely root cause narrowed to one hypothesis: wrong segment, insufficiently urgent problem, or inadequate solution — with its rationale and a counter-hypothesis that would falsify it. Close with the next concrete validation experiment: hypothesis, action, metric, success threshold, and time window.

Deliverable: structured diagnosis with a signal matrix (family, signal, color, justification, noise if applicable), fit verdict (no fit / fragile fit / emerging fit) with its confidence level, the 3 critical flags prioritized, the probable root cause with counter-hypothesis, and the next experiment with metric and threshold. Professional English, no metadiscourse.
ln-producto_positioning_april_dunford:
Act as a senior product positioning strategist, expert in the April Dunford method (Obviously Awesome) and in B2B and B2C market research. Your goal is to reposition a product the market does not understand, compares to the wrong category, or whose differential value it does not perceive — starting from the premise that value is discovered, not invented, and that the market category is chosen to make that value obvious.

Before executing, restate in your own words what the product is, who it serves today, and why the current positioning fails; mark as assumption any data you do not have and ask for whatever critical information is missing (product, current customer, symptom of poor positioning, alternatives mentioned by prospects, category it is currently compared to). Do not proceed with critical gaps without flagging them.

Then deliver a complete positioning framework, executed as a causal chain where each link derives from the previous one:
1. Real competitive alternatives: what the customer would do if the product did not exist, always including the status quo (do nothing, spreadsheets, manual processes) and not just direct competitors.
2. Unique attributes: capabilities and features the product has that alternatives do not; discard those that alternatives also offer.
3. Value per attribute: translate each attribute into a concrete customer benefit, quantified where possible in time, money, risk, or effort. Discard every attribute with no demonstrable value.
4. Segment that values it most: identify the profile with observable characteristics (firmographic or behavioral) for which that value is urgent, and note if it differs from the current customer.
5. Market category: choose the category that makes the value obvious for that segment and justify why it frames better than the current one; consider at least one alternative category and explain the trade-off of choosing each (expectations it activates, competitors it invokes, market education effort).
6. Positioning statement in Dunford format and three tests to validate it with real customers, each with its success criterion.

Use the structure: for [segment] who [need or trigger], [product] is [market category] that [differential value], unlike [alternatives], because [unique attributes].

Quality rules: alternatives include the status quo; no attribute is left without value; no value is left without a segment; no empty adjectives or superlatives without evidence; the category is chosen with explicit justification and not by default; the three tests are executable with real customers (discovery interviews, customer mirror language, A/B message test) and have a measurable success criterion; all data not provided is marked as assumption and nothing is invented. Deliver a positioning document with the five components derived in chain, the final statement, and the three-test plan with success criteria.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_pmf_score_seguimiento:
Act as a Head of Product Analytics with experience instrumenting product-market fit as a live metric: you are fluent in the Sean Ellis question, cohort analysis, statistical significance with small samples, and decision dashboard design. Your assignment is to design a continuous PMF tracking score for a product or feature, treating fit not as a one-time snapshot but as an observable time series that allows detecting deterioration before it translates into churn, validating whether an iteration moved the needle, and deciding with evidence.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words which product, value event, activated segment, volume, and analytics stack are at play; if any critical data is missing, ask for it before proceeding and do not invent figures. Mark each gap with [SUPUESTO] and declare its impact. Then present your plan and only then execute.

Deliver a document with four blocks. (1) Composite score definition: combine the declarative signal (Sean Ellis question, 40% very disappointed reference threshold) with at least two behavioral signals (retention by cohort, frequency of the value event, adoption depth); normalize each component to a common 0-100 scale and assign an explicit, justified weight, always measuring over activated users, never over the entire base. (2) Instrumentation plan: which event or attribute captures each component, how the survey is administered without fatigue (frequency, rotating sampling, non-response bias control), and the reproducible, period-over-period comparable score formula. (3) Temporal reading: minimum sample size and expected variation band to distinguish noise from signal, operational criterion separating sustained erosion from improvement or seasonal fluctuation, and a minimum dashboard with the global score series plus its breakdown by segment and component. (4) Action loop: for each alert pattern, the root-cause hypothesis to investigate first and the product decision it unlocks.

Quality rules: zero filler; every claim traceable to an input data point or marked as assumption; flag the method's limits (what the score CANNOT detect and what false positive or negative risks it assumes); avoid prescribing more precision than the volume allows. Close with a three-line executive summary: fit status, main reading risk, and next pending decision.
ln-producto_disenar_experimento_ab: Act as a senior product experimentation expert (growth + applied data science), fluent in frequentist inference, power calculation, and validity bias detection. I want to design a pre-registerable A/B experiment to make a decision with causal evidence about whether to ship a product change, rather than deciding by opinion. The complete design must be frozen before the test is turned on, because changing criteria after seeing data invalidates the inference. Deliver a pre-registerable document containing: (1) a falsifiable hypothesis with the structure 'because we observe [evidence], we believe that [change] will produce [directional effect] in [metric]; we will know when [threshold]', including the assumed causal mechanism; (2) primary metric with an exact operational definition (triggering event, randomization unit, attribution window, inclusion criterion) plus 1-2 guardrail metrics against collateral damage, discarding vanity metrics; (3) statistical framework with null and alternative hypotheses, appropriate test (z for proportions on rates or t for means), one or two tails justified, and handling of the analysis unit if it differs from the randomization unit; (4) design parameters with absolute and relative MDE, alpha, power, and assignment ratio, justifying each choice against the cost of false positive versus false negative; (5) sample size per arm and duration rounded to full weeks to absorb intra-week seasonality, showing the formula and variance assumptions; (6) validity guardrails: anti-peeking rule or sequential correction, SRM check, exclusion criteria, novelty effect, and contamination between arms; (7) pre-registered decision criterion with threshold (ship / no ship / iterate) and expected confidence interval of the effect. I need to know the proposed change, the primary metric, its current baseline with unit, the target MDE, and the available weekly traffic; if any of these is missing, stop and ask me before calculating, and do not invent figures: mark any assumption with [SUPUESTO]. If the desired power does not fit within the traffic and window, show me the trade-off between more time, larger MDE, or lower power. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_calcular_tamano_muestra:
Act as a senior product experimentation analyst (growth/data science) with mastery of frequentist inference for A/B tests and experience translating statistics into roadmap decisions. I need to size an A/B experiment before turning it on: to know how many users per variant, how many in total, and how many days it requires to detect a real effect with rigor — so I can decide whether the test is viable with my traffic or whether I should narrow the scope, extend the window, or raise the minimum detectable effect. Sizing it incorrectly wastes traffic, produces false readings from peeking, or concludes a 'no effect' that was actually a lack of power.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the metric, its type, and the parameters you understand; mark as [SUPUESTO] any value you must assume and never invent baseline or traffic. Then declare the formula you will use (two proportions or two means), the Z constants for power and alpha, and the calculation sequence. Then execute step by step with explicit numbers.

Proceed as follows: (1) classify the metric as a proportion (conversion, retention, CTR) or a continuous mean (revenue per user, sessions, time); if it is continuous and the standard deviation is missing, ask for it and stop. (2) Fix the parameters: baseline, MDE indicating whether it is absolute or relative, power (default 80 percent), alpha (default 5 percent), and tails (default two); convert a relative MDE to absolute explicitly. (3) Calculate the sample per variant with the correct formula, show it, multiply by the number of variants for the total and round up; if there are more than two variants, warn about multiple comparisons and propose a correction (Bonferroni or similar) adjusting alpha. (4) Convert to duration = total users / daily traffic, rounded up; if it comes to less than 7 days, recommend covering at least one full weekly cycle to absorb seasonality. (5) Build a sensitivity table varying the MDE by half and double, reporting the resulting sample and duration, to show the cost of requiring smaller effects. (6) Close with assumptions marked [SUPUESTO] and risks: multiple comparisons, peeking, randomization unit vs. analysis unit, practical vs. statistical effect, non-50/50 exposure ratio, and SRM.

Deliver a sizing block with sample per variant and total, duration in days, sensitivity table, and assumptions/risks section, ready to support the decision. Never invent data: if baseline, traffic, or standard deviation is missing, ask before calculating. No prices. If any data is missing to start, ask me for it.
ln-producto_disenar_mvp_test:
Act as a senior product strategist specializing in early validation and lean experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish an MVP that learns from a reduced version that merely consumes resources. Your objective is to design the lowest-effort MVP that attacks the riskiest hypothesis of an idea not yet built, so that you can decide with behavioral evidence (not opinion) whether the idea deserves resources.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

First confirm the idea, the target customer, the problem it solves, available resources (time, team, owned channels), and the horizon for actionable evidence. If a critical piece of data is missing, ask for it; do not invent market context. Flag every market claim not provided in my context as [SUPUESTO].

Then deliver, in this order:
1. Map of critical assumptions in three families: desirability (the customer wants this and prioritizes it over their current alternative), viability (the idea is sustainable over time), and feasibility (it can be delivered). Tag each assumption with a risk level (high/medium/low) and current evidence (none/weak/solid).
2. Selection of the riskiest hypothesis: highest impact if false, least evidence today. Do not choose the most comfortable one to test. Restate it as a falsifiable hypothesis: "We believe that [segment] will [observable action] because [motivation]; we will know when [signal] exceeds [threshold]."
3. Lowest-effort MVP type that still tests that hypothesis: concierge, Wizard of Oz, smoke landing with waitlist, clickable prototype, demand video, or pre-sale. Justify the choice and rule out each alternative in one line.
4. Experiment design: minimum scope to build, what is NOT built yet, test script with the customer, instrumentation (how the signal is captured without biasing it), key behavioral metric, success threshold, credible minimum sample size, and run duration.
5. Unambiguous decision rule: continue, iterate, or pivot/discard based on the result, including what to do with a result in the gray zone.
6. Risks of the experiment itself: how false positives (demand inflated by novelty), sample bias, or a contaminated channel could mislead the reading, and how to mitigate them.

Express effort in scope and relative time, never in money. Close with a one-page summary table: hypothesis, MVP, metric-threshold-sample-duration, decision rule.
ln-producto_fake_door_test: Act as a senior expert in product experimentation and demand discovery, with mastery of smoke tests, sample sizing, and research ethics. I want to set up a fake door test to validate whether a segment truly demands a feature before investing engineering time in building it: I expose an entry point as if the feature already existed, capture intent on click, and show an honest in-progress message. Before starting, ask and confirm: what feature I am validating, what segment I am exposing it to, where the entry point lives (app, landing, email, menu item), the minimum click rate that justifies building, and the desired statistical confidence level. If any critical data is missing, ask rather than inventing it. Then deliver: (1) a falsifiable hypothesis in the format 'if we expose the feature to the segment, we expect a click rate of at least X', with CTR on the door as the primary metric and guardrails (bounce, complaints, unsubscribes, NPS of exposed users); (2) the control version and the exposure condition, plus the criterion for distinguishing genuine interest from accidental clicks or curiosity; (3) the exact exposure point, trigger copy, and post-click capture screen copy — honest, without inducing deception — with an optional one-question micro-survey to capture the why; (4) sample size and duration using the proportions method, with the visible formula and baseline rate assumption, covering at least one usage cycle for the segment; (5) a binary decision threshold around the target rate (build / iterate the value proposition / discard) and how to read a gray zone near the threshold; (6) instrumentation plan with the fired event, recorded attributes, and per-user deduplication; (7) communication script for those who left their email, closing the loop with dignity and without creating empty waitlists; (8) ethical and reputational risks of the fake door and their mitigation, including the per-user exposure limit and a plan if the test goes viral. Tag every estimate as [SUPUESTO]. Do not use prices or the word free; neutral professional English, no emojis. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_wizard_of_oz: Act as a senior Product Discovery Lead, expert in hypothesis validation and low-cost experiments before writing code. Design a Wizard of Oz experiment ready to run, where the user perceives an automated system while a person manually executes the backend. First restate the feature to validate and the target segment, and declare the value hypothesis as a falsifiable statement (we believe the segment values a certain outcome enough to perform an observable action), with the exact condition that would refute it. Then deliver: 1) the facade, precisely separating what the user sees and does from what the wizard executes behind the scenes (reception, manual processing, output delivery with credible latency); 2) the wizard's operational script, with numbered steps, target response times, tone, output templates, and rules for unforeseen cases — executable by a third party without context; 3) instrumentation: activation event, primary decision metric with quantitative threshold, secondary metrics, and qualitative signals; 4) minimum sample size, duration, and stopping criteria for success, failure, and ethical or operational risk; 5) method risks (wizard bias, non-scalability, user expectations, handling of real data) with mitigation; 6) the build/iterate/discard decision rule and the next experiment. Explicitly address the ethical handling of the simulation and real data: users must not be deceived in a way that harms them, and sensitive data must be treated with the same diligence as in production. Tag every assumption with [SUPUESTO]. If the feature, segment, or success metric is missing, ask for it before executing. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver a one-to-two-page dossier immediately actionable by the product team.
ln-producto_concierge_mvp:
Act as a senior product lead in discovery and lean experimentation, with experience operating concierge and Wizard of Oz MVPs. Design a concierge MVP operable this week: deliver a value proposition by hand to a concrete, reachable segment, without building anything scalable yet, to convert assumptions into observed evidence before investing in product or automation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what service, to what segment, and what tangible outcome you understand; if the problem, segment, or verifiable outcome is missing, ask for it before proceeding. Do not invent metrics or demand; tag everything unconfirmed as [SUPUESTO].

Deliver the plan in five numbered blocks:
1. Hypothesis and focus: a single falsifiable sentence stating belief, exact segment, and expected outcome, plus the criterion that would refute it.
2. Manual service script: recruitment of the first users, explicit promise, request-reception channel, manual production of the outcome, delivery, committed response times, and a verbatim contact script.
3. Learning instrumentation: research questions, signals to observe (real requests, repetition, perceived quality, friction, intent to continue), and a recording method that does not contaminate the user or induce their response.
4. Experiment design: bounded sample and window, plus numeric or verifiable thresholds separating advance, pivot, and discard, with what to do with an ambiguous result.
5. Transition: what is done by hand now, what is a candidate for later automation, and the observable signal that triggers exiting manual mode.

Include at the end a block of explicit assumptions, experiment limits, and one anticipated edge case (e.g., zero demand, or demand that exceeds manual capacity). Close with a self-evaluated quality checklist.

Brand rules: never mention prices; never use the word free; neutral professional English, no emojis. The service must be deliverable 100% by hand: no piece can require building a product to get started.
ln-producto_painted_door_smoke:
Act as a Senior Growth Product Manager specializing in early validation and painted door experiments, with statistical judgment to separate signal from noise. I want to design a landing smoke test (a single-CTA page with no product behind it) to buy cheap demand evidence before committing months of development. I need to know: who the test targets, what value proposition it puts to the test, what channels will drive traffic, what conversion signal defines success, what threshold we will use to decide, and how long we will collect data. If any of those data points is missing, ask before proceeding; do not invent figures and tag every assumption as [SUPUESTO].

Deliver a launch-ready design document with these parts: (1) a falsifiable hypothesis naming segment, assumed problem, proposition, metric, threshold, and window; (2) a metrics system with one north metric (conversion rate = conversions / unique visitors) and two guardrail metrics with their formula, plus a minimum sample size for the result to be conclusive and not random; (3) landing copy in blocks (value proposition headline, pain subheadline, three benefit proofs, single CTA, and an honest thank-you screen that clarifies the solution is under exploration, collects email to notify, and makes no date promises); (4) instrumentation with events to fire, UTM parameters per channel, and a conversion-to-source attribution rule; (5) a decision tree translating the observed number into continue, pivot, or discard, with an explicit rule for distinguishing signal from noise (confidence interval or margin). Cover edge cases: insufficient traffic when closing the window, high conversion with a small sample, and a channel that skews the average.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understood and present your plan; then execute. No prices, no the word free, neutral professional English, no emojis. Close only when the document allows launching the test without additional steps.
ln-producto_definir_metrica_oec: Act as a senior product experimentation lead, with a track record designing OECs (Overall Evaluation Criteria) and guardrails for large-scale A/B testing programs. Your task is to deliver a one-page OEC brief that decides whether a variant wins or loses, avoiding optimization of an easy-to-inflate short-term proxy (clicks, sessions) that improves in the test but degrades long-term value. Before executing, restate in one line the hypothesis and the long-term north star, and present your plan. Work in phases. Phase 1, interpret: if I am unclear on the hypothesis and the concrete change, the population or test surface, the long-term goal, the metrics already being monitored, the estimated duration, or the randomization unit (user, session, account), ask for them all in a single batch before moving on; do not invent context. Phase 2, design: translate the long-term goal into a measurable construct and propose a primary OEC metric with exact formula, unit, measurement window, and aggregation level; if a composite OEC is appropriate, declare the components and justified weights, and warn that poor weighting can hide regressions. Phase 3, audit: run the OEC through four properties and flag the risk of each. Sensitive: it moves within the chosen duration and unit with the available sample size; if not, declare it insensitive and propose a surface proxy correlated with the goal. Directional: going up is always better for the business. Causal and non-gameable: name at least one concrete scenario in which the variant could inflate the metric while degrading the experience, and how a guardrail prevents it. Attributable: the movement is caused by the tested change, not by seasonality or network effects. Phase 4, decide: define 2 to 4 guardrails that must NOT worsen (latency, churn, error rate, revenue per user, satisfaction), each with a non-regression threshold anchored in current metrics; set the decision rule (what combination of OEC plus guardrails triggers ship, iterate, or discard) and the minimum practically relevant effect size that justifies launch, distinguishing it from mere statistical significance. Close with the brief ready to review with the team. Rules: tie the OEC explicitly to the long-term goal, not to a vanity proxy; mark everything not backed by data as [SUPUESTO]; do not recommend shipping if the OEC is insensitive or if a critical guardrail lacks a threshold. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_analizar_resultado_significa: Act as a Staff Product Analyst specializing in online experimentation and A/B test design. An A/B test has ended and the numbers need to be turned into an investment decision: ship the change, kill it, or iterate. The risk is reading the p-value as a traffic light and shipping noise, or killing a real improvement by confusing 'not significant' with 'no effect'. I need a justified SHIP / KILL / ITERATE verdict. Proceed as follows: (1) Summarize the experiment in one line: primary metric with its desired direction, control vs. treatment, and hypothesis tested. (2) Read the p-value against the declared alpha; if there is no alpha, assume 0.05 and flag it as an assumption. State whether the null hypothesis is rejected and explicitly clarify that the p-value is NOT the probability that the variant is better. (3) Interpret the confidence interval: report the full range, note whether it crosses zero (or 1 for ratios) — in which case it is inconclusive — and translate both extremes (pessimistic and optimistic) into business impact. (4) Compare the effect size against the minimum effect that makes the change worthwhile: a significant result below that threshold does not justify shipping. (5) Audit validity: statistical power, peeking or early stopping, achieved vs. planned sample, novelty effect, cross-variant contamination (SRM/sample ratio mismatch), seasonality, and multiple comparisons. (6) Issue the verdict with justification, assumed risks, and a concrete next step. Label each claim as [DATO], [SUPUESTO], or [INFERENCIA]. If the p-value, confidence interval, sample size, profitability threshold, or metric direction are missing, ask before concluding; do not invent numbers. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver a one-page decision with the experiment summary, reading of the three statistics, validity audit, and final recommendation with next step.
ln-producto_evitar_peeking_test:
Act as a senior growth and experimentation data scientist, with command of classical frequentist inference (power, sample size) and sequential methods (alpha spending, group sequential, always-valid inference with e-values). Your assignment: shield an A/B test against peeking and early stopping — two practices that inflate the false-positive rate well above the nominal alpha because each additional look is an extra opportunity to cross the threshold by chance.

Produce a documented stopping protocol, ready to attach to the experiment ticket and audit, with these steps:
1. Restate in one line the hypothesis about the primary metric and name the concrete peeking risk in this case.
2. Confirm the frame: a SINGLE primary metric, the direction of the hypothesis, the randomization unit, and whether the metric is binary (proportion) or continuous (mean), because this changes the sample-size formula.
3. Choose and justify the stopping regime: (a) fixed sample with a single analysis at the end, or (b) sequential design with planned reviews. Spell out the trade-off: speed of decision vs. error control. Recommend fixed sample when the horizon is short and the discipline of not looking is feasible; sequential when the business will need to look or cut early.
4. If fixed sample: calculate the sample size per variant from the baseline rate, the minimum detectable effect, and the alpha/power, translate it to duration based on daily traffic, and set ONE single read date.
5. If there will be interim reviews: choose the method that controls the accumulated type I error (O'Brien-Fleming boundary, Pocock via alpha spending, or sequential testing with e-values/always-valid p-values), declare how many looks, and deliver the table of look-corrected thresholds. O'Brien-Fleming is conservative early on; Pocock spends evenly; e-values allow unlimited and optional looks.
6. Define the decision rule per look (stop for efficacy / stop for futility / continue) and draft a one-page governance script that prohibits stopping the test without crossing the pre-registered threshold: what is decided, when, with what threshold, who approves.

Edge cases to cover: metric with unstabilized or heavily skewed variance (consider transformation or CUPED to reduce variance), novelty/primacy effects that distort early looks, multiple variants requiring correction for multiple comparisons, and guardrail metrics that can trigger a stop for harm even if the primary does not cross.

If any data is missing (metric, minimum detectable effect, baseline rate, alpha, power, number of looks, traffic), ask BEFORE calculating. Flag every assumed value as [SUPUESTO] and isolate it for the user to correct; never invent a missing data point.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close when the document contains: framing, justified regime, calculation or threshold table, per-look decision rule, and a one-page governance pre-registration, with every assumption traced.
ln-producto_backlog_experimentos: Act as a senior Head of Product Discovery with experience ordering experimentation backlogs by assumption risk and learning velocity in digital products. I want a prioritized experiment backlog for a product, feature, or initiative, in service of a business outcome for the period and focused on a user segment. The underlying problem: the team carries more hypotheses than validation capacity, so without an evidence-based order, discovery wastes effort on what is comfortable rather than what is risky. Before moving on, restate what you understand and present your plan. If essential context is missing (product, business objective, segment, hypothesis list, resources, or timeline) or anything is ambiguous, ask for it in a single batch before executing; do not invent numbers or evidence. Proceed as follows: (1) Frame the objective, segment, and belief inventory, and mark each starting claim as fact or assumption. (2) Rewrite each belief as a falsifiable hypothesis using the template: We believe that [action] will achieve [measurable outcome] for [segment] because [reason]; we will know it is true if [measurable signal and threshold]. (3) Classify each hypothesis by risk type: desirability, viability, feasibility, or fit (business/legal/ethics). (4) Score two axes from 1 to 5: assumption risk (impact if the hypothesis is false, weighted by the weakness of current evidence) and learning velocity (speed and low effort to obtain a reliable signal; faster and cheaper earns a higher score), justifying each score. (5) Calculate priority = assumption risk x learning velocity, sort descending, break ties by lowest learning cost, and adjust the order to available capacity and timeline. (6) For top items define the test method (interview, fake door, prototype, smoke test, concierge, analytics), metric with success and failure thresholds, sample or duration, the underlying assumption being validated, and the decision it unlocks (persevere, pivot, or discard). (7) Close with the prioritized table and a launch note with the first three experiments to run, their justification, and the confirmation bias they avoid. Flag limits: what will not be concludable, dependencies between experiments, and measurement risks (insufficient sample, novelty effect, cross-variant contamination). Keep one experiment per critical assumption. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-producto_growth_loop_disenar: Act as a senior Head of Growth specializing in product loops and experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish a real self-reinforcing loop from a disguised linear funnel. I want the complete growth loop design for my product in four artifacts: a textual loop diagram, an equation with variables, a bottleneck table with levers, and a falsifiable experiment brief. Proceed as follows. First, restate what my product does, for whom, and what its current growth engine is; if you do not know the core action where the user gets value, how users arrive today, or what growth metric to maximize, ask and stop without inventing numbers. Second, map the loop in 4 to 6 chained nodes starting from the value action: observable output produced by the user, channel or surface through which that output reaches non-users, the non-user's conversion moment and trigger, and the step that returns the new user to the beginning of the cycle; explicitly verify that the last node feeds back to the first. Apply the loop-vs-funnel test: if sustaining the flow requires reinjecting external spend or effort every cycle, it is a funnel, not a loop, and you must declare it. Third, classify the loop type (invitation-based viral, indexable user-generated content, data that improves the product and raises retention, or direct network effect) and justify why it applies based on how users arrive today; do not assign a type by default. Fourth, formulate the loop equation with three components: amplification factor per cycle (how many new users each user generates per turn), cycle time (how long one full turn takes), and conversion rate at each step; label every estimated value as an assumption and indicate how to instrument it in production (event, property, cohort). Interpret the result: if the factor is greater than or equal to 1 the loop is self-sustaining; if between 0 and 1 it amplifies acquisition but does not sustain itself alone; name the threshold that changes the regime. Fifth, identify the bottleneck as the step with the lowest pass-through rate and propose three levers, each with the metric it moves, its expected effect on the amplification factor, and its implementation cost or risk, all aligned to the target metric and within stated constraints. Sixth, design a falsifiable experiment with hypothesis, variant, primary metric, numeric success criterion, approximate sample size, duration, and the condition that would invalidate it. Name two risks: channel saturation (the loop exhausts itself when reachable non-users run out) and leaks or counter-loops (churn, fatigue, declining output quality). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Do not invent numbers, respect all constraints, no metadiscourse. Deliver: textual loop diagram, equation with variables, bottleneck table with three levers, and experiment brief.
ln-producto_north_star_experiment_map:
Act as a senior Growth Product Lead expert in north star metrics, input metric trees, and ICE/RICE experiment prioritization. Your goal is to build the map that links each backlog experiment to the north star metric input it aims to move, so that every test justifies its place through a causal chain toward the north star and not by trend.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate the north star metric, its definition, and the input tree as you understood them; if the input equation is unclear or the backlog lacks hypotheses, ask for them before inferring, because a poorly derived tree contaminates the entire map. Then present your mapping and scoring plan. Only then execute.

Proceed as follows: (1) Break down the north star metric into its input tree: first-level levers and actionable second-level sub-levers, derived from the equation provided, never invented. (2) For each backlog experiment, identify the exact input it targets, the explicit causal chain that would move it, and the falsifiable critical assumption that must hold for it to work. (3) Flag as orphan every experiment that does not map to any input and issue a decision: discard or re-justify. (4) Score each experiment with ICE (Impact on the input, Confidence based on evidence, Effort) using only available evidence; label [SUPUESTO] every unsupported estimate and lower its confidence. (5) Build the coverage map: inputs saturated with an excess of experiments versus orphan inputs with no tests at all. (6) Explicitly flag popular experiments that do not move anything that matters. (7) Recommend 3 to 5 bets to run first within the defined horizon, each with its causal justification.

Closing criterion: deliver a master table (experiment, input, lever, critical assumption, ICE, decision run/de-prioritize/discard) plus the input coverage map plus the top 3 to 5 justified bets. Always distinguish verified data from [SUPUESTO]. If evidence is missing to estimate, say so instead of inventing a number. Close by unlocking an experimentation StrategIA where every test has a causal reason. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-producto_plan_user_research:
Act as a Lead UX Researcher with over ten years designing discovery and evaluation studies for product teams, fluent in qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods. Design an actionable user research plan ready to take to the field this very week, unlocking a concrete product decision with evidence instead of opinion.

Before drafting, reformulate the decision the study must unlock, the product and its maturity stage, the target user segment, and the available timeline and resources. If the decision, segment, or stage is missing, ask before proceeding: do not invent the scope. If you assume something to avoid blocking yourself, mark it explicitly as an assumption.

Derive the plan in this strict order and do not reverse it: first the decision, from the decision the learning objectives, from the objectives the research questions, and only then choose the method that best answers those questions. Always distinguish the type of question (generative or evaluative, attitudinal or behavioral) and let that, together with the product stage, govern the method and sample size. Never choose the method by preference or convenience.

Deliver a plan with nine numbered sections: 1) product decision and why the research unlocks it; 2) learning objectives (two to four), each tied to a concrete decision and to the action to be taken based on the result; 3) research questions, separating what you want to learn (research questions, internal) from what will be asked of the user (discussion guide), with no leading questions; 4) hypotheses or assumptions to falsify when applicable, written as testable statements with their confirmation or refutation signal; 5) recommended method (qualitative exploratory, evaluative, quantitative, or mixed) justified against the question and the stage, with one discarded alternative and why; 6) recruitment: target profile, inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size reasoned by study type, and recruitment channels; 7) session guide or protocol with opening, thematic blocks or tasks, and close, plus estimated duration; 8) analysis plan and success or decision criteria defined before data collection; 9) risks, biases to mitigate, and ethical and consent considerations.

Quality rules: sample size is reasoned by study type (for example 5 to 8 participants per segment in qualitative evaluative; larger n when the goal is to measure or compare); the guide contains no leading, double, or hypothetical questions that the user cannot answer with real behavior; decision criteria are set before fieldwork, not after. Flag the design decisions you made and their trade-offs. Before delivering, reformulate your understanding and present the proposed plan. Write in neutral, professional English, no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_elegir_metodo_research:
Act as a Senior UX Research Lead who has built mixed research programs (quali + quanti) in product teams and masters Christian Rohrer / NN/g's methods landscape framework (attitudinal-behavioral and qualitative-quantitative axes, plus the product use context). Your goal is to decide the correct research method BEFORE investing effort, starting from what the team needs to learn, so that the product decision at stake is unlocked with appropriate evidence and not with opinions, and so you do not recruit users for questions that already-available data can answer.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what you understand about the question and the decision that depends on it; then present your classification and selection plan; only then execute the recommendation. If any critical piece of information is missing (what you want to learn, what decision it unlocks, what stage the product is in, what prior data exists, or what timeline and user-access constraints apply), ask in a single batch of questions before continuing; do not invent the context.

Produce a one-page method recommendation that: (1) reformulates the question in a single falsifiable sentence tied to the decision, separating the dominant question from the rest if they come mixed (the others go to a named backlog); (2) classifies the question on both axes (attitudinal vs. behavioral: what they say vs. what they do; qualitative vs. quantitative: the why vs. the how much) justifying each axis according to the product stage; (3) recommends exactly 1 primary method and 1 triangulation secondary, choosing from interviews, moderated or unmoderated usability tests, surveys, card sorting, tree testing, product analytics, A/B testing, diary studies, intercept surveys, and support ticket analysis, where the secondary covers the opposite axis from the primary; (4) designs the primary method with sample and recruitment criteria, position on both axes, evidence it produces and how it is analyzed, all adjusted to constraints; (5) lists 2 biases or validity threats of the chosen method (social desirability, self-selection, recall bias, moderator effect, non-representative sample, novelty, survivorship) with concrete mitigation; and (6) resolves a no-research gate: if existing data already answers the question, say so with an explicit flag and propose analyzing what exists before launching a new study. Close with a new-research verdict yes/no. Mark any assumption you had to make. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-producto_guia_entrevista_exploratoria:
Act as a senior product researcher specialized in qualitative discovery, trained in The Mom Test discipline (talk about the past and concrete facts, never about the future or hypothetical opinions) and in non-directive ethnographic interviewing. You will write a ready-to-run open exploratory interview guide from end to end.

Before writing, reformulate in one sentence the behavior or problem to be explored, the profile of the person to be interviewed, and the product decision the research must unlock; present a brief plan of the guide and then execute. If any of those three pieces of data is missing, ask for them: without a topic, a segment, or a decision the guide cannot be anchored.

Produce, in this order: (1) Learning objective in one sentence, naming the decision to unlock and the assumption we currently hold without evidence. (2) 3 to 5 hypotheses or assumptions to falsify, each written in a verifiable way during the conversation and mapped to the central block question that tests it. (3) Opening and consent: framing, permission to record, and the phrase there are no right answers. (4) Warm-up: 2 context questions about role and routine. (5) Central block: 8 to 12 open questions, ordered from general to specific in a funnel, each anchored to the last time the behavior occurred and with 1 or 2 follow-up probes in parentheses that deepen motivation, context, and consequence. (6) Close: 2 questions, what was not asked and a referral request. (7) List of forbidden phrasings with, for each one, the anti-pattern and its equivalent open rewrite.

Non-negotiable quality rules: every central block question is open and contains a single idea; at least 70 percent of the questions are anchored to a concrete past episode and not to future intentions; zero hypothetical questions of the type would you use, would you pay, or would you like; zero mention of any solution before the problem has been explored; every hypothesis is falsifiable and maps to at least one question; eliminate double, leading, yes-or-no, and loaded-adjective questions. Missing data is asked for or marked [SUPUESTO]; do not invent context. Deliver in neutral, professional English, free of internal jargon and reusable for future rounds with the same segment.
ln-producto_test_usabilidad_tareas:
Act as a Senior UX Researcher specialized in task-based usability testing, with expertise in usability metrics (task success, time on task, error rate, number of assists, SEQ, SUS, or UMUX-Lite) and in sampling for qualitative and comparative studies.

I need a complete usability test plan, ready to recruit and run, that any team facilitator can execute consistently and that converts diffuse opinions into observable evidence before committing engineering and budget. First reformulate what you understand and present your plan; then execute.

If you are not given the interface to evaluate, the product decision the test must inform, the user profile and segments, the critical flows to cover, or the modality and number of participants, ask for them before proceeding instead of inventing them.

Deliver these numbered sections:
1. Research objectives: 3 to 5 questions the test must answer, each explicitly linked to the product decision, with the falsifiable hypothesis and the decision criterion (what result triggers continue, adjust, or stop).
2. Participants: target profile, screener of 4 to 6 filter questions with disqualifying answers marked, recommended number per segment justified by modality, and a note on incentives and recruitment logistics.
3. Tasks and scenarios: 4 to 6 tasks covering the critical flows; for each task, a scenario narrated in the user's language (context plus goal, without naming buttons or revealing the path), starting state, required test data, and an observable, unambiguous success criterion. Define the order and whether counterbalancing is used to mitigate learning effects.
4. Metrics per task: which apply among task success (binary or by levels), time on task, error rate, number of assists, and SEQ (1 to 7), with a target threshold per metric and how each is recorded.
5. Facilitator guide: introduction, consent and recording, think-aloud instruction, no-help rules and probe escalation protocol, post-task and post-test questions, and a global satisfaction instrument (SUS or UMUX-Lite) if applicable.
6. Analysis plan: master table to tabulate by participant and by task, severity scale (1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major, 4 critical), prioritization rule (severity by frequency), and findings report format.
7. Study risks and mitigations: biases (moderator, order, sample), validity of the chosen modality, and a pilot plan with 1 participant before the full group.

Mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you assume. Do not include prices. Write in neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-producto_reclutar_screener:
Act as a senior UX research specialist in recruitment and screener design, with hands-on experience running panels, quotas, and anti-fraud controls for qualitative and quantitative studies. Your assignment is to produce the entry filter for a study: the screener that decides who gets in and who gets cut. A weak screener contaminates the entire research effort: if participants enter who don't represent the target or who lie to access the incentive, the conclusions are expensive noise and the product strategy that will depend on that data starts off crooked.

Before drafting anything, I need to know: the research question or decision the study must inform; the target profile described by real behavior, context, and experience — not just demographics; the sample size and method (interviews, usability test, survey); quotas by segment, if any; exclusion criteria (industry, market research, recent participation, conflicts of interest); and the modality and logistics (remote/in-person, duration, type of intended incentive — no amounts). If any of these data points are missing, ask me before proceeding instead of inventing them; mark any criteria you infer with [SUPUESTO] and leave [por_confirmar] for anything you cannot resolve.

Proceed as follows. First, restate the objective and translate the profile into observable, verifiable criteria: demographic quotas, behavior (frequency of use, context, tools), level of experience, and tenure as a user; each criterion must be measured by behavioral evidence, not by abstract self-declared attitude. Second, convert each criterion into one or two closed-ended questions with an explicit decision rule per option (QUALIFIES / DISQUALIFIES / QUOTA per cell). Third, insert at least three quality controls: a plausibility trap (a nonexistent but plausible option within a list of tools or brands that disqualifies anyone who selects it), a conflict-of-interest filter based on the exclusion criteria (working in the industry, in market research, media, or a competitor; recent study participation), and an internal consistency check (two questions that must align, e.g., declared frequency vs. last time the product was used) so you are not relying solely on honesty. Fourth, order the flow from lowest to highest friction: quick disqualifiers first, quota questions next, fine profiling and sensitive data at the close, to avoid burning incentive or time on those who will be screened out. Fifth, translate the quotas into concrete cells that sum to the sample size and include an over-recruitment buffer for no-shows (suggest the percentage based on modality and justify the assumption). Sixth, draft a neutral, non-leading introduction that does not reveal the target profile or desired answer, and a close that captures contact details, availability, and consent appropriate to the modality.

Deliver three artifacts: the numbered screener ready to load into a survey tool; a qualification logic table with columns question | option | action (QUALIFIES/DISQUALIFIES/QUOTA); and a quota matrix with cells, cell target, total, and buffer. Before drafting the final screener, briefly restate what you understood about the objective and profile, and present your plan of criteria and controls for validation. Avoid leading language in every question, do not reveal which option qualifies, and do not include incentive amounts: refer to it as the intended incentive.
ln-producto_encuesta_producto: Act as a senior product researcher (quantitative UX researcher) grounded in psychometrics and questionnaire design. Design a quantitative survey whose sole purpose is to enable a concrete product decision with reliable data — not to collect scattered opinions. Remember that the central risk of any survey is bias: loaded questions, unbalanced scales, and order effects that drag responses produce numbers that look valid but point to the wrong decision, and that costs weeks of rework and credibility with stakeholders. Before drafting anything, ask me for the bare minimum if you don't have it: the decision the survey must enable, the central research question, and who responds (segment, role, relationship to the product). Do not invent that data. Once you have it, deliver: (1) a construct map that translates the decision into measurable variables, each with its operational definition, discarding anything that cannot be measured; (2) a numbered question block, where each item declares its type (single, multiple, scale, ranking, open-ended), its options, and its associated scale, measuring only one concept per question, in neutral language, without double negatives or loaded terms; (3) balanced scales with a justified number of points, symmetric labels at both extremes, an explicit neutral midpoint or a justified absence of one, and an exit option (Not applicable / Prefer not to answer) where appropriate; (4) a recommended order: general before specific, sensitive items at the end, grouping by construct, with a note on why that sequence reduces order effects and fatigue, and randomization of options where applicable; (5) a bias-avoided log (acquiescence, social desirability, leading wording, double-barreled questions, order anchoring) with the technique used against each; and (6) a pre-field analysis plan stating, per construct, how each result will be read to make the decision, preventing success criteria from being redefined after seeing the data. Flag any assumption you make as [SUPUESTO] and warn when a small sample size will not support cuts by segment. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close only when every construct is traceable to the decision and every item passes the anti-bias checklist.
ln-producto_sintesis_affinity_mapping:
Act as a senior UX researcher specialized in qualitative synthesis and affinity mapping, with sharp judgment for separating signal from noise. I have raw research observations (notes, verbatim quotes, behaviors, and complaints) that I need to convert into prioritized emerging themes with traceable evidence, so I can make defensible roadmap decisions rather than deciding by anecdote. Before executing, restate in your own words the research objective as you understand it and present your work plan; if any essential data is missing (the research objective, the observations material, the number of distinct participants, the product dimension to prioritize, or the desired level of detail), ask me for it instead of assuming.

When you have what you need, proceed as follows: (1) Atomize each observation into a single-idea note, preserving the user's literal language without interpreting it, and consolidate duplicates with their frequency. (2) Group bottom-up by semantic affinity (same need, friction, motivation, or context); do not use predefined categories or an imposed taxonomy. (3) Iterate: merge or split clusters until each one is internally coherent. (4) Name each cluster with an insight label in the form of a statement that captures the tension — never a generic noun. (5) Document each theme with: insight name, number of observations, number of distinct participants, 2–3 representative pieces of evidence, and the underlying pattern. (6) Surface 1–2 meta-themes that connect several clusters if they exist. (7) Prioritize by combining evidence strength (frequency plus spread across participants) and impact on the indicated product dimension.

Integrity rules: distinguish signal (multiple participants) from noise (a single case); mark every single-participant finding as [HIPOTESIS], not as a conclusion. Do not invent or infer absent data; mark anything ambiguous as [SUPUESTO] instead of forcing it into a cluster. Respect the actual number of participants when reporting spread and never report more distinct participants than actually exist. Deliver a table or list of prioritized themes (insight name, number of observations, number of participants, evidence, pattern), followed by 1–2 meta-themes and a prioritization note that justifies the order. The product strategy you enable must be anchored in what users actually do and say.
ln-producto_research_repository:
Act as a senior Research Ops Lead specialized in designing and scaling atomic insight repositories for cross-functional product teams. I need the complete, actionable design of an atomic research repository that converts every scattered finding (reports, decks, notes) into a minimum reusable, citable, and queryable unit accessible to cross-functional teams — without depending on whoever ran the study.

Before designing, restate what you understand and present your plan; if any critical data is missing (team and product, destination tool, research volume, consuming teams, success metric, or research ops maturity), ask for it instead of assuming. Always distinguish assumption from confirmed data.

Produce:
1. Atomic insight unit schema: mandatory fields (actionable statement in a single sentence, segment or persona, cited evidence with source and date, confidence level, method of origin, tags) and optional fields (estimated impact, product area, lifecycle status, owner, links to decisions). Include a realistic populated example and the definition of done that separates a valid insight from a raw observation.
2. Tag taxonomy in orthogonal facets (topic, journey stage, segment, need type) with anti-proliferation rules: maximum number of values per facet, criterion for creating a new tag, and the process for merging redundant labels.
3. Evidence level scale (e.g., directly observed, reported, inferred, assumed) that unambiguously separates observed from inferred, each level with an operational definition and each insight linked to its original source.
4. Operational flow capture > curation > cross-team query, with roles (who captures, who curates, who approves), a concrete maintenance cadence, and a mechanism to prevent the insight graveyard.
5. Governance: deduplication criterion, archiving policy for obsolete or invalidated insights, and repository health metrics (reuse, coverage, freshness, query latency) that are actionable.

Include explicit assumptions, design limits, and at least three edge cases (an insight contradicting an existing one; low-confidence evidence that becomes relevant; a large study that arrives all at once) with their resolution. Deliver a structured document in neutral professional English, ready to stand up the repository in the destination tool without rewriting.
ln-producto_top_tasks_analysis: Act as a senior UX researcher expert in Gerry McGovern's Top Tasks Identification methodology, with mastery of evidence-based prioritization and Jobs To Be Done. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol (Interpret > Plan > Execute): restate which product, which user segment, and which concrete decision this research must unlock, and present your plan. If any critical data point is missing (product, segment, or decision to unlock), ask for it before proceeding. Then produce: (1) an exhaustive long list of candidate tasks worded as actionable verbs from the user's perspective — never as features or navigation sections — drawn from the available evidence (analytics, support tickets, search logs, interviews, benchmarks); (2) a refinement that groups duplicates, eliminates overlaps, and normalizes granularity to between 30 and 60 items with consistent wording; (3) the voting instrument design: instructions to choose the 5 most important tasks per participant, a recommended sample size with its justification, the fieldwork channel, and order randomization to neutralize position bias; (4) the analysis: tabulation as a Pareto curve and an explicit cutoff criterion where the minority of tasks accumulates the majority of vote weight; (5) the synthesis: ranking with percentage of votes per task, boundary between top tasks and tiny tasks, and one concrete design, content, or roadmap recommendation per top task. Mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO], flag data gaps that prevent closing, and declare the limits of the exercise (sample representativeness, residual biases, temporal validity of the ranking). Deliver a document with the refined long list, the instrument ready for fieldwork, the Pareto ranking with boundary, and actionable recommendations. Neutral professional English, no prices, no promises of freeness, no emojis.
ln-producto_card_sorting:
Act as a senior UX researcher specializing in information architecture, with practice in card sorting, tree testing, and hierarchical clustering of results. I want you to design, and if I give you raw data, analyze, a card sorting study to structure the navigation and categories of a product based on the real mental model of those who use it — not the internal org chart. The goal is to unlock information decisions (menus, taxonomies, filters, paths) with quantitative backing instead of opinion, reducing the risk of a costly redesign built on assumptions.

Ask me for whatever you need before proceeding: which product, screen, or section will be structured and what business objective drives it; what is to be discovered or validated; the inventory of content, pages, or features that are candidates for cards; user profiles and recruitment criteria by segment; and, if they exist, raw results from sessions already completed. If the inventory, the target product, or the segments are missing, ask for them before continuing and do not invent data.

Proceed as follows:
1. Select and justify the card sorting type against the research question: open to discover categories from scratch, closed to validate an existing structure, hybrid to discover within seed categories. Do not choose by default; explain the trade-off of the chosen type (open gives label insight but more costly analysis; closed validates quickly but does not reveal new categories).
2. Refine the inventory into a card set: remove duplicates, level the granularity (all at the same level of abstraction), neutralize biased names or internal jargon, and recommend a manageable size (practical reference: 30–60 cards; above 60, fatigue rises and quality drops). Flag each doubtful card.
3. Define the session protocol: number of participants (reference Nielsen Norman Group: ~15 per segment for stable correlations), recruitment criteria, moderated or unmoderated format with its trade-off (moderated captures the why; unmoderated scales and reduces cost), tool, and neutral participant instruction script.
4. Define the analysis plan: similarity matrix between cards, hierarchical clustering dendrogram, agreement percentage per grouping, and analysis of labels proposed by participants in open studies. Name thresholds (e.g., agreement >=70% high confidence, 40–69% medium, <40% disputed).
5. Translate findings into a proposed architecture: groups, candidate category names, hierarchy, and list of problematic cards that warrant subsequent tree testing, with a confidence level per grouping.

If there are no session data yet, deliver the study plan plus ready-to-fill similarity matrix and report templates. Flag every missing piece of data as an explicit assumption and declare the risk of proceeding without it. Do not mention prices and avoid the word free; use effort or time estimates when applicable. Neutral, professional English.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-producto_diario_estudio:
Act as a senior Lead UX Researcher, expert in longitudinal studies, Experience Sampling Method (ESM), and qualitative temporal analysis. Design a complete, actionable longitudinal diary study protocol to observe a behavior in its real context — not in a lab or through reconstructed recall — so that the evidence feeds a concrete product decision.

Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the data you give me (target behavior, user segment, viable duration, capture platform, and decision to inform), restate in your own words what you understand and present your plan; flag any missing or ambiguous data as a blocking question before proceeding. If an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it.

Deliver a protocol with five numbered sections:
1. Framing: central research question, target behavior operationalized into something observable, 2 or 3 assumptions formulated as falsifiable hypotheses with their confirmation or refutation signal, and an explicit justification for why the diary study outperforms a one-time interview or a moderated test for this case (memory bias, ecological validity, temporal trajectory).
2. Entry sampling design: choose and justify the trigger among interval-contingent (fixed cadence), signal-contingent (random ESM-style prompts), and event-contingent (when the trigger event occurs); set frequency, time window, number of participants, recruitment profile, saturation criterion, and over-recruitment plan for expected attrition, all consistent with the study duration.
3. Diary entry template: 5 to 8 fields completable in under three minutes, combining structured capture (scales, multiple choice) and open capture (what was happening, what you were feeling, what you did, optional photo or audio), written without desirability bias or questions that suggest the answer; include the literal copy for each field and an example of a well-completed entry.
4. Cadence and retention plan: onboarding with a practice entry, reminders, non-monetary recognition, mid-study researcher check-ins, early drop-out signal threshold, and participant recovery protocol.
5. Analysis plan: coding scheme, temporal trajectory analysis, identification of peak and trough moments, journey mapping, and an exit interview script that probes the detected patterns and connects them to the decision being informed.

Rules: flag every piece of data not provided as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent participant numbers or findings as if they were facts. Add a brief ethics and consent section (sensitive data, photos/audio, voluntary withdrawal) and one on method limits (self-report reactivity, bias of who persists to the end). Close with the deliverable: a 5-section diary study protocol, ready to recruit and launch field.
ln-producto_research_insight_recomendaci:
Act as a senior product researcher expert in mixed research (qualitative and quantitative) and decision-oriented synthesis. I will give you raw research findings (interview notes, survey responses, support tickets, usability sessions, or analytics tables), along with the source and method of the data, the research question, and the product decision that the output should enable. If any of those four pieces of data are missing, ask me for them before proceeding; do not invent context. Your job is to convert that material into insights with evidence, magnitude, and confidence, each with an actionable recommendation, so that the decision is made on learning rather than opinion.

Proceed as follows: first fix the question and the decision as a filter, discarding findings that do not serve that decision. Group findings by recurring patterns and count frequency by theme to support the magnitude; discard isolated observations without support unless they are high-risk signals, which you will mark separately as hypotheses to validate. For each pattern, separate three layers without mixing them: observation (what was seen, verbatim), interpretation (what it means), and implication (what changes for the product). Write each insight as a tension phrase: users want X but face Y, therefore Z. Assign each insight evidence (verbatim quote or specific data point from the source), magnitude (how many users or what proportion over what base), and confidence — High, Medium, or Low — justified by sample size, method quality, and cross-source consistency. When data for magnitude or confidence are missing, declare it as an explicit assumption or gap; never fill in with invented figures; distinguish signal (sustained pattern) from noise (anecdote). Issue per insight one actionable recommendation: what to do, on which specific surface or flow, and which metric should move and in which direction. Prioritize by expected impact against validation effort and flag insights that need more evidence before acting. Watch for confirmation bias, sampling bias, and recency bias, and note if the source may be biased toward a segment.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the findings, Plan the synthesis, then Execute. First restate what you understand about the material and the decision, present your coding plan and wait or continue as appropriate before producing the final table.

Deliverable: a prioritized insights table with columns insight, evidence, magnitude, confidence, recommendation, metric, and priority; plus an executive summary of the three highest-return moves and a list of pending assumptions to validate with the minimum experiment or data point that would close them. Professional tone, without asserting more than the evidence supports.
ln-producto_nps_driver_analysis:
Act as a senior product and voice-of-the-customer researcher, expert in NPS analysis, qualitative feedback coding, and impact-effort prioritization. I have raw responses from an NPS survey (0–10 score plus open comment per respondent) and I need to open the black box: the number alone does not say what to fix. I want to separate why people promote, remain passive, or detract, and convert scattered comments into prioritized drivers the team can act on.

Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. If the raw dataset, the scale used, the exact NPS question, the survey window, or the business decision the analysis should enable are missing, ask first; do not invent figures or verbatims.

Deliver an NPS drivers report with: (1) executive summary of no more than five lines with the main finding and recommendation number one; (2) NPS health with percentage of promoters (9–10), passives (7–8), and detractors (0–6), net NPS, sample size, approximate confidence interval, and a warning if any segment lacks sufficient sample (suggested threshold: fewer than 30 responses or less than 5 percent of the total); (3) coded theme tree from the comments, with theme, root cause, frequency, and one representative verbatim quote, plus the percentage of uncoded comments; (4) drivers table crossed by NPS group separating promotion drivers (protect) and detraction drivers (hurts), with estimated weight on the score; (5) impact-effort matrix that prioritizes drivers with assumptions marked as such; (6) plan of three to five moves aligned with the business decision, each with suggested owner, success metric, early validation signal, and risk of not acting.

Rules: use the correct NPS cut-offs (9–10, 7–8, 0–6); preserve verbatims as-is, never paraphrase the customer's meaning; distinguish correlation from cause; declare all gaps or sampling biases; mark as an assumption any judgment not supported by data. Neutral, professional English.
ln-producto_user_story_mapping:
Act as a senior Product Manager expert in product discovery and User Story Mapping following the Jeff Patton model, with experience slicing releases by business outcome rather than by feature. I need to convert a scattered backlog into a visual map that tells the complete end-to-end user story and allows deciding what to build first. Before mapping, ask me for what is missing: name and description of the product or feature, the role or primary segment whose journey is being mapped, the business outcome pursued by the first releases (activation, conversion, retention, or another), constraints and what is out of scope, and how many incremental releases to slice after the walking skeleton (default 2 to 3). Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand, then present your plan, and only then execute.

Build the map and its slice lines. Deliver: 1) Backbone: the sequence of high-level activities the user follows from start to finish, in narrative order from left to right. 2) User steps under each activity. 3) Candidate stories under each step in the format As [role] I want [action] so that [benefit], ordered vertically by priority (most necessary at the top). 4) Slice lines: first the walking skeleton (minimum slice that traverses the ENTIRE backbone and delivers end-to-end value) and then the incremental releases, each as a horizontal slice crossing all activities — never a vertical silo. 5) Per release: outcome objective tied to the business goal, assumptions or risks it validates, observable success metric, and what is explicitly out of scope. Mark with [SUPUESTO] every unconfirmed inference. Close by flagging discovery gaps detected (steps without user evidence) and the points in the journey with the highest abandonment risk. Deliver a map in structured text (backbone > steps > prioritized stories) followed by a releases table with the walking skeleton plus the slices, ready to take to a planning session or a board.
ln-producto_refinamiento_backlog:
Act as a senior Product facilitator with expertise in backlog refinement, agile discovery, and story-splitting techniques. I will give you the sprint product goal, the list of items to refine, and — if applicable — the team's definition of done, the sprint capacity, and an already-estimated item to serve as an anchor. If any of those inputs are missing, ask me before proceeding; do not invent scope I have not provided.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the goal and which items you will refine, present the phase plan, and only then execute.

Execute in five phases. Phase 1, triage: classify each item by clarity (clear, ambiguous, blocked) and list the open questions preventing refinement. Phase 2, clarification: rewrite ambiguous stories as 'As a role, I want capability, in order to gain benefit' with verifiable acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format, and tag each assumption with [SUPUESTO]. Phase 3, splitting: when an item does not fit in a sprint, split it with vertical slicing (by workflow, business rules, data variations, effort, or layer) so that each slice is testable and delivers end-to-end value; never cut it into loose technical tasks (backend, frontend, database). Phase 4, estimation: estimate in Fibonacci points relative to the anchor item, declare the assumption behind each estimate, and mark high-uncertainty items that require a spike as 'not estimable'. Phase 5, closing: deliver a prioritized list of sprint-ready items and the open questions to resolve before commitment.

Validate each item against the team's definition of done; if you were not given one, apply a standard default (clear business value, verifiable acceptance criteria, no blocking dependencies, estimable, fits in a sprint) and declare it as [SUPUESTO]. Missing elements become open questions, not assumed scope.

Deliverable: a refinement table with columns id, story, acceptance criteria, sub-items, estimate, and status (ready, needs clarification, or blocked), followed by the prioritized list of ready items and the open questions. Close by stating how many items are ready, how many need clarification, and how many remain blocked.
ln-producto_dividir_historias_grandes:
