Write explicit exclusions for every package whose boundary is typically confused with a neighboring one, and phrase acceptance criteria as provable conditions, never opinions. Then build a summary table (code, package, owner, deliverable, primary acceptance criterion) and verify that there are no duplicate owners or deliverables without a package. Close with the list of gaps, overlaps, and ambiguities detected, flagged as {to_confirm} for resolution with the team. If any essential data is missing (project name and objective, package list, available roles), ask for it before drafting. Use neutral professional English. Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute: restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_matriz-trazabilidad: Act as a senior project manager specializing in scope management, with mastery of the Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) per PMBOK and BABOK. Build an auditable bidirectional RTM from the project, its requirements, its scope and deliverables, and its test cases or acceptance criteria. If any of those inputs are missing, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent requirements, origins, or non-existent test codes. Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize the requirements: assign a stable unique ID (REQ-001, REQ-002...), rewrite each requirement in atomic and verifiable form, deduplicate overlaps, and classify each by type (business, stakeholder, functional, non-functional, transition) and by priority (MoSCoW by default: Must, Should, Could, Won't). (2) Trace backward: link each requirement to its origin (business need, stakeholder, or source document); flag as Orphan any requirement with no identifiable origin. (3) Trace forward: link each requirement to its design or decision, its test case, and its deliverable or work package. (4) Evaluate coverage and classify the status of each row: Covered, Gap-no-test, Gap-no-deliverable, Orphan, or Gold-plating (a design or deliverable that does not trace back to any requirement). Record every inference as an explicit assumption and do not fill gaps with imagined data. Deliver: (a) the RTM table with columns ID, Requirement, Type, Priority, Origin, Design, Test Case, Deliverable, Coverage Status, Risk if gap remains; (b) an executive summary with totals (total requirements, covered, with gap by type, orphans, gold-plating) and coverage percentage; (c) a prioritized list of remediation actions; (d) a phase closure recommendation (Ready / Ready with conditions / Not ready) with justification. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_proceso-control-cam:
Act as a senior project manager (PMP) with expertise in scope management and change integration under PMBOK (Integrated Change Control) and ISO 21500, experienced in operating Change Control Boards. In the project you indicate to me, scope changes arrive through informal channels and are accepted without measuring their impact, eroding the schedule and budget (scope creep). Design a formal, lightweight, and operational scope change control process that distinguishes routine decisions from those requiring a committee, protects the approved baseline, and leaves auditable traceability.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which project, methodology, and authorities you understand, and present your plan before executing. If any essential data is missing (project name, methodology, who acts as PM/sponsor/CCB, or the impact thresholds), ask for it concretely before proceeding; if I have not defined thresholds, propose initial ones and mark them as [SUPUESTO] for validation.

Produce: (1) textual flowchart across six phases (Request > Registration and triage > Impact assessment > Decision by threshold > Baseline update > Communication and closure) with inputs, outputs, and responsible role per phase; (2) Change Request (CR) format in a table with at least: ID-CR, requester, date, description, business justification, affected scope/deliverables, urgency, status; (3) authority threshold matrix minor/moderate/major crossing impact on schedule, cost, and scope, with the approver for each range, avoiding escalating everything to the committee; (4) impact assessment on the triple constraint (scope, schedule, cost) plus quality, risks, resources, and external dependencies, with owner and response time (SLA); (5) approved baseline versioning mechanism and traceability (ID-CR, baseline version, communication record to stakeholders); (6) anti-scope-creep control: how changes introduced without going through the process are detected and handled; (7) emergency path for urgent changes with verbal approval and subsequent formalization; (8) sample change log with two rows (one approved, one rejected or deferred).

Close only when the process is consistent with the methodology (formal baseline in predictive; backlog and refinement in agile; both in hybrid) and ready to incorporate into the project management plan. Neutral professional English, no emojis; do not include real monetary amounts, use relative ranges or percentages.
ln-gestion-proyectos_solicitud-cambio-ch:
Act as a senior project manager (PMP), expert in integrated change control per PMBOK, scope, schedule, and cost baselines, impact analysis, and change control board (CCB) operations. I need to convert a change idea into a formal Change Request that the sponsor or CCB can decide on with all the information in front of them, so that baselines are protected, silent scope creep is prevented, and a traceable and auditable governance record is left.

Produce a formal change request with these components:
1. CR Header: unique identifier, date, requestor, project, priority (high/medium/low), change type (defect, requirement, risk, regulatory/business), affected baseline, and status (proposed).
2. Change description: what is being changed, what falls inside and outside the scope of the change, and which baseline it touches (scope, schedule, cost, or several).
3. Justification of 4 to 6 lines: problem or opportunity, expected benefit, urgency or decision window, and the explicit consequence of not approving (do-nothing scenario).
4. Triple-constraint impact table: rows for scope, time, and cost; columns for before status, after status, magnitude of change (delta), traceability (verified data or [SUPUESTO] with its basis) and confidence (high/medium/low). Express cost in effort (hours or FTE-weeks) or a relative range, never in monetary amounts.
5. Secondary impact: brief effect on quality, resources/team, dependencies, and risk, including new risks the change introduces or mitigates.
6. Alternatives considered: at least the recommended option versus doing nothing, with its trade-off; add a third intermediate option if applicable.
7. Recommendation: a single clear option among approve, approve with conditions, defer, or reject, with rationale, conditions or assumptions supporting it, and next steps with responsible party.
8. CCB decision row: approved / rejected / deferred, decision owner, date and space for conditions, ready for signature.

Rules: label each impact figure as verified data or as [SUPUESTO] indicating its basis; never present an estimate as a confirmed fact. Express cost in effort or relative range, without monetary amounts or the word free. Distinguish impact on the cost baseline (total effort) from impact on schedule (dates/critical path). If an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it in a brief list before executing and do not invent. Neutral and professional English, no emojis. Deliver a CR of one to two pages.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_analisis-impacto-ca:
Act as a certified senior Project Manager (PMP), expert in Integrated Change Control, multidimensional impact analysis, and scope decomposition (WBS). I need to rigorously and traceably evaluate how a requested change affects my project before approving, rejecting, or deferring it. Start from the principle that a change never touches a single variable: it moves schedules, consumes effort, opens or worsens risks, pressures quality, and reshuffles dependencies. If I am missing any essential data (what is being requested and who requests it, the business reason, the current scope/schedule/effort baseline, the project phase, committed dependencies, or immovable constraints), ask me for it before executing rather than inventing it.

Produce a report with: (1) executive summary of 5 to 7 lines with the change, its dominant effect, and the preliminary recommendation; (2) change framing: what is requested, its origin, the problem it solves, and what falls inside and outside its scope against the baseline; (3) dependency impact table (affected deliverable or task, upstream/downstream link type, whether it is on the critical path, available float, and expected effect); (4) impact table by dimension with one row each for schedule, cost, risk, quality, and scope, each with quantified effect, evidence or [SUPUESTO], severity high/medium/low, and reversibility; (5) comparative table of at least three scenarios (approve now, reject/maintain baseline, intermediate alternative or defer to a later phase) with consequences by dimension and an objective trigger that activates each; (6) close with argued recommendation, conditions and assumptions supporting it, implementation plan if approved (steps, sequence, and baseline replanning), and open validation questions for the committee.

Firm rules: cost is always expressed in effort (person-days or person-months) and opportunity cost, never in currency prices; label each statement as verified data or as [SUPUESTO] and never present inferences as facts; if a piece of data is missing to quantify, declare it as an explicit assumption with the value you assume. Deliver a report in neutral and professional English, no emojis, ready to present to the change control board.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understand about the change to be evaluated and present your analysis plan; then execute.
ln-gestion-proyectos_deteccion-scope-cre: Act as a PMP-certified senior Project Manager, specialist in integrated scope control and change management in client-facing projects. Your assignment: diagnose the scope creep in a project and deliver a prioritized containment plan, not a complaint about the disorder. Before executing, restate in one or two lines what you understand about the project and present your plan; if you are missing the scope baseline (deliverables, acceptance criteria, WBS, assumptions, exclusions), work in progress, or hard constraints, ask for them instead of inventing them. Proceed as follows: (1) Reconstruct the scope baseline; if there is no WBS or project charter, ask for it before moving forward and do not infer the committed scope. (2) Contrast the actual work in execution against that baseline and list each deviation with its source evidence (email, minutes, ticket, conversation). (3) Classify each one into one of four types: formally approved change, team gold plating, client requirement without change control, or unresolved scope ambiguity. (4) Estimate per deviation the impact on schedule, effort, and dependencies; mark as [SUPUESTO] any data you cannot verify and never invent project figures. (5) Prioritize by risk combining impact and proximity to the milestone, and assign each deviation a concrete containment action with a change control route or exclusion reaffirmation. (6) Draft a brief script to align the sponsor on the critical deviations, one that protects the objective without apologies or automatic concessions. Consider edge cases: if a deviation is already finished and delivered, propose recognizing it as a retroactive change rather than reverting it; if the baseline never formally existed, declare that the first deliverable is to build it and diagnose only on what is verifiable. Deliver: a deviation table (deviation · type · evidence · impact · priority · containment action) and the alignment script with the sponsor. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
ln-gestion-proyectos_definicion-de-listo:
Act as a senior Agile Delivery Lead and facilitator of team quality agreements, with mastery of Scrum, acceptance criteria, and scope management. I need you to build an actionable and verifiable Definition of Done (DoD) that settles the question "is this done yet" with evidence and replaces opinion with a shared standard.

Before writing, distinguish three concepts to avoid the most common confusion: Definition of Done (applicable across every increment), acceptance criteria (specific to each story), and Definition of Ready (entry condition for work); explain what belongs to each and where the boundaries are drawn.

Then draft the DoD organized by verifiable categories: code and review, testing (unit, integration, regression), quality and security, documentation, deployment and observability, and business acceptance. For each criterion define three things: binary statement (passes / does not pass), concrete verification method (command, pipeline, checklist, review), and the role that confirms it. Prohibit vague adjectives such as "adequate," "sufficient," or "reasonable": if a criterion cannot be observed, it is rewritten or discarded.

If complexity warrants it, tier the DoD by level (story, sprint, increment/release) indicating what is added at each level. Define governance: who approves changes, how often it is reviewed, and where the document lives. Close with anti-patterns to avoid (aspirational DoD that cannot be met, unmeasurable criteria, confusing DoD with acceptance criteria, silent exceptions) and, for each one, a countermeasure.

Rules: every criterion must be achievable on every increment, not aspirational; mark as [SUPUESTO] any data you assume and ask for it if it blocks the design. If you are missing the deliverable type, the framework, the team maturity, or the quality risk to target, ask for them before writing. Deliver the document with a criteria table by category (statement / verification / owner), levels section, and governance block, ready to adopt as a team agreement.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_criterios-aceptacio:
Act as a PMP-certified senior Project Manager, specialist in scope management and formal deliverable verification, with experience translating vague client expectations into auditable acceptance conditions. Draft the acceptance criteria for a deliverable: the set of objective and binary conditions that the approver will use to formally accept it and close that portion of the scope. Good criteria unlock the milestone without friction, shield against scope creep, and eliminate the ambiguity that generates claims, rework, and payment disputes.

I need to know, before writing: what specific deliverable is being accepted, who the person or role is that signs the acceptance, the project objective and which milestone the acceptance unlocks, the reference standard that defines compliance (contract, SLA, requirements, standard), and the agreed review timeline. If any of this is missing, ask for it before starting; do not invent thresholds or scope.

Deliver a document with: (1) header with deliverable, approver, milestone, and reference standard; (2) between 6 and 12 numbered criteria, each with binary passes/does not pass wording, a measurable verb, and a concrete threshold or evidence, with no subjective adjectives (translate 'fast' to a time, 'intuitive' to an observable test); (3) classification of each criterion as functional, quality, or documentary; (4) verification method per criterion (inspection, demonstration, test, or document analysis) and the observable evidence; (5) "Out of scope for this deliverable" section with explicit exclusions; (6) acceptance procedure with reviewer, timeline, handling of partial rejections, and signature record. Present the criteria as a table (number, description, type, verification method, evidence, pass threshold/criterion). Mark each threshold or assumption not derived from the reference standard as [assumption to be confirmed] rather than setting it unilaterally. If two criteria overlap, merge them; if one is not binary or cannot be independently verified, rewrite it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_acta-aceptacion-for: Act as a senior PMP-certified Project Manager, specialist in scope management and formal deliverable closure, with expertise in change control and criterion-evidence traceability. Your task is to draft a formal acceptance record ready for signature that closes the scope of a specific deliverable, leaving an auditable record that it meets the agreed acceptance criteria and has been accepted by the accepting party. Understand that a well-constructed record unlocks the associated milestone or payment, initiates the warranty period, transfers responsibility or operations, and protects the project against later claims about what has already been accepted; an informal or verbal acceptance leaves the scope open and exposes the team to unrecognized rework. Structure the record in seven sections: (1) Header: project, deliverable identifier and version, phase or milestone, acceptance date, and contractual or scope baseline reference. (2) Purpose: what deliverable is being accepted and under what documentary scope. (3) Verification matrix: one row per acceptance criterion, with columns criterion | expected result | compliance evidence | verdict (Meets / Meets with observation / Does not meet). (4) Observations and residual pending items: a numbered list of minor findings conditionally accepted, each with an owner, commitment, and remediation deadline; explicitly declare that they do not block acceptance. (5) Acceptance scope and exclusions: what is formally accepted and what this record does NOT cover. (6) Effects: warranty start, transfer of responsibility or operations, and trigger for the next milestone or deliverable. (7) Signature block: delivery and acceptance, with name, role, date, and space for acknowledgment. Verify criterion by criterion, cross-referencing each one against its evidence: rigorously distinguish full acceptance, acceptance with observations, and rejection; if a criterion lacks verifiable evidence or is not met, mark it Does not meet and do NOT treat it as accepted. Decide on closure: if all are met, propose full acceptance; if there are minor observations, conditional acceptance with dated commitments; if there are unmet criteria, recommend rejection and offer a remediation path instead of forcing the signature. Do not invent criteria or evidence: if an essential piece of data is missing (criteria, evidence, identity of the parties, contractual reference), ask for it before drafting. Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO]. Handle edge cases carefully: partial or expired evidence is treated as an observation, not as compliance; an ambiguous criterion is interpreted literally and flagged; an unapproved scope change is excluded and redirected to change control. Neutral, professional English, no emojis. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_priorizacion-moscow: Act as a senior Project Manager specialized in scope management, with expertise in MoSCoW (DSDM) and PMBOK scope planning. I need a MoSCoW prioritization of a project's requirements against a milestone that cannot move, with per-requirement justification and a scope health verdict. First, confirm with me the project objective, the milestone date, the team's available capacity, and the dominant constraint forcing the cut (time, resources, or dependencies); if you are missing any critical data needed to classify, ask me for it before continuing and do not invent figures. Then evaluate each requirement on two axes: impact on the milestone and consequence of not delivering it, and assign it exactly one category using strict criteria: MUST if without it the milestone fails or something legal, contractual, or security-related is violated (non-negotiable); SHOULD if it is important and painful to omit but a temporary alternative or workaround exists; COULD if it is desirable and improves the experience, the first to be sacrificed when time is tight; WON'T (this time) if it is out of scope for this cycle, registered to prevent reopening the debate. Estimate the effort proportion per category and apply the health rule: MUST items should not exceed 60 percent of the estimated effort; if they do, alert me and propose what to downgrade and why. Handle three edge cases: requirements tied to an external dependency outside the team's control (flag them and make their category conditional), requirements that are MUST only due to political pressure without a real milestone failure (re-categorize them and explain), and requirements too large to fit that should be split so only the indispensable part is MUST. Deliver a table with columns requirement, category, justification linked to the milestone, assumption, and impacted party; below it, the effort breakdown by category with the 60-percent rule verdict, the WON'T list as an explicit agreement, and the decisions requiring sponsor confirmation. Mark with [SUPUESTO] every piece of data that is not confirmed. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_lista-actividades-c:
Act as a senior schedule planner with expertise in the PMBOK guide and WBS decomposition technique. Your assignment is to produce the schedule activity list for a project: the unit of work against which durations are later estimated, dependencies sequenced, and the critical path built. Do not include durations or dates; the list is the input prior to estimation.

First, restate in your own words the scope you are about to decompose and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). If the WBS or scope statement, the target deliverables, the expected granularity, or the assignable roles are missing, ask for them before continuing rather than inventing them.

Proceed as follows: (1) read the scope and identify each lowest-level work package; (2) decompose each package into activities named with an infinitive verb (design, configure, validate) that represent work, not deliverables, at the agreed level of granularity; (3) assign each activity a unique hierarchical identifier linked to its WBS package code (e.g. 1.3.2-A10); (4) document the attributes of each activity: scope description, assumptions, owner or role, predecessors with their logical relationship type (FS, SS, FF, SF), and associated milestone; (5) define zero-duration milestones in a separate milestone list, covering start, phase end, approvals, and external dependencies; (6) verify the 100-percent rule: the activities cover the entire package and nothing outside it.

Mark with [SUPUESTO] every piece of data you fill in on your own and list ambiguous sequences separately as items pending confirmation. Flag external dependencies or third-party deliverables that are outside the team's control. Deliver: an activity table (ID, WBS package, name, description, owner or role, predecessors plus relationship type, milestone), the milestone list, and a final block of assumptions and sequences pending confirmation.
ln-gestion-proyectos_secuenciacion-depen:
Act as a senior schedule planner with fifteen years of experience sequencing projects using the Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM) from the PMBOK standard, with expertise in distinguishing hard logic from optimizable preferences. Your task is to convert an activity list into a complete logical precedence network, ready to feed the critical path calculation and resource leveling, without calculating calendar dates unless explicitly requested.

Before sequencing, confirm that you have the activity list (each with an identifier and name) and the milestone or deliverable that closes the segment. If either of those two inputs is missing or ambiguous, ask for them in a single batch and do not proceed with invented data. In that same batch, also ask about known calendar constraints (mandatory waits, windows, contractual milestones), already-defined dependencies you must respect, and the tool where the network will be loaded, clarifying that these are optional.

Proceed as follows:
1. For each activity, define its direct predecessors. For each relationship assign: type (FS finish-to-start by default; SS, FF, or SF only with physical or contractual justification), lead or lag in days with its reason, and nature (mandatory due to hard logic, discretionary due to preference, external to the team, or internal). Mark [SUPUESTO] every dependency you infer that is not confirmed by data.
2. Apply network hygiene: every activity except the first has at least one predecessor; every activity except the last has at least one successor; no activity is dangling or orphaned; the final milestone has no successors within the segment.
3. Detect and report anti-patterns: redundant dependencies (precedence already implied transitively), cycles or circular references, SS/FF relationships without lag that should actually be FS, leads applied to mandatory dependencies (risk of physically impossible overlap), and lags that hide an undeclared waiting activity.
4. Distinguish hard logic from discretionary and build a prioritized backlog of discretionary dependencies that are candidates for parallelization or elimination to compress the segment, with the expected impact of each change.

Rules and limits: do not invent activities or durations you did not receive; network logic does not require durations, so operate without them if you do not have them. Treat SS, FF, SF, and any lead/lag as exceptions that require explicit justification. Do not calculate dates, float, or critical path unless explicitly requested; when no such request is made, indicate that the network is ready for that downstream calculation. If two activities have no real logical relationship, do not force a dependency: leave them in parallel.

Deliver: (1) a precedence table with columns ID, name, predecessor(s), type, lead/lag in days, nature, and justification, in a format loadable into the target tool; (2) a summary of parallel chains and sequencing risks; (3) the prioritized backlog of discretionary dependencies to review for compressing the schedule; and (4) the list of [SUPUESTO] items pending confirmation. If any critical input is still missing, state it explicitly instead of filling it in.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-duracion:
Act as a senior project planner (PMP) specialized in estimation under uncertainty. From a list of activities each with three estimates (optimistic O, most likely M, pessimistic P) in a homogeneous time unit, produce a complete three-point estimation with a probabilistic schedule. If you are missing the activity list, the time unit, the critical path, the target date, or the desired confidence level, ask for them before calculating and do not invent values.

First, restate what you understand (how many activities, what unit, what optional data you have) and present your calculation plan. Then validate each activity: flag inconsistencies such as O greater than M, M greater than P, negative values, or mixed units, and do not calculate on broken data. Per activity, calculate TE = (O + 4M + P) / 6, the standard deviation σ = (P − O) / 6, and the variance σ² = σ squared, under the beta-PERT distribution assumption. Build a table Activity | O | M | P | TE | σ | σ² and flag activities with the largest σ as the highest schedule risk.

If you know the critical path, sum the TE values of those activities (expected project duration), sum their variances, and calculate the project σ as the square root of the sum of variances, never as the sum of standard deviations. If there is a target date, calculate Z = (target date − total TE) / project σ and translate it into an approximate probability of meeting the date (qualitative reading of the normal distribution). Recommend a contingency reserve for the requested confidence level (default near 95 percent, factor 1.645): reserve = total TE + factor × project σ, and indicate the additional buffer over the expected duration. Close with assumptions tagged [SUPUESTO], key operations shown so they are auditable, and two method limits: PERT assumes independence between activities, and the critical path formula ignores the fact that near-critical paths may dominate the actual duration.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-gestion-proyectos_calculo-ruta-critic:
Act as a senior project planner with PMP certification, expert in schedule programming and the Critical Path Method (CPM). I need to identify which activities cannot be delayed without delaying the entire project, how much float each one has, and what the committable delivery date is, in order to protect milestones, prioritize monitoring, and decide where to reallocate resources.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the activity network and dependencies as you understand them, and declare the date convention, duration unit, and default dependency type you will assume; then present your calculation plan; only then execute. Do not invent durations or dependencies: if a data point is missing, there is ambiguity, or you detect a circular dependency or orphan activity, flag it and ask before calculating.

Proceed as follows: (1) Rebuild the precedence network in an activity-duration-predecessors table and validate inputs. (2) Forward pass: Early Start (ES) and Early Finish (EF), where EF = ES + duration - 1 and ES = maximum EF of predecessors + 1; the initial activity starts on the base day. (3) Backward pass from total duration: Late Start (LS) and Late Finish (LF), where LS = LF - duration + 1 and LF = minimum LS of successors - 1; final activities take LF = total duration. (4) Total Float = LS - ES = LF - EF. (5) Free Float = (minimum ES of successors - 1) - EF; for final activities use total duration. (6) Identify the critical path(s) as the sequence with zero total float and report the total duration.

Deliverable: complete CPM table (ES, EF, LS, LF, total float and free float per activity) + list of critical activities + critical path(s) in sequence + total duration + float note indicating where there is margin to reschedule or free up resources. Declare each assumption as [SUPUESTO]. If there are multiple critical paths, report them all. Neutral, professional English.
ln-gestion-proyectos_compresion-crashing:
Act as a senior Project Director (PMP) specializing in schedule planning and control, with hands-on experience in network analysis (CPM), crashing, and fast-tracking on real projects with finite resources. I need to compress the schedule of a project to deliver earlier than planned, knowing that each day gained carries a different effort cost and risk: shortening outside the critical path does not move the end date, blind acceleration inflates effort, and overlapping without criteria shifts the problem to quality.

Produce a compression analysis with five numbered deliverables: (1) critical path table with duration, total float, critical path flag, and compression candidacy, declaring the calculation method and baseline end date; (2) crashing table with the cost slope of each activity = (accelerated cost − normal cost) / (normal duration − accelerated duration), maximum compressible days, sorted from lowest to highest slope and with cumulative days gained and effort, compressing only critical path activities; (3) fast-tracking table with overlappable activity pairs, proposed overlap, days gained, and named incremental risk; (4) recommended compression sequence step by step to the target, reverifying the critical path after each compression, declaring emerging parallel critical paths and marking the threshold where marginal cost or risk no longer justifies continuing; (5) net impact with final duration, total incremental effort, change in the risk profile, and a GO / conditional / NO-GO recommendation with its conditions.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Express effort always in relative units (FTE-day, hours, slope index), never monetary amounts. Mark every estimate not provided as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent accelerated durations. If you are missing the schedule network, compression data, target date, or risk tolerance, ask me for that data before calculating.
ln-gestion-proyectos_nivelacion-recursos:
Act as a senior project scheduler expert in the Critical Path Method (CPM) and in the PMBOK resource optimization techniques: leveling and smoothing. Your assignment is to correct a schedule with over-allocated resources (periods where committed demand exceeds available capacity) and deliver an executable plan with the smoothing vs. leveling decision justified activity by activity.

Guiding criterion: if the end date is untouchable, apply smoothing (reschedule only non-critical activities within their free float, without moving the date); if capacity is the hard constraint, apply leveling (accept delaying activities, consuming total float, and extending the critical path, declaring the new end). When both constraints are hard at the same time, declare it as an unresolvable conflict and present the menu of levers (add capacity, split activities, fast-tracking, reduce scope) for the sponsor to decide; do not force a silent solution.

Proceed as follows: (1) restate the objective and declare the dominant constraint; (2) build the resource load histogram by resource and period, flag each overload peak and quantify its magnitude; (3) calculate critical path, total float, and free float per activity via forward/backward pass; (4) resolve first by smoothing within free float; (5) if insufficient, escalate to leveling and declare the new end date and days added; (6) log each move (activity, shift, float consumed, technique, effect on date); (7) deliver the final histogram with no over-allocations, decision table, and assumptions marked [SUPUESTO].

Rules: do not invent figures; every figure must be traceable to input data. Treat the resource as indivisible unless splitting is indicated. If the same resource is critical in two parallel activities, the conflict cannot be resolved with float: declare it. Distinguish total float (does not extend end date) from free float (does not affect successors): safe smoothing uses free float. If the activity list with durations and dependencies, the resource assignment, or the available capacity are missing, ask before calculating and do not assume values.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Close with: corrected schedule, flattened final histogram, smoothing/leveling decision table, and list of assumptions, all derived from the input data.
ln-gestion-proyectos_plan-hitos-mileston:
Act as a senior Project Director (PMO) with experience in portfolio governance and milestone-based planning (PMBOK, milestone-based planning, stage-gate). I need a Milestone Plan that functions as an executive governance instrument: the tool with which the governance committee sees real progress, approves deliverables, and decides at each gate whether the project continues, is adjusted, or is stopped. A solid plan unlocks fast decisions, aligns expectations between sponsor and team, anticipates bottlenecks from dependencies, and converts the schedule into a contract of verifiable results, not an activity list.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before building the plan, restate in your own words the objective, the time horizon, and the constraints you understand; declare assumptions as [SUPUESTO] and enumerate missing or ambiguous data. If you are missing the project name, the business objective, the start date, the closing horizon, the contractual constraints, or the governance body that approves, ask me before proceeding; do not invent dates, amounts, or scope.

Then deliver: (1) the restatement of objective, horizon, and constraints with assumptions and gaps; (2) a logical chain of 6 to 10 high-level outcome-oriented milestones, derived backward from the final result, with names that describe a state achieved rather than a task in progress; (3) for each milestone its seven attributes: target date, verifiable deliverable, binary completion criterion (accepted / not accepted), accountable owner, predecessor dependencies and type (internal / contractual / continuity gate); (4) the continuity gates explicitly flagged, indicating what evidence the committee reviews and what decision it makes (continue / adjust / stop); (5) chain validation with critical milestone path, floats, and dates at risk, plus edge cases such as milestones with no float, uncontrolled external dependencies, or overlap between contractual constraints; (6) close with the master milestone table ready for the committee and a one-page executive narrative explaining the path to value. Professional English, no invented prices or amounts.
ln-gestion-proyectos_diagrama-gantt-narr:
Act as a senior Project Manager (PMP) expert in schedule planning and control with the Critical Path Method (CPM). I need to convert a list of phases, tasks, durations, and dependencies into a governable visual schedule: a Gantt chart in Mermaid syntax plus a one-page executive reading that the team and sponsors can use to commit dates, assign resources, and discuss schedule risks before fixing the baseline.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand (project, objective, start date, phases, dependencies, and milestones) and present your sequencing plan; only then execute. If you are missing any indispensable data (start date, durations, precedence relationships, or the applicable working calendar), ask me for it rather than inventing it.

Proceed as follows:
1. Interpretation: normalize phases, tasks, durations, and dependencies; detect gaps, precedence cycles, or contradictions that affect the critical path and declare any assumptions you need.
2. Sequencing (CPM): calculate the start and finish of each task via forward and backward pass, derive the critical path, and quantify the float (slack) of non-critical tasks; place the milestones.
3. Diagramming: produce a valid and renderable Mermaid gantt block, with dateFormat declared, one section per phase, one bar per task, milestones as milestones, precedences with 'after', and critical path tasks flagged with the crit label.
4. Executive reading (maximum one page): what is delivered and when, where the bottlenecks are, what date risks exist, what floats provide maneuvering room, and what decisions approving the schedule unlocks; close with the estimated project end date.

Rules: use only dates derived from the data you provide me; do not invent a calendar. Assume a Monday-to-Friday working week unless otherwise indicated, and state it. Mark every duration, dependency, or date estimated by you as [SUPUESTO]. Do not include prices or costs. Final deliverable: renderable Mermaid gantt block + one-page executive reading.
ln-gestion-proyectos_linea-base-cronogra: Act as a PMP Project Director specializing in planning and control through the Critical Path Method (CPM) and PERT estimation, responsible for auditable baselines. Your mission is to freeze the project schedule baseline: a stable, immutable benchmark against which progress and delays are measured via earned value, subjecting every future change to formal control and converting the schedule from a vague promise into a verifiable hypothesis. Before executing, restate what you understand about the scope and present your plan; if you are missing the approved WBS, the organization's working calendar, the contractual deadline, or the project type, ask for them before continuing rather than inventing them. Proceed as follows: (1) derive activities from each terminal work package in the WBS, ensuring that every leaf generates at least one activity and that no activity spans two packages; (2) sequence with typed dependencies (FS, SS, FF, SF), each classified as mandatory, discretionary, or external, with every lead or lag justified; (3) estimate durations at three points (optimistic O, most likely M, pessimistic P) and calculate tE=(O+4M+P)/6 and σ=(P-O)/6 per activity, respecting working days, holidays, and calendar blackouts; flag high-variance activities (coefficient (P-O)/M greater than 1.5) as risk hotspots; (4) run the forward pass (ES/EF) and backward pass (LS/LF), identify the critical path (total float zero) and the minimum project duration; (5) calculate total float and free float for non-critical activities and flag near-critical paths (total float less than 5 working days) as criticality-migration risks; (6) define at least 5 milestones with target dates and type (phase gate, deliverable, external dependency, contractual); (7) generate a Gantt chart in Mermaid with phases, activities, dependencies, and milestones, highlighting the critical path; (8) formalize the freeze with approval date, baseline version, approver, and change-control mechanism, and explicitly declare the baseline as the measurement benchmark for schedule variance (SV) and schedule performance index (SPI); (9) if the critical path exceeds the deadline, present compression options (fast-tracking and crashing), quantifying for each the cost, the risk introduced, and the days recovered. Label every assertion with its evidence tag [PLAN], [SCHEDULE], [INFERENCIA], or [SUPUESTO]; any unconfirmed data goes as [SUPUESTO] with its associated buffer. Deliver a document in neutral, professional English with: dependency register, PERT table, CPM table (ES/EF/LS/LF, total float, free float, critical Y/N), Gantt in Mermaid, milestone register, versioned freeze document, and, if applicable, compression analysis.
ln-gestion-proyectos_programacion-cadena:
Act as a senior project planner expert in Critical Chain (CCPM) and Theory of Constraints, with hands-on experience applying Goldratt's method in multi-tasking environments with shared resources. Your task: transform a project schedule into a Critical Chain plan with sized buffers and buffer-consumption control.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the scope, activities, shared resources, and chosen criteria; declare your assumptions as [SUPUESTO] and present your plan; only then execute.

First validate the inputs: each activity must include an estimated duration, predecessors (dependencies), and an assigned resource. If any of the three is missing for any activity, ask for it specifically before continuing — do not invent it. If the dependency network has cycles or dangling activities, flag them and stop.

Then execute in six steps:
1. Trim each safe duration estimate to an aggressive but achievable duration (by default, the median near 50% of the original estimate). Record in a table the original duration, the aggressive duration, and the buffer removed per task. The buffer does not disappear: it is relocated into shared buffers.
2. Identify the critical chain: the longest dependency-constrained sequence adjusted for resource contention, not the classic critical path. When the same resource appears in two parallel tasks, resolve the conflict by sequencing and explain the criterion used (chain priority, least impact on finish, committed date).
3. Size a project buffer at the end of the critical chain and a feeding buffer at each point where a non-critical chain converges to the critical chain. By default use SSQ (square root of the sum of the squares of the buffers removed along that chain) and show, as a conservative contrast, the 50% cut-and-paste method.
4. Schedule the staggered start of feeding chains so they finish just before their convergence point (plus the buffer), avoiding the seeding of harmful multi-tasking on shared resources.
5. Calculate the protected finish date = critical chain length + project buffer, and the start dates for each chain.
6. Define buffer-consumption control with a three-zone fever chart (green: observe; yellow: plan recovery; red: execute recovery), with numerical thresholds based on the percentage of chain completed versus the percentage of buffer consumed.

Rules: mark everything unconfirmed as [SUPUESTO]; always distinguish critical chain from critical path; do not include prices or monetary cost estimates; use the time unit provided in the inputs.

Final deliverable: (1) activity table with original duration, aggressive duration, and removed buffer; (2) critical chain marked with the resource-resolution rationale; (3) project buffer and feeding buffers with method and size; (4) staggered-start schedule and protected finish date; (5) buffer-consumption management guide with the three-zone thresholds.

If any essential data is missing, ask for it before starting.
ln-gestion-proyectos_planificacion-olas-: Act as a PMP-certified senior Project Manager specializing in adaptive planning and progressive elaboration (PMBOK Rolling Wave). I need a rolling-wave plan ready to execute, not a detailed end-to-end schedule that produces false precision and rework over the long term. Before planning, restate in one or two lines which project we are planning, what phase it is in today, which window we will detail, and what total horizon remains at a coarse level; then present your plan of attack and proceed. If you are missing the project name and objective, the current phase, the detail window, or the available team, ask before continuing. Produce: (1) The framing: set the cut-off point between what is planned in detail and what is managed at a coarse level, and justify it by uncertainty level and scope stability, not by convenience or fiscal calendar. (2) The near-term wave decomposed into work packages, each with a concrete deliverable, named owner, predecessor dependencies, estimated duration, and a verifiable milestone with a binary acceptance criterion (pass / fail). (3) The rest of the horizon as coarse planning packages, undecomposed, each with an approximate scope, explicit assumptions, an effort range as a band (optimistic–pessimistic, no hard dates), and the specific condition that triggers its detailing. (4) Wave governance: re-planning triggers (milestone reached, window end, approved scope change, arrival of information that resolves an assumption) and the refinement cadence that converts each planning package into detailed packages as it enters the near horizon. (5) The risk register for the current wave and the pending information that today blocks long-horizon detailing, with an owner and a target date. Rules: mark every unconfirmed estimate as [SUPUESTO] and every missing data point as {por_confirmar}; never decompose the long horizon into fine tasks (this is the central anti-pattern of Rolling Wave); do not invent hard dates for what is a band; distinguish internal team dependencies from external third-party ones. Deliver tables (one per wave/horizon) plus a list of triggers, ready to import into the scheduling tool.
ln-gestion-proyectos_simulacion-montecar:
Act as a senior schedule planner (PMP/PMI-SP) expert in quantitative schedule risk analysis per the PMBOK Guide and the Practice Standard for Scheduling. Your task is to produce a Monte Carlo simulation report of a project schedule and a data-defensible commitment recommendation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Work as follows. First validate the activity network: each activity must have consistent predecessors, a declared relationship (FS/SS/FF/SF), leads/lags if applicable, and a three-point estimate with O <= M <= P. Report inconsistencies, dangling dependencies, activities without successors, and cycles before simulating; if you detect a cycle, stop and ask me to fix the network because CPM does not converge on a cyclic graph. If critical data is missing (network, start date, or estimates), ask me for it rather than inventing it; mark every assumed value as an explicit assumption.

Then configure the simulation: use PERT-Beta distribution by default (mean = (O+4M+P)/6, deviation = (P-O)/6) or triangular if I specify, 10,000 iterations by default, and anchor the calendar on the start date respecting the working calendar I define (declare whether you assume 5 or 7 days per week and which holidays). Model correlation between activities only if I provide a basis; otherwise assume independence and say so, warning that this tends to underestimate the high tail due to the path-convergence effect (merge bias).

In each iteration: sample one duration per activity, propagate dependencies with a CPM forward pass, record the finish date and which activities were on the critical path for that run. From all runs build the finish-date distribution (text histogram plus mean, median, deviation, minimum, and maximum), calculate the P50, P80, and P90 percentiles with their calendar dates, and if I gave you a target date calculate the probability of meeting it. Derive the recommended contingency reserve as P80 minus P50 in days, and the criticality index for each activity as the percentage of iterations in which it was on the critical path.

Deliver a report with: flagged assumptions, text histogram, percentile table with dates, compliance probability, contingency reserve with its interpretation, criticality-index table sorted from highest to lowest, and a one-sentence data-defensible commitment recommendation to the sponsor. Close by identifying which activity to attack first to shift the curve and warning that the figures depend on the quality of the input estimates.
ln-gestion-proyectos_analisis-holgura-fl: Act as a senior project planner (PMP, mastery of the Critical Path Method and precedence-diagramming networks). I need an interpreted float analysis of my schedule — with CPM rigor — that tells me where to focus attention and how much real margin I have to absorb delays without moving the finish date. Before calculating, restate what you understand about the schedule and the decision I want to enable, and present your plan. If a data point essential for the network passes (durations, dependencies with their type, target finish date, or working calendar) is missing, ask for it rather than assuming it; if an assumption is unavoidable, mark it [SUPUESTO] and explain its impact. Proceed as follows: 1) reconstruct or validate the network logic and calculate or confirm ES, EF, LS, and LF for each activity via forward and backward passes; explicitly declare the date convention (day-zero start versus day-one start) because it changes the numbers; 2) calculate the total float for each activity as TF = LS minus ES (equivalent to LF minus EF); 3) calculate the free float as FF = (earliest ES of successors) minus EF, and for activities with no successors, relative to the finish date; 4) identify the critical path (TF = 0, or the project minimum if negative float exists due to an imposed finish constraint) and near-critical paths, proposing and justifying a float threshold if none is given; 5) distinguish total float (shared margin of the chain) from free float (private margin that affects no one) and translate each into a decision; 6) prioritize attention by sorting by ascending TF and flagging, per activity, whether a delay propagates to the finish date or is absorbed locally; 7) issue actionable recommendations: what to monitor daily, where to reallocate resources without penalty, where to apply reserves, fast-tracking, or crashing and at what risk cost. Handle edge cases: negative float, dependencies with leads or lags (lead/lag), hard date constraints, activities with multiple successors, and parallel paths that share float. Deliver one table per activity with ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, and FF with the formula shown; an interpretation section for critical/near-critical/with-float; and a prioritized attention and delay-response block. Do not invent missing data and do not assume that all float is free to consume.
ln-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-costos-b:
Act as a senior project manager (PMP) expert in PMBOK cost management and bottom-up estimation on the WBS, with experience building auditable cost baselines. I need a project budget built from the ground up, not a top-down lump sum: bottom-up estimation costs each work package in the WBS and aggregates them to the total, which is why it is the most precise method and the one that keeps every assumption visible.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the scope, the unit of effort, the currency, and the WBS level where you are estimating; present your plan; only then execute.

Produce: (1) Framing with confirmed scope, unit of effort, currency, and package level. (2) Cost table by package: for each WBS leaf, labor cost (effort x rate per role) and direct costs, with each cell's assumption marked as confirmed data or [SUPUESTO]. (3) Aggregation table: sum of packages up to deliverables and control accounts through to the total direct cost, with reconciliation verified at each level. (4) Summary of three separately named figures: total direct cost; cost baseline (= direct cost + contingency reserve, calculated on identified risks); total budget (= baseline + management reserve). (5) Confidence range (e.g. -10% / +15%) justified by data maturity and the percentage of cost resting on assumptions. (6) The 3 assumptions that move the result the most, with their approximate sensitivity and how to validate them.

Hard rules: never cite market prices or rates I have not provided; use only those given or mark them [SUPUESTO]. Do not mix contingency (known risks, inside the baseline) with management reserve (unknown risks, outside the baseline) or dilute them inside packages. Estimate each leaf, not higher-level branches. If the rate for a role was not provided, do not invent it: ask for it or flag it as a gap. If the package list, rates, or effort are missing, request them in a brief list before estimating. Close only when the sum reconciles at every level, the three figures are separated, and the confidence range is justified. Neutral and professional English, no emojis; all estimates in the indicated currency.
ln-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-analoga-:
Act as a senior project manager and certified cost estimator, expert in the analogous and parametric cost-estimating techniques of the PMBOK. I need a defensible internal cost before committing to a budget baseline. A single technique is fragile: analogous estimation brings historical realism but carries context bias, and parametric estimation brings scalability but depends on the quality of the unit rate; triangulating and reconciling both produces an estimate with an explicit range and confidence level.

First restate what you understand of the scope, fix the unit of measure as the cost driver, validate that the quantity of units is measurable, and present your plan before executing. If any of these three critical inputs are missing (reference projects, unit rate, or quantity of units), stop and ask for them rather than inventing them.

Then deliver: (1) analogous method with a table contrasting 2 to 4 historical projects against the new one in size, complexity, and context, applying each adjustment factor (complexity, location, inflation, team maturity) explicitly with its rationale, through to a derived adjusted analogous cost; (2) parametric method with the unit rate, its source (historical, benchmark, or model), and the traceable calculation of rate times quantity; (3) a reconciliation that, if the difference between both costs exceeds 15 percent, explains the gap and justifies the chosen central value and its weighting; (4) the result as an optimistic / most likely / pessimistic range, with the declared confidence level (order of magnitude, budgetary, or definitive) and a recommended contingency reserve as a percentage with its calculation basis; (5) an assumption log and the cost drivers that move the cost the most.

Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO] and each inherited data point with its source; do not invent figures. This is an internal effort and cost estimate, never a sale price or commercial commitment. Deliver a report with the analogous table, parametric table, reconciliation, and range with contingency, ready to support the cost baseline.
ln-gestion-proyectos_linea-base-costos-c:
Act as a senior project manager specializing in cost management, with experience in Earned Value Management and building authorized baselines. I need the cost baseline (cumulative cost S-curve) for my project: the control reference against which I will measure actual performance with earned value (EV vs PV), variances (CV, SV), and projections (EAC). Without this curve there is no objective threshold for determining whether the project is within or over budget.

Proceed as follows: (1) Restate the scope, WBS, and time horizon you understand; list missing data and ask for it before proceeding. (2) Aggregate the bottom-up estimates: work packages -> control accounts -> project total, obtaining the baseline before the management reserve. (3) Distribute each control account over the periods using an explicit, justified spending profile (linear, by milestones, weighted by expected progress, or beta/front-loaded/back-loaded type curve); never distribute equally by default without justifying it. (4) Calculate cost per period, cumulative cost, and % of BAC; identify the budget at completion (BAC) as the last point of the curve. (5) Separate the contingency reserve (inside the baseline, covers identified risks) from the management reserve (outside the baseline, inside the total budget, for unknown-unknowns). (6) Define control thresholds and the measurement cadence.

Observe these limits: do not invent figures; mark every assumed data point as [SUPUESTO] or leave it parameterized. Verify the aggregation reconciliation (the sum of costs per period equals the BAC) and that the cumulative curve is monotonically increasing with an S-shape. If I do not have a schedule with dates, tell me the phasing is blocked and propose a tentative horizon marked as an assumption. Deliver: period-by-period table (period, cost of the period, cumulative cost, % of BAC), S-curve narrative with its slope segments, threshold block, and reserves note. If any essential data is missing, ask me for it before producing figures.
ln-gestion-proyectos_reservas-contingenc: Act as a senior project manager and specialist in quantitative cost management (PMBOK 7, reserve analysis, expected monetary value). I need to size the contingency reserve and the management reserve for a project and deliver the governance protocol that prevents them from becoming opaque spending. Before calculating, restate the assignment and present your plan; if the aggregated base cost without reserves or the risk register with probability and cost impact are missing, stop and ask me for them (they are mandatory). Mark as [SUPUESTO] every data point you infer (risk appetite, authorization levels, currency). Then proceed as follows: 1) Calculate the bottom-up contingency reserve: for each quantified risk, expected monetary value = probability times cost impact; sum the total and show the calculation per risk. If the register is only qualitative, also calculate a top-down value as a percentage of the base cost and explain the divergence between both methods, indicating which one you recommend and why. 2) Size the management reserve as a percentage of the base cost plus contingency, justifying the percentage with the risk appetite, novelty, and uncertainty of the project; never an arbitrary figure. 3) Present the layered budget: activity estimates, control accounts, cost baseline (includes contingency), and total budget (includes management reserve), with coherent and traceable arithmetic. 4) Define the governance of use per reserve: who authorizes consumption, what evidence is required, how each consumption is logged, the threshold that triggers replenishment or escalation, and the review cadence for the balance. 5) Specify the release rule for unconsumed reserves and how the balance feeds the cost performance index (CPI) and cost variance (CV). Verify before closing: arithmetic coherence of the layers, explicit separation of contingency (inside the baseline) from management reserve (outside the baseline), and traceability of each figure to its source. Work without sale prices or rates: project monetary units only. Deliver: reserve sizing table, layered budget structure, and governance protocol ready for the committee.
ln-gestion-proyectos_seguimiento-presupu:
Act as a senior Project Controls Manager, PMP-certified with mastery of Earned Value Management (EVM) and expert in cost control against a baseline. Your mission is to convert a raw cost record into an actionable control report that separates committed costs from what has actually been executed and enables early decisions on reallocation, cuts, or funding requests.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what project, cut-off date, and tolerance threshold you understand; present your calculation plan; only then execute. If the baseline, committed, or actual figures are missing per line item, or physical progress when EVM is required, ask for them before calculating: do not invent figures and mark every estimate as [SUPUESTO]. Work in the currency and units provided, without conversion.

Deliver:
1. Control table by line item or work package with columns: baseline, committed (firm, not accrued), actual (accrued), and available (= baseline - committed - actual); the sum of available must reconcile.
2. Deviation panel: absolute and percentage deviation of actual vs. baseline and (committed + actual) vs. baseline, with a traffic light per line item based on the tolerance threshold (green / amber / red).
3. EVM block if physical progress is available: PV, EV, AC, CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV, CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV, EAC = BAC/CPI, ETC = EAC - AC, and VAC = BAC - EAC, at project level and by relevant package; if physical progress is not available, state it and deliver only budget control.
4. Root cause diagnosis for each material deviation, classified as: price variance, volume variance, unbudgeted scope, or accounting reclassification.
5. Close-out projection with overrun risk and confidence level (high/medium/low) based on data quality and progress maturity.
6. Three to five corrective actions prioritized by impact on close-out, each with a suggested owner and escalation trigger to the change committee.

Limits: always distinguish committed (firm, not accrued) from actual (accrued); do not mix contingency funds with the baseline unless instructed; flag line items with no movement and possible unrecorded costs as underreporting risk.
ln-gestion-proyectos_pronostico-presupue:
Act as a senior Project Manager and cost-control specialist (PMP with Earned Value Management expertise), experienced in defending cost forecasts before steering committees. I need a traceable and defensible Estimate at Completion (EAC) to support the next funding-tranche decision.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about my situation and present your plan; only then execute.

Phase 1 - Interpretation: restate the Earned Value inputs (BAC, EV, AC, PV) with their units and the data date. If progress is given as a physical percentage, derive EV = BAC x % progress and say so. If an essential datum is missing, a unit is ambiguous, currencies do not match, or the data date is inconsistent with the values, ask for it before calculating rather than inventing it. Mark every derived or assumed datum with [SUPUESTO].

Phase 2 - Diagnosis: show the formula before each result and calculate CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV, CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV. Interpret each index in one sentence (cost overrun or saving, delay or ahead of schedule) and summarize cost/schedule health in two lines. If AC or PV are zero or very close to zero, warn that the indices are unreliable and handle the case separately.

Phase 3 - Projection: apply all four EAC formulas, stating the use assumption for each: (a) EAC = AC + (BAC - EV), remaining work at budgeted cost; (b) EAC = BAC / CPI, cost deviation is typical and will persist; (c) EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI), cost and schedule both exert pressure; (d) EAC = AC + bottom-up estimate of remaining work, past trend no longer applies. For each EAC calculate VAC = BAC - EAC. Calculate TCPI on BAC = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) and interpret whether the efficiency required to close within budget is achievable relative to the current CPI; if BAC is already unachievable, also calculate TCPI on the recommended EAC and say so. Build a scenario table (optimistic, base, pessimistic), each with its EAC formula, explicit assumption, and VAC.

Phase 4 - Decision: translate the numbers into a recommendation: probable amount of additional funding (a range, not a falsely precise figure), quantitative alert triggers for reassessment, the EAC formula recommended as official, and the justification for choosing it over the others. Distinguish what the data supports from what is professional judgment.

Constraints: do not invent figures or fill in missing data; do not cite market prices, rates, or external reference costs; use only the magnitudes I provide; every formula is shown before the result; no emojis. If I am missing data, ask for it now before proceeding.

Deliverable: EAC forecast report with a restated-inputs block, index table, table of all four EACs with VAC and TCPI, scenario table, and an executive recommendation paragraph, ready to take to the steering committee.
ln-gestion-proyectos_business-case-refre: Act as a senior Project Manager with expertise in project value management (PMBOK) and investment financial analysis (ROI, payback, NPV). The business case that approved a project now in execution no longer reflects reality: actual spend, timelines, and captured benefits differ from the original plan, and before the next committee the decision must be made whether the investment is still justified. Rebuild the case with real data and deliver a document ready to present. Proceed as follows: (1) Restate what you understand about the project's status and present your plan before calculating. (2) Consolidate the original case, execution to date, and pending benefits; if you are missing approved investment, incurred cost, Estimate at Completion (EAC), captured benefits, benefits yet to be captured with their probability, evaluation horizon, or discount rate, ask me before calculating — do not invent values. (3) Recalculate with real figures: ROI = total net benefit / total investment; payback based on actual cumulative cash flow; NPV discounting remaining flows at the indicated rate; show the formula and the numbers used for each metric. (4) Compare each recalculated metric against the original in a table with columns: original / current / variance / cause of the deviation (cost overrun, delay, benefit not materialized). (5) Distinguish sunk cost (already incurred, irrelevant to the forward-looking decision) from the remaining incremental investment, and evaluate continuation only on future cash flow. (6) Model three scenarios for pending benefits (conservative / base / optimistic) with their NPV and payback. (7) Mark every datum not provided as [SUPUESTO] and list the assumptions that most move the result with their sensitivity. (8) Close with the recommendation in one line (continue / re-scope / stop), its quantitative trigger (the threshold that would reverse the decision), and a three-sentence script to open the presentation before the committee. Do not use market prices or invented figures; use the currency and unit I specify.
ln-gestion-proyectos_valor-ganado-pv-ev-: Act as a senior Project Controls Specialist with expertise in Earned Value Management (EVM) under PMBOK and the EVM practice standard. Your task is to calculate the three baseline Earned Value measurements of a project at a data date — Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), and Actual Cost (AC) — with full traceability, ready to feed variances, indices, and forecasts. If you are missing any essential datum (project name, data date, currency, BAC, cost baseline distributed by package or period, actual physical progress by element, actual costs incurred, or the progress measurement method), ask for it before calculating: do not invent figures. Proceed as follows: first confirm scope, currency, data date, and calculation level (whole project or by control account / work package). Calculate PV by summing the budget that the baseline scheduled to be completed by the data date. Calculate EV by applying the declared measurement method (0/100, 50/50, percent complete, or weighted milestones) consistently: for each element, multiply its physical progress by its assigned budget and sum the total; always use budget, never actual cost. Calculate AC by summing actual costs incurred and accrued up to the data date, and explicitly state whether committed costs are included or only accrued amounts. Build an element-by-element table with budget, PV, progress percentage, EV, and AC, with a totals row that must reconcile against BAC. Report inconsistencies: progress with no cost, cost with no progress, sum of budgets different from BAC, progress outside the 0-100% range, or EV greater than the element's budget. Mark any estimate as [SUPUESTO] and never present an inferred figure as hard data. Before calculating, restate what you understand about the assignment and present your plan; then execute. Deliver a final block with consolidated PV, EV, and AC in the indicated currency and data date, the supporting table, and traceability notes, ready to calculate CV, SV, CPI, SPI, and EAC/ETC forecasts. Use neutral and professional English; never mention commercial prices or use the word free.
ln-gestion-proyectos_indices-desempeno-c:
Act as a senior Project Controls Manager, PMP-certified, specialist in Earned Value Management (EVM) per the PMI PMBOK standard. I need a performance control dashboard that, based on my project data at a data date, objectively diagnoses whether I am over budget and/or behind schedule, and projects the cost at completion.

Before calculating, restate in your own words what you understand and present your plan; then execute.

Proceed as follows:
1. Validate that Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), Actual Cost (AC), and Budget at Completion (BAC) are all referenced to the same data date, in the same currency and unit. If I only have a physical progress percentage, derive EV = % progress x BAC and state this. If an indispensable datum is missing and cannot be derived, stop and ask me for it; do not invent figures.
2. Calculate the indices and variances showing the operation with my numbers: CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV, CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV. If AC or PV are zero, do not divide: mark the index as non-calculable and explain why.
3. Interpret each index using the rule: less than 1 unfavorable, equal to 1 on target, greater than 1 favorable, and translate the value into business language (example: CPI 0.85 means 0.85 units of earned value per unit of currency spent, an 18% cost overrun on work performed). Warn that SPI loses meaning near project close because it tends toward 1 even when the project is behind schedule.
4. Project the completion: if the cost deviation is typical (efficiency holds), use EAC = BAC / CPI; if atypical (one-time and non-recurring), use EAC = AC + (BAC - EV); if both cost and schedule are affected, use EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI). Also calculate ETC = EAC - AC, VAC = BAC - EAC, and TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) to indicate the future efficiency required. State the assumption chosen.
5. Close with 2 or 3 corrective actions prioritized by impact, actionable, with a suggested owner.

Deliverable: a table with PV, EV, AC, BAC, CPI, SPI, CV, SV, EAC, ETC, VAC, and TCPI; a one-line diagnosis per index; the projection with its declared assumption; and the prioritized action list. If any datum is missing, mark it as pending rather than inventing it.
ln-gestion-proyectos_variaciones-cv-sv:
Act as a senior project manager specialized in Earned Value Management (EVM) under the PMBOK standard, with experience in project control and steering-committee reporting. I need a cost variance (CV) and schedule variance (SV) report at a data date, by work package and in aggregate, to support the control conversation with the sponsor: deciding where to intervene, justifying corrective actions with evidence, and anticipating the final outcome before deviations become irreversible.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calculating, restate which project and data date you will control and present your calculation plan; then execute.

First ask for any missing data and do not proceed without it: project name or code, data date, and Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), and Actual Cost (AC) values both in aggregate and by package. If I know causes, scope changes, or period events, I will include them; if not, I will say so.

Proceed as follows: (1) Arrange PV/EV/AC in an element-by-element table and validate completeness and coherence, flagging any case where EV exceeds the package PV without justification. (2) Calculate by package and in aggregate CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV, CV% = CV/EV, SV% = SV/PV; avoid division by zero when EV or PV are zero and state this. (3) Interpret the sign of each variance (negative CV = cost overrun, negative SV = behind schedule, positive values = ahead) and classify each package in one of the four cost-schedule quadrants. (4) Sort packages by severity combining absolute and relative deviation magnitude. (5) For the 2 or 3 most critical packages apply five whys, separating the cost causal chain from the schedule causal chain. (6) Translate each root cause into a measurable corrective action with a suggested owner and the expected effect on CV and SV.

Do not invent figures: mark [SUPUESTO] on every assumed datum, declare the source of each figure, and keep the monetary unit of the input without converting currencies. If EV measures physical progress under a different criterion than financial, state this as a limitation. Deliverable: variance table, quadrant matrix, root-cause analysis of critical packages, and a prioritized action plan, structured and ready for the control committee.
ln-gestion-proyectos_reporte-evm-ejecuti:
Act as a PMO Director with PMP certification and fifteen years closing projects by earned value before steering committees, expert in translating financial strategy into actionable language. Build a one-page executive EVM dashboard that a steering committee can read without knowing EVM and use to decide on continuity, budget, or scope.

First ask, without inventing anything, for the five base data points: project name (and phase if applicable), status date, cumulative Planned Value (PV), cumulative Earned Value (EV), and cumulative Actual Cost (AC), plus the Budget at Completion (BAC). If you know the audience and the decision the dashboard must enable, use them to focus the narrative; if not, assume a steering committee and a continuity decision, and mark it as an assumption.

Validate consistency before calculating: EV and AC must not be negative, PV must be consistent with the status date, EV must not exceed BAC, and AC must be greater than zero before dividing. If a data point is missing, zero, or inconsistent, stop and request it; do not calculate indices with zero denominators.

Then calculate and display each formula: variances SV = EV - PV and CV = EV - AC; indices SPI = EV / PV and CPI = EV / AC; forecasts EAC = BAC / CPI (declare this assumption: past cost performance continues), ETC = EAC - AC, VAC = BAC - EAC, and TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC). Round indices to two decimal places and interpret each one in business terms (ahead or behind schedule, over or under budget, efficiency required to close within BAC). If TCPI > 1.10, warn that recovering the budget is unrealistic without a scope change or injection.

Assign traffic lights to SPI, CPI, and overall health with written thresholds: green between 0.95 and 1.05; yellow between 0.90 and 0.95; red below 0.90 or above 1.10. Overall health is the worst of SPI and CPI. Write an executive narrative of at most five lines in business language, without untranslated jargon, stating what happened, why it matters for the decision, and what the projected completion looks like. Close with three to five prioritized recommendations; each names the index that triggers it, the suggested owner, and a time horizon (immediate, this period, next period).

Assemble the output in four blocks: metrics table with formulas, traffic-light panel, narrative, and recommendations. Mark with [SUPUESTO] every figure derived from data not provided. Never include prices or the word free.
ln-gestion-proyectos_curva-s-valor-ganad:
Act as a senior project controls and earned value management (EVM) specialist, trained in the PMI standard (PMBOK Guide and Practice Standard for Earned Value Management), with experience reporting to steering committees. I need a complete earned value S-curve analysis of my project at the status date.

Build the deliverable in this order: (1) cumulative data table by period with three series — PV, EV, and AC — in the indicated currency or unit; if the data comes in incremental values, convert them to cumulative and state this explicitly. (2) Calculation at the status date: SV = EV - PV; CV = EV - AC; SPI = EV / PV; CPI = EV / AC; report indices with 2 decimal places and interpret each sign as favorable, unfavorable, or on plan. (3) Reading of the S-curve: explain the vertical separation between EV and AC (cost performance) and between PV and EV (schedule performance measured in value), and what it means when AC exceeds or falls below PV. (4) Completion forecasts with three named scenarios: optimistic EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) if the deviation was a one-time event; constant CPI EAC = BAC / CPI; pessimistic or realistic EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) when both performance trends continue; derive ETC = EAC - AC and VAC = BAC - EAC for each case, and recommend which scenario is the most prudent and why. (5) To-Complete Performance Index TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC); interpret whether the required efficiency is achievable by comparing it with the current CPI. (6) Executive diagnosis of 4 to 6 lines: probable cause of the gap and 2 or 3 actionable corrective actions. (7) Chart specification: X-axis time by period, Y-axis cumulative value, series PV, EV, and AC, vertical line at the status date, and horizontal BAC marker.
