(2) Cross-filtering map as a table from source to destination with direction (unidirectional or bidirectional), exempt visuals with their reason, avoiding circular filtering and double-counting; trace propagation as a directed graph and detect cycles. (3) Advanced parameters and interactivity: what-if, metric or scenario selectors, drill-through and bookmarks, with range, step, default, and expected effect. (4) Precedence and reset: application hierarchy when filters conflict, reset button behavior, and selection persistence across pages. (5) States: default on open, empty or no-data state with a message per sensitive visual. (6) Performance: high cardinality, lazy loading of lists, pre-aggregations, indexing or partitioning, and multi-selection limits for the specified engine.

Classify each filter by the decision it enables, not by habit. Tag with [SUPUESTO] everything assumed and justify each decision in one line. Close with a prioritized summary of coherence and performance risks (impact and probability) with their mitigation. The deliverable is an interactivity design document with the six tables and the final summary.
ln-datos_dashboard_accesibilidad_color: Act as a senior accessible data visualization specialist, with experience applying WCAG 2.1 and color-blind-safe palettes (Okabe-Ito, ColorBrewer) in production dashboards. I want you to audit the color accessibility of a visualization and redesign its palette. First confirm with me the chart type, the series or categories to distinguish and how many there are, the current palette in hex, the target WCAG level (AA or AAA), and the usage context (background and medium); if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask for everything in a single round before continuing. Then diagnose the palette on three axes: color-blindness safety by simulating deuteranopia, protanopia, and tritanopia and flagging color pairs that collapse; contrast by calculating the ratio of each color against the background and between adjacent series against the applicable thresholds (3:1 for non-text graphical elements and borders, 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text); and exclusive dependence on color. Then redesign the palette: assign each series a hex from a named, validated system, ordered by maximum perceptual distance; use a single-hue sequential scale for magnitude and a diverging scale with a neutral center for deviation from a baseline. Add at least one redundant encoding layer appropriate to the chart type (marker shape, fill pattern, direct label, line weight or style, order or position). Clearly distinguish the print version from the projection version if the context includes them, because they degrade contrast. Do not invent brand colors or assume the BI tool; tag every unconfirmed piece of data as an assumption. Deliver: a palette table (series, hex, contrast against background, redundant layer), a report of the non-compliant pairs with their numeric ratio, a verification checklist with instructions for validating with a color-blindness simulator and contrast checker, and a final compliance verdict stating whether the target level is met or listing the pending adjustments with their priority. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_dashboard_alertas_umbral:
Act as a senior Business Intelligence analyst specializing in operational alert design and business observability. I need to convert a set of metrics into a traffic-light and alert system ready to implement, with defensible thresholds, anti-noise measures, and notifications with an owner, so that the report governs attention rather than competing for it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. If you are missing a target, tolerance, data source, or alert owner, ask before proposing thresholds — do not invent them.

Deliver in this order: (1) threshold rules table per metric with desired direction (higher is better / lower is better / range), threshold type (fixed vs. target, relative to period or budget, statistical by deviation), and the resulting numeric rule; (2) green/amber/red band matrix with numeric justification for each threshold; (3) anti-noise rules: minimum persistence window, debounce or grace period to resume, and suppression of false positives due to seasonality or expected events; (4) accessible conditional formatting that combines color with an icon or text label — never color alone — readable by color-blind users; (5) notification matrix per amber and red band with channel, owner, message that includes metric, current value, crossed threshold, and suggested action, plus an escalation path if the condition persists; (6) assumptions log tagging [SUPUESTO] on every inferred piece of data.

Close when every threshold is traceable to a target or tolerance, anti-noise measures exist against alert fatigue, every alert has an owner and an actionable message, and no threshold was invented without a basis.
ln-datos_dashboard_narrativa_anotaciones:
Act as a senior Business Intelligence analyst expert in data storytelling, with mastery of visual hierarchy and executive dashboard design. Your task is to convert a raw-metrics dashboard into a decision-making tool that can be read in seconds and makes the suggested action explicit.

MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate which dashboard, metrics, period, audience, and events you understand; name the 2–3 dominant findings), then Plan (present the reading order and the finding-to-chart-to-title-to-annotation mapping), and only then Execute. If you are missing any essential piece of data (dashboard description, metrics with values, period, or audience), ask before continuing — never invent figures or causes.

Deliver four components ready to apply: 1) Actionable titles: rewrite each chart title using the format subject + figure + direction + cause (when the cause is in the data), in a table showing current title vs. proposed actionable title. 2) Contextual annotations: for each relevant series, one annotation anchored to a specific point (date or value), classified as event, anomaly, or critical threshold (target, SLA, break-even point), with a brief label explaining the why; in a table: chart, point/date, type, label. 3) Executive summary: 3 to 5 sentences to place at the top of the dashboard that answer what happened, why it matters, and what decision it suggests; deliver it in a version with real data and in a template version with placeholders to regenerate when the data changes. 4) Reading order: order the recommendations according to the F or Z pattern, with critical items at the top left and justification for that choice.

Tag with [SUPUESTO] every cause or figure that is not confirmed. Close by confirming that every title carries a figure and direction, every annotation is anchored and classified, the summary does not exceed 5 sentences in both versions, and no metrics were invented. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-datos_dashboard_self_service: Act as a senior self-service analytics and BI architect, with experience in semantic layer modeling, data governance, and adoption programs. Design a self-service analytics experience that allows business users to explore their data domains autonomously on the available BI platform, without generating parallel reports with contradictory figures or making decisions on non-certified data. Before executing, restate what you understand about the context and present your plan. If you are missing key data (sector or industry, BI platform, priority data domains, user analytics maturity, and adoption target), ask first instead of inventing; tag any assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver a design document with five blocks. 1) Semantic layer: 2 to 4 domain datasets, each with declared grain, dimensions, certified metrics with their business formula in plain language, source of each field, and explicit separation between certified and experimental; include one anti-pattern to avoid (metrics with the same label but different formulas). 2) Library of reusable visualization templates (KPI tracking, time comparison, ranking, distribution, funnel), each derived from the business question it answers and with guidance on when to use it and when NOT to. 3) Governance guardrail matrix: row-level and domain permissions, PII and sensitive data handling, freshness and quality validation, visible certified vs. non-certified label, and limits to prevent queries that degrade performance. 4) Enablement model: consumer, explorer, and author levels, a learning path per level, promotion criteria, and an explicit process for elevating an ad hoc analysis to certified content. 5) Success metrics dashboard: adoption, autonomy, reduction of data team requests, and trust in the figures, each with a definition and measurement method, plus a baseline and a frequent adoption risk with its mitigation. Close with acceptance criteria for the document. No prices. Neutral, professional English, no invented figures or tools.
ln-datos_metrica_definir_north_star: Act as a Head of Product Analytics with a track record defining North Star metrics and input metrics at digital product companies. Your deliverable is the recommendation of ONE North Star metric (NSM) with its input metrics tree and guardrails, ready to be defended before a leadership committee. Before executing, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand, Plan the approach, and only then Execute. I need you to know what the product does and for whom, the business model and how it monetizes, the aha moment or value moment, the product stage (pre-PMF, early growth, or scale), and the metrics the team tracks today along with available data. If any of those inputs is missing or ambiguous, ask before proceeding; when an assumption is unavoidable, mark it as [SUPUESTO] and record how to invalidate it. Proceed as follows: (1) articulate in one sentence the core value the product delivers, expressed as a user action verb rather than a feature; (2) propose 3 to 5 NSM candidates, each with a definition, exact formula, time window, unit of measurement, value behavior it captures, and connection to growth according to the business model; (3) score each candidate 1–5 against six criteria: reflects delivered value, is leading with respect to revenue, is actionable by the team, is measurable with current data, resists gaming, and is understandable by leadership; tabulate the scores; (4) recommend ONE single NSM and justify the rejection of each alternative; (5) decompose it into 3 to 5 input metrics within an explicit growth equation (for example breadth x frequency x depth), assigning each input a lever and the responsible team; (6) define 2 to 3 counter-metrics or guardrails that protect product health when optimizing the NSM, each with its alert threshold. Close by explicitly distinguishing the NSM (one) from input metrics (many) and from discarded vanity metrics, and flag the risks of the chosen definition. Neutral, professional English, no prices or cost figures.
ln-datos_metrica_arbol_drivers:
Act as a senior data and business analytics analyst specialized in driver trees and metric decomposition, with experience connecting outcome KPIs with operable inputs. Your deliverable is a driver tree with explicit causal relationships, an actionable-leaves table, a leverage ranking, and the selection of focus drivers. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows:

1. Framing. Confirm the definition of the outcome metric (formula, unit, period, population) and its current value. If the definition is ambiguous, propose two possible interpretations and declare which one you assume. Mark every piece of data that was not provided as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent baselines or elasticities. If critical context is missing (which metric to move, how the business operates and makes money, or within what window action will be taken), ask before decomposing.

2. Decomposition. Decompose the metric into first-level drivers with an EXPLICIT mathematical relationship per node (product, sum, or weighted average) and drill each branch down to leaves that are actionable inputs, not aggregates. A leaf is actionable if a concrete team can move it with a decision; if it is still an aggregate, keep decomposing. Avoid double-counting: the same quantity cannot appear in two branches that are later summed.

3. Nature of each edge. For each edge, distinguish accounting identity (certain by definition, e.g. revenue = customers x ticket) from causal hypothesis (assumed correlation that may not hold). Mark hypotheses as [SUPUESTO] when no data supports them and note their expected direction and strength.

4. Leaf card. For each leaf define: input name, formula or event that measures it, current baseline (or [SUPUESTO] if data is missing), unit, concrete lever that moves it, and responsible area or owner.

5. Leverage. Estimate how much a 10-percent change in each leaf moves the outcome metric according to the tree relationship, make the elasticity assumption explicit, and sort from highest to lowest. When data is insufficient to calculate, prioritize by judgment, marking it [SUPUESTO]. Distinguish theoretical leverage (how much it moves the needle) from real actionability (how much control there is over the leaf within the decision window): a high-impact leaf without control is not a focus.

6. Focus and protection. Recommend the 2–3 drivers with the greatest leverage AND real control within the decision horizon, one lever per driver with its tracking metric, and 1–2 guardrails against side effects (e.g. moving conversion without degrading margin or churn).

Expected deliverable: indented tree with the mathematical relationship per node and an identity/hypothesis label per edge, leaves table (input, formula/event, baseline, unit, lever, owner, leverage) sorted by leverage, and the 2–3 focus drivers, one sentence each, with lever, tracking metric, and guardrail. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-datos_metrica_especificacion_calculo: Act as a senior analytics engineer with more than a decade designing semantic layers and metric dictionaries (dbt Semantic Layer, LookML, Cube), responsible for unique and auditable definitions. I need you to produce a versioned specification card (metric spec) for a business metric, ready to implement without reinterpretation. Before writing, restate in your own words the metric, its source, and its grain, and present your plan; mark any missing data as a question rather than inventing it. Then deliver: (1) the metric in one business sentence and the question it answers; (2) the formula as numerator / denominator, or base aggregation if it is a count or sum, naming each field and source table; (3) granularity (what one row represents) and the unit of measurement; (4) valid slicing dimensions and filters that ALWAYS apply; (5) time window, dating criterion (by which date the event is attributed) and canonical time zone; (6) explicit resolution of edge cases: division by zero, nulls, duplicates, refunds or reversals, late-arriving data, currency and conversion, definition changes over time (slowly changing); (7) the final formula in readable pseudo-SQL; (8) two worked numeric examples step by step, one normal and one edge case; (9) actionable validation tests: expected ranges, reconciliation against a source of truth, behavior on an empty partition, and at least one non-regression test. Label each rule as CONFIRMED (comes from an existing source or definition) or [SUPUESTO] (inferred, requires validation from the metric owner); do not invent numbers or field names. Close with a list of assumptions to confirm and the proposed version of the card. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_metrica_evitar_vanidad:
Act as a senior product and data analyst, specialist in actionable metric design (AARRR/pirate frameworks, North Star Metric, and the vanity vs. actionable distinction from Lean Analytics). You will audit a team's or product's metrics dashboard and convert it into a system of signals that change decisions, not a wall of counts that only go up.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which metrics I have, which decision they should inform, and what the moment when the user receives real value is; flag anything ambiguous (funnel, who decides, time window) and if something blocks the analysis, ask before continuing. Then present your plan. Only then execute.

Execution:
1. Inventory each metric and apply the actionability test: what concrete decision would change if that number went up or down 20 percent. If the answer is none, it is a vanity candidate.
2. Classify each one as Actionable, Vanity, Questionable, or Guardrail (a health metric that does not trigger a decision but protects against harm). Justify in one line.
3. For each Vanity, design an actionable replacement, preferably a ratio or normalized rate (over cohort, session, or stage) rather than an absolute count, anchored to the value moment.
4. Define each new metric: name, explicit formula, owner, threshold or range that triggers action, and the decision it enables.
5. Flag gaps: metrics that are missing to cover the full funnel or the decision at stake.

Edge cases: if a metric is leading for an Actionable one, mark it Questionable and explain the link; do not remove guardrails even if they do not drive decisions; if two metrics measure the same thing, recommend consolidating. Do not invent figures or business data; everything unverifiable is marked [SUPUESTO].

Deliverable: an audit table (metric | classification | why | replacement) and a block of new metric definitions (name | formula | owner | threshold | decision) ready to paste into the dashboard. Close with the 3 highest-leverage metrics. If you need to know which metrics I have, what the team decides, or what the value moment is, ask before auditing.
ln-datos_metrica_framework_aarrr: Act as a senior Analytics Lead with fifteen years instrumenting product funnels and defining actionable metrics with Dave McClure's AARRR framework (Pirate Metrics) and retention cohort analysis. I need a metrics dashboard that makes the entire user lifecycle measurable before optimizing anything: it exposes where value is gained and where it leaks, connects the stages with comparable conversion rates, and enables a defensible effort-investment decision. To start I need four inputs; if any is missing or arrives ambiguous, ask for all of them in a single round before continuing: the business model that defines the funnel, events or sources already instrumented today, the reference time window for metrics and cohorts, and the concrete decision the dashboard must enable. Proceed as follows. First, frame: confirm inputs, fix the business model and the A-A-R-R-R order; do not assume benchmarks or market figures, and if you infer anything mark it as an assumption. Second, define each AARRR stage (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) with: operational definition (entry event and advancement event), main metric with explicit numerator/denominator formula and window, instrumentation events marked [DATO] if they already exist or [SUPUESTO] if missing, and conversion rate to the next stage (advanced / entered) with consistent denominator and window to chain the funnel. Apply the focus proper to each stage: Acquisition by channel and effort cost with no monetary figures; Activation on the aha moment; Retention measured by cohorts and distinguished from aggregate retention; Referral with an invitation coefficient; Revenue with conversion to payment and expansion. Third, consolidate a funnel table (stage, main metric, formula, conversion to next, data source), declare a North Star metric aligned to the decision and explain how it relates to the five stages, and identify the stage with the greatest drop-off (likely bottleneck) with the quantitative signal that would confirm or rule it out. Defer all optimization tactics to a later phase: the deliverable is metric definition, not an improvement plan. Close by declaring the active assumptions and instrumentation gaps that would block the calculation. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_metrica_okr_a_indicadores:
Act as a senior Analytics Engineer and Head of Data, an expert in the OKR framework of Andy Grove and John Doerr and in metric trees with a leading/lagging distinction, with a track record of translating objectives into instrumented metrics without losing ambition. Your assignment: take a set of OKRs that are already drafted but not instrumented (the Key Results sound ambitious but have no formula, source, baseline, or owner, and no one can tell whether they are moving) and convert them into a catalog of measurable indicators that unlocks real tracking, exposes gameable or pure-activity KRs before instrumenting them, and connects each Objective to leading indicators that allow timely course-correction.

Before executing, ask me in a single batch for the minimum required data if I have not provided it: the full text of the OKRs (each Objective with its Key Results as they are today), the organizational level they apply to (company, area, squad, or individual), the data sources available for instrumentation (systems, tables, events: product analytics, CRM, data warehouse, tickets), and the target closing horizon. Optionally: instrumentation constraints, data governance, privacy, or team. Ask in one batch only; do not invent source systems or baselines.

Proceed as follows. First, diagnose the measurability of each Key Result: classify it as an outcome KR or an activity KR (flag activity as a weak signal that measures effort, not impact), and detect ambiguous, duplicate (measuring the same thing), or gameable KRs (optimizable without achieving the objective), proposing a reframe that preserves the Objective's ambition. Second, operationalize each valid KR into an eleven-field card: (1) name, (2) definition in one sentence, (3) formula with unit and numerator/denominator separated where applicable, (4) concrete source drawn from the available systems or tagged [SUPUESTO] with an acquisition method, (5) granularity and cut dimensions, (6) baseline (data point or [SUPUESTO] with how to obtain it), (7) target at the end of the horizon and alert threshold, (8) leading or lagging classification with justification, (9) measurement cadence, (10) data owner, (11) gaming risk and countermeasure. Third, build a metric tree that connects each Objective (lagging) to its leading indicators, marks the north metric for each Objective, and flags Objectives with no actionable leading indicator. Fourth, deliver a summary table and a list of KRs to reframe with the proposed reframe.

Firm rules: every unverifiable source or baseline is tagged [SUPUESTO] with an acquisition method; zero invented figures or systems; every formula with an explicit unit; metric and target always separate; every indicator with a cadence and owner; respect privacy and governance constraints. Never include prices or invented monetary figures. Close by confirming that each Objective has at least one actionable leading indicator, or by flagging the gap.
ln-datos_metrica_leading_lagging:
Act as a senior business metrics analyst specializing in designing balanced measurement systems (leading/lagging) and validating causal chains. I need to convert a business objective into a balanced metrics dashboard, in table format, ready to review with stakeholders on a single page.

The business objective is to reduce B2B customer churn over the next 6 months. The decision horizon is weekly: I need to be able to act each week. The available data sources are the CRM (accounts, sales activity), product events (logins, feature usage, ~1-day latency), and billing (renewals, downgrades, monthly latency). The main operational lever is the Customer Success team. The dashboard is reviewed by the Customer Success committee every week. I have 18 months of historical data available to validate correlations.

Proceed as follows: 1) Restate the objective and confirm the anchor lagging indicator: formula, unit, frequency, typical reaction lag, target, and baseline. 2) Propose 2 to 4 leading indicators obtainable from the available sources, each with an explicit causal hypothesis (moving X should move the result because...), formula, frequency, expected direction, and the lever that controls it. 3) Build the leading vs. lagging balance table with anticipation window, expected relationship strength, and validation method using the historical data. 4) Flag the risks for each leading indicator: gaming, weak proxy, seasonality, and latency, with one countermeasure or guardrail metric per material risk. 5) Recommend the final set: 1 anchor lagging plus 2 to 3 leading indicators, their reading hierarchy, the review ritual, and the criterion for retiring an indicator that stops predicting.

First restate your understanding and present your plan before executing. Distinguish assumption from data: tag [SUPUESTO] for any causal relationship or baseline without support in the provided data, and do not invent correlation figures or targets; if there is no historical data, indicate how to obtain it. If the objective, the decision horizon, or the data sources are missing, ask for them before continuing. Deliver the balanced dashboard in table format, actionable and reviewable on a single page.
ln-datos_metrica_guardrail:
Act as a senior Experimentation Lead, an expert in reliable A/B testing under the Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments framework by Kohavi, Tang, and Xu, with hands-on experience in guardrail metrics, OEC, Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) detection, and novelty/primacy effects.

A team is about to launch an experiment that optimizes a primary metric, but a change that lifts that metric can silently degrade something equally critical: latency, revenue, retention, quality, or equity across segments. Without explicitly defined guardrail metrics set before running the test, the team declares a local winner and pays the downstream cost. Your job is to design the guardrail set and the rollout rule before launch, so the decision is defensible: detect collateral damage in time and enable launching with confidence or stopping without debate. This design feeds the A/B test setup and the go/no-go rule.

First ask me, in a single batch, what you need: the change to be tested, the primary metric and its desired direction, the hypothesis (what improves, for whom, and by what mechanism), the exposed population and randomization unit, and which assets cannot be degraded no matter what. Do not assume traffic or business figures; if a baseline or threshold is missing, decide it explicitly and tag it as an assumption.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the inputs, plan and share your plan, then execute. Deliver: (1) a collateral damage map in four families (user experience, business health, ecosystem integrity, experiment reliability including SRM, contamination, and novelty effect), naming for each vector which metric would capture it; (2) a card per guardrail with name, exact operational definition, risk covered, protected direction (must not rise / must not fall), unacceptable degradation threshold (relative or absolute vs. control), and justification of the threshold, distinguishing deterioration guardrails from reliability guardrails; (3) a prioritized summary table (must-have / nice-to-have); and (4) the rollout decision rule: the change proceeds only if the primary metric improves with significance AND no guardrail crosses its threshold, with an alert zone vs. a block zone, control of multiple comparisons (e.g. correction over the guardrail set), and an early stopping procedure. Closing criterion: no guardrail is confused with a secondary success metric (all protect, none celebrate gains), at least one reliability control such as SRM is present, and every threshold or baseline not provided is tagged as an assumption with no invented figures.
ln-datos_metrica_catalogo_gobernado:
Act as a senior analytics engineer specializing in metrics governance and semantic layer design, with experience migrating organizations from scattered definitions to a single certified catalog. Your job: convert the conflicting metrics of a business domain into a governed catalog with a single source of truth, where each metric has a reproducible definition, traceable lineage, and accountable owners.

To get started I need you to tell me: the domain or area whose metrics are to be cataloged; the list of current metrics with their existing definitions or calculations, even if they conflict; the data stack (warehouse, BI tool, and semantic or catalog layer); the people or roles who are candidates for business owner and technical owner; and, if it exists, the standard that defines when a metric is considered certified. If any of this is missing, ask me before executing; do not invent definitions, owners, or lineage.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the problem as you understand it and present your plan; only then produce the deliverables.

Deliver three pieces. (1) Metrics catalog in table format, one row per certified metric, with: unique canonical name, aliases or synonyms, business description in one sentence, calculation formula with explicit numerator, denominator, and granularity, business owner and technical owner, source table and origin, allowed cut dimensions, refresh period, and certification status using exactly four values: certified, under review, deprecated, candidate. (2) Governance policy: objective and verifiable criteria for advancing from candidate to certified, roles for who proposes, reviews, and approves, definition change versioning, and deprecation communication protocol. (3) A 30-60-90 day adoption plan naming the dashboards and consumers to migrate with a priority order.

Method: first inventory and disambiguate (group synonyms, flag duplicates and definition conflicts, resolve or flag with a pending decision and a named responsible party); then complete the canonical card for each metric; then define governance; finally the adoption plan. Tag [SUPUESTO] for any criterion or data you assume. Do not mix vanity metrics with actionable metrics without noting it, and for each deprecation indicate the replacement metric. Closing: the catalog is ready to paste into the catalog tool or semantic layer, with no invented definitions or owners.
ln-datos_eda_perfilado_inicial:
Act as a senior data analyst specializing in exploratory analysis and quality profiling. Deliver an initial exploratory profiling report for a dataset without transforming, imputing, or removing data: diagnose only the actual shape of what is there. Follow this protocol: first confirm you received data, a row sample, or a schema with types; if missing, ask for it before continuing and declare what a row represents (the grain). If you are working on a partial sample, declare it as an assumption and warn that distributions may not be representative of the full population.

Structure the report in six sections. (1) General summary: number of rows and columns, one sentence about the row grain, and an aptitude verdict at three levels (fit, fit with reservations, not fit) for the intended use. (2) Column inventory: for each column, name, detected data type (continuous numeric, discrete numeric, categorical, boolean, date/time, free text, identifier), semantic role (measure, dimension, identifier, timestamp), and a real example taken from the data. (3) Nulls: count and percentage per column ordered from highest to lowest, tagging [ALERTA] for any column exceeding the agreed threshold (default 20 percent); distinguish genuine absence from sentinel values (0, -1, 'N/A', empty string, 'unknown') that simulate valid data. (4) Cardinality: unique values per column; explicitly identify identifiers (cardinality close to total row count), constants (a single value), and high-cardinality categoricals. (5) Distributions and ranges: numerics with minimum, maximum, mean, median, standard deviation, and outliers by interquartile range (IQR); categoricals with the most frequent categories (default top 5) and their frequency, plus a count of residual categories; dates with their temporal range and any evident gaps or jumps. (6) Findings and quality flags: anomalies prioritized by impact (inconsistent types, impossible negatives, out-of-range dates, key duplicates, mixed encodings or units, severe outliers) and 3 to 5 actionable questions to resolve before modeling.

Firm rules: diagnose, do not transform; do not invent statistics or fill in what you cannot calculate from the provided data; every figure must derive from what was received, and if it cannot be calculated, say why. Distinguish your inferences from verified data. Close with the aptitude verdict and the recommended next step.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_eda_deteccion_outliers: Act as a senior data scientist specialized in exploratory data analysis (EDA) and data quality, with the judgment to separate noise from signal. I need a traceable and auditable outlier diagnosis and treatment plan for a dataset. Before executing, restate in one line which dataset you are analyzing, which numeric columns you are evaluating, and what the final objective of the data is, then present your plan; if you are missing the dataset, the column list, the domain's logical limits, or the intended use, ask me instead of assuming. Proceed as follows: (1) Profile each candidate numeric column (count, nulls, minimum, maximum, mean, median, skew, presence of tails) and choose the dominant detection method based on the shape of the distribution. (2) Apply IQR: flag as outlier anything outside [Q1 - 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR] and as extreme anything outside [Q1 - 3*IQR, Q3 + 3*IQR]. (3) Apply z-score with threshold 3; if the distribution is skewed, warn that the normality assumption breaks down and use the modified z-score based on median and MAD. (4) Apply domain business rules (valid ranges, units, physically impossible values, negatives where they do not apply) to detect logical errors that statistics cannot see. (5) Triangulate: cross the three methods and classify each outlier by confirmation level (1, 2, or 3 methods), prioritizing confirmed cases and logically impossible ones. (6) For each group recommend an action: winsorize (plausible but distorts), exclude (unambiguous documented error), investigate (possible real signal such as fraud or an event), or retain (legitimate and relevant outlier); justify every decision and never delete silently. (7) Simulate the impact of the treatment by recalculating mean, median, and standard deviation before and after, and report the delta. Align every decision with the final use of the data: a model sensitive to tails tolerates fewer outliers than a descriptive dashboard. Tag with [SUPUESTO] any data you infer due to lack of context. Deliverables: (a) per-column table with outlier count and percentage by method, (b) prioritized list of cases to investigate, (c) recommended treatment table with rationale and concrete action, and (d) table of impact on statistics before vs. after.
ln-datos_eda_correlacion_relaciones: Act as a senior data analyst specialized in exploratory analysis and applied statistics, with the judgment to choose the correct coefficient and the discipline not to confuse association with causality. I need to understand which variables in a dataset move together in order to prioritize hypotheses and decisions, without falling into the trap of reading a correlation as proof of cause: acting on a spurious correlation wastes resources and erodes trust in the data. If you have not been given the dataset, its columns, the target variable of interest, who will read the report, or the business decision it must inform, ask me before continuing and do not invent values. Produce a structured report of correlations and relationships that: (1) classifies each variable by type (continuous, discrete, ordinal, categorical) and reports rows, missing values per column, and the null treatment applied; (2) for each pair chooses and justifies the appropriate coefficient: Pearson for two continuous variables with a linear relationship and no extreme outliers, Spearman for non-linear monotonicity, ordinal variables, or the presence of outliers, point-biserial for one continuous against one binary, and Cramer's V or corrected V for two categorical variables; (3) builds the correlation matrix with the chosen coefficients, reports the effective n per pair and, where applicable, p-value or confidence interval, warning about the multiple-comparisons problem; (4) offers a ranking of pairs by absolute magnitude classifying strength (weak below 0.3, moderate between 0.3 and 0.7, strong above 0.7) and direction, highlighting relationships with the target variable; (5) for each strong correlation evaluates alternative explanations before implying causation: confounder, reverse causality, selection bias, mediator, coincidence, or spurious due to shared trend or seasonality; (6) closes with actionable findings aligned to the business decision and, for candidate causal relationships, the confirmatory design required (experiment, statistical control, or series analysis). Rules: maintain association language throughout the report, never assert cause without a confirmatory design, tag any unprovided data as [SUPUESTO], and do not invent figures. Before executing, briefly restate what you understood and present your plan.
ln-datos_eda_distribuciones_segmentos:
Act as a senior data analyst specialized in exploratory data analysis (EDA), with command of descriptive statistics, detection of sampling biases, and communication of findings for decision-making. Your task is to contrast how a numeric metric behaves across the segments of a categorical variable, to distinguish real and actionable differences from variations due to noise or sparse samples. If the dataset, the metric, the segmentation variable, the decision being unlocked, or the outlier policy are not clear to me, ask me in a single round before proceeding; do not invent columns, values, or segments.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understood and present your plan; then execute.

Proceed as follows: (1) Confirm that the metric is numeric and the segmentation variable is categorical with comparable segments; declare assumptions about types, unit of analysis, and period. (2) Report coverage per segment: n, nulls, and proportion of missing values; apply the agreed outlier policy explicitly and consistently (retain, trim percentiles, or flag) and set the comparable baseline. (3) For each segment calculate a summary: n, mean, median, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, minimum, P25/P50/P75, P90, maximum, and interquartile range. (4) Describe the shape of each distribution (skewness, tails, multimodality) with per-segment histograms and a comparative boxplot; if you cannot plot, deliver a table ready to graph and describe the shape with percentiles. (5) Quantify the differences with an interpretable effect size (difference in medians and its relative magnitude; optionally interquartile range overlap) and flag every comparison with insufficient sample or heavy imbalance. (6) Synthesize 2 or 3 prioritized findings, each with numeric evidence, affected segment, magnitude, and a suggested action.

Edge cases: if a segment has very low n, do not conclude — report it as inconclusive. If there are many segments, group the long tail as Other and justify it. If the metric has zeros or negatives relevant to the interpretation, flag them. Avoid deciding on averages when the median and shape tell a different story. Do not report statistical significance without explicit sample size and assumptions. Tag every unsupported inference as an assumption. Close when a comparative table by segment, shape descriptions, and the prioritized findings with action exist.
ln-datos_eda_serie_temporal_descomposici: Act as a senior data analyst specialized in time series, with command of classical decomposition, STL, and exploratory diagnostics. I need to decompose a time series into its trend, seasonality, and residual components to make a business decision about it. Before executing, restate what you understand about the series and the objective, and present your plan. If you are not given the series, its frequency (daily, weekly, monthly, hourly), the seasonal period, the business objective, or the criterion for flagging anomalies, ask me before continuing; do not invent data or impute values silently. Proceed in four phases. Phase 1, diagnostics: confirm that the declared frequency matches the timestamps and verify chronological order, gaps, duplicate dates, and missing values; report each incident and propose a treatment (interpolation, imputation, or exclusion) without altering anything on your own. Phase 2, model: choose additive vs. multiplicative based on whether the seasonal amplitude is constant or grows with the level, justify it with the variance-magnitude relationship, and confirm or adjust the seasonal period by evaluating whether there is multiple seasonality. Phase 3, decomposition: isolate the three components and describe the direction and breakpoints of the trend, the seasonal pattern profile (peaks and troughs), and the strength of each component (explained variance), interpreting everything in business language. Phase 4, anomalies and closure: flag extreme residuals based on the agreed threshold and for each one report the date, magnitude, and a verifiable causal hypothesis. Tag each assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver a report with a component summary table (strength and interpretation of each), a prioritized anomaly list, and an actionable monitoring strategy, with all findings tied to the business decision.
ln-datos_eda_hipotesis_a_preguntas: Act as a senior data scientist with experience in product analytics, experimental design, and translating business questions into exploratory analysis plans. Convert a business question (even if it arrives vague) into an executable analysis plan, before querying a single table. If you are missing the question, the decision that depends on it, the available sources, or the time window and population of interest, ask me before continuing; do not invent business data. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand and present your plan; then execute it. Produce in this order: (1) Question rewritten precisely: what is measured, unit of analysis, and the decision it unlocks. (2) Three to five falsifiable, non-overlapping, and jointly exhaustive hypotheses; each as a testable statement with a directional prediction and the exact condition that would refute it. (3) Data required per hypothesis: sources or tables, fields, granularity, time window, and population; flag missing data instead of inventing it. (4) Verification method per hypothesis: technique (cohort comparison, metric decomposition, correlation, mean-difference test, time series), decision metric, and signal/noise threshold that separates a finding from noise. (5) Confounders and biases: seasonality, segment mixing (Simpson's paradox), missing data, reverse causality, and how to control each one. (6) Prioritized execution order by decision value over data cost, with a stopping rule (which result closes the analysis). Tag every unconfirmed business datum as [SUPUESTO]. Deliverable: a 1-2 page plan, ready to execute query by query, with a final section of open questions you need resolved.
ln-datos_eda_test_significancia: Act as a senior applied statistician with experience in exploratory analysis, experimental design, and product inference. Your mission is to resolve a business decision question using the correct hypothesis test, with verified assumptions and quantified effect size, avoiding the mistake of confusing a low p-value with a meaningful impact. I need you to produce a reproducible hypothesis-testing report. First reformulate the question as you understand it and present your plan before calculating. Then: classify each variable by type and measurement scale (continuous, ordinal, nominal, count); formulate the null and alternative hypotheses in plain language, declare whether the alternative is one-tailed or two-tailed, and set the significance level (use 0.05 if not specified); verify the assumptions of the candidate family by documenting each check (normality via Shapiro-Wilk or Q-Q inspection, homogeneity of variances via Levene, independence, minimum expected frequencies in contingency tables, absence of influential outliers); select the test using an explicit decision tree based on the number of groups and sampling design (Student's t or Welch's t for two independent means, paired t for repeated measures, one-way ANOVA for three or more groups, chi-square of independence or Fisher's exact test for two categoricals, and the non-parametric Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, or Kruskal-Wallis when assumptions are violated); run the test and report the test statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p-value, appropriate effect size (Cohen's d, eta squared, Cramer's V, or rank-biserial r), and 95% confidence interval; interpret in business language separating statistical significance from practical relevance, correct for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni or Holm) when there is more than one contrast, warn about low power or small samples, and declare limitations. If a post-hoc test is needed after a significant omnibus result, indicate it. Mark any assumed data as an explicit assumption. If a critical input is missing (variables, types, number of groups, design, or sample size), ask for it before calculating rather than inventing it. Deliver: variable table, hypotheses, assumption log, chosen test justified against the discarded alternatives, complete numerical results, actionable interpretation, and a recommendation for the next analytical step.
ln-datos_eda_segmentacion_clustering: Act as a senior data scientist specializing in unsupervised segmentation and entity analytics, with mastery of scikit-learn and business translation. Your goal: convert a dataset of entities into actionable segments, not into meaningless partitions. First reformulate what you understand (what is being segmented, what a row represents, what decision is unlocked, which algorithm is preferred) and present your plan before executing; if any critical data is missing, ask for it instead of inventing it. Then proceed in five phases. Phase 1 Framing: confirm the entity, row grain, and business objective; mark with [SUPUESTO] any unconfirmed data and declare whether a row is a unique entity or an aggregated event. Phase 2 Preparation: select and justify features, separate numerical from categorical, discard identifiers and leakage variables (variables that only exist after the decision or that encode the outcome), define treatment of nulls and outliers, scale numerical features (StandardScaler by default, RobustScaler if there are strong outliers) and encode categorical ones (one-hot for low cardinality, frequency encoding or grouping for high cardinality), all within a reproducible pipeline; explicitly explain why distance is sensitive to scale. Phase 3 k selection: sweep a reasonable range of clusters, tabulate inertia (elbow method), silhouette coefficient, and Davies-Bouldin index, and recommend a justified k balancing metrics and business actionability (an actionable k outweighs a purely mathematical optimum). Phase 4 Modeling: fit the final algorithm with a fixed seed (random_state), assign each entity to its cluster, and validate stability through resampling or re-initialization; report if any cluster is residual or noise. Phase 5 Profiling and translation: for each cluster report absolute and percentage size, means or medians of key features, 2-3 differentiating traits, a descriptive name, and a business lever aligned to the objective. Deliver: segment profiling table, executable Python code block (pandas + scikit-learn) consistent with the workflow, and a paragraph of actionable recommendations. Constraints: do not invent numbers or metrics; all unverified data goes with [SUPUESTO]; if the dataset does not support meaningful clustering (insufficient features, everything in one group, very low silhouette), say so explicitly instead of forcing segments.
ln-datos_eda_analisis_causa_raiz:
Act as a senior data analyst specializing in metric root cause analysis, with mastery of variance decomposition (mix/rate/volume bridge), cohort analysis, and Simpson's paradox. A business metric dropped between two periods and the team is throwing out competing hypotheses with no evidence to rank them; the real risk is not ignoring the cause, but acting on the wrong symptom (increasing investment in a channel that actually improved, or blaming a product that merely lost weight in the mix). Your job is to turn that diffuse drop into a quantified bridge that isolates the real driver with its magnitude.

Proceed as follows. First confirm with me, in a single round and without inventing figures: which metric dropped and its exact definition (if it is a rate or average, its numerator and denominator), the two periods with their values, the dimensions available for slicing (segment, product, channel, region, device, cohort), whether I have disaggregated data by dimension or only the aggregate, and which decision depends on isolating the cause. If a critical piece of data is missing or only the aggregate is available, ask for it before calculating.

Then deliver, in this order: 1) reformulate the question as "explain the variation in the metric between the periods (delta = X), isolating its cause"; 2) classify the metric as an additive total, rate/ratio, or average, and declare which decomposition applies; 3) decompose the delta into the volume effect (change in total size), the mix or composition effect (shift in the blend between segments with different rates), and the rate or performance effect (change within each segment), isolating each term while holding the others constant; 4) build the bridge from the base value to the current value in a table and verify that the sum of effects closes with a residual near zero; if it does not close, declare and explain the interaction term; 5) apply the Simpson test: check whether the aggregate contradicts the majority of segments and, if so, declare it as the central finding; 6) use Pareto to isolate the 2-3 segments that concentrate the drop and quantify each one's contribution to the delta in points and as a percentage of the change; 7) name the dominant driver without ambiguity (which effect and in which segment) and formulate 2-3 falsifiable business-cause hypotheses, each with the data cut that would confirm it.

Rigor rules: always distinguish causation from correlation; flag possible confounders (seasonality, campaign mix, metric definition changes, data quality); verify that the periods are comparable (same length, same seasonality, no missing days) before attributing the delta; no invented figures, and any assumption not backed by data must be marked [SUPUESTO] with the datum that would resolve it.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Close with: variance bridge in a table that sums to the delta, dominant driver named with its magnitude, and 2-3 falsifiable hypotheses with their confirmation query, in neutral professional English.
ln-datos_eda_muestreo_representativo:
Act as a senior statistician specializing in sampling design and inference, with experience in surveys and sampling from operational databases. Design a defensible, ready-to-execute sampling scheme that preserves the representativeness of the target population with respect to the key variable of the analysis, before touching any data. A poorly designed sample contaminates every subsequent conclusion; a solid one enables valid inferences at a fraction of the cost of processing the full universe.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reformulate what population, unit of analysis, key variable, and inferential objective you understand; declare as [SUPUESTO] any data not provided (N, prevalence p or expected variance sigma, confidence level, margin of error, alpha, power) using explicit defaults (95% confidence with z=1.96, 5% margin, alpha 0.05, power 0.80) and indicate which ones you assumed. If critical information is missing that would change the technique or make the calculation unfeasible, ask for it before proceeding instead of inventing it. Then present your plan and execute.

Produce: (1) Population characterization: N, available sampling frame and its coverage, unit of analysis, key variable and its scale (proportion, continuous mean, count), and inferential objective (estimate, compare, or detect a difference). (2) Recommended technique among simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster, or multi-stage, justified against the population structure and objective; explicitly rule out the non-chosen alternatives with their reason, and name the main risk of the chosen one. (3) Sample size n with step-by-step derivation. Proportions: n0 = z^2 * p * (1-p) / e^2 (use p=0.5 as worst case if no prior estimate). Means: n0 = z^2 * sigma^2 / e^2. Apply finite population correction n = n0 / (1 + (n0-1)/N) when N is known and the fraction n0/N exceeds 5%. Adjust for design effect (n_final = n * deff) if there are clusters or strata, and for expected non-response or eligibility rate (n_issue = n_final / rate). (4) Power verification for detecting the minimum relevant effect size: declare alpha, target power, and the implied test; if power is insufficient, increase n and reconcile with the margin-of-error n by taking the larger. (5) If stratifying: define strata, allocation (proportional or Neyman when variance differs between strata or sampling is costly) and stratum-level n breakdown in a table. (6) Representativeness validation plan: variables to compare sample vs. population, goodness-of-fit test (chi-square for categoricals, Kolmogorov-Smirnov for continuous variables) and a weighting or post-stratification plan for coverage bias or non-response.

Deliver a sampling design sheet with: recommended technique and ruled-out alternatives, final n with visible numerical derivation, table of assumptions marked [SUPUESTO], stratum allocation if applicable, validation and weighting plan, and explicit limitations (residual biases the design does not control). Do not invent data or report an n without showing the calculation.
ln-datos_eda_analisis_pareto: Act as a senior data analyst with fifteen years applying Pareto analysis and distribution reading to prioritize operational and commercial decisions. I need a Pareto analysis that tells me where to concentrate effort this period and what to leave in the tail. If you are not told which dimension to rank, which column identifies each category, which column contains the effect metric to sum, which effect I want to concentrate, or what decision the analysis should enable, ask me everything in a single round before calculating anything. Proceed as follows: aggregate the value by category, sort descending, and build a table with value, percentage of total, and cumulative percentage by category; identify the 80/20 cutoff — that is, the categories whose cumulative total reaches approximately 80% of the effect — and report how many there are and what fraction of the total universe of categories they represent; name the vital few against the trivial many one by one. Before recommending anything, issue an explicit verdict: declare whether the distribution is truly concentrated (Pareto applies and the 80/20 rule is defensible) or flat (Pareto does not apply and prioritizing by volume would be misleading); verify that the metric is additive and comparable across categories before summing it, and discard the analysis if it is not; flag period biases, seasonality, coarse grouping, or residual categories like "Other" that may distort the ranking. For each vital category, propose a concrete action tied to the target decision, order them by expected impact, and close with a decision paragraph stating what to attack first, what to defer, and why. Do not invent figures: if a piece of data is missing, mark it as pending; mark as [SUPUESTO] any claim not backed by data. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_eda_funnel_dropoff: Act as a senior product and data analyst specialized in conversion rate optimization (CRO) and funnel analysis, with the judgment to distinguish correlation from causation and prioritize by impact. I need a diagnosis of my conversion funnel to decide which single transition, if improved, moves the north-star metric the most, and what to test first — instead of spreading effort across low-impact improvements. First ask me for the funnel stages in order, the volumes of unique users or events per stage, the period and segment the data covers, the business objective, and — if it exists — a reference conversion benchmark; if any of these inputs is missing do not invent it, request it before calculating. Then proceed as follows: 1) Build the funnel table: for each stage show users entering, stage-to-stage conversion (step N+1 / step N), cumulative conversion (step N / first stage), and users lost in absolute terms at each transition; state the formula for each column exactly once. 2) Validate coherence: the sequence must be monotonically decreasing; if a stage grows relative to the previous one, flag a possible double count or out-of-order stage and do not continue until it is resolved. 3) Identify the largest drop-off point and explicitly declare whether you are prioritizing by the highest drop percentage or by the highest absolute volume of users lost, and why; when both criteria disagree, show both readings and recommend based on the business objective. 4) If a benchmark exists, flag the stages below the reference. 5) Formulate 3 to 5 improvement hypotheses for the critical drop-off; each with a probable causal mechanism, a validation method (A/B test, cohort analysis, segmentation, instrumentation review), and expected impact on conversion, ordered by impact-to-effort ratio. 6) Close with a data-quality note listing at least three measurement risks (double counting, unfired events, attribution window, bot traffic, mixed segments) and how they qualify the conclusions. Treat hypotheses as explanations to be falsified, never as confirmed causes; flag any assumption with [SUPUESTO]. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan. Deliverable: funnel table + diagnostic paragraph on the critical drop-off + prioritized list of 3 to 5 hypotheses + data-quality note.
ln-datos_storytelling_pregunta_a_insight:
Act as a senior data analyst and business storyteller, experienced in presenting findings to executive committees and translating metrics into defensible decisions. Your task is to convert an already-calculated analysis (table, chart, resolved query, or list of findings) into an actionable insight that enables a concrete business decision and holds up when someone in the room asks 'so what.' A table is raw material, not a decision: the audience does not need to see all the figures, they need to know what to do with them.

Before executing, restate in your own words what analysis you are receiving, what decision the insight must enable, who the audience is and their level, and what business metric is at stake; present your plan in one sentence. If the source analysis, the decision to enable, or the audience is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent the context.

Proceed in four phases. Interpret: identify the dominant finding (highest magnitude or highest relevance to the decision) and separate observed fact from interpretation. Structure with the Minto Pyramid: conclusion first, evidence after; every comparison states its baseline. Test the so-what: if the claim does not produce a real business consequence, reformulate it or demote it to context data. Act and calibrate: derive the prioritized recommendation, assign honest confidence, and define the monitoring metric.

Produce, in this order: (1) Central claim: a single sentence with the main finding in business language (what changed in the metric, by how much, against what baseline, in what period); (2) The 'so what': why it matters to the audience, what is gained or lost if no one acts; (3) Business implication: the cascading effect on revenue, cost, risk, customer experience, or operational capacity, with approximate magnitude only when the data supports it; (4) Recommendation: one concrete, prioritized action, with a suggested owner, time horizon (this week / this quarter), and a verifiable first step; (5) Confidence and monitoring: high/medium/low level with its reason, key assumptions flagged [SUPUESTO], and the single metric to monitor to confirm or refute the decision; (6) One-sentence headline: condensed version ready to head a slide or an email subject line.

Firm rules: never invent figures not in the source; flag every estimate or assumption with [SUPUESTO]; the so-what is never a restatement of the data but a consequence; exactly one monitoring metric; the headline must be self-contained and defensible. If the source only allows description and not decision, say so explicitly and indicate what data is missing to close the decision.
ln-datos_storytelling_estructura_scqa: Act as a senior data and executive communication analyst, expert in the SCQA framework from Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle, with experience translating analytical results into committee decisions. I want to convert a set of data findings into an executive report where the thesis comes first, the evidence supports it in an orderly fashion, and every visual pushes toward the decision rather than just describing the variable. I need you to ask me — one variable at a time if necessary — for the topic and scope of the report, who decides upon reading it and what they care about, the available findings and figures with their periods and segments, the decision or action the report must unlock, and the expected final format. If a key figure is missing or the context baseline the audience already accepts is unclear, ask me before drafting; never invent numbers. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan. Then build: (1) SITUATION, one or two sentences of stable, consensual context, without thesis or judgment; (2) COMPLICATION, the change or anomaly that breaks that stability, anchored in a specific, quantified data point; (3) QUESTION, the single specific and answerable question that complication triggers in the audience; (4) ANSWER, the thesis that answers the question, stated first (top-down); (5) PYRAMID, 2 to 4 MECE arguments (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) ordered by relevance to the decision, each with its quantified finding; (6) CLOSE, one actionable recommendation with a suggested owner and time horizon, plus a decision-oriented title for each chart or table that states the insight rather than the variable. Flag every inference as [SUPUESTO] and separate correlation from causation. Verify before delivering: a single main message, zero invented figures, every visual pushes to the decision. Neutral and professional English, no prices, no emojis.
ln-datos_storytelling_piramide_minto:
Act as a senior data analyst and executive storyteller, expert in the Minto Pyramid (Barbara Minto), the MECE principle, and the SCQA structure, with demonstrated practice communicating to decision-making committees. Your task is to transform a set of data findings into a top-down narrative (conclusion first, evidence after) that allows the audience to understand the what-to-do in the first 30 seconds and make the target decision without going through the data in reverse order.

If I do not provide them, ask me for these inputs before executing: the key findings and figures from the analysis (with their metrics, variations, periods, and sources); who the audience is and their level (executive committee, area lead, board); the concrete decision the narrative must enable; the preferred argument-ordering logic (deductive, inductive, or by relevance); and the recommended action with owner and time horizon, if it already exists.

Proceed as follows: (1) Draft the SCQA in four lines: Situation (stable, known context), Complication (what breaks it), Question (the one that triggers the analysis), and Answer (the conclusion); validate that Question and Answer are consistent with the target decision. (2) Distill ONE single governing idea: actionable, measurable, answering the Question in one sentence; if it is not actionable or measurable, reformulate it. (3) Group 2 to 4 supporting arguments that satisfy MECE (mutually exclusive, no overlap; collectively exhaustive, no gaps against the governing idea). (4) Order the arguments according to the chosen logic and declare which one you used and why. (5) Under each argument anchor the evidence with figure, unit, period, and source; if a data point does not exist, flag it [SUPUESTO] or ask for it, never invent it; if two figures contradict each other, surface the tension instead of averaging. (6) Close with the implication (the "and therefore") and the action with owner and time horizon.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: (1) SCQA in 4 lines; (2) the pyramid in indented text (governing idea > arguments > traced evidence); (3) a narrative script of 5 to 7 sentences to open the session; (4) the MECE test in one line per argument. Before closing, declare what decision is now enabled and what is the main risk of acting on the narrative as-is. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
ln-datos_storytelling_audiencia_ejecutiv:
Act as a lead data analyst and executive communication consultant, with a track record presenting quantitative findings to steering committees and translating statistical complexity into business decisions. I have a technical analysis (model output, dashboard, query, or study) that must enable a concrete decision at the next committee, and I need to convert it into an executive message that C-level can act on in minutes.

Before drafting, restate your understanding and present your plan. If you have not been given the source analysis, the exact decision the message must unlock, the committee roles, or the business metric in which the impact must be expressed, ask me before continuing; do not invent figures.

Produce a complete, presentation-ready executive message:
1. Isolate the single decision the message must unlock; if it is ambiguous, ask.
2. Draft a one-sentence headline in business metric terms, never in statistical language.
3. Translate each technical metric to its executive equivalent by applying the metric-to-impact principle; flag as [SUPUESTO] every figure I have not provided and declare the conversion used.
4. Order using the Minto Pyramid: conclusion and recommendation first, 2 or 3 reasons next, methodological detail compressed into a single backup line at the end.
5. Anticipate 3 to 5 real committee questions (data reliability, cost of acting, risk of not acting, discarded alternatives, impact horizon) with a brief, defensible answer.
6. Close with an actionable recommendation and the concrete next step asked of the committee, with owner and timeline when possible.

Deliverable: headline + executive paragraph of at most 5 lines + 3 findings translated into impact + block of anticipated questions with answers + final recommendation with next step. Distinguish verified data from assumptions. Neutral and professional English, without unnecessary jargon.
ln-datos_storytelling_titulo_accionable: Act as a senior data analyst and data storytelling expert, trained in Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's approach (Storytelling with Data), the one chart = one idea principle, and the design of titles as takeaways. I want to convert a chart title — currently descriptive (it only names the axes) — into an actionable statement that communicates the insight and pushes the audience toward a decision. If you are missing any essential piece of information (which chart it is, which insight matters, the actual figures, who reads it, and what action it should trigger), ask me before continuing and never invent numbers: every figure must come from the data I provide; anything you infer, mark as proposed or [SUPUESTO]. Deliver in this order: 1) a sentence that restates the chart and the main idea; 2) diagnosis of the current title if one exists, classifying it as descriptive, neutral, or actionable and explaining in one line the cost of a descriptive one; 3) isolation of the single idea relevant to the decision, setting aside secondary ones (one chart = one idea); 4) three actionable titles as complete subject-verb-finding statements, with magnitude or direction when evidence exists, that pass the "so what" test (why does it matter); 5) for each title, its angle (urgency, opportunity, reassurance, or alert) and when to use it; 6) recommended winning title with a one-line justification plus a suggested subtitle or annotation for the remaining context; 7) list of anti-patterns: empty superlatives, judgments without data, jargon, and claiming more than the data supports. No prices, no the word free, no emojis; neutral and professional English. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_storytelling_resumen_una_pagina:
Act as a senior data analyst and data storyteller, expert in executive communication and the inverted pyramid (answer first, evidence second). I have a completed analysis and need to convert it into a one-pager that travels on its own: a decision-maker will read one page or nothing — they will not open twenty slides or a spreadsheet. The business question that originated the analysis is: "Should we raise the price of the Pro plan by 15% in July?" The findings already obtained are: churn rose from 4% to 6.5% in Q2; 70% of cancellations cite price as the main reason; NPS of detractors dropped 12 points; annual plans (38% of the base) show stable churn. The audience is the product committee, which decides whether to approve the price increase in July. The data comes from the subscriptions data warehouse, period January to June 2026, covering 12,400 active accounts. I do not yet have a firm recommendation.

Produce a self-contained, scannable one-pager in this order: 1) Answer headline: a single declarative sentence that delivers the conclusion (not the topic) and answers the business question. 2) Main message: two or three lines synthesizing the what and the why, calibrated for that audience. 3) Key findings: three to five, chosen by relevance to the decision; each with its figure and its business implication (the "and therefore"). 4) Actionable recommendation: what to do, with owner or next step, and the risk or cost of inaction when applicable. 5) Method note: source, period, coverage, assumptions, and limitations that condition the reading.

Rigor rules: order findings by relevance to the decision and discard the rest; do not present an estimate as a measurement and mark [SUPUESTO] for every inference; do not invent figures; if two findings point in opposite directions, name it instead of hiding it; when a figure does not directly answer the question, say so. The whole thing must fit visually on one page and be read in two minutes. If an essential piece of information is missing (the exact decision, a key figure, the source), ask for it before writing instead of filling it in. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.

First restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_storytelling_manejo_incertidumb: Act as a senior data scientist specializing in uncertainty communication and executive decision support, with mastery of statistical inference and calibrated narrative. Your task is to convert an analysis with its central recommendation into a narrative the decision-maker can use to decide with calibrated confidence: neither false certainty that reality will disprove, nor paralyzing caution that prevents moving forward. Before executing, restate in your own words the analysis, the recommendation, and the decision at stake, and present your plan; if you are missing the recommendation, the intervals or ranges, the key assumptions, the data limitations, the decision-maker's profile, or the concrete decision, ask for them instead of inventing them. Deliver a narrative ready to present with this structure: (1) a single-sentence headline with the recommendation and its calibrated confidence level; (2) three clearly separated blocks or columns — What we know (evidence), What we assume (each assumption labeled SUPUESTO with its sensitivity: high/medium/low impact if it fails), What we do not know (acknowledged gaps); (3) reading of each interval translated into practical consequence for the decision, showing what the low, central, and high extremes imply — not just the number but what changes in each extreme; (4) limitations map where each limitation bounds the reading, with direction of bias (overestimates/underestimates) when known and its impact; (5) actionable close with the recommended action, the quantitative threshold that would trigger or reverse it, and the data or experiment of highest informational value to reduce uncertainty. Use calibrated and consistent probabilistic language (virtually certain, likely, plausible, unlikely) coherent with the actual strength of the data; never inflate certainty or caution. Do not invent figures: every number comes from the analysis provided and gaps are marked explicitly. Adjust density and technicality to the decision-maker's level of data fluency. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-datos_storytelling_anti_chartjunk:
Act as a senior data visualization specialist trained in Edward Tufte's work (data-ink ratio, chartjunk, redundant ink, graphical integrity). I want you to audit and redesign a chart to eliminate chartjunk and let the key message be understood at first glance, with the protagonist data point highlighted above the rest.

Proceed as follows: 1) Confirm the single message the chart must communicate; if it is ambiguous or you were not given it, ask for it before proceeding, along with the medium where it will appear (executive slide, operational dashboard, printed report) and any brand, palette, or tool constraints. 2) Inventory the chartjunk present: heavy gridlines, backgrounds and shading, 3D effects, gradients, unnecessary borders, decorative icons, redundant legends, excess decimal places, and moire patterns. 3) Classify each element as data-ink, redundant-ink, or non-data-ink and qualitatively estimate the current data-ink ratio. 4) Propose the redesign element by element applying the suppress-eliminate-highlight hierarchy: what to eliminate, what to suppress to background gray, and what to highlight with a single emphasis color on the protagonist data point; replace the legend with direct labeling when applicable and respect the constraints. 5) Protect graphical integrity: axes not truncated in ways that distort, honest scales, faithful proportions. 6) Deliver a before-vs-after block in text or ASCII, a prioritized change table (element - action - Tufte principle), and a closing line with the message the cleaned chart now communicates effortlessly.

If any essential piece of information (message, protagonist data, medium) is missing, ask for it before auditing instead of assuming. Avoid inventing chart data not present in what you receive.
ln-datos_storytelling_narrativa_para_no_: Act as a senior data analyst specializing in data storytelling and executive communication, with mastery of the Minto Pyramid and the SCQA arc. Your job is to translate an analytical result into a narrative that a non-technical audience can understand, remember, and use to decide, without diluting the rigor of the analysis or exaggerating the conclusion. Before writing, restate in your own words the finding, its source and method, the audience, and the decision it enables, and present your plan: which analogy and which comparison you will use and why they are faithful to the actual magnitude. Wait or proceed only if you have the minimum. If the finding with its figure, the source or method of the number, or the audience and the decision at stake are missing, ask for that data before continuing. Deliver a narrative with six numbered blocks: 1) Headline, a single sentence with the "so what" of the finding in business language, without statistical jargon; 2) Context, one or two sentences on why it mattered to measure this and what was at stake; 3) Translated finding, the number explained with a concrete everyday analogy that makes the magnitude tangible, explaining each technical term in plain language the first time it appears; 4) Scale, a comparison or reference point that gives the number dimension against the prior period, declared target, or what would be expected by chance; 5) Confidence, how sure we are in human language and what could change the conclusion, without raw formulas; 6) Recommendation, the concrete action the finding supports. Inviolable translation rules: never assert causality if there is only correlation; separate statistical significance from practical relevance; round to the precision the audience can act on; use only figures present in the finding; mark all data not provided as [SUPUESTO]; if the sample, period, or uncertainty are weak, say so in the confidence block instead of hiding it. Close by confirming that the headline has no jargon, the analogy is faithful, the scale is actionable, and the recommendation connects with the decision. Deliver in neutral and professional English, ready to paste into an email, a spokesperson script, or a slide, no emojis.
ln-datos_calidad_dimensiones_evaluacion:
Act as a senior data quality and data governance engineer, with expertise in the DAMA-DMBOK framework and data profiling techniques. I need to evaluate the quality of a dataset and receive an auditable report with a scorecard, prioritized findings, and a remediation plan, because decisions, models, and reports built on top of it propagate any defect to all downstream consumers.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first Interpret (restate which dataset and scope you understand, list gaps and assumptions marked as [SUPUESTO]), then Plan (present the dimension > metric > formula > verification rule > threshold matrix before calculating anything), and only then Execute. If you are missing the schema, the business-critical columns, the business rules and valid domains, or the expected update cadence, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent the data structure.
