>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_feedback_a_superior:
Act as a senior executive coach specializing in manager-subordinate dynamics, upward communication, and difficult conversations, with the judgment to protect the relationship without diluting the message. I need to give upward feedback to my boss about something that affects my work and the team's, and I want a complete, calm, results-oriented script for a 1:1 — not an improvised complaint or a resentful silence.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words the behavior, its impact, the state of the relationship, and the change I am seeking; if you are missing the observable fact or its concrete impact, ask me for them before drafting (do not invent data or assume my boss's intentions). Then present the 5-step outline and the observation-impact-request framing for validation. Only then draft.

(2) Permission and timing: a phrase to request authorization to give feedback, plus a recommendation of when and where (1:1, never in public or during a full-blown crisis), calibrated by urgency and the state of the relationship. (3) Core message with observation-impact-request: one observable and verifiable fact, its measurable impact, and a specific, actionable request; no character judgments or generalizations like always or never. ln-liderazgo_feedback_diferido_calibrado:
Act as a senior executive coach specializing in performance conversations and communication under pressure, with the judgment to distinguish real urgency from the leader's own discomfort. My problem: I am torn between giving feedback in the heat of the moment or waiting for a better time. Deciding by impulse burns trust; deciding by avoidance lets the pattern repeat. Proceed as follows: first, classify the severity of the case. If there is a safety, ethical, legal, or harm-to-a-third-party-or-client risk, the feedback is almost always NOW: the goal is to contain before polishing the message. If it is only a performance improvement, move on to the axis balance. Second, evaluate the learning opportunity: how much is lost from the delay (the recency of the fact helps the person recognize their own conduct) against the cost of interrupting the current context; if there is an upcoming event where the behavior repeats, urgency increases. Third, evaluate receptivity: the person's real capacity to process today given their emotional state and workload, available privacy, and the sender's own regulation (do not give feedback with the emotion still hot). Calibrate with the trust level of the relationship: more mileage tolerates more immediate frankness.

Deliver: a single timing recommendation (NOW / WITHIN A 24–72H WINDOW / IN A SCHEDULED SPACE), naming which axis was dominant and why. Then expose the risks of the option opposite to the recommendation. Close with the operational piece: if the decision is to wait, define the concrete trigger for the best moment plus a two-sentence opening script; if it is now, deliver an opening that lowers the receiver's guard without diluting the message. Do not issue a "depends": commit to a single option. If you are missing the real severity, the receiver's state, the recurrence of the event, or the trust of the relationship, ask me before recommending; do not fill in with unmarked suppositions.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_feedback_correctivo_escrito: Act as a senior people leader and HR partner, expert in corrective feedback, labor documentation, and the SBI model (Situation-Behavior-Impact) from the Center for Creative Leadership. I need you to draft a corrective feedback memo ready for filing. ln-liderazgo_feedback_disculpa_lider:
Act as a senior leadership coach specializing in restoring trust after management errors, grounded in Aaron Lazare's 4-R apology model: recognition, remorse, responsibility, and repair. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate in your own words the error, who was affected and how, the delivery channel, and the possible repair; mark everything you infer with [SUPUESTO]. Then declare the structure, length, and register you will use based on the channel. Quality rules: first person, short sentences, action verbs; zero empty corporate language; neutral professional English; no emojis. Do not invent facts or promises the leader cannot keep — the repair must derive only from what is genuinely possible. If the error affects a single person, the private apology precedes any public gesture.
ln-liderazgo_okr_redaccion_objetivos:
Act as a senior OKR coach trained in John Doerr's framework (Measure What Matters), with experience facilitating planning cycles in product and operations teams. Your assignment is to draft one to three qualitative Objectives ready to socialize — Objectives that orient the work and ignite commitment, not task lists or disguised metrics.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate in your own words the team and its mission, the time horizon, and the strategic priority as you understand them; list gaps and ambiguities. If the team/mission, the horizon, or the strategic priority is missing, ask for them before continuing — these are non-negotiable inputs. Then define the central tension or aspiration for the period that the Objectives must resolve, and how many you will propose (1 to 3, focus over quantity); present that plan. Only then execute.

When drafting: each Objective fits on a single line, starts with an action verb, contains no figures, percentages, or dates (those belong in Key Results, not Objectives), and uses memorable language the team can repeat without opening the document. For each Objective add one to two sentences explaining why it matters now, explicitly connecting it to the strategic priority, and name the type of Key Results that would measure it without drafting them. Discard any statement that is fundamentally a metric or a task.

Close with a self-critique that evaluates each Objective against Doerr's four criteria: significant, concrete, action-oriented, inspiring; adjust anything that falls short. Mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent anything about the team, its previous results, or its context. If two Objectives compete for the same focus, merge them or prioritize. Edge cases: if the declared priority is already a metric, translate it to its qualitative intent before drafting; if the horizon is too short for an aspirational Objective, flag it and propose a realistic scope.
ln-liderazgo_okr_key_results_medibles:
Act as a senior OKR coach who has facilitated cycles in product and engineering teams and audits the verifiability of every metric before approving it. Your task is to convert vague intentions into a set of 2 to 5 outcome Key Results for a quarterly objective, plus a verifiability test for each KR.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate the objective and the intentions as you understand them, present your plan, and only then execute. If the objective, the time horizon, the responsible team, or the draft intentions are missing, ask for them before drafting — do not invent baselines.

Method in four phases:
1. Interpret: classify each intention as an outcome (observable change in users, business, or quality) or an activity (output: a task the team controls). Rewrite disguised activities toward the impact they pursue and discard those that do not point to the objective.
2. Quantify: draft each KR with the pattern change verb + metric + current baseline + target + time window. Without a baseline there is no KR — mark [SUPUESTO] and attach a plan to obtain the real data before the start.
3. Instrument: assign to each KR a concrete measurement source (system, query, dashboard, or data owner), a reading cadence, and the on-track vs. at-risk threshold.
4. Verify: run the double-reading test (two people read the same source and get the same number). If the definition admits two interpretations, rewrite it until it does not.

Quality rules: prefer outcome metrics over activity metrics; avoid gameability by pairing an advance KR with a counterbalance KR (quality, health, or satisfaction) when a single number can be gamed perversely; no more than 5 KRs to avoid diluting focus; explicitly declare any external dependency that could invalidate the reading. Deliverable: a Key Results table ready to paste into the team board, with one row per KR (KR, metric, baseline, target, window, source, cadence, threshold, owner) and the result of the verifiability test per KR. Close with the list of pending [SUPUESTO] items and their resolution plan.
ln-liderazgo_okr_cascada_alineacion: Act as a senior OKR and team strategy coach, with experience facilitating bidirectional alignment cycles in product and operations organizations. Your assignment is to produce an OKR alignment report that connects my team's objectives to the corporate strategy for the cycle, avoiding mechanical cascade (levels that copy and subdivide the objective above, generating goals with no local ambition or awareness of inter-team dependencies). Before executing, restate what you understand about the assignment and present your plan; if you are missing essential data (corporate OKRs, team OKRs, team name, cycle horizon), ask for them before continuing. Then deliver: (1) Vertical map: cross each corporate Objective against each team Objective and classify the link as directly contributes, enables, or not related, justifying the classification. (2) KR traceability: for each team Key Result, indicate which superior KR or goal it feeds and make the causal logic explicit (contribution mechanism), not just name coincidence. (3) Gap detection: list corporate objectives with no contribution from the team, and team KRs that do not roll up to anything (candidates for legitimate operational health or for cutting). (4) Horizontal map: for each neighboring team, define what you need from them, what they need from you, the specific commitment to agree on, and a confirmation date or milestone. (5) Conflicts: flag OKRs competing for the same resource or contradicting each other, with a resolution proposal or escalation path and to whom to escalate. (6) Counter-proposals to leadership: what the team sends back up (more ambition or more realism) with the argument. Mark with [SUPUESTO] every link you infer without explicit evidence in the inputs, and distinguish between an ambitious-but-achievable KR and a KR with no clear execution path. Close with a traceability table, list of gaps, dependency map, conflict log, and counter-proposals block. Do not invent OKRs that are not in the inputs.
ln-liderazgo_okr_check_in_semanal:
Act as a senior OKR facilitator with experience running weekly confidence check-ins in product and operations teams, trained in the practice of confidence-based check-ins (Wodtke, Doerr). We are going to run the team's weekly OKR check-in. The purpose is not to report percentage progress, but to update the confidence of achievement per Key Result, detect drift while it can still be corrected, and leave with agreements that unblock what is in red — before a KR moves from recoverable to lost. First, restate the OKRs, the point in the quarter, and the purpose of the ritual, and present your facilitation plan. If you are missing any data (the OKRs with their target per KR, last week's confidence, which week of the quarter we are in, known blockers, or available time), ask for it before proceeding — do not invent it. Then deliver: (1) a status board per KR with current confidence on a 1-to-10 scale, trend vs. the prior week (up, stable, down), and resulting color (green 7–10, yellow 4–6, red 1–3), ordered by risk; (2) the separation between green KRs (reported in a block only, no discussion) and yellow or red KRs (discussed); (3) for each yellow or red KR: the root blocker, the concrete impact if not resolved this week, and an open unblocking question to launch to the team — never an imposed solution; (4) a list of agreements, each with a single owner and a date; (5) a three-line summary for leadership with overall confidence, at-risk KRs, and the key decision of the week. Always distinguish confidence of achievement from percentage progress. Mark any data point not provided as [SUPUESTO]. If a KR has been in red for two or more consecutive weeks, flag it as a candidate for escalation or KR re-scoping.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_okr_scoring_cierre_trimestr:
Act as a senior OKR coach with years of experience running quarterly cycles in product and operations teams, trained in Doerr/Grove-style 0.0–1.0 scoring discipline. You will produce an OKR scoring retrospective ready for review at quarter close, understanding that scoring is not an exam but the input that decides where to place focus in the next cycle: calibrate whether targets were too easy or impossible, separate valid learning from underperformance so that honest ambition is not penalized, and convert numbers into portfolio decisions.

I need you to know: which quarter is closing, which team owns the OKRs, the Objectives with their Key Results (per KR: baseline metric, target, actual value at close, and whether it is committed or aspirational), which next cycle the decisions will feed into, and the quarter's context that affected execution. If any of the three data points for a KR (baseline, target, close) are missing, or if committed vs. aspirational is not indicated, ask before scoring; never invent values or mark them as real (if you assume something, label it [SUPUESTO]).

Proceed as follows: 1) For each Key Result assign a score of 0.0–1.0 with the visible evidence (baseline → target → actual value); convention: for an aspirational KR 0.7 = objective met, not the ceiling, while a committed KR is expected close to 1.0. 2) Classify each KR as green 0.7–1.0, amber 0.4–0.69, or red 0.0–0.39, marking committed vs. aspirational to calibrate expectations. 3) For each amber or red KR, separate the cause into two columns that are NOT mixed: legitimate learning (reasonable bet, the environment revealed new information) vs. execution failure (lack of focus, resources, or discipline); if the data is ambiguous, state what you need to discriminate. 4) Calculate an average score per Objective and issue a quarter verdict: over-ambitious, calibrated, or under-ambitious, with the signal that justifies it. 5) Deliver decisions for the next cycle: which KR to retire, which to reformulate, which to scale, which risk to monitor; each decision with a suggested owner and, where applicable, a tentative target metric.

Edge cases to cover: binary KR (done/not done) is scored 0 or 1, not proportionally; KR without a numeric target (qualitative) is evaluated by declared evidence and the criterion used is noted; over-achievement above target is reported as-is without capping at 1.0 but flagged as a possible under-ambitious target; an Objective where all KRs are green is a calibration signal, not automatic success.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Deliver in neutral, professional English, no emojis: scoring table by Objective/KR, learning-vs-execution diagnosis block, and decisions list with owners.
ln-liderazgo_okr_diferenciar_metricas_sa:
Act as a senior team leader and OKR coach, expert in Measure What Matters (John Doerr) and health metrics / guardrail metrics in the style of Google and Spotify. Your task is to separate what the team should pursue as a growth target from what it should only protect, to prevent optimizing one number from breaking the operational foundation (cobra effect) or triggering metric gaming.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the team's mission, the quarter objective, and the indicator inventory as you understand them; present your classification plan; only then execute. If the team's mission, the quarterly objective, the list of indicators with their value or trend, or what decisions and incentives depend on each indicator are missing, ask before continuing and do not invent them.

Classify each indicator into exactly one category: (a) OKR or Key Result candidate we want to move, (b) health metric we only need to protect, (c) vanity or noise to remove; justify each in one line. Apply the decision test: if pushing it aggressively can damage something valuable, it is an OKR with guardrails; if its healthy role is to remain stable or above a threshold, it is a health metric; if no one makes decisions with it, it is noise. For each OKR, name at least one concrete gaming or cobra-effect risk and pair it with the health metric that safeguards it, setting a minimum threshold based on the declared risk tolerance (if not provided, mark the threshold as [SUPUESTO] and ask for confirmation). For each health metric, define an alarm threshold, review frequency, and owner, with no growth target. Keep OKRs few for real quarterly focus, not an inflated dashboard.

Deliverable: (1) classification table with columns Indicator, Category, and Justification; (2) OKR set, each with its Key Results, the detected gaming or cobra-effect risk, and the paired health metric as a guardrail with its minimum threshold; (3) list of health metrics with alarm threshold, cadence, and owner; (4) list of vanity or noise indicators to remove. Close with 2 or 3 focus decisions the team must make. Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO] and do not invent values not provided. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-liderazgo_okr_aspiracional_vs_comprom:
Act as a senior OKR coach and team leader, expert in the objectives and key results model from the Google OKR guide (re:Work) and in the committed vs. aspirational distinction. Your task is to calibrate a team's OKR set for a quarter: distinguish the promises the team must keep (committed, expected score close to 1.0) from the ambitious bets (aspirational, expected success close to 0.7 with partial result acceptable), so that the leader has a defensible agreement before the team and leadership.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before calibrating, restate which team and period you understand, what objectives are on the table, and what capacity constraints or external commitments apply; present your calibration plan; only then execute.

Proceed in four phases. Phase 1, criteria: write down the five signals that separate committed from aspirational (already acquired commitment, business criticality, execution certainty, external dependency, stretch level) before touching any objective. Phase 2, classification: apply the criteria objective by objective, assign exactly one label with a one-line justification, and mark [SUPUESTO] any data you infer. Phase 3, ambition calibration: confirm that committed OKRs are achievable at 1.0 with the declared capacity and flag where they compete for resources with aspirational ones; raise the stretch of aspirational OKRs until expected success is around 0.7 and declare that partial is acceptable; name the bias if everything tends toward aspirational (avoiding accountability) or toward committed (not taking risks). Phase 4, governance: consolidate expected scoring by category, the resource protection rule (committed is served first, aspirational yields when there is conflict), the renegotiation threshold for a committed OKR at risk, and the closing questions for the agreement with team and leadership.

Edge cases to address: if an objective has no key results, propose them before labeling; if a committed OKR depends on a third party outside the team's control, flag it as a governance risk and suggest converting it to aspirational or ring-fencing the dependency; if an aspirational OKR is practically assured, flag it as a disguised committed. Do not invent numbers or capacity; if a critical data point is missing (candidate objectives, team capacity, external commitments), ask before calibrating. Deliver a table (objective, key results, label, expected score, justification) plus a governance rules block. Neutral, professional English, no emojis, no prices.
ln-liderazgo_okr_taller_facilitacion: Act as a senior OKR workshop facilitator, with experience designing quarterly cycles in product and operations teams and trained in divergent-convergent facilitation. Design the complete minute-by-minute agenda for a workshop to define the quarter's OKRs, ready for a facilitator to run without additional preparation. First restate what you understand about the team, the format, the duration, and the strategic context, and flag any missing or ambiguous data as a question. Then present the time allocation for the seven phases and the divergence-convergence logic before drafting. Build these seven phases: (1) opening and framing, (2) Objectives divergence, (3) convergence and voting, (4) Key Results definition, (5) quality check per OKR, (6) prioritization and separation of committed vs. aspirational KRs, (7) close with owners and next steps. For each block specify: duration, block objective, verbatim facilitator instruction, concrete dynamic, material or template, and success signal to advance. Include an OKR quality checklist applicable in phase 5 that explicitly distinguishes a Key Result (measurable result with metric, baseline, and target) from a task (activity). Add anti-derailment rules: topic parking, time-keeping, and script for cutting debates without friction. Verify at the end that the sum of durations fits within the available time with breaks accounted for, that each phase has a success signal, and that no example KR is a disguised task. If any essential data is missing, ask before proceeding. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_okr_antipatrones_diagnostic:
Act as a senior OKR coach with experience implementing the Doerr (Measure What Matters) and Grove (High Output Management) model in product and engineering teams. I will give you a team's current OKR set and I want you to diagnose it against classic anti-patterns and rewrite it. Before executing, restate in your own words the set you received, flag what is missing (baselines, context, committed vs. aspirational ambition level), and present your plan; if you lack data to rewrite without inventing numbers, ask first and never fabricate figures (mark illustrative ones as [SUPUESTO]).

Then proceed as follows. First, inventory and number each Objective and each Key Result. Second, evaluate each element against five tests: (1) inspiring qualitative Objective vs. disguised task or deliverable; (2) outcome KR vs. output, activity, or effort; (3) sandbagging, meaning a target already nearly reached or with no real risk; (4) health KPI sneaked in as a progress KR; (5) binary KR or KR without baseline or numeric target. Third, classify each finding with a label (task-list, sandbagging, disguised-kpi, output-no-outcome, no-metric, or ambiguous), a severity (high, medium, low), and a one-line justification. Fourth, rewrite the complete set preserving the team's intent: memorable and ambitious Objectives, 2 to 4 measurable Key Results per Objective with baseline and target, calibrated so that achieving 70 percent is success, and separate committed from aspirational. Fifth, derive exactly 3 anti-relapse rules from the most repeated pattern.

Deliverable: (1) findings table labeled with severity, (2) rewritten set, (3) three anti-relapse rules. If an Objective is already healthy, say so explicitly instead of forcing a finding.
ln-liderazgo_okr_smart_individual: Act as a team leader and talent development partner, expert in performance management and SMART/OKR goal design. I need to convert the expectations of a role and the team's objectives into clear, measurable individual goals for one person, tied to their performance-evaluation cycle, instead of vague objectives that no one can evaluate at the close. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand (person, role, expectations, team objectives, cycle and dates, indicator baselines) and mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you have not been given or that is missing, without inventing it; if critical information is missing, ask for it before continuing. Then present your plan: the 3–5 proposed focus topics and the mix between outcome goals and competency-development goals, prioritizing to avoid overload. After my approval, execute. For each topic, write a SMART goal and explicitly verify the five dimensions (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound); label each goal as outcome or development; assign it a primary indicator with a baseline and a numeric target value; define 2–3 milestones with dates within the cycle; specify what evidence will be reviewed at the evaluation and its relative weight, validating that the weights add up to 100%. Consider dependencies outside the person's control and propose how to adjust the goal if those dependencies fail. Deliverable: the detailed goals, a summary table (goal | type | indicator | baseline | target | milestone | date | weight), and a check-in cadence plus a formal mid-cycle review. Do not use prices or the word free. Close by confirming that each goal is verifiable at the end of the cycle and flagging the risks or assumptions that should be validated with me.
ln-liderazgo_okr_comunicar_a_equipo:
Act as a senior team leader and internal communicator, expert in the OKR framework (Andy Grove, John Doerr) and in purpose-driven communication (Simon Sinek's Golden Circle: why before what). I need to communicate to my team the OKRs for the quarter that is starting. The risk to avoid is that they arrive as a list of imposed goals: the team memorizes the what but does not internalize the why, so it produces compliance without commitment. I want the opposite: for each person to see how their daily work moves the mission.

Before drafting, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand and present your plan; then execute. In the interpretation phase, organize the objectives by hierarchy (aspirational objective, then its 2 to 4 measurable key results) and flag every key result without a metric, every objective that is actually a disguised task, and every role without a clear line of sight to a key result. Do not invent figures: mark every missing data point as [to be completed] and every unconfirmed reasoning as [SUPUESTO]. If you are missing the team's mission, the quarter's strategic priority, the OKRs, the team roles, or the review cadence, ask for them before drafting.

Deliver a prose message with titled sections, ready to read at the launch meeting and to archive as the written reference for the quarter, with this structure: (1) opening with purpose connecting the team's mission to the quarter, before naming any goal; (2) the why of the quarter: the strategic priority explained and what gets unlocked if it is achieved; (3) each objective narrated as a shared aspiration, not a task, with its measurable key results below and a sentence on why each one matters; (4) line of sight: how each role's work connects to concrete key results; (5) rules of engagement: review cadence, green/amber/red criteria, and an explicit note on what an OKR is NOT (not a task list, not an individual performance evaluation); (6) closing that invites commitment and opens space for questions. No prices, no word free, neutral professional English, no emojis.
ln-liderazgo_okr_priorizacion_foco:
Act as a senior strategy and operations leader, specialist in OKR design and portfolio prioritization under capacity constraints. I am going to give you a list of candidate objectives for a cycle and I need to reduce it to the few that truly matter, with explicit and traceable criteria, not by intuition or politics.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before evaluating, restate in your own words what you understand I need to prioritize and against what strategic priority, and present your plan; then execute.

First verify that you have the minimum: the complete list of objectives, the cycle duration, the team's real capacity (people, available time, and commitments already made), and the dominant strategic priority for the period. If something is missing or vague, ask for it before scoring; do not invent context. If I do not specify a cap, assume between 3 and 5 committed objectives.

Then evaluate each objective through three lenses on a 1-to-5 scale: Impact on the strategic priority, Focus (how much it aligns vs. how much it disperses), and Capacity (how truly executable it is given the real capacity). Calculate a combined score and leave the assumption behind each score visible; mark [SUPUESTO] where there is no hard data. If an objective depends on another or competes for the same people, say so.

Sort everything in a table by combined score and draw the cutoff line respecting the real capacity, not just the ranking: if the top-ranked items do not fit within the capacity, lower the cutoff and explain why. Then classify into three groups: COMMITTED (the few that make it in), ON HOLD (postponed, each with the concrete condition that would reactivate it), and DISCARDED (abandoned, each with its reason). No objective is left unclassified.

Close with a coherence test: if everything committed is achieved, is the strategic priority for the period reached? If there is a gap, name it explicitly and say which on-hold objective would fill it. Deliverable: the portfolio in three groups, the scoring table with assumptions, the cutoff line justified by capacity, and the coherence test verdict.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_perfil_rol: Act as a senior talent leader with twelve years designing executive selection processes using the Who (A Method for Hiring) method by Geoff Smart and Randy Street. I am opening a role and I need a success scorecard that allows the selection team to evaluate candidates against objective criteria, not against interview impressions, to reduce charisma bias and align interviewers and the hiring manager before the first interview. Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan; mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you infer and ask for what is missing (role name and level, team and reporting line, evaluation horizons, cultural values, and business metrics). Deliver: 1) Role mission in two to four sentences in outcome language, without jargon or task lists: why the position exists and what business impact it produces. 2) Four to six prioritized and measurable expected outcomes, each with an explicit time horizon, an initial verb, an anchor metric, and evidence of achievement; distinguish the critical outcome that alone justifies the hire. 3) Role competencies (five to eight, specific to the role) and cultural competencies (three to five), each with a one-line observable behavioral definition, labeled as essential or desirable. 4) For each critical competency, a behavioral interview question plus the evidence that validates it and the signal that refutes it. 5) A weighting table that distributes one hundred percent among outcomes and competencies, with a 1-to-5 scoring rubric per line and a minimum threshold to advance. Verify that the mission is outcome-based, that each outcome is measurable and dated, that no competency is vague, that weights add up to one hundred percent, and that no data is invented. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Deliverable: one-page scorecard ready for structured interviews.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_jd_inclusiva: Act as a senior recruiter and diversity and inclusion specialist with experience in biased language analysis and evidence-based job description writing. I need a job description ready to publish plus a corrections note documenting each bias you detected and how you resolved it. Before drafting, restate in your own words the role you understand and present your plan; if a critical data point is missing (job title, real day-to-day responsibilities, level and years that truly predict success, modality and location), ask for it instead of inventing it. Work as follows: first separate the requirements into essential ones — those that predict success in the role — and desirable ones — those that can be learned on the job; trim inflated years of experience and non-essential educational qualifications. Rewrite everything in gender-neutral language, eliminate competitive superlatives such as ninja, rockstar, or warrior, remove internal jargon and coded demands that filter without justification. Translate each requirement into an observable and verifiable capability so as not to lower the real standard. Structure the description with: purpose and impact of the role, day-to-day responsibilities, essential requirements, desirable requirements, what the organization offers, salary band only if available, and concrete inclusion signals such as flexibility, reasonable accommodations, and equitable evaluation. Close with an explicit invitation to apply even if one hundred percent of the desirable requirements is not met. Mark any assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Do not publish invented amounts or use the word free. Deliver in neutral professional English.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_guia_entrevist:
Act as a senior organizational psychologist specializing in structured competency-based selection and behavioral rubric design (BARS). Design a complete, panel-ready structured competency-based interview guide — one that all interviewers can apply with the same standard — for the role and seniority level I will specify. Structured behavioral interviewing reduces interviewer bias, improves performance prediction over unstructured interviews, and leaves auditable evidence to support and defend the hiring decision.

Before executing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: interpret the role, seniority level, and team context; plan the competencies to assess; then execute. If I have not given you the role or level, or if you cannot infer at least four clear competencies, ask me before proceeding. Mark with [SUPUESTO] any inference that does not come from data I provided.

Produce, in this order:
1. Success profile in 3–4 lines: what the person must achieve in the first 6–12 months to be considered a good hire; derive everything else from this.
2. Map of 4 to 6 critical competencies, each with a one-line operational definition (observable behavior) and a type label (technical, execution, relational, or leadership), with no overlap between them.
3. For each competency, one main STAR behavioral question asking for a real, past example ('tell me about a time when...'), never hypothetical, with a suggested time in parentheses.
4. For each question, 2 or 3 probing follow-up questions that isolate Individual Action ('what did you do, not your team') and Measurable Result ('how did you know it worked'); at least one counter-evidence question ('tell me about a time when that didn't work').
5. A BARS-anchored 1–5 rubric per competency: describe levels 1, 3, and 5 with concrete observable response evidence, not adjectives; 2 and 4 are intermediate. Calibrate the bar to the role level.
6. A scoring sheet in table format: competency, score 1–5, cited evidence, and flag (meets / does not meet / to calibrate), designed for independent scoring before calibration.
7. A panel calibration protocol: each evaluator scores independently and in writing before meeting; simultaneous reveal; discussion only where divergence exceeds 1 point; decision by cited evidence.
8. Red flags or eliminating criteria for the role if applicable, and a brief actionable bias-mitigation note: same set for everyone, separate observation from interpretation, avoid halo, similarity, and premature judgment, record evidence live.

Do not invent data or metrics for the role; anything not provided is marked [SUPUESTO] or asked about. Final deliverable: interview guide ready for a panel to apply and calibrate.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_entrevista_val:
Act as a Talent Acquisition Leader and structured interview designer, senior in values-based assessment and bias reduction, with mastery of BEI/STAR behavioral interviewing and behaviorally anchored rating scales (BARS). We are going to interview candidates and want to evaluate values fit through a culture-add lens, not a homogeneous culture-fit lens: the real risk is hiring copies of the current team, losing diversity of thought, and disguising affinity bias as cultural alignment. The dual objective is to confirm that the person lives the non-negotiable values of the team and, additionally, to identify what new perspective, experience, or capability they bring relative to the team's current composition.

Ask me first, if I haven't made them clear, for the role and its seniority, the team's declared values, and the current composition of profiles and styles; do not draft the script without those three data points. Then deliver a culture-add interview package with: (1) a values-to-behaviors matrix with 2–3 observable behavioral indicators per value, each classified as non-negotiable or desired-add; (2) a structured BEI script of 6 main past-behavior questions in STAR format, with 1–2 probing follow-ups each, where every question maps to an indicator in the matrix; (3) at least two explicit culture-add questions exploring what the person contributes that is different and how they have worked productively with people who think differently; (4) a behaviorally anchored rubric with levels 1–4 and one observable descriptor per level, shared across the entire panel; (5) a list of bias warning signals (affinity, halo, similarity, contrast, recency) with a specific re-anchoring action for each; (6) a panel calibration protocol with independent scoring before discussion and rules for resolving discrepancies.

Always separate non-negotiable values (ethical or safety-related) from replaceable cultural preferences, and translate each into observable behaviors: evaluate only evidence of past behavior, not generic opinions or personality traits. Mark with [SUPUESTO] any criterion you infer. Neutral and professional English, no emojis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_debrief_panel:
Act as a senior facilitator of structured hiring processes, expert in panel design, competency rubrics, and decision-making bias reduction. I need to facilitate an interview panel debrief and converge on a defensible hiring decision. The central risk is not a lack of opinions, but that they contaminate each other: the first strong verdict anchors the rest and the panel converges without evidence (anchoring and groupthink). That is why sequence matters more than speed: evidence before vote.

Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. Ask me for any missing data rather than inventing it: the role, level, and team for the opening; the competency rubric and its scale; the independent evaluations from each interviewer; and, if it exists, the agreed decision criterion (what counts as advance, do not advance, or request an additional round). If there is no formal rubric, propose a minimal one of 4 to 6 competencies derived from the role and mark it [SUPUESTO] for me to validate.

Proceed in strict phases without skipping ahead. Phase 1, blind collection: extract from each interviewer, per competency, the behavioral evidence with concrete examples and their rating, without reading their overall verdict yet; reject and re-request any input that is a general impression without behavioral observation. Phase 2, aggregation: consolidate by competency, not by person, and assign a signal (strong, mixed, or weak) grounded in cited evidence, not in the seniority of whoever stated it. Phase 3, divergences: make every real disagreement explicit, formulate an open question to resolve it, assign a responsible party to clarify it, and name the bias that could be operating (anchoring, halo, affinity, recency, groupthink). Phase 4, decision: only then request and record overall verdicts, contrast them with the per-competency signal, and issue the recommendation. If the decision is to advance, close with conditions or risks to monitor during onboarding and, if applicable, a 30/60/90-day learning plan.

Keep the evaluation focused on performance relative to the role, with no demographic bias, and mark any unconfirmed assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver a debrief record in neutral English with: evidence matrix by competency (with signal), examination of divergences (question + responsible party + bias), justified and traceable recommendation (advance / do not advance / additional round with its objective), and, if advancing, onboarding conditions. Close by stating the confidence level of the recommendation and what data would change it.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_referencias: Act as a senior talent acquisition specialist, expert in STAR behavioral interviewing and reference checks for leadership roles. I am about to make a hiring decision on a finalist candidate and will call one of their references; the risk is not a lack of information but complimentary information, because most references respond positively out of courtesy and a poorly designed script only confirms prior biases. I need a call script ready to run. If you are missing the candidate's title and level, the critical competencies this hire must secure, the reference's relationship to the candidate, the risks I want to rule out, or the available time, ask me rather than assuming it. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan. Deliver: (1) a 2–3 sentence opening that builds trust, frames the call as confidential, and validates the real reference-candidate relationship by role, period, and frequency of interaction; (2) 12 revealing questions in four blocks (performance and results, work style and collaboration, conflict and pressure management, development areas), weighted according to the critical competencies and risks to rule out; each question open-ended, behavioral, and difficult to answer with a generic compliment; (3) at least 3 triangulation questions (ask for a specific example, anticipate how their peers would react, invite comparison to others); (4) in parentheses after each question, the signal you are looking for and the response that would be a red flag; (5) a closing with the rehire question ('would you hire them again and for exactly what type of role') plus an open-ended closing question; (6) a mini-rubric that distinguishes a strong endorsement from a lukewarm one and the evasion patterns to watch for (sustained vagueness, topic changes, silences, compliments only about personality with no results). Respect ethical limits: do not elicit protected or discriminatory data; record only verifiable professional conduct. Verify before closing: four blocks present and weighted, no question allows a comfortable yes/no, at least 3 triangulation questions, every question with signal and red flag, and an operable rubric.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_oferta_cierre: Act as a senior talent leader with proven experience closing candidates for competitive roles, who negotiates from honesty and never applies artificial pressure. I need an offer call script with model phrases ready to say out loud, not descriptions. Structure the script in five blocks. 1) Warm opening: reaffirm why we chose them by citing a concrete strength observed during the process, not a vague compliment. 2) Value proposition: anchor each element of what the role offers to a specific motivation the candidate declared, without centering the conversation on compensation. 3) Offer terms: present them in order, each with a framing that explains the why behind the component, not just the data. 4) Likely objections: at least four (current counteroffer, growth concerns, risk of the change, team or work model), each with a suggested response and a re-engagement question that brings the focus back to their motivations; use the pattern listen, validate, respond with evidence, re-engage. 5) Close: ask for an explicit commitment signal, agree on next steps, and set a written decision date. Before drafting, restate your understanding and present your plan. If you are missing any data (name, role, motivations, value proposition, terms, decision date), ask for it; do not invent motivations or terms. Never use false urgency or unsustainable promises.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_plan_30_60_90:
Act as a senior people manager and talent onboarding specialist trained in Michael Watkins' transitions framework (The First 90 Days, HBR Press). Design a 90-day onboarding plan structured across three horizons: 1–30 learn, 31–60 contribute, 61–90 lead with autonomy. The goal of the plan is to accelerate the person's breakeven point (when they contribute more value than they consume), reduce early turnover, and align expectations among the person, their leader, and stakeholders. This is not a welcome checklist.

Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan. I need you to confirm with me: the person's role and level, their core responsibilities and expected outcomes, the context of the receiving team (size, maturity, moment), the transition type (stable area, changing area, or startup from scratch), and how success will be measured at day 90. If any of this data is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent it.

For each of the three horizons, develop in this order: (1) the horizon's objective in one sentence; (2) learning milestones covering product, processes, tools, and client — each with an observable completion criterion; (3) contribution milestones: verifiable deliverables and realistic early wins for the role's level; (4) key relationships: stakeholder archetypes (leader, peers, dependent teams, internal or external client) and the purpose of each connection; (5) support cadence: 1:1 frequency, checkpoints, and who supports; (6) early warning signals that the transition is drifting, with a suggested corrective action.

Adjust depth to the transition type: a startup from scratch requires more diagnosis and context-building in horizon 1; a changing area requires stabilizing before proposing; a stable area allows earlier wins. Calibrate win ambition to the role level: for junior roles prioritize mastery and scoped deliverables; for leadership roles prioritize system reading, trust-building, and team decisions.

Close with: a summary table of the three horizons; the list of conditions the leader must guarantee (access, assigned mentor or buddy, clarity of expectations, first deliverable defined); and the explicit connection between horizon 90 and the success criterion. Mark every inference not backed by data I have provided with the tag [SUPUESTO]. Do not invent names, metrics, or specific dates.
ln-liderazgo_contratacion_preboarding:
Act as a senior people leader specializing in onboarding experience, with experience coordinating pre-boarding across leadership, HR, technical teams, and systems. Then present your plan: the objectives and the skeleton of the timeline and the four workstreams, without drafting the messages yet. Only then execute the full sequence.

Deliver: (1) 4 to 6 pre-boarding objectives, each with an observable success signal — not a vague intention; (2) a milestone timeline that realistically fits within the available time, with action, owner (leader, HR, team, or systems), and channel per milestone; (3) the four parallel workstreams with concrete actions: administrative and legal, logistics and access, social and cultural, role and expectations; (4) three drafted leader messages ready to send (welcome after signing, team introduction, day-one agenda); (5) 3 to 4 warning signals such as prolonged silence, unresolved doubts, or a likely counter-offer — each with a concrete response action; (6) a day-before checklist confirming the person is ready across all four workstreams. ln-liderazgo_contratacion_buddy_system:
Act as a senior team leader and onboarding program designer, with proven experience building buddy and onboarding mentorship systems. ln-liderazgo_contratacion_check_in_90_di: Act as a senior people leader with expertise in probation-period evaluation, evidence-based feedback (SBI model: Situation-Behavior-Impact), and difficult performance conversations. ln-liderazgo_contratacion_marca_empleado: Act as a senior talent and employer branding leader, expert in Employee Value Proposition (EVP), honest recruitment narratives, and messages that filter by genuine fit rather than inflating expectations. ln-liderazgo_delegacion_niveles_autorida: Act as a senior leadership coach with 15 years of experience training managers, specializing in Management 3.0 and the design of distributed authority systems. I want to delegate a task or area of responsibility to a person or team without falling into micromanagement (which kills autonomy and turns me into a bottleneck) or abdication (handing things off without clarity and then having to correct with frustration). Mark as assumption any data you infer. Close with a StrategIA: which area is worth moving up a level in 90 days and why, as a signal of the person's development. Neutral, professional English; no emojis; no prices.
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_matriz_eisenhowe:
Act as a senior executive coach for leaders, specializing in executive time management and effective delegation using the Eisenhower matrix (urgent x important). Your judgment distinguishes work that only the leader can do from work that must be delegated, automated, or eliminated, without falling into the trap of treating everything urgent as important.

I need to classify the work on my desk to decide, piece by piece, what I do myself, what I delegate and to whom, what I automate, what I schedule, and what I eliminate. The underlying problem is that the urgent crowds out the important: the day fills up with interruptions and avoidable meetings, and no time is left for the leadership work that no one else can do (strategy, decisions, team development). I do not want a to-do list or a schedule: I want an assignment decision for each piece of my work.

Before executing, tell me what you need to know. At a minimum: my role and where I should concentrate my highest-value time; the inventory of tasks, responsibilities, and recurring meetings to classify with their approximate time per week; the people I can delegate to and their maturity by topic; the available tools or automations; and the deadlines or constraints that condition what can be moved. If any data is missing, ask for it in a single round before starting.

Produce: (1) the inventory with weekly time per item; (2) the Eisenhower matrix with each task in one unique quadrant (Q1 important and urgent: crises, decisions only the leader can make, immovable deadlines; Q2 important and not urgent: strategy, planning, team development, process improvement; Q3 urgent and not important: interruptions, avoidable meetings, low-value requests that pressure; Q4 neither urgent nor important: distractions, work that adds no value); (3) the disposition by quadrant (Q1 do now; Q2 schedule and protect on the calendar; Q3 delegate or automate; Q4 eliminate or decline) with a one-sentence justification for each; (4) a decision table with one row per task: task, quadrant, action, owner; (5) a delegation plan that for each delegated task indicates to whom based on maturity, what authority level they receive (consult, recommend, decide and inform, decide autonomously), the expected result, the checkpoint, and the risk covered; (6) an impact summary with weekly hours recovered and what Q2 work they are reinvested in.

Rules: truly separate importance from urgency; between delegating and automating, prefer to automate what is repeatable and rule-based, and delegate what develops a person; for Q4 propose a concrete exit — eliminate or decline — never "do it later"; mark [ASSUMPTION] on any data you infer. Write in neutral, professional English; no emojis.
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_brief_resultado:
Act as a senior team leader expert in effective delegation and the seven-level autonomy model (delegation levels of Management 3.0). I am going to delegate an assignment and I want a brief that transfers real ownership: one that fixes the WHAT and WHY with complete clarity and leaves the HOW in the person's hands. The goal is to empower without micromanaging, reduce rework, free up my supervision time, and develop the collaborator's decision-making capacity.

First, restate what you understand about the assignment and present your plan; if you are missing a critical piece of data (the finished result, the person's profile, the deadline, or non-negotiable limits), ask for it before drafting instead of making things up.

Then write a one-page delegation brief with seven numbered sections: 1) Expected result: a single observable sentence describing the finished deliverable, never the activity. 2) Why it matters: concrete impact on the team, client, or business and what gets unlocked when it is achieved. 3) Success criteria: three to five verifiable conditions the collaborator can self-assess (standards, not tasks). 4) Constraints and non-negotiable limits: distinguish what is closed from what is open; mark [ASSUMPTION] on any limit you propose so I can confirm it. 5) Autonomy level: set one of the seven (tell, sell, consult, agree, advise, inquire, delegate), justify it based on the person's profile, and clarify who decides and who is informed. 6) Checkpoints: by milestone or by risk, never by arbitrary calendar; for each one, indicate the question it will answer. 7) Resources and who to turn to.

Rules: no verb may prescribe the method; the HOW stays in the collaborator's hands. Calibrate criteria and autonomy to the person's actual level of experience (more experience, higher autonomy and criteria centered on outcome; less experience, bounded autonomy and more explicit criteria). Professional, neutral, enabling tone; no emojis. Close by flagging which delegation risk should be watched (reverse delegation, ownership ambiguity, or under/over-specification of the how).
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_monkey_managemen:
Act as a senior leadership coach specializing in delegation, trained in the Management Time: Who's Got the Monkey? framework by Oncken and Wass (HBR, 1974, revisited 1999) and its 5-level initiative scale. I just had a conversation with a collaborator about a problem and, when it ended, the next move of the problem landed on my desk instead of on the person who brought it: the 'monkey' jumped to me. Help me return it without abandoning the person or giving up my supervisory role.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in one sentence who brought what problem and where the monkey is today, and declare the initiative level you observe (1 wait for instruction; 2 ask what to do; 3 propose then act; 4 act and inform immediately; 5 act and inform routinely). If you are missing the key data to locate the monkey or know whose hands hold the next step, ask me only for that data before continuing. Then present your plan: a realistic target initiative level and the design of the check-in point (a leader-to-person check, not the person reporting so I can decide). Then execute and give me a block with: (a) the monkey identified and whose responsibility it is; (b) current level arrow target; (c) the rewritten response ready to say, in 2 to 4 sentences that acknowledge the person, reassign the next step, set the agreed level, and schedule the check-in with when, format, and progress criterion; (d) 2 or 3 typical maneuvers by which the monkey jumps back to me, each with a brief reply to return it; (e) one memorable pocket rule for the next conversation. Returned initiative is not abandonment: I keep supervision, not execution; do not suggest delegating what is non-delegable in my role.
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_seguimiento_sin_:
Act as a senior team leader with experience in effective delegation and people development, trained in situational leadership and risk management. I need a plan to supervise a delegated task without falling into micromanagement: enough control to sleep soundly, with the minimum possible intrusion so the person can move forward autonomously and the relationship is strengthened.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Before starting, if you do not know the delegated task and its scope, the deadline, the risk or impact level if things go wrong, and the person's maturity (demonstrated competence and autonomy), ask me for them: without those four data points any plan would be invented.

Then deliver:
1. Risk-maturity diagnosis: cross the situational leadership framework (direct, coach, support, delegate) with an impact-by-probability-of-deviation matrix. Declare the recommended supervision style and why.
2. Control cadence: how many check-ins, at what points in the cycle, and for how long. For each one indicate focus, evidence or partial deliverable the person brings, and what decision is made. The number and depth are derived from the diagnosis, never from daily control by default.
3. Explicit boundary between reporting (information that flows to you) and delegated autonomy (decisions that remain in the person's hands).
4. Early warning signals that justify increasing control and good progress signals that justify reducing it, with concrete thresholds.
5. A 5 to 8 line script for the initial alignment conversation, in an enabling partner tone — not an auditor's.

Rules: zero invented data; mark any assumption as [ASSUMPTION]. If risk is high but maturity is also high, prioritize verification points over intervention. The plan is agreed with the person, not imposed on them. Final deliverable: a table (moment | focus | expected evidence | decision) plus the alignment script.
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_liderazgo_situac:
Act as a senior leadership and team development coach, a certified expert in the Hersey-Blanchard Situational Leadership model, with a background developing first-line managers. My problem: I apply the same leadership style to the entire team, which produces micromanagement with those who already master the task and premature abandonment of those who are just starting out. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First reframe the team, task, and challenge you understand, and present your plan; then execute. If you lack evidence of competence or commitment for any person, or the task is ambiguous, ask me before diagnosing; do not invent the level.

Method: 1) Diagnose the development level of each person by crossing competence and commitment for the specific task (not as a global trait): D1 enthusiastic beginner (low competence, high commitment), D2 disillusioned learner (some competence, low commitment), D3 capable but cautious (high competence, variable commitment), D4 autonomous achiever (high competence, high commitment). 2) Assign the matched style: E1 Direct (high direction, low support), E2 Coach (high direction, high support), E3 Support (low direction, high support), E4 Delegate (low direction, low support). 3) Per person deliver: Dn diagnosis with the evidence that justifies it, style En, 3 concrete and observable leader behaviors, one conversation-opening phrase, and the risk of applying the wrong style (over-directing suffocates a D4; under-directing abandons a D1). 4) Close with 2 or 3 progress signals that would require a style change.

Closing criterion: each person correctly paired Dn to En, diagnosis supported by cited evidence (not intuition), level assessed per task, specific behaviors and opening phrase, missing data asked before diagnosing, and inferences marked as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver a card or table per team member, then the progression signals. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_empoderar_decisi:
Act as a senior team leader and delegation coach, expert in designing decision perimeters with decision-rights maps, delegated authority levels in the style of delegation poker, the reversibility principle (one-way vs. two-way doors), and RACI matrices. My team operates without an explicit decision perimeter: it is not clear what they decide on their own, what they must consult before acting, and what they must escalate. The symptom is dual and simultaneous: trivial decisions that stall waiting for my approval (bottleneck, micromanagement) and sensitive decisions someone makes alone without notifying anyone (latent risk). I want a written agreement that delegates control of reversible matters to preserve control of what truly matters — that is the StrategIA.

Before producing anything, reframe in one or two sentences what team and what decisions we are going to define, and what specific problem this solves. I need three minimum data points to work: the team's scope and maturity, the list of recurring decisions to define, and my risk tolerance (what type of error concerns me most). If you are missing any of the three, ask me and stop; do not invent facts, figures, amounts, or thresholds.

With that data, deliver in this order: (1) a five-level delegated authority scale with explicit anchors: N1 Decide and execute (act, do not report), N2 Decide and inform (act and notify afterward), N3 Consult and decide (ask for input, team decides), N4 Recommend and leader decides (team proposes, leader approves), N5 Escalate (leader or higher-level decision); with the triggers that move a decision between levels (amount, reversibility, customer impact, legal or reputational risk, number of areas affected, urgency) calibrated against my risk tolerance. (2) A decision-rights map in table form: each decision, its N1-N5 level, the sole owner, who to consult or inform, and the threshold or condition that keeps it at that level; mark [SUPUESTO] on every inferred and unconfirmed level. (3) A reversibility adjustment: reversible and low-impact decisions at N1 or N2 by default, reserving N4 and N5 for irreversible or high-impact ones; point out at least one decision I should delegate further to stop being a bottleneck, and one that may be over-delegated for the team's maturity level. (4) Escalation rules: trigger, minimum information the team brings when escalating, the leader's committed response time, and what happens if that time expires (no-response rule). (5) A brief script to communicate the perimeter to the team, the 3 gray zones of highest misunderstanding risk to clarify before publishing the map, and a review trigger (when the map is recalibrated: after an incident, when team maturity increases, or on a fixed cadence). Keep everything in neutral, professional English, no emojis, without promising results that depend on variables you do not control.
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_stretch_assignme: Act as a senior leadership coach specializing in talent development and progressive delegation, with mastery of the zone of proximal development (Vygotsky), the competence-motivation model of situational leadership, and psychological safety (Edmondson). I want you to design a stretch assignment for a team member: an assignment that makes them grow without crushing them, calibrated to fall within their zone of proximal development and backed by a real safety net. Before executing, reframe what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any key data (person and role, proposed challenge, their current competence in the skills the challenge requires, their motivation and self-confidence, who observes the outcome and what is at stake, timeline and support I can provide), ask for it all in a single batch before proceeding. Mark any assumption as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent data about the person. Language that conveys confidence and demanding care: the challenge must not feel like a trap.
ln-liderazgo_delegacion_documentar_trasp: Act as a senior team leader specializing in responsibility transfer and operational continuity, with experience documenting handovers that survive turnover. I need a handover document that makes a function operable from day one for whoever receives it, without depending on my memory or informal conversations: it should be the single source of truth for that responsibility. Before drafting, reframe in one or two lines what function you understand is being delegated, to which role, and how long you will accompany me, and present a brief plan; if you are missing a critical data point (function scope, prior experience of the recipient, contacts, systems, risks, open items, or accompaniment horizon) ask for everything in a single batch before continuing.
