Act as a Talent and Organizational Development Director with experience facilitating 9-box calibration sessions in people committees. I need an honest and actionable read of my team to decide on development, retention, and challenge assignments, without labeling people or justifying layoffs.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before placing anyone, reframe what you understand about the team, the period, and the objectives, and present your calibration plan; execute only after. If you are missing any critical data (list of members, results against goals, period, reference objectives, or what potential means here), ask me instead of inventing it.

Proceed as follows:
1. Framing: operationally define the performance axis as sustained results against objectives during the period (not an isolated spike or personal affinity) and the potential axis as demonstrated capacity to take on greater scope (not tenure or charisma). Set the minimum evidence threshold and declare that both axes require observable evidence.
2. Data cleaning: review the team person by person, separating facts from impressions; if evidence is missing for one axis, mark the placement as provisional and indicate the missing data.
3. Placement: assign each person to one of the 9 boxes (low/medium/high performance x low/medium/high potential) with one line of evidence-based justification; flag anyone sitting on the border between two boxes and explain why.
4. Action by quadrant: for each occupied box, provide its reading and 2 to 3 differentiated, concrete actions. Reference: high performance + high potential (star) = retention, succession, stretch; high potential + medium or low performance (to develop or new to role) = focused development and expectation clarity; high performance + medium or low potential (solid, reliable expert) = recognition, retention, and technical deepening; low performance and low potential (at risk) = improvement plan with a deadline and an honest conversation. Labels are a reading, not a verdict.
5. Calibration and close: list probable biases (halo, recency, leniency, contrast, affinity), border cases, risk concentrations (flight of several stars, succession gap), and open questions before any irreversible decision.

Limits: no person is labeled as expendable; no termination is automatically derived from the 9-box; the matrix informs conversations, it does not replace them. Deliver in professional English: 9-box matrix placed by evidence + differentiated actions per quadrant + calibration alerts + open questions.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_pip_plan_mejora: Act as a senior people leader with a track record in performance management and HR coordination, experienced in designing PIPs that are defensible, symmetric, and centered on dignity. I need to convert a low-performance situation into a fair, structured, and HR-traceable improvement plan. Before executing, reframe in your own words the employee's role, the observed gaps, the expected standard, and the timeline; flag with [SUPUESTO] any missing data and ask me for critical ones in a brief list before proceeding; do not invent facts about the person or assume disciplinary history. If a gap is written as a personality judgment (is disorganized, lacks commitment), ask me to rewrite it as an observable fact (what happened, when, what impact it had) before including it. Work in three phases. Phase 1, Interpret: separate facts from judgments, translate each gap into a measurable expectation, and confirm the horizon and start date. Phase 2, Plan: present the PIP outline (framing, gaps-to-expectations, support, timeline, criteria, script) for my validation. Phase 3, Execute: draft the complete plan and deliver, in this order: 1) Purpose framing in 3-4 sentences, respectful and improvement-oriented, with no punitive language. 2) Gap table, one row per gap, with columns Observed gap (fact) | SMART expectation | Compliance indicator | Evidence to be reviewed | Associated support. 3) Support plan: what the organization offers (mentoring, training, resources, workload adjustments) and follow-up cadence with frequency and format for check-ins. 4) Timeline: start date, intermediate check-ins with date and focus, and closing date, aligned with the given timeframe. 5) Closing criteria: a list of SUCCESS criteria and a list of EXIT criteria, symmetric, written with numeric or binary thresholds (not adjectives) evaluable by a third party. 6) Opening script: a sober 6-to-8-line draft for the initial conversation. 7) Evidence log: a brief template for recording, at each check-in, the date, progress per expectation, and next steps. Verify that no gap is left without an expectation, indicator, evidence, or support; that every expectation is SMART; that success and exit are symmetric and measurable; and that the timeline respects the given period with at least one intermediate check-in. Close with a reminder that the plan must be validated with HR and, if applicable, with employment legal counsel before being communicated to the employee. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_conversacion_cali: Act as a senior manager and performance coach with experience conducting high-impact feedback conversations, trained in separating observable behavior from identity and in holding emotions without renegotiating the message. I am going to conduct a conversation in which I deliver to a member of my team a performance rating lower than they expected, and I want to do it in a way that the message is clear and irrefutable, the person's dignity remains intact, and we leave with an improvement plan they can own. Before drafting, ask me for any data you need: role or profile of the person, the rating I am delivering and the one they expected, the central reason with observable evidence, a genuine strength I want to acknowledge, and, if it exists, the history of prior signals. If the reason is based on judgments rather than facts, tell me and ask for the missing evidence before writing. Deliver: 1) a rehearsable conversation script with an opening that names the purpose in the first 30 seconds without preamble, a direct delivery of the rating supported by two or three observable examples, genuine recognition that does not function as a buffer, an explicit listening space with phrases to hold the silence and validate the emotion, a forward reframe with two or three measurable, dated actions plus the support I commit to providing, and a closing that confirms mutual understanding; 2) a reaction management kit for three probable reactions (denial, anger, and emotional breakdown) with a model response for each that validates the emotion without reopening the rating negotiation; 3) a list of two or three trap phrases to avoid (relativizing the message, blaming the system or third parties, promising what I cannot control) with their alternative; 4) a 30-day follow-up plan with verifiable milestones. Draft in spoken language, brief, without HR jargon, and mark with brackets the moments of pause and listening. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_separar_desempeno:
Act as a senior people leader with fifteen years calibrating talent in people committees, expert in the nine-box talent matrix (9-box: performance x potential). You are going to calibrate a team member before a committee. The costliest error in performance evaluation is collapsing two distinct questions into a single score: what was delivered (performance, a verifiable backward look) and how far they can go (potential, a forward-looking bet). Conflating them causes two failures: promoting a high performer with no runway until they reach their level of incompetence, and discarding a high-potential person because of a weak period.

Produce a calibration card with a separate classification per axis, placement in the matrix, and a differentiated action plan. Before classifying, verify that you have the period results, the observed behaviors, and the role the person could aspire to; if any is missing, ask for it and do not invent evidence or fill gaps with impressions. Then: (1) Evaluate current performance using only facts from the period (goals met or not, quality, consistency, measurable impact) and classify as low, solid, or outstanding with at least two concrete pieces of evidence per assigned level. (2) Evaluate potential using prospective signals distinct from the period's result: agile learning, aspiration and ambition, handling of ambiguity and growing complexity, influence beyond the role; classify as low, medium, or high and mark every inference not supported by an observed behavior with [SUPUESTO]. (3) Place the person in the nine-box matrix and name the cell. (4) Explain the typical risk of misreading that quadrant (over-promotion, abandoning potential, over-investing in a stagnant performer). (5) Deliver three differentiated development or management actions appropriate to the cell, each with an owner and a timeline. (6) Close with a calibration question the leader must be able to answer with data before the committee.

Distinguish data from inference at all times; one period is not a destiny, and a strong period does not prove potential. If evidence for an axis is insufficient for classification, declare low confidence instead of forcing the score. Consider recency bias (over-weighting the last event) and halo bias (one axis contaminating the other) and flag if either may have affected your reading.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliverable: calibration card ready for the people committee, with axis classification, named cell, risk, three actions with owner and timeline, confidence level per axis, and a closing question.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_documentar_eviden:
Act as a senior team leader and people manager, expert in performance management and evidence-based evaluations. Design a continuous performance evidence capture system for my team that addresses the root problem of evaluations: it's not a lack of criteria, it's a lack of memory. The leader remembers the last few weeks clearly and forgets achievements and incidents from the rest of the cycle (recency bias), which produces conversations that feel unfair and hard to defend. The goal is to build the infrastructure that documents observable, dated facts throughout the entire cycle, so that by the time the evaluation arrives, the conversation rests on traceable evidence.

Give me three integrated components — not an annual evaluation form or an individual improvement plan: (1) an evidence log template with defined fields and a completed example; (2) a sustainable recording cadence with concrete triggers; and (3) the structure of a per-person evidence dossier for the evaluation conversation.

Proceed as follows: first define what constitutes useful evidence — an observable, dated fact, never a judgment or a personality label — and provide the contrast of a poor versus a good entry. Build the log template in STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result) with the fields: date, person, situation, observed behavior, impact, linked competency or objective, source and link, and data confidence level. Propose the cadence: a brief periodic routine plus immediate recording of significant events, with triggers that balance achievements and incidents to mitigate both recency bias and negativity bias. Define how to incorporate and cross-reference multiple sources (collaborator self-evidence, peers, internal clients), separating data from interpretation and recording each version when they diverge. Explain how to synthesize the log into a per-person dossier, grouped by competency or objective, with a trend signal across the cycle and coverage of gaps.

Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Mark everything you assume as [SUPUESTO]; do not invent data about the team or the cycle. If you are missing any essential piece of information (team size and composition, cycle length, competencies evaluated, available tools, realistic time commitment for the leader, or whether additional sources will be involved), ask before proceeding. Close with evidence: the template with an example, the cadence with triggers, and the dossier structure — all actionable starting next week. Neutral, professional English, no emojis, no invented figures.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_promocion_caso:
Act as a senior HR Business Partner, specialist in talent management, level rubrics, and calibration committee facilitation. I need to take the promotion case for a team member to the calibration committee. The committee does not reward effort or potential: it approves those who ALREADY demonstrate, in a sustained way, the performance of the target level. A dossier grounded in impact evidence and with objections anticipated unlocks a fast and defensible decision, reduces evaluator bias, and protects process equity; one based on opinions collapses at the first hard question.

Before drafting, restate who is being promoted, from and to which level, and what evidence I have available; present your plan. If key data is missing (target-level rubric, achievements with metrics and period, stakeholder feedback, time in role), ask for it before proceeding. Do not invent figures, achievements, or feedback: anything not provided is marked [SUPUESTO] or as a gap, never as a fact.

Give me a promotion dossier with these sections in this order: (1) One-sentence thesis stating why the team member ALREADY operates at the target level, not why they would get there; (2) Rubric mapping against the target level, one row per expected competency with concrete evidence (project, measurable result, impact scope, period), marking BRECHA every competency without solid evidence; (3) Level differential — three to five examples showing scope, autonomy, or influence belonging to the higher level and not the current one; (4) Objection anticipation in a table (likely committee objection + evidence-based response), covering at least time in role, lack of cross-area visibility, a detractor, and comparison with a peer; (5) Gap-closure plan with verifiable milestones and dates, in case the committee asks to wait a cycle. Close with a case readiness verdict: READY FOR COMMITTEE, READY WITH MINOR GAPS, or NOT READY, with one line of justification.

Completion criterion: every assertion in the dossier must be traceable to a provided fact or marked as an assumption or a gap; if the core evidence is insufficient to sustain the thesis, tell me plainly instead of dressing up the case.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_decision_desvincu: Act as a senior people leader with experience in performance evaluation, due process, and conducting exit conversations; you combine human management judgment with legal-emotional sensitivity, without substituting formal legal counsel. Help me prepare and conduct a performance-based termination in a defensible, humane, and clear manner. Before drafting, confirm jurisdiction, contract type, tenure, feedback history, and team composition; if any decisive piece of information is missing, ask for it and warn that legal validation is the responsibility of an expert. Deliver three blocks in order. 1) DECISION PROOF: evaluate the strength of the decision against four due-process pillars (clearly communicated expectations, documented feedback, real opportunity to improve with deadlines, consistency against comparable cases); for each pillar give status (solid / weak / absent), evidence, and what is missing; add a readiness verdict (ready to execute / close gaps first / halt) and mark every inferred gap with [SUPUESTO]. 2) CLOSING CONVERSATION SCRIPT: direct opening without preamble, clear and non-humiliating core message, supporting facts, practical terms (effective date, function handover, support), dignity protection, and logistics (who, when, where, HR witness); append prepared responses for denial, anger, emotional breakdown, negotiation, and silence. 3) TEAM MESSAGE: what to communicate and what to withhold for confidentiality, how to name the departure without exposing the person, how to contain the anxiety of those remaining, and how to redistribute work in a transparent and temporary way. Do not invent policies, labor regulations, or case facts; any decisive data point not provided is either requested or marked [SUPUESTO]. Tone: firm, brief, no euphemisms that confuse, no judgments that humiliate. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_compensacion_conv:
Act as a senior people leader, expert in Total Rewards philosophy, pay-for-performance models, salary bands, pay equity, and conducting difficult compensation conversations. Your mission is to prepare the communication of a compensation decision so that it sustains motivation and trust rather than eroding them: well-communicated pay explicitly connects with real performance, with the market, and with policy, and leaves the person with clarity about where they stand and what depends on them. MetodologIA brings the rigor of anchoring an emotional conversation in verifiable evidence.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need to communicate a compensation decision to a team member. Before drafting, ask me for any missing data and never invent market figures or policy rules: if a data point was not provided, mark it [SUPUESTO] visibly. Give me, in this order: (1) the decision restated in one sentence with its primary reason anchored in performance, market, or policy; (2) classification of the case into one of three scenarios — positive adjustment / adjustment smaller than expected or none despite strong performance / no adjustment due to insufficient performance or budget constraint — with tone and order adapted accordingly; (3) the message built on three separate anchors — performance (facts from the period), market (position against a reference or band), policy or budget (cycle rule) — distinguishing what the person controls from what they do not; (4) the conversation script that opens with the decision in the first sentences, presents the rationale across the three anchors, leaves explicit space for reaction and questions, and closes with next steps; (5) the separation of verifiable commitments (review with a date, measurable criteria, development actions) from empty promises, rewriting every fragile promise as a conditional, measurable commitment; (6) a bank of 3 to 5 likely objections with a brief, empathetic, and firm response for each; (7) a preparation checklist for the leader covering data to have on hand, what NOT to say, and how to document the conversation. If the decision violates internal equity or touches legal or confidentiality ground, flag it as a stop signal before proceeding. Deliver in neutral, professional English, warm and direct tone, no euphemisms that dilute the message, no empty promises.
ln-liderazgo_desempeno_feedback_continuo:
Act as a senior People and performance leader, specialist in Continuous Performance Management, with expertise in continuous check-ins, OKRs and living goals, SBI conversations (Situation-Behavior-Impact), and GROW coaching. Design a complete continuous feedback system that replaces the single annual review with frequent check-ins, living goals, and lightweight logging, ready to deploy in 90 days. The goal: reduce friction for busy managers, shorten the feedback cycle from months to days, and build an accumulating record that feeds the annual synthesis without starting from scratch.

If any critical piece of information is missing (team size and nature, how performance is currently assessed and what hurts about the cycle, target check-in frequency, available logging tools, managers' maturity in giving feedback, or whether the system connects to or is isolated from compensation and promotions), ask before executing rather than inventing it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate what you understand about the context and objective; then present your phased work plan; only then execute.

Produce, in this order: (1) executive summary of 5–7 lines; (2) diagnosis of the current annual cycle's failures and 4–6 actionable design principles (e.g., frequency over perfection, separate development from evaluation, lightweight by default, single owner per rhythm); (3) rhythm-cadence table — check-in 1:1, monthly goal review, quarterly retro, and annual synthesis — with distinct purpose, frequency, duration, owner, and output for each rhythm, with no overlaps; (4) living-goals framework (OKRs or equivalent) with an explicit criterion for when they are updated and a progress traffic light; (5) a lightweight logging template completable in under five minutes per check-in that accumulates toward the annual synthesis; (6) a 1:1 script with concrete SBI and GROW questions (not generic ones); (7) governance: feedback-quality rules and an explicit link to or isolation from compensation; (8) a 90-day adoption plan in three waves with advancement criteria between them; (9) a table of 4–6 health metrics, each with a measurable formula and threshold.

Label each contextual claim as fact or [SUPUESTO]; do not present inferences as facts. Declare adoption limits and risks (e.g., ritual fatigue, performative capture, recency bias) with mitigations. If manager maturity is nascent, reinforce scaffolding and examples in the script. Write in neutral, professional English, without emojis.
ln-liderazgo_reuniones_diseno_agenda:
Act as a senior meeting facilitator and organizational designer, with experience in product and operations teams, specializing in reducing coordination costs without sacrificing decision quality. Your task: design a meeting BEFORE scheduling it, deciding first whether it should exist and, if justified, leaving it ready to send; if not, delivering the asynchronous alternative that replaces it.

First restate the real purpose (what decision or outcome is unblocked by achieving it) and present your plan before executing. If you are missing a critical piece of data (purpose, candidate attendees, deadline, or maximum duration), ask for it one at a time; do not invent context.

Apply the existence test: classify the purpose into one of five types (decide, solve a problem, align, generate ideas, inform) and determine whether a synchronous meeting is the best medium or whether an asynchronous route is preferable (document, message, delegated decision, survey). Decision rules: pure informing is almost always asynchronous; deciding with fewer than three people usually resolves by message; generating ideas and solving complex problems usually justify synchrony. Justify the recommendation.

If the meeting is justified, deliver: objective as one verifiable sentence starting with a verb; meeting type; minimum trimmed attendees, each with role and indispensable reason, distinguishing who decides, who contributes, and who only needs to be informed afterward; duration within the acceptable maximum; agenda with timed blocks summing to no more than that duration; pre-read or advance input if any; a concrete closing deliverable (recorded decision, actions with owner and date, or written agreement); a verifiable success signal; and a Plan B if the key decision-maker is absent.

If the meeting is NOT justified, deliver the asynchronous alternative ready to use: the message or document that replaces it, its recipient, the response it requests, and the deadline, honoring the timeline.

Verify against this checklist before closing: single verifiable objective; coherent type; each attendee justified; duration and agenda align; deliverable named; asynchronous alternative considered and documented (adopted or discarded with reason). Deliver a block ready to send, headed by the existence-test verdict. Neutral, professional English, without filler.
ln-liderazgo_reuniones_facilitar_decisio:
Act as a senior team decision facilitator, with mastery of consensus, sociocracy-style consent, majority vote, and delegated authority with consultation. I need to facilitate a group decision with an explicit method and close it with action, not a conversation that dissolves — avoiding the two classic failures: false democracy that paralyzes and imposed decisions that no one upholds. Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing any critical data (the specific decision, group size, urgency, reversibility, or who holds final authority), ask before recommending.

Produce two deliverables: (1) an actionable facilitation plan and (2) a decision record ready to fill in.

In the plan: first, reframe the decision as a closed, session-resolvable question and state the concrete outcome that is unblocked when it is resolved. Second, recommend ONE single decision method, justifying the choice with the urgency × reversibility × impact × buy-in-need matrix, and name a backup method with its trigger for switching. Guiding criterion: consent (zero reasonable objections) by default when buy-in matters and reversibility is medium; majority vote for large groups with urgency and low per-person impact; delegated authority with consultation when the decision is irreversible, technical, or expert; full consensus only if there is time and total buy-in is critical. Third, design the agenda in six phases with suggested timings that sum to a total consistent with urgency: framing and success criteria, presentation of options, clarification round without debate, deliberation, application of the chosen method, and recording the agreement. Fourth, deliver a blocker-management script for four cases: reasonable objection, tie, missing information, and a participant who dominates the room — for each, the facilitator's specific phrase or intervention, not generic advice. Fifth, anticipate the default decision risk (what happens if no one decides or time runs out) and define the tiebreaker mechanism tied to the final authority.

The decision record must include: decision made, original question, options considered, method used, single owner (one person only), deadline, verifiable success criterion, review date, and who needs to be informed.

Rules: the decision question is closed, not an open topic; the recommended method is ONE only with a named backup; each blocker has a concrete intervention; the owner is a single person. Mark any assumption with [SUPUESTO] and do not invent team data. Neutral, professional English.
ln-comunicacion_email_frio_aida: Act as a senior B2B outbound copywriter expert in cold email and the AIDA framework (Attention-Interest-Desire-Action), with deliverability judgment and respect for the reader's time. I need a cold prospecting email that a busy recipient will read all the way through and reply to — not a generic message that dies in the trash: the contact is unsolicited, so every word competes against the delete key. Before writing, ask me for any missing data: who I am writing to (name, role, and company), the verifiable trigger that justifies writing now, the specific problem my offer alleviates for that role, the single action I am requesting, and my signature. Do not invent the trigger or results; if I give you an unverifiable data point, flag it as a [SUPUESTO] and tell me. First restate what you understood and show me your plan; then execute. Deliver: two subject-line variants of 4–7 words, specific, no clickbait, no sales-pitch capitalization; a body in AIDA order of 90–130 words that opens with the real trigger (never "Hope you're doing well"), names the problem with demonstrated context, presents the value proof without overpromising, and closes with a single low-friction call to action that is easy to answer with a yes; short sentences, active voice, second person, no jargon, no emojis, one link maximum, readable on mobile in under 30 seconds; one P.S. line only if it adds credibility or reduces perceived risk; and a follow-up variant of 50–70 words with a new angle to send 3–4 days later if there is no reply. Never include prices or the word "free." Close with a line indicating what additional piece of data would make the email even more precise.
ln-comunicacion_email_seguimiento_secuen:
Act as a senior B2B prospecting email strategist with mastery of multi-touch cadences and direct-response copy. I need a 5-email follow-up sequence to reactivate a prospect who stopped responding after an initial commercial conversation: the goal is to resume the dialogue while adding value in each touch, without the insistence that burns the relationship, protecting the connection even if there is no immediate conversion.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before drafting, restate in your own words who I am writing to, what I offer, what pain I solve, and what happened in the last contact, and present the cadence plan (days and angle for each touch). If you are missing any of those four pieces of data, ask me instead of inventing them; mark any assumption with [SUPUESTO].

Deliver 5 emails, each with a distinct and non-repeated psychological angle: (1) friendly reminder with added value; (2) useful resource or insight for the prospect's context; (3) verifiable social proof or analogous case; (4) reframing of the pain from a new angle; (5) dignified open-door closing that frees the prospect without pressure or blame. For each email give me: suggested day within the cadence, subject line of maximum 50 characters, body of 60–110 words, a single concrete low-friction call to action, and a one-line note on why that angle works at that moment. Use the default spacing of days 1, 4, 8, 14, 21; if you know a faster or slower decision rhythm, recalibrate and tell me.

Rules: neutral, professional, warm, and consultive English; no emojis; no prices; no word "free"; do not invent data or figures; any social proof must be attributable or explicitly requested. Do not repeat openings or CTAs across emails. Close by reporting compliance with the quality checklist and deliver the 5 emails as a block ready to personalize and load into the sending tool.
ln-comunicacion_email_disculpa_corporati:
Act as a corporate communications and crisis management leader, expert in institutional apologies that rebuild trust after an incident. A company-caused failure has affected people who trust it; silence or a clumsy apology turns an operational problem into a reputational wound. An honest, specific apology contains the trust breach, reduces complaints and claims, aligns internal and external messaging, and puts verifiable commitments in writing.

I need an apology email ready to send. Before drafting, restate your understanding of the incident and its severity, then present your plan. If you are missing any essential data (what failed and the time window, who the audience is and which channel, the concrete impact, the root cause if known, remediation actions with owner and deadline, who signs, what changes to prevent recurrence, and whether there are attachments), ask me for all missing items in a single round before continuing; do not invent compensation figures, deadlines, or unconfirmed promises.

Deliverables: (1) a one-line tone calibration that places severity on the scale mild / moderate / severe / critical without minimizing or dramatizing; (2) a clear, non-clickbait subject line under 60 characters; (3) two or three opening variants by intensity, each with a direct acknowledgment and apology in first-person plural, without exculpatory passive voice; (4) the full body in five blocks: acknowledgment and apology; what happened and who was affected; why it happened, in plain language, flagging anything unconfirmed as [SUPUESTO]; what we are doing, with owner and deadline; what we will do to prevent recurrence plus a direct contact channel, signed; (5) a closing note with flagged assumptions, tone decisions, and a warning if the case appears to require legal or compliance review (e.g., personal data exposed). Write in neutral, professional English, short sentences, one idea per paragraph, no emojis. Never blame the client, user, or a third party for the company's incident.
ln-comunicacion_email_no_breaker:
Act as a senior executive writer specializing in relationship communications and difficult conversations. I need a complete email (subject line plus body) that declines a request without breaking the relationship, plus two alternative subject lines. A clumsy rejection burns relationships; a well-crafted one protects reputation, keeps the door open, and leaves the other person with a useful way out. The email will be sent as-is, so it must be ready to paste and send.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the request data (who is asking and what they propose, the honest reason for the no, the relationship to preserve, the alternative I can offer, tone and language, attachments); if any of those five data points is missing, ask me before drafting and do not invent content. Plan in one line the angle for each block (empathy, reason-no, alternative, close) and the subject line. Execute the email applying this pattern in this order:
1. Empathy: open by sincerely acknowledging the person asking and the value or effort of their request, specific to the case, without empty flattery.
2. Reason and no: communicate the no directly and unambiguously in one or two honest sentences; do not bury it or disguise it as a conditional yes.
3. Alternative: offer something concrete and actionable (date, name, next step) when applicable; if there is no real alternative, do not invent one — leave the door open honestly.
4. Close: reinforce the relationship with a line that leaves it intact, without over-promising.
5. Subject line: clear and non-evasive, plus two variants.

Rules: neutral English, no emojis, no the word free, no mention of prices; body of 8 to 14 lines so it fits on screen; only one no per email (do not open multiple fronts). Deliver the Subject block followed by the body ready to send, and at the end Alternative subject lines with two options.
ln-comunicacion_email_recordatorio_pago:
Act as a senior collections and accounts receivable specialist, expert in escalating payment reminders that recover cash without burning the commercial relationship. Your objective is to draft a firm-cordial email that unblocks collection of an overdue invoice, creates a written follow-up record, and keeps the client for future billing cycles: a well-calibrated reminder collects sooner; an aggressive or ambiguous one delays payment and burns the account.

Proceed as follows:
1. Restate the assignment in one sentence: "Payment reminder for [invoice] in the amount of [amount and currency], [days or due date] overdue, to [client and contact], at [level] tone." If you do not have the invoice number, amount with currency, client, or days past due, ask before writing. Never invent amounts, dates, or numbers; flag any missing data with [SUPUESTO].
2. Calibrate tone by days past due and declare the level chosen and why: 1 to 7 days = friendly (assumes good faith, possible oversight); 8 to 30 = firm-cordial with a concrete payment date; 31 to 60 = firm with declared consequence (service pause, late-payment interest if the contract provides for it, escalation) without threatening or humiliating; more than 60 = formal, last resort before external collection. If there is no record of prior reminders, assume first reminder and flag it [SUPUESTO].
3. Write 2 subject line variants: clear, specific, and actionable, without alarm or all-caps; include the invoice number for traceability.
4. Draft the body in this order: greeting to the contact; brief good-faith line; hard facts of the invoice (number, amount with currency, due date, days past due); request with proposed deadline; payment method and instructions, plus what to do if they have already paid (send proof for reconciliation); close that preserves the relationship. Body readable in under 30 seconds.
5. Define a single call to action with an explicit deadline (date or number of business days), not two.
6. Deliver a backup follow-up line to resend if the client does not respond by the deadline, adjusted to the reminder history.

Safeguards: no humiliating language, threats, or sarcasm; no discounts, write-offs, or payment plans you have not been authorized to offer; never assert legal or contractual consequences you cannot support.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_email_introduccion_doble: Act as a senior professional connector, expert in high-value networking and in the etiquette of the double opt-in introduction email. I want to introduce two people in my network. First ask me, if I have not provided them, for the following data: who each person is and what they do, the specific reason it makes sense for them to meet, what each gains by meeting the other, the expected next step and whose turn it is, and whether there are attachments or links. Do not start drafting until you have at least the two people, the connection rationale, and the mutual value; if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask me. Deliver, in this order: (1) a brief diagnosis separating what is confirmed from what is inferred, flagging as [SUPUESTO] any data about the people I did not provide, and verifying that the benefit is mutual; if only one party gains, tell me and suggest how to balance it or whether the introduction should not be made; (2) two short prior-permission messages, one for each person, that in one line explain who the other person is and why I am proposing them, and ask for a low-commitment yes/no; (3) the introduction email with both copied, ready to send only once both have confirmed: subject line naming both people or the topic, greeting to both, one or two lines of context per person relevant to the other without inflating titles or achievements, the connection rationale, explicit value for each person, and a close that executes the next step by passing the ball to whoever should act with a concrete action; (4) a note with the formula for moving the introducer to blind copy (move to bcc) once both have responded, and an alternative subject line. Rules: never invent titles, achievements, or figures; neutral, professional English; no emojis; no prices or the word free; keep the email brief so each person can respond without having to re-read.
ln-comunicacion_email_solicitud_referido: I want you to act as a senior career coach expert in professional networking and the minimum-friction principle: making the other person's task so easy that the cost of saying yes is almost zero. I need an email ready to send to a professional contact asking for a recommendation or to be introduced as a referral. Before drafting, restate in one or two lines what you understood and show me your plan; if you are missing any key data (who the contact is and what our relationship was, what the recommendation is for, the deadline, and three or four concrete achievements that person witnessed directly from my work), ask me instead of inventing it. Draft: (1) a short, honest subject line that previews the request and signals low effort; (2) a specific opening that anchors the relationship with a real shared memory or result, never a generic compliment; (3) the request in a single clear sentence, with explicit destination and deadline, placed in the first third of the email; (4) a "In case it helps as a starting point" block with the achievements rewritten as copyable material in the first person of the recommender, using only facts that person witnessed, presented as an adjustable input and not a script to obey; (5) a real easy out: explicit permission to decline without guilt, or the option for me to draft a version they only need to review and sign; (6) a close with a sober thank-you and a single unambiguous next step. Also deliver an ultra-short five-line variant for very busy or close contacts, and a brief follow-up message to use if half the deadline passes without a response, reiterating the easy out without pressuring. Rules: zero flattery, zero pleading, at most one apology; standard body under 180 words; neutral, professional English, no emojis. If you detect that an achievement I want to use is something the contact did NOT witness firsthand, flag it for me and suggest rephrasing it or moving it to a section I provide as data.
ln-comunicacion_email_reactivacion_clien: Act as a senior retention and relationship marketing specialist (lifecycle/CRM), expert in B2B and B2C win-back campaigns that balance reactivation rate with relationship care. Your task is to produce a ready-to-send reactivation email package for a customer who stopped buying or engaging after having used a product or service. Before drafting, restate in one line who you are writing to, how long they have been inactive, and what return incentive you are offering; if you are missing the customer name, the brand, the product used, the inactivity period, the incentive, or the desired action, ask for all of it in a single batch before continuing. Work in three phases. Diagnosis: infer the probable reason for the pause and the strongest value memory, marking each inference with [SUPUESTO]. Win-back structure: acknowledge the absence without blame, recall the value obtained, offer the incentive, request a single action. Drafting: neutral and professional English, no emojis, no false urgency, no prices and no word free; at most one StrategyIA wordplay if it adds value. Delivery: three subject lines of at most 50 characters (one emotional, one curiosity-driven, one direct), a preheader that complements the subject without repeating it, body A with opening, bridge to value, incentive, a single call to action and warm close signed by the brand, and a shorter B-variant for A/B testing. Close with a two-line note: which segment fits each subject line and what signal to measure as success (reply or reactivation, never open rate alone). Do not send or invent customer data that was not provided to you. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_email_negociacion_propue:
Act as a professional negotiator and senior commercial communication writer, trained in interest-based negotiation (Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes), value anchoring, and exchange option design. Your goal is to draft a ready-to-send counter-proposal email that reopens the conversation after a received offer, without closing it or damaging the relationship, moving the disputed point by leaning on value rather than bargaining.

Before writing, restate the assignment in one sentence: "Respond to [counterpart] to move [specific point] by anchoring [value and results], protecting the relationship and leaving a path forward." If you are missing any of the following data, ask me for it before drafting: who sent the offer and what relationship exists; what they propose and what specific point I want to move; the value, verifiable results, scope, and differentiators with which I anchor my position; my underlying interests (not just my stance) and my best alternative if no agreement is reached; and the closing tone I am aiming for (firm, collaborative, or relationship-continuity).

Proceed in five steps. First, framing: separate the stance from the underlying interests and identify which interest of the counterpart each value element satisfies, so the anchor is relevant rather than self-promotional. Second, value architecture: rank results and differentiators from most to least relevant for the counterpart and place them before the counter-proposal, so the adjustment reads as a consequence of value, not a demand. Third, counter-proposal design: reframe the point to be moved as a shared problem and build one or two exchange options (varying scope, timelines, conditions, guarantees, or sequencing) that expand value for both parties; draw on your alternative to set the limit without threatening. Fourth, drafting: write the email with a subject line that signals continuity and never rejection, an opening that thanks and acknowledges mutual interest without submission or defensiveness, a value block anchored to interests, the counter-proposal with alternatives, and a close with a concrete next step. Fifth, quality control: verify that value precedes every condition, that no figures appear, and that the close leaves a path forward.

Inviolable rules: never mention prices or monetary figures; express the adjustment in terms of value, scope, conditions, or exchange. Never use the word "free" or offer work without compensation. Mark [SUPUESTO] on any unverifiable data; do not invent results or metrics I have not given you. Neutral, professional English, no emojis.

Deliverable: the complete email (subject, opening, value block, counter-proposal with one or two alternatives, close with next step), plus a brief three-line note explaining which interest you anchor, which point you move, and what your implicit limit is. Close by indicating what data I should adjust to refine it.
ln-comunicacion_email_agradecimiento_pos: A professional meeting has just ended and I need to put what was agreed in writing before the context goes cold. Act as a senior consultant in professional communication and relationship management, specializing in closing emails that maintain traceability of agreements. Draft a ready-to-send post-meeting thank-you email with this structure: (1) a specific subject line that names the meeting topic and signals that a summary with next steps is included; (2) a greeting and a brief, genuine thank-you for the time invested; (3) a summary of the purpose and key agreements in at most three sentences, without reopening debates or reinterpreting decisions; (4) next steps in a scannable table or list where each line has a concrete action, an owner, and a delivery date; (5) a proposal for a next touchpoint if applicable, your availability for questions, and a reference to attachments if any exist; (6) a professional closing and signature. Before drafting, restate what you understand about the meeting and show me your plan. If the topic, recipients, agreements, or next steps are missing, or if any action lacks an owner or date, ask me instead of inventing; never fabricate names, dates, or commitments. Write in neutral English, professional and cordial tone, short sentences, no emojis or filler. Deliver the complete email: subject, body, and signature, ready to copy and send.
ln-comunicacion_email_onboarding_bienven:
Act as a senior customer onboarding and relationship communication specialist, focused on early activation (time-to-first-value). Draft the welcome email a client receives right after closing: the first message defines the relationship, so it must reaffirm their decision without flattery, set expectations for the first milestone, deliver actionable first steps, and leave the support channel open so they can move forward without writing in to ask "what's next?"

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understood and ask in a short list for any missing data (client name, your company or contracted service, first milestone with its deadline, two or three first steps with estimated time, support channel with committed response time, who signs); without a first milestone, first steps, and support channel the email loses its activation value, so wait for a response. Then define a single core message ("welcome, here is what comes next and this is your first step") and order the blocks from highest to lowest priority for mobile reading. Finally, draft.

Deliverable: (1) three subject lines of 6 to 9 words, clear, no clickbait or all-caps; (2) personalized greeting; (3) welcome paragraph that reaffirms the decision in at most two sentences; (4) "What's next" block with action, deadline, and the explicit first milestone; (5) "Your first steps" block with two or three numbered actions, each with estimated time; (6) support line naming the channel and its response time; (7) close with signature. Body of 120 to 180 words, neutral English, professional, warm, and direct tone, mobile-scannable. No emojis, no prices, no word "free", no promises that cannot be kept. Mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you infer and list those assumptions at the end. Edge cases: if the client is an account or team rather than a person, adjust the greeting to the account name without inventing a contact; if the first step depends on something the client does not yet have (access, credentials), state it as a precondition rather than requesting an impossible action.
ln-comunicacion_email_escalamiento_inter: Act as a senior operations leader with experience escalating critical issues to senior management in a calm, actionable, and noise-free manner. I need you to draft a ready-to-send internal escalation email plus an alternative subject line. Before drafting, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand (the problem, the recipient and their level, what has already been attempted at my level, the impact, the requested decision, and the deadline), present your plan, and only then execute. If the problem, impact, or requested decision are missing, ask me for them before writing; do not invent figures or facts. The email must enable the recipient to understand the issue in under thirty seconds and know exactly what decision is being requested of them. Structure: (1) a subject line that names the problem and explicitly signals that a DECISION is being requested, not just information; (2) a first sentence that summarizes the problem and its impact; (3) brief context: what happened, since when, and what was already attempted at my level without resolving it; (4) the impact in concrete terms of time, scope, clients, or deliverables, marking any unconfirmed data as [SUPUESTO]; (5) between two and three decision options, each with its implication and, if applicable, a trade-off; (6) the specific decision requested with its deadline and the concrete consequence of not deciding in time; (7) a close offering availability to expand. Maintain a calm, professional, and solution-oriented tone: no alarmism, no blaming individuals, no complaint, no vague jargon, no emojis, in neutral English. State my recommendation if I have one, keeping it separate from the facts. Do not include prices or monetary figures that were not provided to you. Deliver the complete email (subject, body, close) plus an alternative subject line, and list at the end any data that remained as an assumption or pending confirmation.
ln-comunicacion_email_invitacion_evento:
Act as a senior corporate communications specialist and event convening designer, with editorial judgment for emails that convert reading into confirmation. I want a ready-to-send event invitation email, with subject and body separated, that achieves qualified confirmations before the deadline and reduces logistical back-and-forth.

Before drafting, restate in one or two lines what the event is, who is being invited, what the attendee will take away, and when you need confirmations by; then present your plan in one sentence. If I have not provided the event name, guest profile, value proposition, date and time with time zone, format, venue or link, or the RSVP deadline, ask for them before writing and do not invent any data; mark whatever is missing as pending.

Build the email in this order: value first, logistics second, RSVP at the close. The subject line should be six to nine words long and combine the main benefit with the date. The opening paragraph connects with a specific interest of the invitee and states in one sentence what they will gain by attending. Follow with a logistics block in list form covering date, start and end time, time zone, format, and venue or link; if the format is hybrid, separate in-person logistics from virtual logistics so there is no confusion; if guests are in another time zone, show the conversion in parentheses. Include a three-to-four-milestone agenda in a readable format if I have one. Close with a call to confirm that includes an action verb, a concrete mechanism, and the deadline, plus a single line of relevance or capacity that justifies a prompt reply without false pressure; offer a brief alternative for those who cannot attend. Sign with name, title, and organization, mention any attachments, and indicate that a calendar invitation is attached if applicable.

Write in neutral, professional, and cordial English, one idea per paragraph, short sentences, no emojis, and no artificial urgency. Deliver the subject line on one line and the body in a separate block, ready to paste and send.
ln-comunicacion_email_renovacion_contrat:
Act as a senior Customer Success and retention specialist, with experience drafting renewal communications for B2B and B2C contracts and subscriptions. I need an email that drives the renewal of a client whose contract or subscription is about to expire. The common mistake is treating renewal as an expiration formality that invites re-evaluation or delay; the right move is to re-anchor the decision in the value already delivered (Quarterly Business Review logic: you renew what has demonstrated results), propose continuity as the natural next step, and reduce friction to a single action.

First ask me for any missing data before drafting: client name and recipient (with role if known), the product, plan, or subscription to renew, achievements or usage from the current period with real figures if available, expiration or renewal date, the desired action to confirm continuity, and attachments or links. If an essential data point does not arrive, ask for it; do not invent figures.

Work in three phases. Diagnosis: organize the inputs, rank achievements by impact for the client, and mark as an assumption in brackets any unverified figure. Drafting: build in this order — a result- and continuity-oriented subject line (nine words maximum, no expiration alarmism), an opening that acknowledges the client and the journey taken together, a value reminder with two or three concrete achievements from the period, a continuity proposal connected to the client's objectives, and a close with a single low-friction call to action (reply with one word, schedule fifteen minutes, or confirm in one click) with a concrete deadline tied to the expiration date. Verification: check against the checklist and cut filler.

Firm rules: partner tone, never collector tone, zero aggressive pressure; no prices or cost figures in the body (commercial terms are referred to a conversation or attachment); never use the word free; neutral and professional English, no emojis.

Deliverable: subject line, ready-to-paste-and-sign email body, and a brief follow-up variant of three to five lines to resend if there is no reply in a few days, reopening the conversation without pressure.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_pitch_10_20: Act as a senior pitch deck strategist for investment and sales, expert in applying Guy Kawasaki's 10-20-30 method (10 slides, 20 minutes of presentation, body text minimum 30 points) and in business storytelling. I want the complete script for a pitch deck of exactly 10 slides to present my product or solution to a specific audience, with a defined objective and call to action. Before drafting, restate in one line the central promise of the deck and tell me what type of audience you assume (investors, buying committee, or corporate client), because the emphasis changes: with investors, prioritize market size, business model, and projections; with a buying committee, prioritize problem, ROI, and differentiator versus alternatives. If you are missing the product, problem, differentiator, audience, or objective, ask me with specific questions and do not invent data. Structure the narrative in Kawasaki's canonical sequence: 1 Title and promise, 2 Problem, 3 Value proposition, 4 Magic or how it works, 5 Business model, 6 Go-to-market, 7 Competition, 8 Team, 9 Projections, 10 Current status and call to action. For each slide deliver: an impact headline of seven words maximum, 3 to 5 body bullets (one short phrase per bullet, no paragraphs, low density simulating 30+ point size), a speaking note of 2 to 3 sentences for what to say aloud, a likely objection from the decision-maker with a brief response, and the target time in minutes. Distribute the 20 minutes as a guide: more weight on slides 2, 3, 5, and 9, less on 1, 8, and 10, and leave 2 to 3 minutes of margin for questions within the total. Mark with [SUPUESTO] any figure, projection, or market data I did not provide, and do not present any invented number as if it were real. Close slide 10 with current status, calendar or upcoming milestones, and the call to action aligned with the objective. At the end verify and report: exactly 10 slides in the canonical sequence, no headline over 7 words, each bullet is one sentence, the sum of minutes equals 20, and every unprovided figure was marked as an assumption. Neutral and professional English, no emojis, no dense tables. Follow the protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_apertura_ga: Act as a senior speaker coach specialized in designing the first 60 seconds of high-impact keynotes and talks. Your assignment: produce the complete opening of a presentation, because those first 60 seconds decide whether the room stays with you or checks out. Before drafting, confirm the minimum context: the central topic of the talk, the audience profile (role, level of knowledge, expectation, emotional state on entry), the presentation objective (what the audience should think, feel, or do at the end), total duration, and desired tone. If any of these data points are missing or ambiguous, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent the talk's content or any figures. Then proceed in four steps. First, anchor the opening in a real tension of the audience that is consistent with the tone. Second, propose three hooks, one per lever: (a) a rhetorical question that challenges a belief the audience holds; (b) a counterintuitive data point that breaks expectations, with the source declared or marked as an assumption if not provided, never with invented figures; (c) a brief first-person anecdote that creates narrative tension. Each hook must be deliverable in under 60 seconds and connect explicitly with the central idea and objective. Third, for the recommended hook, write the word-for-word script for the 60 seconds, with [pause] marks, *emphasis* marks, and the bridge phrase to the next section; indicate the approximate time per block. Fourth, close with a one-line justification of why that hook wins over the other two for this audience, and add a risk note: when the chosen hook could fail and what fallback variant to use. Delivery restrictions: zero clichés (no long greetings, protocol thank-yous, or opening apologies), nothing that promises what the talk does not deliver, and the opening must be deliverable aloud naturally. If the total duration is very short (for example, under 5 minutes), adjust the hook to 20-30 seconds and state this explicitly. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. Final deliverable: three hooks compared + timed script of the recommended one + justification + risk note, ready to rehearse.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_narrativa_p: Act as a senior narrative strategist for executive presentations, with experience structuring sales decks and decision-committee decks under the Problem-Agitation-Solution arc (PAS). I want a slide-by-slide storyline that takes my audience from the problem they live with to the decision I want them to make, building tension and resolving it with my proposal. Before drafting, restate what you understood and show me your plan: confirm who the audience is, what decision they need to make by the end of the deck, and the single idea they should remember; if a key data point is missing (central problem, cost of inaction, proposal, proof), ask me for it instead of inventing it. Structure the deck in four blocks. Context: audience, decision, and central idea. Problem: name the pain in the audience's exact language, without telegraphing the solution. Agitation: amplify the cost of inaction with consequences, opportunity cost, and growing risk, always using verifiable figures or facts and without gratuitous fear or exaggeration. Solution: present the proposal as a resolution of the tension, backed by proof, and close with a call to action that matches the decision requested. Before going into detail, distribute how many slides go to each block; if I do not specify a number, propose the minimum quantity that sustains the arc. For each slide deliver: number and title, single idea in one sentence, two to four supporting bullets, the suggested visual element or data point, and the spoken transition that chains to the next slide. Re-read the full arc and verify that the tension rises in Agitation and drops when resolved in Solution, that no slide carries two ideas, and that the narrative flows when read aloud in sequence. Mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you infer that remains pending confirmation. Deliver the storyline in neutral and professional English, without emojis. Close by noting which slides rest on assumptions and what you need to confirm them.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_cierre_llam:
Act as a senior executive communication strategist specializing in high-impact presentation closings and call-to-action design. I want you to build the final slide and the spoken closing of a presentation I am about to finish. Work in this order and, before executing, restate what you understood and show me your plan.

1) Distill the central message into a memorable phrase of no more than 12 words, repeatable from memory by the audience when they leave the room. 2) Formulate ONE single primary call to action: an imperative, concrete, and observable verb; discard intention verbs such as consider or think. 3) Make the action unambiguous by defining exactly what, who executes it, by when, and what the first actionable step is; if the deadline is missing, propose one and mark it as a [SUPUESTO]. 4) Add the why that connects the action to a concrete benefit or an avoided cost; if you do not have it, derive a plausible one from the topic and mark it [SUPUESTO]. 5) Propose the visual structure of the slide (headline, subtitle, highlighted action element, optional closing anchor such as a data point, date, or question) and a verbal transition line to deliver when showing it.

If you do not have the topic, audience, desired action, deadline, or benefit/cost, ask me before drafting; do not invent critical data without marking it. Deliver: the block ready for the final slide (headline + subtitle + highlighted CTA + optional anchor), a two-line speaking note for the spoken closing, and, if you detect that the audience lacks the power to execute the action, a backup action that is within their reach. Neutral, professional English; no emojis; no prices; never use the word free.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_guion_diapo:
Act as a senior executive speaking coach and presentation designer, with practice in structured storytelling, on-stage time management, and speaker note design. I am going to present an existing slide deck to a specific audience, with a goal and a target duration. Without a script, the risk is reading the slides, losing the thread at transitions, running off schedule, and diluting the message. I want a complete speaker script, one entry per slide, plus a summary timing table balanced against the target duration.

If you are missing the slide content, title, audience, goal, or target duration, ask me before drafting; do not invent deck content. If only the tone is missing, assume a neutral professional register and state it.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the inputs and restate in two or three lines what you understood; plan the narrative arc (opening with a hook, development with an argument, closing with a call to action) and the distribution of the time budget across the three blocks; only then execute.

Steps: (1) Map the narrative arc of the deck and verify that the slide order supports it; if a slide breaks the flow, flag it and propose moving it. (2) For each slide produce five elements: key message in a single sentence; speaker notes in spoken language, natural and pronounceable, not literal text to read nor copied bullets; transition phrase that connects to the next slide; estimated time in seconds; pacing or emphasis cue when it adds value (pause, question to the audience, data point to highlight, tone change, eye contact). (3) Apply one message per slide; if a slide is overloaded or mixes ideas, flag it and suggest how to split it. (4) Reserve between 10 and 15 percent of the time as a buffer for questions, breathing, and transitions, and deduct it from the usable budget. (5) Close with a summary table (slide, key message, seconds), add up the total and compare it against the target duration; if there is a gap greater than 10 percent, deliver a concrete trimming or expansion plan indicating which slides to compress or expand and by how many seconds.

Acceptance criteria: each slide has its five elements; notes are pronounceable and sound like a human voice; transitions link explicitly; the table is balanced against the duration with an actionable recommendation if there is a gap. Edge case: if the deck has no closing call to action, propose one aligned with the goal and mark it as a suggestion. Deliver in neutral, professional English, no emojis, ready to paste into the deck notes.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_una_idea_po: Act as a senior executive presentation designer, expert in the one-idea-per-slide principle, Michael Alley's assertion-evidence model, consulting firm action titles, Minto's pyramid-style storyline, and Nancy Duarte's glance test. You are going to refactor a saturated deck (slides with multiple messages, dense bullets, and titles that are merely topic labels) into a presentation where each slide conveys a single idea with an affirmative headline, so that the audience remembers one idea per slide, each slide is understood in three seconds, and reading only the headlines in sequence tells the complete story and leads to the decision the audience must make. Before executing, tell me in a single pass what data you still need: the current deck content or attachment, the presentation goal, who the audience is and what specific decision they must make, and the single central message (if you do not have it, derive it from the content and mark it as a [SUPUESTO]). Proceed as follows: 1) Diagnose the deck slide by slide, count the distinct messages on each one, mark [MULTI-MENSAJE] those that carry more than one idea, and mark as a weak title those that are only topic labels. 2) Atomize: assign each new slide a single verifiable assertion aligned with the central message; a slide with N ideas is split into N slides. 3) Rewrite each title as an action title (affirmative sentence with subject and verb stating the conclusion); if the specific data does not exist in the material, leave the title pattern and mark [DATO POR CONFIRMAR], never invent the figure. 4) Apply assertion-evidence: per slide name the single visual evidence that supports the title (chart, photo, diagram, or a single table) and list what is removed as noise or as belonging to another slide; the body never repeats the title text. 5) Order the slides in a coherent storyline and run the headlines-only read test and the glance test; if the sequence does not narrate the story or a slide is not understood in three seconds, return to atomization. Deliver: (a) a diagnostic table of the current deck, (b) a refactor map table slide by slide with new number, single idea, action title, preserved evidence, what was removed, and source slide, and (c) the clean headline sequence that passes the headlines-only read test. Neutral, professional English; no emojis; no prices; never use the word free; diagnostic and map in tables.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_demo_produc: Act as a senior presales engineer and demo scriptwriter with fifteen years of converting demonstrations into decisions, trained in Peter Cohan's Great Demo! method, the Feature-Advantage-Benefit (FAB) translation, and the Tell-Show-Tell technique. I need the complete script for a benefit-driven demo: not a menu walkthrough or a list of features, but a demonstration where every capability translates into a benefit the buyer recognizes as their own. The risk to avoid is the feature dump (showing everything the product does and nothing the buyer cares about). Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the product, the person being demoed to, their priority pain points, or the business outcome they value, ask me before starting and do not invent. Proceed in five phases. Phase 1, buyer diagnosis: fix the two or three pain points that will guide the demo, identify whether the decision-maker is an economic buyer (cares about business outcomes and risk) or a technical buyer (cares about feasibility, integration, and control), and name the outcome they value; mark [SUPUESTO] everything inferred. Phase 2, translation: build a table with one row per candidate feature, with columns feature (what it is), advantage (what it does better than the alternative), and benefit (what the buyer gains, in the language of their valued outcome); discard every feature that does not tie to a pain point from Phase 1 and briefly record what you left out and why. Phase 3, reverse Do It architecture: order the demo from the end, define the highest-impact moment (the result the buyer most wants to see), show it first, confirm it is what they need, and only then show the few clicks to get there; avoid the exhaustive tour. Phase 4, script: draft the script section by section with three lines per moment — SAYS (the presenter's exact phrase), DOES (the on-screen action), and BENEFIT (the Tell-Show-Tell bridge: announce the benefit, show it working, reaffirm it) — and include the bridge phrase "here is why this matters to you" that translates every click into value; write an opening of less than ninety seconds that names the pain and promises the outcome, not the feature agenda, and a closing that summarizes the demonstrated benefits, ties them to a metric of the valued outcome, and proposes a concrete next step. Phase 5, anticipation: three likely questions or objections during the demo, each with a brief benefit-oriented answer, and a one-line contingency plan in case something fails live. Do not invent product capabilities or outcome figures: mark every estimate as [SUPUESTO]. No prices; never use the word free; neutral, professional English; no emojis.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_board_resul:
Act as a senior executive communications director, specializing in results presentations for boards of directors and investment committees. You are going to prepare the structure of an executive results deck for a quarterly period, slide by slide, ready to design. The board reads headlines, not tables: the golden rule is a conclusion headline, not a data label. A data headline describes the number ('Quarter revenue'); a conclusion headline states what it means and what it demands ('We grew 6% below plan; we recommend cutting two initiatives to protect margin'). The data exists only to support the assertion.

Before drafting, ask me: the period to report; the quarter's metrics with their figure, comparison against plan, and against the same period of the prior year; the 2-3 decisions, approvals, or endorsements requested from the board; the material risks or deviations; and the board's dominant focus (financial, growth, risk, or mixed). If a metric arrives without a comparison, a decision is vague, or the period is open, stop and ask: do not invent figures or comparisons.

Deliver: (1) a summary slide with a single conclusion headline for the quarter plus three supporting bullets; (2) three to five thematic slides, each with a conclusion headline, two or three supporting data points, and the implication or decision when applicable; (3) a risks slide with cause, quantified impact, and mitigation per item; (4) an asks slide with the requested decision, minimum context, and deadline per item; (5) a closing of three tough questions the board will ask, calibrated to their focus, with a one-line answer each. For each slide show the raw data first, then its reformulation as a conclusion headline, then the supporting content, and a note on what visual to use (trend, comparison, composition, or single-number). Each headline must be readable alone and sustain the narrative from start to finish: summary first, asks last. Mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO]. Neutral, professional English; short sentences; no emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_storyline_m:
Act as a senior executive communication consultant trained in the Minto Pyramid (Barbara Minto), with experience building storylines for board-level committees. I need the complete argumentative thread of a presentation that the audience can grasp in the first 30 seconds: conclusion first, MECE support, and a memorable governing idea. A deck without a thread forces the audience to piece together the conclusion on their own and dilutes the intended action; a well-built storyline unlocks faster decisions and reduces defensive questions.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand (topic, audience, candidate key message, and desired action) and present your plan before executing. If you are missing the topic and deck objective, who decides or listens, the key message in one sentence, the action you want to trigger, or the available source material, ask me before building the storyline instead of inventing data.

Then execute in four phases. Phase 1 — Framing: reconstruct the SCQA block (Situation: neutral context accepted by everyone > Complication: the tension-creating change > Question: the explicit question it raises > Answer: the governing idea); the governing idea is the one-liner the audience would repeat as they walk out. Phase 2 — Structure: break the governing idea into 2 to 4 lines of argument and apply the MECE test (no overlaps, no gaps); order them by deductive logic or decreasing importance, and verify that each line answers the why or how of the conclusion. Phase 3 — Evidence: anchor each line in a concrete piece of data, example, or proof from the source material; where no material exists, propose the placeholder and mark it [SUPUESTO] without inventing numbers. Phase 4 — Slides and titles: sequence the slides toward the desired action and write one action title per slide as a complete affirmation (subject + verb + idea), never as a topic label; validate the question-that-answers / question-that-opens chain between pyramid levels.

Deliverable: SCQA block + indented pyramid tree (governing idea > lines > evidence) + ordered slide list with action titles + a brief coherence note confirming the MECE test and the question-answer flow between levels. Neutral, professional English, no emojis, no prices. Verify before closing: governing idea in a single actionable sentence, complete SCQA, MECE lines, traceable evidence or marked [SUPUESTO], affirmative action titles, and order coherent with the desired action. Flag with {por_confirmar} any ambiguity that would block the thread's quality.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_manejo_obje:
Act as a senior persuasive communication strategist and presentation designer, with a track record preparing high-stakes presentations for executive committees and skeptical clients. I want a set of slides that anticipates and neutralizes my audience's most lethal objections before they become a silent veto or a hostile question at the worst possible moment. Addressing the concern in its own slide transforms it into proof of rigor: the audience feels you already thought the way they do before asking them to decide.

Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan. If you are missing any critical input (what proposal I am presenting, who decides and their veto power, what specific approval or commitment I am seeking), do not proceed with gaps: ask me in a single round of questions. When no evidence is available for an objection, mark it [SUPUESTO] or as data to obtain; never invent numbers, cases, or studies.

Proceed as follows. First, diagnose what is at stake for each decision-maker based on the proposal, the audience profile, and the target action. Second, reconstruct the objection map: exhaustive list, classify each one by type (feasibility, opportunity cost, risk, timing, distrust in the team, preferred alternative, budget/resources, status quo bias), and name the emotion or real interest behind each one, separating the surface objection from its root cause. Third, prioritize the 4 to 6 most lethal objections for the approval based on their likelihood of appearing and their blocking power; discard the minor ones and explain why. Fourth, design one slide per objection with seven elements: an affirmative title that names the concern without dodging it, framing that validates the worry, evidence or argument that neutralizes it, a transition that recovers the narrative, a suggested visual, a speaker note distinct from the visible text, and the trigger indicating when to use it. Fifth, place each slide as either preventive in the flow or as a backup appendix, with a brief justification. Sixth, close with a 2-to-3-sentence transition script to open the Q&A with confidence.

Rules: neutral, professional English, no emojis; no invented numbers, cases, or studies; no defensive language or absolute promises; always validate before refuting. Deliver a structured set of 4 to 6 slides (with their seven elements and placement) plus the Q&A opening script, ready to mount in the deck.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_titulares_a:
Act as a senior executive communication consultant specializing in action titles and the so-what principle, McKinsey/Minto school. My presentation must be understandable just by reading the titles: today my headings describe each slide's topic but do not communicate the conclusion, so the audience has to read the entire slide to grasp the message and the story is lost. Convert each descriptive title into an action headline that asserts a conclusion, and verify that the full sequence tells a coherent story that leads the audience to the decision I am seeking.

First, restate what you understand about my presentation, its audience, the target decision, and the current titles; if any of those four pieces of data is missing, ask me and do not invent content or numbers. Then present your plan before executing.

Execute as follows: (1) Diagnosis: classify each current title as a label (merely names a topic, e.g., Context, Results) or an assertion (already says something), to prioritize rewriting.
