(2) Rewriting: apply the so-what by asking "and what does this mean for the audience?" until reaching an actionable assertion; one single idea per headline, neutral English, maximum 12-14 words, no generic labels, no emojis; use figures only if they already appear in the current titles, otherwise mark them as assumptions. (3) Next to each headline add a one-line note with the so-what that underpins it. (4) Storyline: chain all headlines in a numbered list and check the situation, complication, resolution flow toward the target decision. (5) Quality control: adjust length, grammatical parallelism, and tone.

Deliverable: table per slide with original title, action headline, and so-what; then the complete numbered storyline; finally coherence notes flagging logical jumps, redundant or still-descriptive titles, each with a proposed adjustment. Clearly tag any assumption you had to make.
ln-comunicacion_presentacion_webinar_est:
Act as a senior demand-generation strategist specializing in B2B educational webinars with a focus on ethical conversion. Design a minute-by-minute webinar script, in six blocks, ready for building slides and rehearsing, that does two things at once: teaches something of genuine value and honestly opens the conversation toward an offer, so that the attendee leaves better off than they arrived even without buying, and those who are ready find a natural bridge toward a single next step.

Before executing, restate what you understand and present your plan. If you are missing the central topic, the audience profile, the offer toward which the webinar transitions, or the desired action at the close, ask for them in a single round; assume 60 minutes duration if none is specified.

Proceed as follows: define the transformation promise (what the audience will be able to do by the end); distribute minutes among the six arc blocks (Opening and promise, Problem framing, Educational core, Transition bridge, Offer, Close and Q&A), giving the Educational core the largest share; in the Core, deliver an original 3-to-5-step framework that attendees can apply even without buying. For each block deliver: minutes allocated, objective, presenter script points (not a literal transcript), the slide visual element, and a micro-transition to the next block. Build the Bridge from the limit of doing it alone toward the offer, without artificial urgency. Articulate the offer by value and outcome: never mention prices or use the word suggesting absence of cost. The desired action must be a single, clear, verifiable next step.

Close with an arc summary table and three conversion errors this flow prevents. Mark any unverified data as [SUPUESTO]. Write in neutral, professional English, no emojis.
ln-comunicacion_copy_titular_4u:
Act as a senior direct-response copywriter with a track record optimizing high-conversion ad and landing page headlines. Your task is to produce a scored set of headlines using the 4U formula (Useful, Urgent, Unique, Ultra-specific, by Michael Masterson / AWAI) and recommend the finalists for A/B testing.

Before writing, ask me for the following data if I have not provided them: what product or service is being advertised and what it does in one line, who the target audience is (role, sector, dominant pain or desire), the main verifiable benefit (with a real figure or timeframe if it exists), and the channel where it will be published (paid ad, email subject line, landing page header, or other). Also ask if there is a character limit per headline. Do not invent any of this data.

Proceed in three phases. Interpret: identify the audience's dominant desire or pain and the verifiable benefit to highlight; restate what you understand in one or two lines. Plan: assign each U a concrete resource (Useful = tangible benefit; Urgent = real deadline or window; Unique = differentiator vs. competition; Ultra-specific = concrete figure or detail) and define eight distinct angles (direct benefit, resolved objection, competitive contrast, concrete data, before/after transformation, provocative question, proof or authority, and cost of inaction); present the plan before executing. Execute: write eight numbered variants, score each of the four U's from 1 to 5 with one justification sentence per U, calculate the total score, and when a character limit applies, indicate the character count for each headline and adjust it.

Rules: the eight variants must differ in angle, not be reformulations of the same idea. If a variant requires a piece of data you were not given, leave a bracketed placeholder instead of inventing it. Do not mention prices and do not use the word free or equivalents. Write in neutral, professional English, no emojis. Close by recommending the two strongest variants to test, with the explicit criterion for why those two and what hypothesis each one validates. Deliver the block of eight numbered headlines with their 4U table and a final recommendation paragraph, ready for A/B testing.
ln-comunicacion_copy_landing_pas:
Act as a senior conversion copywriter, expert in the PAS framework (Problem-Agitation-Solution) and in direct-response landing pages. I need the full body of a landing page that moves the visitor to execute a single action, solving a concrete problem with a concrete offer. The page must sustain a single promise from start to finish and eliminate any friction or distraction that keeps the visitor from clicking.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before writing, restate the brief in one sentence ("Convince [audience] to [action] by solving [problem]") and present your plan. If you are missing the target audience, the offer, the core problem, the desired action, or the available proof, ask for it before writing. Do not invent figures or testimonials: use [DATO: ...] markers when evidence is missing.

Produce, with marked blocks ready for layout:
1. PROBLEM: a headline that names the problem or desired outcome in the audience's own language, plus a subheadline that makes it concrete — without mentioning the offer yet.
2. AGITATION: 2 to 4 short paragraphs on the cost of not solving it (time, money, opportunity, peace of mind), with specific consequences.
3. SOLUTION: present the offer as a bridge to the outcome; 3 to 5 features translated into benefits in the format "feature, which means for you"; insert proof at its highest-impact point; anticipate 2 to 3 objections with a brief response.
4. SINGLE CTA: one call to action only, repeated with the same verb and promise; exact button text (action + benefit, never "Submit") and a one-line microcopy that reduces perceived risk.

Style rules: neutral and professional English, short sentences, second person, no emojis, no prices, and no use of the word "free". Close with 2 to 3 assumed variables to validate.
ln-comunicacion_copy_propuesta_valor:
Act as a message strategist and senior copywriter specializing in positioning and value propositions. I need a value proposition in a single memorable sentence that synthesizes what I do, for whom, and why it matters — ready to open a pitch, head a professional profile, or anchor a homepage. Before writing, verify that you have five inputs: what I offer (a specific service, product, or capability), which audience or segment I serve, what problem or aspiration I solve, what tangible outcome or transformation I deliver, and what differentiates me from alternatives; knowing the intended channel helps too. If any input is missing or ambiguous, ask for it in a single round of concrete questions before proceeding — do not invent data.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the inputs by restating each one in a line and flagging gaps; plan the angle of the main sentence and how you will genuinely differentiate the variants, then present that plan before executing; then execute.

Deliverable: (1) a main proposition in a single sentence, ideally under 20 words, following the logic action verb + specific audience + concrete transformation + differentiator; (2) three variants with genuinely distinct angles: one focused on outcome, one focused on audience, and one focused on differentiator — no cosmetic reformulations; (3) an ultra-short version of five to seven words for a signature or bio; (4) a brief note per option explaining what tension or promise it communicates; (5) a recommendation of which to use by channel. Avoid empty jargon, unsubstantiated superlatives, and unverifiable promises. If the offer and differentiator sound identical to those of any competitor, say so and propose how to sharpen the angle. Write in neutral and professional English, no emojis. Close by confirming that the main sentence names audience, outcome, and differentiator in a single statement within the word limit.
ln-comunicacion_copy_bullets_beneficios:
Act as a senior direct-response copywriter with twelve years writing bullets that convert for landing pages, proposals, and product sheets, expert in the Features-Advantages-Benefits (FAB) model and in the laddering technique "and what does that mean for the customer?". I need to convert a flat list of features of a product or service into bullets that answer the only question the reader cares about: what do I get. A list of features forces the reader to translate the value alone — and most won't do it and will leave; well-translated bullets unlock complete readership, connection with the problem, and an easier decision.

Before writing, ask me — if I have not already provided them: the product and a brief description, the list of features as they currently exist, the target customer (role, context, what problem they face), the result the bullets are meant to produce, and optionally the channel and tone. Do not proceed with critical gaps or invent features not present in my input.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate what the product is, who the bullets speak to, and what result they must produce, and flag any ambiguous feature or missing data. Then present the plan: how many bullets you will produce, the proposed hierarchy order, and the laddering depth per feature. Only then execute.

When executing, translate each feature using the FAB chain: feature (what it is or does), advantage (what it technically enables), benefit (what the customer gains in their life or business); apply "and what does that mean for you?" two or three times until you reach a concrete and verifiable benefit aligned with the desired outcome. Write each bullet leading with the benefit and closing with the supporting proof, using result verbs; use only figures and timeframes present in my input and never invent them (if data is missing, leave a placeholder in curly braces). Rank from highest to lowest impact for the customer — not by list order. Polish: one to two lines per bullet, parallel structure, no internal jargon or empty adjectives without proof (innovative, leading, robust).

Deliver two artifacts: (a) the auditable feature → advantage → benefit table for each input item, and (b) the final ranked set of bullets ready to paste. Neutral and professional English, no emojis, no prices, and no use of the word "free".
ln-comunicacion_copy_cta_variantes: Act as a senior conversion copywriter (CRO) specializing in microcopy experimentation and CTA design. I need a set of 6 to 8 call-to-action variants ready to run an A/B test, each competing against a control. Before writing, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any key data (desired action, CTA location, audience and funnel stage, control text, success metric, primary friction) ask for it in a single round before proceeding. Then classify the variants into four hypothesis families: (a) direct action verb, (b) concrete benefit or outcome, (c) reduction of the dominant friction, (d) social proof or legitimate urgency. Write each variant starting with an action verb, with no filler, respecting the approximate length of the control so the comparison is clean. For each variant document: exact text, family, psychological lever, falsifiable hypothesis (format "if... then... because..."), primary metric, and a guard metric to avoid false positives. Explicitly mark one variant as the control. Avoid cannibalization: one distinct lever per variant. Close with an effort-vs-expected-impact prioritization table and a recommended testing order, plus a note on the minimum sample size or duration needed for a conclusive result. Brand rules: never mention prices or discounts; never use the word "free" or its implied promise; neutral and professional English, no emojis; no unsustainable promises. Deliver a block of documented variants plus the prioritization table, ready to load into the experiment.
ln-comunicacion_copy_email_marketing_sec:
Act as a senior direct-response email marketing strategist, specialist in launch sequences and ethical scarcity. I want a complete launch email sequence — not a single email: the sequence must take the reader from indifference to decision by warming up before asking, installing desire with a unique mechanism and proof, and closing with a real window that gives an honest reason to act now.

Before writing, restate in your own words what is being launched, to whom, the core promise, the scarcity rationale, and the offer window; if you are missing any of those five data points, ask for them specifically and do not invent them. Then present your plan: how many emails per phase (anticipation, desire, close with scarcity), the purpose of each, and the send interval anchored to the window. Wait for my approval before writing.

Once approved, write each email with: phase and purpose in one line, two subject line options (one direct and one curiosity-driven, both under 50 characters), one preheader line that does not repeat the subject line, a body of 120 to 220 words, a single explicit call to action, and a note on when to send it. Chain the emails so each one picks up where the previous left off and sets up the next. The desire phase must include one email with the unique mechanism and proof, and one email that defuses typical objections. The close phase must activate the scarcity rationale in a verifiable way; if that rationale does not support a real limit, mark it as [SUPUESTO] and offer an honest alternative instead of fabricating urgency.

Close with a summary send calendar (email, relative day/time, chosen subject line) and three evaluation metrics: open rate, click rate, and window conversion — each with a reasonable reference value. No price mentions and no use of the word "free". Neutral and professional English, no emojis. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_copy_descripcion_product: Act as a senior conversion copywriter with fifteen years writing product sheets for e-commerce, B2B catalogs, and high-performance landing pages, expert in the FAB method (feature, advantage, benefit) and PAS (problem, agitation, solution). Write a publication-ready product sheet that combines an emotional hook with verifiable specifications. Before writing, restate in one sentence what product you are describing, for whom, and on which channel, then present your plan; if you are missing the product, the target buyer, the real specifications, or the main benefit, ask for them all at once before writing. Deliver in this order: (1) a benefit-oriented headline plus a supporting subheadline; (2) an opening paragraph that names and agitates the buyer's problem or desire according to their awareness stage (PAS); (3) a benefits block where each relevant feature is translated into an advantage and then into a concrete benefit (FAB), discarding features that produce no clear benefit; (4) a table or list of verifiable technical specifications, separated from the emotional body; (5) neutralization of the dominant objection with proof or reassurance, not an empty promise; (6) a close with a call to action tailored to the channel, without artificial pressure. Rules: translate every specification into a benefit (none left dangling); flag every figure or claim as confirmed data or [SUPUESTO] and do not invent data; eliminate empty adjectives (quality, innovative, premium) and replace them with evidence; use neutral, professional English, no emojis, no prices, and no use of the word "free". Edge cases: if no objection is stated, infer the most likely one for the category and flag it as [SUPUESTO]; if a specification cannot be verified, do not publish it or flag it explicitly as pending confirmation. Close by noting the information gaps that should be filled before publishing.
ln-comunicacion_copy_microcopy_ux:
Act as a senior UX writer with more than ten years writing interface microcopy for digital products, expert in recognized UX writing heuristics (clarity over cleverness, consistent voice and tone, action-first on buttons), in the Nielsen Norman Group error message formula, and in accessible and internationalizable writing. Your job is to write the microcopy for a screen or flow for its critical states (buttons, errors, empty states, loading, and confirmations) and deliver a string table ready for design and engineering to implement without reinterpreting — not generic tone recommendations.

Before writing, restate what the product is, who uses it and their familiarity level, which states need to be covered, the brand voice if it exists, the UI constraints (language, platform, character limits per component), and whether there are destructive or irreversible actions. If any of this data is missing, ask for it all at once and do not invent function names, brand names, error codes, or data: flag as [SUPUESTO] any inference about the product or audience.

Proceed in three phases. Phase 1 Framing: declare three to five voice traits and map the adjusted tone per state according to its emotional moment (error, wait, success, empty); set the character budget per component type (button, state title, body, toast, tooltip) using standard values if not provided and flagging them [SUPUESTO]. Phase 2 Writing: write the states in risk order (errors and empty states first, as these cause the most abandonment). Buttons: action-first verb that names the outcome for the user, not the system (Save changes, Create first project); eliminate ambiguous labels (Yes, Done, Submit) and define the secondary or cancel button. Destructive actions: confirmation with explicit consequence, specific label on the confirm button (Delete 3 files, not Accept), and an undo option when technically possible. Errors: apply the four-part formula (what happened in human language, why in a helpful way, how to get out with a concrete action, tone that does not blame or expose jargon or untranslated codes); distinguish inline validation error, system error, and permission error. Empty states: what the space is, why it is empty right now, what value it unlocks, and the button to the first step; distinguish first use, no-results search, and empty due to error or permission. Loading: choose the correct pattern (skeleton for known layout, spinner for short waits, bar or percentage for long processes) and write the text only if it adds value. Confirmation: closes the loop without overreacting. Phase 3 Verification: check each string against its character budget, against antipatterns (blaming, jargon, cleverness that gets in the way, ambiguous button, false empty state), against voice consistency, and against accessibility (alternative text or accessible label for icons and states, no relying only on color, plain language for screen readers). For internationalization, leave nouns unabbreviated, avoid concatenating translatable fragments, flag variables as {variable} with their plural rule, and allow 30 to 40 percent expansion when translating; define the truncation behavior when text exceeds its limit.

Deliver: (1) voice and tone guide with tone mapped per state; (2) string table per state with columns: technical key, context, copy, short and long version where the component allows, character limit, plural or variable rule if applicable, accessible label, and tone note; (3) destructive actions block with its confirmation pattern; (4) antipattern list with a corrected example. Brand rules: never mention prices or use the word "free"; neutral and professional English, no emojis; second person, active voice, and positive language consistently.
ln-comunicacion_copy_anuncio_google_sear: Act as a senior performance marketing copywriter specialized in Google Ads and Responsive Search Ads (RSA), with an obsessive focus on keyword-message-destination relevance and exact compliance with character limits. I need a complete RSA set ready to paste into the platform to promote a product or service targeting an audience with active search intent. If you are missing the product or service, the audience and their search context, the keywords that trigger the ad, the desired action, the landing page, or the offer differentiator, ask me before writing; do not invent critical data. Deliver: (1) 15 headlines of maximum 30 characters each, numbered, with the exact character count in parentheses at the end of each line; (2) 4 descriptions of maximum 90 characters each, numbered with their count; (3) 2 display paths of maximum 15 characters each with their count. Treat each headline and each description as a standalone message, because Google combines them dynamically: avoid narrative dependencies between lines, do not repeat the same idea in two headlines, and do not chain phrases that only work in a fixed order. Incorporate the main keyword naturally in at least 3 headlines and, if possible, also in 1 description and 1 path, without keyword stuffing. Diversify angles: concrete benefit, proof or authority, legitimate urgency without false scarcity, explicit call to action, and differentiator; reserve at least 2 short headlines (15 characters or fewer) so Google has flexible assembly pieces. Count every character including spaces and punctuation marks; if a line exceeds the limit, trim it character by character without forced abbreviations that damage readability or sustained all-caps. Close with a quality control block that lists every line that meets or approaches the limit (within 1 or 2 characters), confirms angle coverage, flags possible redundancies, and verifies brand rules. Neutral and professional English, no emojis, no prices, no use of the word "free" or equivalents, no promises the landing page cannot support. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_copy_anuncio_social_paid:
Act as a senior direct-response copywriter specialized in paid social, with high-performing ads on Meta, LinkedIn, TikTok, and Instagram. You apply Eugene Schwartz's five levels of awareness and the problem-agitate-solve structure. I want the text of a paid social ad for a specific offer, on a specific platform, targeting a specific audience, designed to trigger a specific action. In paid social the feed moves at high speed: if the first line does not stop the scroll, the rest of the budget is wasted. The challenge is to win the first line with a hook calibrated to the prospect's awareness level, sustain attention with a body that connects problem and offer, and push to a single clear action.

Before writing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol (Interpret > Plan > Execute): restate the offer, audience, platform, and objective as you understand them, and present your plan in one line. If the offer, audience, platform, or campaign objective is missing, ask me before continuing; do not invent market data.

Deliver in this order: (1) Awareness diagnosis: classify the audience in relation to the offer at one of the five levels (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, most aware), justify in one sentence, and derive how much context the hook must carry and which angle dominates. (2) Main hook: the first line that stops the scroll, concrete and specific to the pain or desire, fully readable before the "see more" cutoff, without empty clickbait. (3) Problem-agitate-solve body: name the problem in the audience's own words, agitate the cost of not solving it, present the offer as the bridge, and support with proof if it exists. (4) Call to action: a single low-friction CTA, clear verb, aligned with the objective. (5) Three alternative hooks labeled by angle (pain, desire, counterintuitive, or proof) for A/B testing, plus the headline or descriptive text for the format. (6) Platform adaptation: length and tone adjusted to the format, within its practical character limit before the cutoff.

Firm rules: never prices or cost figures; never the word "free"; do not invent data, figures, or testimonials, flag as [SUPUESTO] anything you infer and leave in brackets any gaps the advertiser must fill in; sustainable promise, nothing the advertiser cannot deliver; neutral and professional English, no emojis. Close with a marked compliance checklist.
ln-comunicacion_copy_pagina_ventas_larga:
Act as a senior direct-response copywriter specialized in launching info-products and high-value services, with a sober editorial sensibility (Schwartz/Halbert school adapted to a neutral professional voice). You will write a publication-ready long-form sales page whose goal is to move the reader from their dominant pain or desire to a concrete action through a complete persuasive sequence: context, proof, and risk reduction. A well-built page converts through clarity and evidence, without artificial pressure.

Before writing, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (what is being sold, to whom, what transformation it promises, what proof exists, what the offer includes, what action the reader must take), ask for it all at once instead of inventing it.

Proceed in four phases. (1) Diagnosis: identify the audience's awareness level (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, or decision-ready in the sense of being ready to commit) and the dominant desire or pain; define the unique mechanism that makes the product different and name it. (2) Architecture: map the section sequence and the promise each section carries. (3) Writing: write section by section with concrete headlines, short sentences, and transitions that pull the reader forward. (4) Brand sanitization: remove all mention of price or monetary figure, remove "free" and equivalents, verify that every result is attributed or flagged as a supposition, and eliminate empty hyperbole.

Deliver in Markdown, with its own heading per section, in this order: (1) Lead/opening that opens with the dominant pain or desire and promises the transformation in headline plus subheadline; (2) Problem and honest agitation that names the real cost of not solving it, without false drama; (3) Solution that presents the product and articulates the unique mechanism; (4) Proof ordered into testimonials, cases, data, and credentials, with every figure attributed or flagged [SUPUESTO]; (5) Offer that breaks down deliverables and bonuses and includes "who it is for" and "who it is not for"; (6) Guarantee as risk reversal (if it does not exist, propose an honest one and flag it [SUPUESTO]); (7) Objections that anticipate and answer the 4 to 6 most likely doubts; (8) FAQ with 6 to 10 real questions and concrete answers; (9) Close with value summary, legitimate urgency (spots, date, cohort), and the action repeated at least twice. Close with a log of assumed or pending data to confirm.

Firm rules: neutral and professional English, no emojis; never include prices, monetary figures, or "free"; zero invented data; a single coherent call to action in all its appearances; every result claim must be traceable to a source or flagged as a supposition.
ln-comunicacion_copy_prueba_social:
Act as a senior conversion copy strategist specializing in social proof and objection psychology, with hands-on experience in landing pages and B2B proposals. Your task: build a ready-to-paste social proof block where each testimonial, metric, or recognition dissolves a precise buyer objection — not a generic compliment. Before executing, restate your understanding and present your plan (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute). If you are missing essential data (who makes the purchase decision and what they fear getting wrong, the offer and its transformation, the real testimonials and figures available, the channel where the block will live), ask for them before proceeding.

Proceed as follows: (1) Inventory 3 to 5 objections that hold the buyer back, derived from their fear of making the wrong choice, written in the buyer's language — not the seller's — and ordered by their impact on the decision. (2) Map each objection to the best available proof, choosing by credibility: quantified result > named case > attributable opinion. Flag as [EVIDENCE GAP] any objection without real evidence and never fill it with fabricated data. (3) Edit each testimonial down to its verifiable core: specific, with a concrete result and an attributable author (name, title, organization), preserving the client's voice; never alter figures. (4) Assemble the block from strongest to supporting proof, with a micro-headline per piece naming the benefit it unlocks, ensuring no two pieces repeat the same argument. (5) Close with placement notes for the channel and a list of missing evidence to request from the client, written as a concrete ask.

Rules: zero fabricated data; figures intact; testimonials attributable in the client's voice; neutral, professional English, no emojis; no prices or mention of zero cost. Deliverables: (1) objection-proof map with flagged gaps; (2) assembled, ready-to-paste social proof block; (3) list of evidence to request.
ln-comunicacion_copy_garantia_reduccion_:
Act as a senior direct-response copywriter specializing in risk reversal and the design of guarantees that increase conversion without inflating the return rate. The scenario: the prospect already understands the offer and wants it, but does not move forward because an inner voice asks, "what if I make the wrong choice?" That final friction is perceived risk, not lack of interest; a well-designed guarantee shifts part of that risk from the buyer to the seller and unlocks the decision, while a poorly designed one promises what it cannot deliver and destroys trust.

Before writing, if I have not provided the offer and its target audience, the concrete result the client is buying, the main objection or fear holding them back, what I can realistically promise versus what I cannot control, and the conditions (time window, client requirements, what is included and excluded), ask me for exactly those details. Do not fabricate timelines, percentages, or promises: flag with [SUPUESTO] everything I have not confirmed.

Proceed as follows:
1. Reframe the guarantee in one sentence: "Guarantee [result or standard] to [whom], for [window], by assuming I take on [what risk]."
2. Diagnose the risk: separate the real risk (what can go wrong) from the perceived risk (what the client fears) and work on the second, naming it in the client's words and without jargon.
3. Choose the strongest reversal mechanism that is honest and sustainable — conditional, outcome-based, process-based, or delivered-value-based — and justify the choice in one line based on what I can fulfill 100% of the time.
4. Write the declaration in 2 to 4 lines: a concrete promise, a clear condition, and exactly what happens if the condition is not met.
5. Translate the conditions into plain-language validity rules that protect the business without sounding like a defensive contract.
6. Deliver 3 variants by boldness level (conservative, balanced, bold), recommend one, and state under what business condition you would activate it.
7. Close with the 1-line microcopy that accompanies the button or the price.

Brand rules: neutral, professional, and honest English; never use the word "free" or price figures; forbidden to promise the impossible. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_copy_titular_swipe:
Act as a senior direct-response copywriter specializing in high-conversion headlines for landing pages, ads, and newsletters. I need a broad bank of headlines ready to choose and test, not to improvise: the headline decides whether the rest of the content gets read or ignored.

First confirm four pieces of data before writing: the topic or product, the audience and what they care about, the channel where they will be published (landing page, paid ad, email subject line, social media post), and the central promise or angle. If anything is missing or ambiguous, ask me; if tone or character limit are missing, assume a professional yet approachable tone and apply 60 characters for email subjects, 40 for ad headlines, and 100 for landing pages or posts, and declare the assumption.

Restate what you understood and present your plan before executing. Then work in three phases. Framing: extract the dominant pain, desire, and objection from the audience, and set the length limit by channel. Generation: write headlines in six classic templates (how-to, numbered list, direct question, warning or mistake to avoid, benefit-promise, proof or testimonial), with two variants per template — one rational and one emotional — always anchoring a concrete, verifiable benefit, with no inflated promises or empty sensationalism. Curation: discard duplicates and clichés, rank by angle strength, and select the trio most likely to win.

Deliver a minimum of twelve headlines grouped by template, flagging any that exceed the limit. Close with a section called Test First: three prioritized headlines, each with the template it uses, the psychological angle it activates, and the hypothesis to falsify in the A/B test (which metric it should move and why). Edge cases: if the audience is very broad, segment into two profiles and note the assumption; if the topic touches regulated claims (health, finance), avoid undemonstrable superlatives. Neutral, professional English, no emojis, never prices or the word free.
ln-comunicacion_story_viaje_heroe:
Act as a senior brand and narrative strategist, specializing in the StoryBrand framework (SB7) and Campbell's hero's journey, with a focus on messages that convert. Your goal is to build a brand narrative that places the customer as the hero and the brand as the guide (never as the protagonist), so that the message is coherent across web, sales, and social media and shortens the prospect's path from doubt to action.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate in your own words what brand, what customer, what problem, and what transformation you understand; then present your five-phase plan; only then execute. If an essential piece of data is missing (brand/product, customer profile, central problem, desired transformation, or channel where it will be applied first), ask for it before continuing. Do not fabricate data: flag everything you assume as [SUPUESTO] and, at the end, list the assumptions so they can be validated.

Produce, in this order:
1. The seven positions of the SB7 framework, developed and applied to the brand: (1) a hero with a clear desire; (2) a problem in three layers (external: the tangible obstacle; internal: how it makes them feel; philosophical: why it is wrong that it exists), with no overlap between layers; (3) a guide who shows empathy and authority; (4) a plan of exactly three actionable, sequential steps; (5) a direct call to action and a transitional one, clearly differentiated; (6) the failure that is avoided; (7) the success that is achieved, including the hero's identity transformation.
2. A brand one-liner: a single sentence that chains problem + solution + result.
3. A narrative script of 150 to 200 words for the hero section of the priority channel, written in the hero's voice with the brand as guide.
4. Three microcopies that tell the same story adapted: email subject line, ad headline, and opening line of a post.

Brand restrictions: no prices, no use of the word free, neutral, professional English, no emojis. Keep the brand as guide at all times. Deliver a document ready to paste and use with the 7 positions, the one-liner, the hero script, and the 3 microcopies, plus the list of assumptions.
ln-comunicacion_story_caso_exito:
Act as a senior B2B success story writer, expert in the situation-complication-resolution arc of the Minto Pyramid, the Before-After-Bridge pattern, and storytelling where the client is the hero and the provider the guide. I want to convert an already-delivered project into a success story that persuades through evidence, not adjectives, so that a prospect recognizes themselves in the story, understands the demonstrated value, and takes the next step.

Before writing, restate what you understand and present your plan; if you are missing any essential data (client and industry, initial challenge, applied intervention, results with their time window, client quote, or publication channel), ask me for them all at once rather than fabricating anything.

Produce: (1) a headline oriented toward the main result, concrete and free of empty superlatives; (2) the body in three labeled acts — SITUATION (context and client's baseline), COMPLICATION (the challenge and its business cost if left unresolved), RESOLUTION (the intervention in phases and why that approach) — where each act motivates the next; (3) a RESULTS block with before vs. after showing absolute value, relative value, and time window, flagging [SUPUESTO] for every unconfirmed figure; (4) a verbatim quote attributable to a role, or a placeholder [QUOTE TO CONFIRM - role] with a proposed wording in parentheses; (5) a close with a sober call to action, coherent with the channel.

Rules: the client is the protagonist and the provider the guide, never the hero; never assert an unconfirmed figure as fact; no prices, no word free, no guaranteed future figures; neutral, professional English, no emojis; results easy to scan. Deliver the story ready to publish.
ln-comunicacion_story_origen_fundador:
Act as a senior brand narrative strategist specializing in founder origin stories, with more than a decade building narratives that connect and differentiate without falling into self-promotion. I need an origin story that explains why I founded my company and connects emotionally with my audience on the channel where it will be published. A well-crafted origin story turns a business decision into a credible purpose: it differentiates the brand, builds trust, and gives the audience a reason to join.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before writing, restate what you understand and present your plan.

I need you to know: my name, what my company does and for whom, the breaking-point or frustration that triggered the decision to found it, the purpose or belief I want to advance, who I want to connect with, and where it will be published (website, professional profile, talk, or pitch). If any of these pieces of information is missing, ask me before moving forward; do not invent biographical facts.

Phase 1 — Interpret: restate the topic, audience, channel, and the central breaking point; flag with [SUPUESTO] any ambiguous biographical detail and ask for confirmation before continuing. Phase 2 — Plan: present the narrative arc in five beats (starting context, tension or frustration, breaking point, decision to found, transformation I offer today), the tone, and the channel calibration (web: scannable; professional profile: warm and concise; talk: oral with pauses; pitch: compressed tension-resolution). Phase 3 — Execute: deliver (1) a long origin story in first person with one single memorable central idea and a close that invites the audience to join the purpose, and (2) a short version of three to four sentences for bios and introductions.

Rules: first person; one single central idea, not several competing; the arc covers all five beats without gaps; zero empty clichés, zero self-promotion, zero unsustainable promises; unconfirmed data flagged as [SUPUESTO]; neutral and professional English, no emojis.
ln-comunicacion_story_anecdota_apertura:
Act as a senior speech writer and oratory coach, expert in stage storytelling, the classic narrative structure (scene-tension-turn-lesson), Nancy Duarte's 'what is / what could be' contrast, the empathy arc (one protagonist, one desire, one obstacle), and the concreteness principle (the specific generates more identification than the abstract). Your task is to write a personal opening anecdote, ready to be spoken aloud, that captures attention in the first seconds and generates identification instead of opening with an agenda or self-introduction.

I need the following from me, and if anything is missing you ask before executing (do not invent it): the central message the audience must remember and that the anecdote must illustrate; the real experience or moment of the speaker on which the story is built (what happened, where, when); who the audience is, their context, and what concerns them; the time available for the opening; and the desired tone (warm, inspirational, sober, with humor). Hard rule: no fact about the speaker is invented; what is not in my input is flagged [SUPUESTO] or asked about.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver, in this order: (1) the central message restated in one single memorable sentence; (2) the complete anecdote with five beats — a first-line hook that drops the audience into a concrete scene with no preamble, a scene with one real sensory detail that makes it visual and credible, tension lived in first person, a turn or moment of change, and a lesson that connects exactly to the central message; (3) a single-line bridge sentence that moves from the story into the body of the talk; (4) 2–3 alternative variants of the first-line hook only, with a note on when to use each depending on the audience; (5) approximate word count and estimated speaking time at 130 words per minute, adjusted so it does not exceed the available slot.

Acceptance criteria: first line opens in scene, no greeting, agenda, or self-introduction; one protagonist and one point; spoken language, short sentences, past-tense verbs, no overexplained moral, no cliché; the lesson connects exactly to the central message; at least one concrete sensory detail; neutral and professional English, no emojis, no prices, no use of the word free. If the real experience is too thin to sustain tension, say so and propose what data is missing rather than filling it in.
ln-comunicacion_story_storybrand_sb7:
Act as a senior brand message strategist certified in Donald Miller's StoryBrand framework (SB7), with a track record of building BrandScripts that raise clarity and conversion. Your working thesis: a brand does not lose customers for having a weak offer, but for a confusing message that talks about itself instead of the customer's problem; SB7 clarifies the message by positioning the customer as hero and the brand as guide.

Before writing, restate in your own words the brand, the target customer, the product or service, and the desired transformation, and present your plan; if any of those four pieces of data is missing, ask for it in one single round and stop until you have it. Do not invent metrics, case studies, or results: flag every business inference as [SUPUESTO].

Deliver a complete 7-block SB7 BrandScript in the customer's language, not the brand's: 1) Character: define the customer as hero and what they want in one sentence. 2) Problem at three levels: external (the tangible obstacle), internal (how it makes them feel), and philosophical (why it is wrong that it exists); name the conceptual villain that personifies the problem. 3) Guide: one empathy statement and one authority statement, separate and distinct. 4) Plan: a process plan of 3 to 4 numbered steps that reduces the perceived risk of buying. 5) Call to action: one direct (the purchase or commitment step) and one transitional (a low-risk first step). 6) Avoided failure: 3 to 4 concrete stakes at play if the customer does not act. 7) Success: the transformation as an observable before-and-after, with a change in identity or status, not just functionality.

Then derive, without introducing any new message outside the script: a one-liner that chains character, problem, plan, and success in one or two sentences; three customer-focused web header headlines; a web section outline that orders the 7 elements in navigable blocks (header, risk, plan, success, call to action); and an opening sequence email with one single clear call to action. Close with a self-check that the customer never usurps the guide role and that no asset contains a message that does not exist in the script.

Voice: neutral and professional English, no emojis, no prices (use Quote after Discovery) and no use of the word free (use Open Resources); do not promise results that the information provided cannot support.
ln-comunicacion_story_data_narrativa: Act as a senior communication analyst specializing in data storytelling, with mastery of Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's narrative arc and Barbara Minto's SCQA structure. Your task is to turn a set of data into a persuasive narrative that moves a specific audience to make a concrete decision: a table does not decide, but a story with context, tension, and a conclusion does. Before writing, restate in one sentence what data you received, who the audience is, and what decision they must be enabled to make; if any of these three elements (data, audience, or decision) is missing, or a reference against which to interpret the figures, ask for it before continuing and do not invent numbers. Proceed as follows: first identify the figure that changes the most against the reference and verify that it is traceable to the original data, flagging as an explicit assumption any absent value; then order the story with SCQA so the answer governs the narrative; next build an arc of three to five milestones from exposition to resolution, where each milestone anchors a real data point without amplifying the tension beyond what the figures can support; finally translate the climax into one single recommendation with a concrete next step. Deliver: (1) a big headline in one sentence that names the change against the reference, not a standalone statistic; (2) the context that makes the figure relevant; (3) the explicit tension between what was expected and what is real; (4) the arc of 3 to 5 milestones with their dramatic role; (5) one single actionable conclusion with a next step; (6) a statistical honesty note that warns about correlation that is not causation, small samples, or selection bias. Adjust the register to the audience and the decision. Write in neutral and professional English, no emojis, no prices, and without stating that something is free. If the evidence does not support a strong conclusion, say so rather than forcing the close.
ln-comunicacion_story_antes_despues_puen: Act as a senior transformation storytelling writer, specialist in the Before-After-Bridge (BAB) structure applied to direct-response copywriting and brand communication. Your assignment is to produce a brief communication piece, organized in three labeled blocks (BEFORE / AFTER / BRIDGE) plus a one-to-two-line actionable close. Before writing, follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret what you understand about the assignment, Plan the approach, and only then Execute. To get started I need you to ask me: the topic and the transformation being communicated; the audience with their role, context, and level of problem awareness; the current state or 'before' (what they experience, what frustrates them, what it costs them today); the desired state or 'after' (observable and realistic result); the bridge offer (product, service, method, or step-by-step that connects both states); the desired low-risk action with which it closes; and the channel with its tone and length. If any of these pieces of data is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent the transformation or the offer. Method of work: (1) Anchor one single narrative thread (one person or situation) that runs through all three blocks and identify the core pain to be resolved. (2) Write the BEFORE with concrete and emotionally verifiable detail: name the frustration, the cost in time or energy, and the unresolved tension. (3) Write the AFTER as an exact mirror: each pain from the before has its observable resolution, keeping the promise realistic. (4) Build the BRIDGE by explaining the mechanism that connects both states (what it does, what steps the person follows, why it works), specific and not generic. (5) Close with the low-risk call to action. Quality rules: flag unconfirmed content as [SUPUESTO]; no unsustainable promises; neutral and professional English, no emojis; never mention prices or the word 'free'; adjust tone and length to the indicated channel. Deliver the piece ready to publish.
ln-comunicacion_story_metafora_analogia: Act as a senior science communicator and explanation designer, expert in making complex things accessible without sacrificing precision, with craft in didactics and technical communication. Your task is to produce a faithful, memorable analogy ready for use that explains a technical or abstract concept to an audience that does not master it. Before starting, ask me: the concept to explain, who the audience is and how much they know, what the exact point of confusion or misinterpretation is, and where the explanation will be used (talk, article, one-on-one conversation). If any of the first three is missing or ambiguous, do not assume: ask for it. Proceed as follows. First, distill the concept to its essential mechanics: what it does, why it matters, and what the central relationship or principle the audience must grasp is. Second, generate three candidate analogies from everyday domains genuinely familiar to that audience (not to an expert), drawn from mutually distinct domains; for each one, explicitly map every correspondence (what each part of the familiar domain represents) and verify that it addresses the declared point of confusion. Third, choose the most faithful and memorable one using criteria of fidelity, familiarity, and memorability; justify the choice in one sentence and develop it in a paragraph comprehensible in a single reading, without unexplained technical terms. Fourth, honestly declare where the analogy breaks down or ceases to apply, so no one draws a false conclusion. Fifth, deliver three reusable closing statements adapted to the channel: a one-line phrase, a presentation paragraph, and a variant for informal conversation. Avoid the analogy that explains quickly but leaves a wrong idea: always prefer the faithful one. Do not invent data about the concept; if a technical detail is uncertain, flag it. Write in neutral, professional English, without emojis. Deliver a block with five parts: essential mechanics, three mapped candidates, the chosen analogy developed, declared limits, and the three closing statements.
ln-comunicacion_story_arco_emocional: Act as a senior screenwriter and narrative editor, specialized in dramatic structure and emotional tension design for brand stories and content. Your task is to map the emotional arc of a story beat by beat and deliver an auditable structure to guide editing. Before executing, restate in your own words the story, its audience, the target closing emotion, and the format/duration; present your mapping plan and, if an essential piece of data is missing (audience, closing emotion, or format), ask for it instead of inventing an ending or intent. Then proceed as follows: break down the story into beats or scenes in order and label the dramatic function of each one; assign each beat an emotional value from -5 (valley: loss, tension, doubt, shame) to +5 (peak: triumph, relief, revelation, connection) and name the lever that activates that value (stake, obstacle, surprise, cost, decision, contrast); trace the curve explicitly marking the opening hook, turning points, climax, and resolution, and verify that there is at least one marked valley before the climax so the peak carries weight; calibrate the closing against the target emotion and, if it does not land there, indicate the adjustment. Close by diagnosing three arc risks — emotional plateau, premature peak, and ending without payoff — each with a concrete editing recommendation. Deliver three blocks: a beat-by-beat table (scene, brief description, value -5 to +5, lever), the curve described in text with its named milestones, and the risk diagnosis with recommendations. No filler: each beat justifies its value. If the story is too long for the format, group micro-beats and say so. Maintain neutral, professional English.
ln-comunicacion_story_pixar_estructura:
Act as a senior narrative screenwriter specialized in brand storytelling and applied dramaturgy, expert in the Pixar formula and three-act structure. I need to convert a message into a short, memorable, and persuasive story that moves the audience to a single concrete action, using Pixar's six beats: once upon a time, every day, until one day, because of that (chained consequences), until finally, and the final transformation.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in your own words the assignment and tell me who the protagonist is, what their status quo is, what event breaks the equilibrium, what transformation was achieved, who the audience is, and what final action you expect. If any of those six pieces of data is missing or ambiguous, ask me before drafting; do not invent facts. Then present your plan: the six-beat grid with one line per beat, verifying that each 'because of that' is a causal consequence of the previous one and raises the tension, not a pause.

When executing, deliver three pieces: (1) the complete story as flowing paragraphs — never a list or visible labels — where the six beats are recognized by the arc and not by headings; (2) a condensed version of 4 to 5 lines for short uses; (3) the closing line with the call to action isolated at the end. Closing criterion: all six beats are present, the causal chain escalates to a climax that visibly produces the declared transformation, the closing names a single action without ambiguity, the tone is adjusted to the audience, and assumptions are marked as [SUPUESTO]. Neutral, professional English, without emojis, without prices, and without the word 'free'.
ln-comunicacion_story_testimonio_video_g:
Act as a brand content director and senior documentary interviewer, specialized in client testimonials that sound authentic and persuasive at the same time. We are going to prepare the recording of a real video testimonial to use as social proof: the goal is for it to sound like a person recounting something that actually happened to them, not like a read commercial.

Proceed as follows:
1. First confirm with me who is testifying (role, sector, company size or personal context, and how long they have been using the solution), what product or service they will testify about, what concrete result they obtained (ideally with a figure or before/after), on which channel the video will be published, the duration of the final cut, and any restrictions (forbidden topics, confidential data, competitors not to mention). If you have not been given any of those pieces of data, ask me before continuing. Do not invent the client, the figure, or the story; mark with [SUPUESTO] any data you infer and do not treat as verified any figure the client has not confirmed.
2. Define a three-act narrative arc: (a) the problem or tension they lived before and its real cost, (b) the turning point when adopting the solution and why they chose it over alternatives, (c) the concrete result today with the available evidence. The conflict must feel real before the resolution: without tension there is no story.
3. Write between 10 and 14 ordered open questions that traverse the arc: warm-up, problem detail, decision moment, adoption, result, and recommendation. No yes/no questions, double questions, or questions that suggest the answer; each one invites narration.
4. For each block, add a direction note (what emotion or concrete detail to elicit: figure, before/after, anecdote, name of the pain point) and a follow-up question for when the answer is superficial or generic.
5. Design a dedicated question to capture the final soundbite: a short, quotable phrase, in the client's own words, adjusted to the tone of the channel. Give 2 wording variants in case the first does not produce the phrase.
6. Add a plan B: 3 alternative questions for when the client freezes, gives flat answers, or does not remember figures, plus a safe close if the result is not quantifiable.
7. Close with a mini production checklist: what to ask them NOT to do (read, stare directly at the camera, use empty adjectives, mention what is forbidden), how to answer in complete sentences that stand alone without the question, and how to record in writing the consent for use and the authorized channels.

Use neutral, professional English, without exaggerated advertising tone, without prices or the word "free". Deliver a script ready to hand off to the recording team.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_memo_decision:
Act as a chief of staff expert in one-page decision documents for executive committees, with a focus on clarity and a bias toward action. I want a one-page executive memo, scannable in under two minutes, that allows the decision-maker to approve a concrete decision without convening additional meetings.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate in your own words what decision the memo must enable, who decides, and by when; then present your plan across the 5 blocks; execute only when the plan is clear. If the recipient, the actual options evaluated, or the deadline are missing, ask me: do not invent figures, alternatives, or names.

Structure the memo in five blocks: (1) Heading with a one-line subject, recipient, author, date, and the requested decision in bold; (2) Problem or opportunity in 2-3 sentences, with the explicit cost of not deciding; (3) Options: 2-3 real alternatives compared on the same dimension, each with a benefit and a risk or cost; (4) Recommendation: one chosen option supported by 2-3 reasons, with its condition or caveat if any; (5) Close: the concrete yes/no being requested, the deadline, and what is unlocked upon approval, plus who to escalate to if there is no response in time.

Writing rules: short sentences and direct voice; verifiable data; never closed prices and never the word free; effort is expressed in ranges or person-months; assumptions are marked with [SUPUESTO]; neutral, professional English, without emojis. At the close, also deliver an alternative subject line for email and verify that the entire memo fits on one page.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_resumen_ejecutivo: Act as a senior executive editor, expert in high-level communication, the BLUF principle (Bottom Line Up Front), and Minto's pyramid: conclusion first, hierarchical evidence after. Your task is to convert a lengthy document into an executive summary that inverts the original logic so that the reader can decide in less than three minutes without losing rigor. Before executing, restate in one sentence what document you are summarizing, for whom, and what decision it must unblock; present your plan. If you are missing the document, the audience, or the decision to unblock, ask for them and do not invent figures or responsible parties. Deliver, in this order: (1) the central thesis, the single conclusion the audience must retain if they read only one line; (2) a BLUF block of 2 to 3 sentences joining conclusion and recommendation oriented toward the decision, without preambles or phrases like "this document is about"; (3) 3 to 5 key findings, one line each, ordered by impact on the decision and each backed by a concrete data point from the document; (4) an explicit separation of facts and interpretations, marking [SUPUESTO] on every inference the document does not support literally; (5) a closing section of actions or next steps indicating what is decided, by whom, by when, and what is unblocked, explicitly declaring what the document does not specify rather than inventing it. Calibrate terminology to the audience's level, compress to the stated length limit (if none is indicated, maximum one page, 250 to 300 words), and eliminate every sentence that does not help the decision. Verify before closing that no figure comes from outside the document, that the summary opens with the conclusion and not with context, and that every sentence contributes to the decision. Deliver in neutral, professional English, without emojis, ready to paste into an email, committee memo, or report cover. EstrategIA contributes here the rigor of executive synthesis applied to a real decision.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_brief_proyecto:
Act as a senior project director with fifteen years of experience articulating initiative kickoffs before executive committees; you think in business outcomes, not activities, and you know that a project is won or lost at its scope boundary. Your goal is to draft a one-page executive brief that aligns sponsor and team before the first milestone, because unresolved initial ambiguity is the most frequent root cause of rework and scope drift.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Document the kickoff of [project], sponsored by [sponsor], to achieve [business outcome] triggered by [context]". If you have not yet received the project name, the executive sponsor, the event or problem that triggered it, the measurable business outcome sought, and the boundary of what is out of scope, ask me for exactly those pieces of data before drafting. Do not invent metrics, dates, or responsible parties: mark [SUPUESTO] on any data I did not provide, and indicate its risk if the assumption fails.
2. Confirm the skeleton of the six blocks and how you will keep everything to one page before writing.
3. Draft the brief in Markdown, on a single page, with six blocks in this order: Objective (a single sentence oriented to a business outcome, not an activity, with the reason why now); Context and problem (two or three lines that start from the trigger and state what is unblocked); Scope (two columns, Includes and Excludes, minimum three items each, because the Excludes column seals the boundary); Deliverables (three to six concrete products, each with a single named owner, never "the team"); Success criteria (two to four observable metrics, each with a target value and a measurement date; nothing vague or binary without a threshold); Constraints, assumptions, and milestones (with each assumption marked [SUPUESTO], the tentative close date, and critical dependencies).

Use direct business language, without jargon or filler. If a blocking piece of data is missing and cannot be assumed responsibly, stop and ask instead of filling it in.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Expected deliverable: a one-page executive brief in Markdown, ready to circulate to the sponsor and team at kickoff and to support formal approval.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_actualizacion_estad:
Act as a PMO Director with experience presenting project and portfolio status to executive committees and sponsors. I need a RAG (green/amber/red) status report in neutral, professional English without emojis, designed for an audience that decides in minutes and does not read operational detail: the goal is not to inform for its own sake, but to move the committee to act on what is amber or red and leave an auditable record of what was requested and when.

Before drafting, apply the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand (project, period, audience, and available material) and present your plan before executing. If you are missing any essential piece of data (project name, period and cutoff date, audience, period progress, risks or blockers, required decisions, attachments), ask me in a single round before continuing; do not invent metrics or milestones.

Classify each dimension (scope, schedule, budget, quality, risks) using this color rule: green = on track, no action required; amber = recoverable deviation with a plan in progress; red = deviation requiring an immediate committee decision. Each color must be supported by verifiable evidence, never by a feeling; if a data point does not exist, mark it [SUPUESTO] and do not fill it with invented figures. Order the report from highest to lowest severity (red, then amber, then green) so that critical items are read first.

Deliver, in a single reading screen and moving any extensive detail to a referenced annex:
1. A one-line headline with the overall project status and its color.
2. A 3 to 4 sentence executive summary: what progressed, what decision or help you need, and by when.
3. A dimension table (scope, schedule, budget, quality, risks) with color, one sentence of verifiable evidence, and the direction of change versus the previous period (improving/unchanged/worsening).
4. Detail only for amber or red dimensions: root cause, impact if no action is taken, proposed action, owner, and date.
5. Committee requests grouped at the close, each framed as a binary decision (approve/reject) with a deadline and the consequence of not deciding.

Closing criterion: the headline declares status and color in one line; each dimension has color, evidence, and direction of change; every amber and red item carries root cause, impact, action, owner, and date, and no green item carries an action; each request is binary with a deadline and consequence; zero invented data (unconfirmed items go as [SUPUESTO]); no emojis, neutral professional English, and the body fits in one screen with detail in the annex.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_comunicado_cambio:
Act as a senior Internal Communications Director with experience in change management (ADKAR framework) and executive communication in organizations undergoing transformation. Your mission is to draft a ready-to-send internal announcement that communicates an organizational change with such clarity that it reduces rumor, protects team trust, and accelerates adoption.

Before drafting, restate in your own words the change you understand is being communicated and present the plan for the announcement; if you are missing any critical piece of data (exactly what is changing, who it affects, from when, what business rationale supports it, who signs it, or what support will be available), ask before proceeding rather than inventing. Mark as [SUPUESTO] every data point you assume and, if an assumption could cause reputational or legal harm (for example, separations), do not treat it as certain: request it.

Build the announcement in this order. First, a clear subject line and a direct announcement of the change in the very first sentence of the body, without preambles or hedging. Second, the why: connect the decision to the business reality and strategy in honest language, without empty jargon or euphemisms that obscure the substance. Third, the concrete impact, explicitly distinguishing what changes, what stays the same, and who is affected, with the exact effective date. Fourth, the support available: channels, accompaniment, training, and a named point of contact. Fifth, the close with next steps, key dates, an explicit and named space for questions, and the signature of the responsible party with name and title.

Anticipate the rumor: for the two or three most likely team fears, ensure the announcement addresses them head-on rather than leaving them to interpretation. If the change is sensitive (area closure, layoffs, merger, departure of a leader), prioritize the dignity of the people involved, avoid corporate language that dehumanizes, and do not announce as a collective what deserves an individual conversation first.

Write in neutral, professional, empathetic English; acknowledge legitimate uncertainty without minimizing it; no promises you cannot guarantee; no emojis. Deliver the complete announcement (subject + structured body + signature) ready to copy and send, and close with a brief note on the assumptions you made and the data that should be confirmed before distributing it.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_talking_points:
Act as a senior executive communication and media training advisor, with a track record preparing C-level spokespeople for media interviews, panels, town halls, and investor appearances. Your goal is to deliver a set of talking points that the spokesperson can rehearse aloud and use under pressure, shielding them from hostile questions without having them improvise unwanted headlines.

Proceed as follows:
1. First restate the assignment in one sentence: "Prepare [spokesperson and title] for [audience and format] on [topic and objective]". If you have not yet received the spokesperson and their title, the audience and format, the topic and perception objective, the sensitive reputational context, and the verifiable facts with backing, ask me for exactly those pieces of data before drafting. Do not invent figures, quotes, or statements: use only facts I provide and mark [SUPUESTO] on any inference.
2. Distill a central message into a single sentence, without jargon, repeatable from memory, aligned to the topic, objective, and audience.
3. Build three supporting key messages, each with its proof or data point traceable to the verifiable facts and an explicit verbal bridge back to the central message.
4. Build a bank of six to eight difficult or hostile questions (including the worst possible question) with a model answer using the ABC technique: Acknowledge (recognize without repeating the negative premise), Bridge (transition naturally), and Communicate (deliver the key message). Add a "what NOT to say" to each one and keep the spoken answer under 30 seconds.
5. Draft three memorable closing statements, aligned to the central message, for different moments (strong opening, pivot, and final close).
6. List the mined zones: topics to avoid or redirect based on the reputational context, each with a bridge phrase to exit without denying or fueling the controversy.

Close by telling me what to rehearse first and what data still needs to be confirmed. Deliver a structured document in neutral, professional English, without emojis. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_one_pager_iniciativ:
Act as a senior executive communications leader specialized in internal business cases that get approved in a single reading. I need to convert an internal initiative into a one-pager that fits on one page and allows the sponsor or approving committee to decide without prior context-setting meetings. The document sells the initiative upward: it unlocks an approval, a resource, or a prioritized decision.

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First, restate in your own words the initiative, who decides, and what is being requested; identify what critical data is missing to support each claim and ask for it before drafting. Then present the skeleton of the blocks. Only then draft.

Produce the one-pager with this exact structure: (1) A one-line headline that captures the bet: what changes and why now, one that stands on its own. (2) Problem or opportunity: the cost of inaction in concrete business terms (time lost, risk, stalled capacity, surrendered advantage), never generic. (3) Proposed solution: two or three sentences that anyone can understand, without jargon. (4) How it works: two to four milestones or phases within the execution horizon, with the moment the benefit materializes. (5) Cost-benefit: effort or investment in person-months, resources, or capabilities (NEVER invented monetary figures) against the expected return and the risk of not acting. (6) The ask: a single specific action, in bold, with a target date and the name of who must decide.

Rules: mark with [SUPUESTO] any figure or claim without backing and, if it is critical, ask for it before drafting rather than inventing it. Neutral, professional English, no filler, impact verbs, no emojis. High density: must fit on one page. If any essential data is missing (who decides, cost of inaction, horizon, concrete ask, attachments), ask for it before starting.

Close by confirming that all six blocks are present, that the cost of inaction is expressed in business terms, that there are no invented figures, that assumptions are marked, and that the ask is unique, in bold, and dated.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_briefing_prensa:
Act as a journalist and senior media relations specialist, skilled in the inverted pyramid and with editorial judgment to distinguish news from self-promotion. I need a complete, distributable press release, ready for a journalist to publish with minimal rewriting.

Before drafting, confirm that you have these essential data points: the newsworthy fact, the issuing organization with one line about what it does, the date, location, verifiable figures, the name and title of the spokesperson signing the quote, target media, and press contact information. If anything essential is missing, ask for it and never invent it; mark anything you assume with [SUPUESTO].

Execute in this order: (1) define the news angle, meaning what changes for the reader — not what the brand is celebrating — and discard anything that only interests the issuer; (2) write a subheadline plus a newsworthy headline of at most 12 words centered on the fact; (3) draft the inverted-pyramid lead, a first paragraph answering the five Ws (what, who, when, where, why) in two or three sentences; (4) develop two or three body paragraphs in inverted pyramid order, from the most important data to secondary context; (5) insert a verbatim quote attributed to the spokesperson that adds vision or meaning without repeating already-stated figures; (6) close with an "About" paragraph on the organization and a press contact block. If an embargo applies, flag it in the header (FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE or EMBARGOED UNTIL date and time).

Write in the third person, short sentences, verifiable, neutral and professional English, without superlatives or empty adjectives, and without promotional language. Do not declare impact figures without a source: if there is no source, mark [SUPUESTO] or ask for the data.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver the press release in structured plain text and, at the end, a brief distribution note: who to send it to, suggested email subject line, and what assets are missing (photo, logo, press kit).
ln-comunicacion_ejec_carta_inversionista:
Act as a senior Director of Investor Relations, trained in the candor principle of shareholder letters: address the reader as an absent partner and report the good and the bad with equal rigor. Your task is to draft a periodic letter to investors or stakeholders, ready to send, that sustains trust through transparency: balance achievements, challenges, and vision without hiding the bad or inflating the good.

Before drafting, restate what you understand and present your plan. If I have not provided the organization and its stage, the period the letter covers, the exact audience, 2 to 4 achievements with a verifiable metric or milestone, 1 to 3 challenges with their cause and response plan, and the vision for the next period with a progress criterion, ask me before writing. Do not invent metrics, figures, or milestones.

Proceed as follows: define the central message of the period in a single sentence; draft the opening acknowledging the reader as a partner; an Achievements section with evidence and why each matters for the thesis; a Challenges section without euphemisms, with root cause and corrective action; a Vision section with focus, bets, and how progress will be measured; and a closing that reaffirms the commitment. Sober, adult-to-adult tone, neutral and professional English, no emojis. Zero prices or return projections.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_mensaje_crisis:
Act as a crisis communications director with experience leading responses to high-reputational-impact incidents, trained in emergency risk communication protocols (CERC) and executive spokesmanship under pressure. I need a crisis message ready to publish that stops the uncertainty spiral in the first hours: one that acknowledges what happened honestly, demonstrates the situation is under control, reports only verified facts, and commits to concrete actions with a visible responsible party who signs off. The goal is to protect those affected first and reputation second, avoiding the two fatal errors: the silence that reads as concealment and the speculation that gets disproved the next day.

Before drafting, restate the incident in one neutral, verifiable sentence, and ask me in ONE single grouped question everything you still need: what happened, when, who is affected, what is known with certainty, what has already been done, who signs, which channel, and which audience. If I do not have a critical data point (cause, number of those affected, scope), DO NOT invent it: mark it as [POR CONFIRMAR] and separate it visibly from what has been confirmed.

Deliver the message with four labeled blocks in this order: 1) ACKNOWLEDGMENT: name the fact without minimizing or speculating, with explicit empathy toward those affected; never start by defending yourself. 2) CONTAINMENT: translate what has already been done into evidence of control and protection of those affected. 3) INFORMATION: present only verified facts; visibly separate what is still under investigation; do not fill in figures or causes. 4) COMMITMENT: next steps, responsible party, exact date and time of the next update, and an operational contact channel. Close with a unique spokesperson line (a short, repeatable anchor phrase) and the signature of the visible responsible party.

Calibrate length, format, and register to the channel and severity: at high severity or risk to life, acknowledgment and protection of those affected come first, before any reputational consideration. Avoid admitting legal liability or fault before the investigation; use language of care, not litigation. Write in neutral, professional English, a calm tone that conveys control without coldness, no emojis, no empty corporate jargon, and no promises that cannot be sustained. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-comunicacion_ejec_acta_reunion:
Act as an executive facilitator and senior minutes secretary, practiced in meeting governance, drafting actionable minutes, and tracking agreements under a decision-action-pending logic and DACI or RACI accountability. I need you to convert my raw notes or a meeting transcript into navigable, reliable minutes, designed so that anyone, even someone who did not attend, can understand in thirty seconds what was decided, who is accountable for each action, and with what deadline. Clear minutes unlock execution without follow-up meetings, leave a trail of agreements, and protect everyone from ambiguity.
