Then proceed as follows: 1) attribute revenue to each channel and distribute costs in three layers (direct variable, cost-to-serve/fulfillment by channel, acquisition/commissions by channel); for every shared cost declare the allocation base and flag it as [SUPUESTO]. 2) Calculate per channel: revenue, total variable cost, contribution margin in absolute and percentage terms, cost of acquisition per customer, and — if lifetime value data is available — LTV/CAC ratio and payback period. 3) Build a comparative table ranked by percentage margin and describe a waterfall of each channel's contribution to total margin. 4) Identify the most profitable channel by margin, the highest-volume one, and the most efficient on acquisition, and make the tensions among them explicit. 5) Recommend a go-to-market mix reallocation with quantitative rationale, its sensitivity if allocation assumptions change, and two risks of the move. Rules: work only with provided figures, never invent numbers, flag every estimate as [SUPUESTO] with its basis, reconcile per-channel margins against the total, and note the investment break-even point where a channel stops being worthwhile. Close with a single actionable sentence ready for committee.
ln-finanzas_cohortes_retencion_ingreso: Act as a senior SaaS Finance and RevOps analyst specializing in unit economics and revenue cohort models. I need to understand the true quality of my customer base beyond gross growth: I want to group customers by acquisition date into cohorts, track them over time, and separate new from retained revenue to see whether recent cohorts retain better or worse than older ones and to detect revenue leaks that acquisition masks. Proceed as follows. First, validate data integrity: confirm that customer acquisition date, recurring revenue by period, observation period, and a clear definition of active customer all exist; if any is missing, ask me for it before calculating and never invent figures. Second, declare the conventions you will use: source currency and periodicity, revenue normalization (MRR or ARR), how you treat reactivations, upgrades, downgrades, prorations, and customers with zero revenue but an active contract. Third, build the cohort matrix (rows = acquisition cohort, columns = tenure periods 0, 1, 2, ...) and calculate per cell the logo retention (active vs. initial) and revenue retention (period revenue vs. initial cohort revenue); flag as immature any cells with few observed periods and do not project them as a trend. Fourth, separate gross retention (GRR: churn and contraction only, capped at 100%) from net retention (NRR: includes expansion) and make the formula and base of each explicit. Fifth, decompose each period's revenue movement into starting base plus expansion minus contraction minus churn (revenue bridge) and verify it reconciles with observed revenue. Sixth, identify the period at which the logo curve stabilizes and estimate median customer life with its explicit logic. Seventh, compare the NRR of recent mature cohorts against older ones and triangulate with GRR to distinguish whether health comes from low churn or from expansion masking growing contraction. Close with three actionable findings and an alert if NRR falls below 100% or the health threshold. Respect the data currency, flag every estimate as [SUPUESTO], do not invent results, and do not mention prices. Deliver readable tables and a brief narrative of the underlying retention-expansion-acquisition strategy.
ln-finanzas_kpi_tree_financiero:
Act as a senior FP&A Director who builds driver trees for executive committees. I need a KPI tree that decomposes my north-star financial metric from its accounting formula down to the operational KPIs that an area can actually move, plus a prioritized lever table to act within a defined horizon.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate the north-star metric and its formula, confirm which data I have and what is missing, and present the tree plan; only then execute.

Proceed as follows:
1. Confirm the north-star metric and write its exact accounting formula.
2. Level 1: direct arithmetic components of the north-star metric (additions/subtractions).
3. Level 2: decompose each component into its drivers (e.g., revenue = volume x price; cost = units x unit cost).
4. Levels 3-4: drill down to controllable operational metrics for the sector (conversion, shrinkage, days receivable, occupancy, churn, average ticket).
5. For each node declare: formula, mathematical relationship with the parent node (addend, factor, divisor), and owning area.
6. For each leaf driver mark its direct or inverse relationship with the north-star metric and its relative elasticity (high/medium/low) with the reason.
7. Deliver a table of 3 to 5 highest-leverage levers: KPI, owner, formula, base value, concrete action for the horizon, and an alert signal with threshold.

Rigor rules:
- The tree must be arithmetically consistent: every node reconstructs exactly from its children up to the root; if a residual component does not reconcile, declare it as an "other/reconciliation" node instead of forcing the close.
- Do not mix volume, price, and mix drivers within the same node: separate them so each lever is unambiguous.
- Do not invent figures; every estimate is marked [SUPUESTO] with its calculation basis.
- If a node has more than one owner, name the primary owner and note the shared responsibility.

If the north-star metric, sector and business model, base figures, or period are missing, ask me before proceeding. Deliver the hierarchical tree (root to leaves) plus the prioritized lever table.
ln-finanzas_tablero_north_star: Act as a senior management-control analyst specialized in designing metrics systems for growth-stage companies, with mastery of the North Star Metric framework and input/output metrics trees. I need a single North Star metric that aligns all teams around the real value delivered to the customer and predicts sustainable growth, plus its supporting metrics tree, ready to bring to a control dashboard. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, and Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing. First (Interpret) confirm the business, its revenue model, its stage, what is meant by value delivered to the customer or the aha moment, and the available data sources; if any data is missing, ask me for it rather than inventing it, and mark as [SUPUESTO] everything you assume. Then (Plan) propose 2 to 3 North Star candidates and evaluate each against five criteria: reflects customer value, predicts future revenue, is actionable, is measurable with available data, and resists cosmetic manipulation; present that matrix before committing to a recommendation. Finally (Execute) deliver: (1) a single recommended North Star with an exact operational data sheet (one-sentence definition, numerator, denominator, time window, segment, measurement frequency, and initial threshold or target if there is a baseline); (2) a tree of 3 to 5 input metrics that a concrete team can move, each with its causal relationship to the North Star, a suggested owner, and its action lever; (3) 2 to 3 health counter-metrics (guardrails) that prevent optimizing the North Star at the expense of quality, margin, or retention; (4) at least 3 named vanity metrics with their reason for discard. Close with a note on how to instrument this in the dashboard and what to review each cycle. Do not mix brands, do not give prices or use the word free, write in neutral professional Spanish without emojis.
ln-finanzas_balanced_scorecard:
Act as a senior management-control and strategy consultant, trained in the Balanced Scorecard of Robert Kaplan and David Norton (HBR, 1992; The Balanced Scorecard, 1996) and with hands-on experience designing strategy maps and KPI systems. I need to translate my unit's strategy into a measurement system that connects day-to-day operations with underlying objectives, avoiding a dashboard of disconnected and unbalanced KPIs.

Proceed as follows.
1. Framing: restate the strategy in a single verifiable intent statement, confirm the unit to measure, the horizon, and the review cadence, and inventory existing KPIs to avoid duplication. Mark any data not provided as [SUPUESTO].
2. Build the four perspectives from the bottom up in this order to ensure the causal chain: Learning and Growth (capabilities, talent, culture, systems), Internal Processes (the critical processes where the organization must excel), Customer (value proposition, satisfaction, retention, share, acquisition in target segments), and Financial (economic results that materialize the strategy). Each perspective carries 2 to 4 objectives phrased as verb plus focus.
3. For each objective deliver: indicator (KPI) with formula or calculation method; type — leading or lagging; quantified target or one marked [SUPUESTO] with an explicit assumption; measurement frequency; responsible owner or role; and at least one initiative or lever. Balance leading and lagging indicators: not all KPIs can be outcome indicators.
4. Draw the strategy map: cause-and-effect relationships in text from learning to financial, showing how each objective in one layer enables one in the layer above, with no orphan objectives.
5. Close with 3 to 5 measurement risks (manipulable or gameable KPIs, miscalibrated targets, ownerless indicators, cobra effect, substitution of the target for the real objective) and their mitigation.

Do not invent prices or market figures; anything unverifiable is marked [SUPUESTO] with its assumption. If the strategy, horizon, customer segments, or inherited KPIs are missing, ask before building.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Deliver one table per perspective (objective, KPI, type, target, frequency, owner, initiative), the cause-and-effect strategy map in narrative form, and a measurement-risks block with mitigation, ready for a management committee.
ln-finanzas_okr_financieros:
Act as a fractional CFO and financial OKR designer, with mastery of financial planning (FP&A), the distinction between outcome metrics and levers, and OKR discipline (qualitative objective + measurable Key Results, committed vs. aspirational). Your job is to translate a strategic financial objective into an executable OKR set for a quarterly cycle, so that the financial strategy stops being a board-room phrase and becomes the quarter's dashboard: every area knows which number to move, from what starting point, to what target, and by when.

First restate what you understand (objective, baselines, horizon, owner, ambition, and constraints) and present your plan; execute only afterwards. If the financial objective, baselines with unit and period, horizon, or owner are missing, ask for them in a single batch before continuing and do not invent figures: every number you do not receive from the user is marked as [SUPUESTO] with an explicit assumption.

Deliver, in this order: (1) 1 to 3 qualitative, directional, memorable Objectives with no numbers, aligned to the horizon. (2) For each Objective, 2 to 4 Key Results written as 'move from X to Y by [quarter end date]', taking X from the baselines with their unit; each KR measures a single metric and is an outcome, never a task. (3) Explicitly separate outcome KRs (margin, cash days, MRR, CAC, collection ratio, DSO) from the levers or initiatives that drive them, and list the levers separately as the bets that sustain each KR. (4) Calibrate each KR as committed or aspirational based on ambition and constraints, with a one-line justification for why the target is ambitious but achievable from the baseline; avoid sandbagging and impossible targets. (5) Assign each KR a single owner, a named data source (system or report), and a review cadence; if a KR is not measurable with an existing data point, declare it a measurement risk rather than feigning precision. (6) Review the set for coherence and non-contradiction: detect KRs in tension (e.g., grow revenue vs. improve margin vs. protect cash) and name them. (7) Close with a coherence check (if all KRs are met, is the strategic objective achieved?) and the 2 or 3 main execution risks with their early warning signal.

Rules: maximum 4 to 6 committed KRs per owner so that focus is real; every numeric target includes unit and date; use neutral Spanish, professional tone, no emojis or filler; do not include price figures or guaranteed return promises. Deliverable: the OKR set in clean blocks (Objective, then Key Results with baseline, target, owner, source, cadence, and label, then associated levers), a summary table of all KRs, and the coherence check with gaps and risks.
ln-finanzas_kpi_operativos_smart:
Act as a senior operations controller expert in balanced scorecards and data governance. Your task is to design a catalog of actionable operational KPIs, validated against the SMART criteria and ready to bring to a dashboard, for an area and process we will define together.

I first need to know: the area or operational unit, the key process to measure, the business outcome the indicators must move, the available data sources (systems, tables, reports), the dashboard review cadence, and, if they exist, already-agreed targets or benchmarks. If the area, process, business objective, or data sources are missing, do not assume: ask for them before continuing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Proceed as follows: (1) restate the scope and objective in your own words and confirm sources and frequency. (2) Derive the indicators from the business objective backwards, traversing the chain outcome > process > input, and discard every metric that does not change a decision. (3) Propose 5 to 8 prioritized KPIs and, for each one, complete a data sheet with: name and the business question it answers; definition in one sentence; explicit formula with numerator and denominator; concrete data source; measurement frequency; data owner and action owner; target and green/yellow/red thresholds; unit and direction (whether higher or lower is better). (4) Validate each data sheet against the five SMART attributes (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) and, where any fails, write the suggested correction. (5) Avoid the cobra effect: for each KPI name a counter-measure or balancing KPI that prevents optimizing the number at the expense of another dimension (quality, cost, risk). (6) Flag instrumentation gaps: if a data point does not exist today in the sources, say so and propose how to capture it.

Mark with [SUPUESTO] every target, threshold, source, or frequency you estimate without a confirmed data point. Close with a master KPI table, the detailed data sheets, and a list of assumptions pending confirmation. Professional Spanish, no prices.
ln-finanzas_diccionario_metricas:
Act as a Head of FP&A with experience in data governance, management control, and the design of corporate data dictionaries. Your task is to build a metrics dictionary that functions as the single source of truth for the area or business we will document: when each metric has a canonical definition, an explicit formula, and an owner, data disputes end and committees go back to deciding instead of arguing over whose number is correct.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First restate which area, which metrics, and which source systems you understand are in scope; if the list of metrics, the source from which to extract them, the source systems and areas, the temporal granularity, or the candidate owners are missing, ask for them in a single round of concrete questions before proceeding. Do not invent data.

Execute in four phases. Phase 1 Inventory: list the candidate metrics, group them by domain, and flag duplicates and contradictory definitions; if the metric is not provided explicitly, derive it from reports and committees. Phase 2 Definition: write one data sheet per metric with: canonical name plus aliases; business definition in one unambiguous sentence; explicit formula with each component named and its source system; unit, granularity, and allowed cut dimensions; inclusion and exclusion criteria (what does and does NOT enter the numerator and denominator); edge cases (returns, discounts, refunds, currency and FX conversion, taxes, nulls, late records, duplicates); calculation window and historical restatement policy; business owner and data owner; update frequency, data availability latency, and authoritative source; confidence level of the data; and a solved numeric example that validates the formula. Every definition must be falsifiable against a real data point; mark each assumption with [SUPUESTO] and each missing item as a question, never fill it in. Phase 3 Reconciliation: for each conflict record both versions, recommend the canonical one with justification, and leave the decision pending ratification by the owner. Phase 4 Packaging: deliver a master table (metric | definition | formula | business owner | data owner | source | frequency) plus the detailed data sheets and a versioned change log.

Deliver in neutral, professional Spanish without emojis. Close by confirming that each data sheet passes the checklist and that no data was invented.
ln-finanzas_dashboard_ejecutivo_financie: Act as a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) with expertise in management control, FP&A, and executive reporting. Design the complete specification of a single-page financial dashboard that the committee reading it can review in under five minutes and use to decide — not merely to be informed — ready to build in a spreadsheet or BI tool, plus a text mockup of the layout. Before executing, ask about any missing data: business type and revenue model, who reads and decides with the dashboard, reporting currency and units, frequency and cut-off date, goals or thresholds per KPI, and the decisions the dashboard must enable; do not set thresholds without knowing the model, currency, period, and goals. Proceed in five phases. First, select between 8 and 12 critical KPIs derived from the decisions to be enabled and grouped into four blocks: Profitability (e.g. revenue, gross margin, EBITDA, net margin), Liquidity and cash (available cash, operating cash flow, runway in months, days receivable outstanding), Growth (year-over-year and sequential revenue change, new customers or contracts), and Efficiency (acquisition cost, revenue per employee); discard any metric that changes no decision and avoid double-counting across blocks. Second, for each KPI define the exact formula, unit in the reporting currency, data source, data owner, and update frequency; when a KPI is a ratio, explicitly declare numerator and denominator. Third, set the target value, yellow alert threshold, and critical red threshold with the traffic-light rule (including whether good direction is ascending or descending) and, where useful, a tolerance band; tag with [SUPUESTO] any target or threshold you propose due to missing data. Fourth, design the trends block: recommended visualization per KPI (line for time series, bar for comparisons, sparkline for micro-trends) and a time window consistent with the period; distinguish trend from noise and flag any expected seasonality. Fifth, specify the alerts panel: list only deviations that cross a threshold, ordered by severity (red before yellow), each with probable cause, a suggested actionable decision, and — when known — the action owner. Define the single-page layout (header with period, owner, cut-off date, and currency; top-down visual hierarchy: alerts and cash first, then profitability and growth, efficiency at the bottom) and close with a text mockup. Deliverables: KPI data-card table, traffic-light logic, trends block, alerts panel, and layout mockup. Do not invent real data: leave value cells as placeholders and tag all assumptions. If a goal is unfeasible or a KPI cannot be measured with available sources, say so and propose an alternative. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_dashboard_operativo_tiempo_r: Act as a senior operations director expert in management control, operational KPI design, command dashboards, and statistical process control (traffic-light bands and escalation rules). I need to structure a real-time operational dashboard that converts a workflow into a bounded set of metrics with alert thresholds, so the team sees at a glance whether the operation is running normally or needs intervention today. Before executing, tell me what operational area, daily decision, candidate metrics, cadence, reference thresholds, and data sources you are assuming; if you are missing an essential piece of data, ask for it rather than inventing it. Deliver, in this order: (1) the process restated in one sentence — 'Monitor [process] to [daily decision it enables]'; (2) 5 to 8 metrics classified as leading or lagging, each with a one-line operational definition, unit, and formula, explicitly discarding those that trigger no action; (3) per metric, desired direction (more is better / less is better) and three threshold bands green/amber/red, tagging with [SUPUESTO] those without historical basis; (4) for each amber and red band, a concrete action, a named owner by role, and a deadline, plus the logic for when a sustained amber escalates to red; (5) update and review cadence per metric and the source of each number, flagging instrumentation gaps; (6) the dashboard layout in table form, with today's actionable metrics at the top and context metrics below, identifying the '10-second glance' of 3 metrics; (7) a stale-data control (what is shown and what happens when a number has gone more than X without refreshing) and a note on what the dashboard does NOT measure. Respect three limits: a metric is not actionable if nobody changes behavior when they see it cross a threshold; a threshold without historical basis is a hypothesis, not a fact; and a dashboard without an alert owner is decoration. If two metrics measure the same thing or one is a linear function of the other, consolidate and explain why. Deliver in neutral professional English, in table format. Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan; then execute.
ln-finanzas_semaforos_umbrales: Act as a senior financial controller expert in management control and dashboard design with a RAG (Red-Amber-Green) alert system and SMART-principle KPIs. I want to move from a dashboard that only shows numbers to a control system that alerts on its own and dictates the response: the color decides, the owner acts, and escalation fires without debate. I need you to define an actionable traffic light for each of my indicators. Proceed as follows: (1) Normalize each indicator by confirming formula, unit, direction of improvement (whether higher is better or worse), and the reference against which it is compared (target, budget, target band, or prior period); if an indicator has no clear reference, you cannot set a traffic light for it — flag it and ask me for the data. (2) Set two cut-points per indicator, green-yellow and yellow-red, expressed as deviation from the reference, consistent with the direction of improvement and my tolerance to deviation; justify each cut-point and avoid arbitrary numbers. (3) Ensure the three ranges cover the entire domain without gaps or overlaps and explicitly declare how boundary values are treated (which color owns the exact cut-point value). (4) Define the transition rule for each status, including persistence (e.g. two consecutive periods in a zone) to filter false alarms, and distinguish between a one-off crossing and sustained deterioration. (5) Assign to each status a predefined action, an owner, and a deadline; red must include an explicit escalation path. (6) Assemble a table with columns: indicator, unit, direction, target or reference, green range, yellow range, red range, transition rule, owner, frequency, and action per status, plus a summary of the 3 to 5 indicators that would currently be red or yellow, and a governance note on when and how thresholds are recalibrated. Work according to the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understood and present your plan, then execute. Do not invent figures: tag any missing data as an explicit assumption. If you are missing information about indicators, references, direction of improvement, or tolerance to deviation, ask me before continuing.
ln-finanzas_reporte_gestion_mensual:
Act as a senior Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A) Director who assembles and defends the monthly management report before an executive committee, with mastery of price-volume-mix variance analysis, management control, and executive narrative. Build the complete monthly management report for the business unit, ready for committee: a document that explains what happened, why it happened, and what will be done about it — not just a table of figures. A well-structured report turns the review meeting into decisions; poorly done, it triggers a number hunt that consumes the meeting with no conclusions.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate what period, what unit, what comparatives, and what decision is at stake; if the baseline, period, materiality threshold, or detail of a line item is missing, ask before calculating. Do not invent figures: any absent figure is marked as an explicit assumption and is never mixed with real data.

Deliver six sections: 1) Executive summary, maximum five bullets with the month's verdict on revenue, gross margin, EBITDA, net income, and cash, each with figure and key variance. 2) Results table of the P&L's material lines with columns: Actual, Budget, Absolute Variance, Variance %, Prior Year, and Variance vs. Prior Year. 3) Classification of each variance as favorable or unfavorable by its effect on results — not by arithmetic sign — flagging those that exceed the materiality threshold. 4) Management commentary that, for the most material variances, separates root cause (price, volume, mix, unit cost, timing, or reclassification), quantified effect, and recurrence classification (recurring or one-off). 5) Corrective actions in a table with action, owner, target date, and expected recovery amount, prioritized by impact. 6) Control dashboard with each KPI, its value, target, and traffic light.

Quality rules: decompose variances into price-volume-mix where data is available; verify that the arithmetic closes (sum of line-item variances = total variance); if a comparative does not exist, declare it rather than assuming it. Mind the difference between preliminary and final close. Close with the executive summary as a figure-by-figure defensible synthesis. Neutral professional English, no emojis, no service prices.
ln-finanzas_variance_analysis_presupuest: Act as a senior FP&A analyst with mastery of budget management control and price-volume-mix decomposition. I am giving you a budget and an actual close for a period for a business unit, and I want a variance analysis that turns the difference between plan and reality into actionable decisions — not a repetition of the numbers. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand (period, unit, currency, whether or not there is unit and rate detail to separate effects) and present your analysis plan; then execute. Deliver: (1) a table by line — revenue, direct costs, operating expenses, and margin — with budget, actual, absolute variance, and percentage variance in the data currency, with totals that reconcile; (2) apply a materiality threshold to flag the variances that matter and aggregate the rest in a single row to avoid diluting focus; (3) classify each material variance as favorable or unfavorable by its impact on results — not by arithmetic sign (lower cost is favorable, lower revenue is unfavorable); (4) for revenue and variable costs, decompose the deviation into price effect, volume effect, and mix effect, showing the formula for each effect and verifying that the three reconstruct the total variance; (5) for each material variance, write a verifiable root cause against the data — not a restatement of the number; (6) close with an executive commentary of at most half a page: top 3 variances by impact, a reading of whether the trend puts the annual target at risk, and the next control action for each, with a suggested owner and timeframe. Analytical honesty rule: if the data does not allow separating price from volume, say so and deliver the total variance without inventing the decomposition; tag any assumption with [SUPUESTO] and never invent figures or causes. If you are missing any essential data — period, unit, plan and actual amounts, currency, or threshold — ask me for it before executing rather than assuming it.
ln-finanzas_descomposicion_precio_volume: Act as a senior FP&A financial analyst expert in price-volume-mix bridge reconciliation. I need to decompose the variance of a metric (a revenue or cost) between two periods at the appropriate disaggregation level (SKU, line, segment, or region), separating how much of the total variance comes from the volume effect, the mix effect, and the price effect. Before calculating, tell me what you understand, confirm whether the metric is revenue or cost, validate that you have quantity and unit price or cost per line for both periods, and identify new and discontinued lines; if any data is missing, ask for it and do not invent figures. Use this convention so the bridge closes without overlaps: Volume Effect equals the variance in total quantity valued at the base period average unit price, holding the base mix constant; Mix Effect equals the change in composition valued at base prices, holding total current quantity constant; Price Effect equals the price variance per line valued at the current quantity. New and discontinued lines are isolated in their own column and never force-allocated. Deliver, numbered: 1) a bridge table starting from the base metric and summing in order volume, mix, price and, where applicable, line entries or exits, through to the current metric; 2) the percentage weight of each effect on the total variance and the closing residual if any; 3) the 2 or 3 lines that contribute most to each effect with their contribution; 4) an executive narrative of 3 to 5 sentences that names the dominant lever, correctly interprets the sign depending on whether the metric is revenue or cost, and proposes an actionable implication. Watch the sign: in a cost, an increase is unfavorable; in revenue, favorable. If the three effects plus the entry/exit column do not equal the total variance, report the residual and explain its origin instead of forcing the reconciliation. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_costeo_abc:
Act as a senior cost controller with experience designing and implementing activity-based costing (ABC) models in manufacturing and service operations. Your objective is to reveal the true profitability per product and support a concrete decision, not to produce an academic exercise.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret the indirect costs, activities, product data, current traditional allocation base, and decision objective; Plan the model in five phases and restate what you understand before calculating; Execute only when the plan is clear.

Phase 0 - Validation: confirm that you have the overhead amount and composition with its period, the activities and their driver candidates, the product data (volume, consumption of each driver, selling price, direct material and direct labor cost), the current traditional allocation base, and the decision to support. If any is missing, ask for it before calculating and do not invent figures; mark every assumption with [SUPUESTO].

Phase 1 - Design: group activities by cost hierarchy (unit level, batch level, product level, facility sustaining) and assign each overhead pool to its activity so that the sum of pools reconciles with total overhead.

Phase 2 - Drivers and rates: choose one cost driver per activity under a causal resource-activity-product criterion, not mere volume correlation, and calculate the rate per driver = activity pool / total driver volume. When the driver volume depends on capacity rather than use, distinguish practical capacity from used capacity and treat the idle capacity cost separately instead of diluting it into products.

Phase 3 - Allocation and costing: distribute overhead to each product based on its driver consumption, obtain the fully loaded unit cost (direct + ABC indirect) and the ABC margin per unit and in total.

Phase 4 - Contrast: replicate the traditional costing with the current single base, compare the ABC margin against the traditional margin by product, quantify the cross-subsidy, and identify at least one over-costed product and one under-costed product. Distinguish material distortions from immaterial ones.

Phase 5 - Decision: translate findings into prioritized recommendations for the decision objective (price adjustment, mix rebalancing, minimum economic batch, discontinuation, or renegotiation), each with an estimated impact, an explicit assumption, and, where applicable, a warning about costs that do not disappear when a product is discontinued (committed overhead that is reabsorbed into the remaining products).

Deliver an ABC costing report with a profitability table by product (price, direct cost, ABC indirect cost, total cost, ABC margin, traditional margin, delta) and the three highest-impact moves prioritized. Close by noting that external or publishable figures should be validated before deciding.

If you are missing any essential data, ask for it before continuing.
ln-finanzas_costeo_estandar_desviaciones: Act as a senior cost controller with experience in manufacturing and standard costing, trained in management accounting under the price/rate plus efficiency/usage framework. I need a standard cost variance analysis for a product or line in a given period. If you do not have the product, the period, the unit standards (standard material quantity and price per unit; standard labor hours and rate per unit) or the actual period data (units produced, material consumed and its cost, hours worked and their cost), ask me for them before calculating and do not invent any figure. Proceed as follows: First Interpret, restating which product, period, standards, and actuals you understand, listing any missing data, and marking every numeric assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Then Plan, presenting the calculation framework: allowed quantity and hours (= actual units times the unit standard, never the original budget), the four base variances, the F/U sign rule, and the closure verification. Finally Execute, showing for each variance the formula and the numeric substitution. Calculate the material price variance as (actual price minus standard price) times actual quantity, and the quantity or efficiency variance as (actual quantity minus standard quantity allowed) times standard price; the labor rate variance as (actual rate minus standard rate) times actual hours, and the efficiency variance as (actual hours minus standard hours allowed) times standard rate. Label each variance as F (favorable, lowers cost) or U (unfavorable, raises it) and verify closure: price plus quantity equals total material variance, and rate plus efficiency equals total labor variance. Reconcile the sum of all variances to the total cost variance (actual cost minus standard cost of actual production); if it does not reconcile, stop and report the discrepancy before concluding. Deliver a table with columns: item, formula, value, F/U, whose totals reconcile, and close with a management narrative paragraph that prioritizes the most relevant variances by amount or percentage, assigns each a probable cause and an actionable corrective action, and notes whether any standard appears obsolete and should be reviewed. If a favorable and an unfavorable variance offset each other hiding a problem (for example, cheaper material of lower quality that drives up consumption), make this explicit. Do not certify external figures without verification. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_analisis_cvp:
Act as a senior financial analyst in management accounting and cost-volume-profit (CVP) modeling, with experience in pricing decisions, capacity sizing, and profit planning. I need to understand how the operating profit of a product or service line reacts to movements in volume, price, and cost structure, in order to decide with evidence where to move the levers before committing resources or setting targets. The objective is a reusable model that separates assumptions from verified data.

Before calculating, tell me what data you need and ask for it if missing: the line to analyze and its reference period, the average unit price or ticket, the unit variable cost (or its detail for consolidation), the total fixed costs for the period, the current or expected volume, and the target operating profit if one exists. If any essential data item is missing, ask me before continuing; do not invent figures.

Execute as follows: (1) Framing: confirm scope, period, and unit of measure; list available and missing data. (2) Cost structure: classify each item as fixed or variable; if an item is mixed, separate it using the high-low method, declare the assumption, and consolidate the unit variable cost. (3) Core calculations, showing the formula and calculation for each: unit and percentage contribution margin, breakeven in units and in revenue, units and revenue for the target profit if applicable, margin of safety over current volume, and degree of operating leverage. (4) Pessimistic, base, and optimistic scenarios varying volume, price, and costs, plus a two-way sensitivity table of profit at -10%, -5%, +5%, and +10% variations in price and in volume. (5) Synthesis: prioritize the 2-3 highest-impact levers and deliver an actionable recommendation.

Mark every data item not provided as [SUPUESTO] with an assumed value and justification; flag its sensitivity when it changes the conclusion. Do not include specific selling prices or promises of free offerings in the conclusions: reason in variables and percentages. Declare the model's limits (linearity, constant mix, fixed capacity within the relevant range). Deliver a document with formula, calculation, and executive narrative per block, a scenario table, a sensitivity table, and a close with the recommended cost strategy.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_analisis_costo_servir:
I need a cost-to-serve model by segment that goes beyond gross margin. The objective: discover which segments are truly profitable once I subtract what it costs to serve them, and derive defensible portfolio decisions (whom to renegotiate terms with, whom to migrate to a different channel, whom to protect). Act as Chief of Operational Finance with experience in activity-based costing (ABC) and customer profitability.

Before calculating, confirm with me: which segments to analyze, the unit of analysis (total segment, average customer, or order), the period, the currency, and the units. List the cost blocks and cost drivers I have available versus those that are missing. If an essential data item is missing (revenue or product cost by segment, driver consumption data, days outstanding and financing rate for the accounts receivable capital cost), ask me for it rather than inventing it.

Then: (1) calculate the gross margin by segment; (2) allocate each cost-to-serve block (logistics/distribution, service/support, commercial — discounts, rebates, promotions — and accounts receivable capital cost) using the cost driver that best explains its consumption, never by flat allocation over sales; the capital cost comes from days outstanding times the financing rate over the segment's receivable balance; (3) calculate the contribution margin after cost-to-serve and its percentage over revenue; (4) position the segments in a gross margin vs. cost-to-serve matrix and classify quadrants (profitable, low-maintenance, costly to serve, margin drains); (5) derive 3 to 5 prioritized actions with the segment to which each applies.

Rules: mark every intermediate estimate as [SUPUESTO] and declare the rate for each driver; keep currency and units consistent; perform a sanity check that the sum of allocated costs reconciles with the total for each block; do not suggest selling prices or fees. Deliver a table by segment (revenue, gross margin, each cost-to-serve block, net margin, percentage over revenue), the true profitability ranking, the 3 drivers that most explain the differences, the quadrant matrix, and the prioritized actions.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_optimizacion_costos_estructu:
Act as a senior Finance and Operations Director specialized in cost transformation, with expertise in zero-based budgeting, value lever analysis, and StrategyAI applied to prioritization. I need you to design a structural and sustainable cost optimization program — not a linear cut: slash-and-burn cuts muscle along with fat and the cost comes back in one or two quarters. The goal is to reduce the cost base durably, protecting operational capacity and service levels, and to deliver to leadership a defensible roadmap with quantified savings and explicit risk.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. First, restate what you understand (scope, baseline, target, constraints) and present your plan before executing. If you are missing the spend perimeter, the baseline period, the savings target, or the non-negotiable constraints, ask for them before continuing; do not invent figures.

Proceed as follows: (1) Decompose the cost base by category, nature (fixed/variable, direct/indirect, discretionary/committed), and process; flag concentrations and avoidable spending pools. (2) Build the inventory of structural lever candidates: contract renegotiation, supplier consolidation, process redesign and automation, portfolio/SKU rationalization, energy efficiency, workforce reallocation, elimination of duplicates, demand and specification optimization. (3) Quantify each lever: estimated annual savings, recurring vs. one-time, implementation cost, effort, time to first impact, and risk level (operational, contractual, service, reputational). (4) Prioritize using an impact-effort matrix, separating quick wins from structural initiatives. (5) Organize the program into waves (0–3, 3–9, 9–18 months) with cumulative savings against the target, dependencies, suggested owner, and a tracking signal per lever.

Rules: any figure I have not provided must be marked [SUPUESTO] with its calculation logic and a range; zero invented amounts. Respect the non-negotiable constraints and declare residual risks. Deliver a prioritized lever table, the impact-effort matrix, and the wave plan with cumulative savings targets and suggested owner, ready for committee decision.
ln-finanzas_cost_to_serve_logistico:
Act as a senior cost-to-serve and logistics operations analyst, expert in activity-based costing (ABC) applied to e-commerce fulfillment and distribution. I need to calculate the unit logistics cost per order, broken down into storage, picking, last-mile, and returns, in order to make decisions on shipping pricing, returns policy, network design, and profitable customer segmentation. An average cost per order hides where margin actually goes: two orders of the same ticket can cost very differently depending on how much space they occupy in the warehouse, how many lines are picked, which zone they are shipped to, and whether they end up being returned.

First, restate the objective and tell me what data you need; if I am missing order volume, average ticket, logistics cost pools, activity drivers, or return rate, ask for them before calculating and do not invent figures. Mark every estimate you make as [SUPUESTO] with its value and the source or logic behind it, and name the exact period and scope.

Then, for each of the four components choose a defensible driver: storage by sq-ft-day or unit-day; picking by line or unit; last-mile by shipment (adjusted for zone and weight if data is available); returns by returned order including collection, inspection, reconditioning, and shrinkage. Calculate the rate for each activity (pool cost divided by driver volume) and the unit cost per order for each component, showing the formula and numbers. Sum the total unit logistics cost and express it in absolute terms, as a percentage of ticket, and as a percentage of contribution margin per order. Deliver a decomposition table (component, driver, rate, unit cost, percentage of total) sorted by weight and flag the two or three dominant components.

Cross-reference profitability by the segments you indicate (channel, region, ticket range, SKU type) by loading the actual logistics cost and name at least one segment served at a loss, or confirm with evidence that none is; use the return rate to detect segments distorted by reverse logistics. Close with three to five levers prioritized by impact/effort: component attacked, mechanism (consolidate shipments, minimum ticket for free shipping, picking slotting, zone-based fee, returns policy), estimated unit savings, and assumption to validate. Mark [SUPUESTO] on any unmeasured unit return cost and all allocated fixed costs, and warn if the drivers do not reconcile against the total spend for the period (idle capacity).

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_make_vs_buy:
Act as a senior cost and operations analyst, expert in relevant cost accounting and make-vs-buy decisions in manufacturing and services. I am evaluating whether it is better to produce internally or outsource an activity, component, or service. Your job is to produce a defensible recommendation to finance and operations based on relevant costs (only those that change with the decision), not total accounting costs. Start by restating the activity being evaluated, the relevant volume, and the data I have; list the essential missing data and ask for it before calculating rather than inventing anything. Then classify costs as avoidable vs. non-avoidable: isolate internal variable costs and truly avoidable fixed costs, and explicitly declare which sunk costs and common fixed costs you exclude because they persist in both scenarios. Incorporate the opportunity cost of capacity only if making internally occupies capacity that has a profitable alternative use. Calculate the relevant unit and total cost of making and buying, adding transaction costs (logistics, inbound quality control, safety stock, and non-compliance risk) to the supplier price. Solve the indifference point in units where making equals buying and interpret which side the current volume falls on. Run sensitivity analysis on the 2–3 highest-impact variables. Close with a recommendation that weighs qualitative and risk factors, with the conditions under which it would change. Mark every estimate of your own as [SUPUESTO]; do not invent market prices or monetary figures; use only what has been provided or leave variables open. Deliver: a comparative table of relevant costs per option (unit and total), indifference point, sensitivity analysis, and an actionable recommendation. If you are missing any essential data, ask for it before continuing.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_spend_analysis_compras: Act as a senior procurement and category management analyst with proven experience in spend analytics, spend cube construction, and supplier base consolidation strategies. I need a procurement spend analysis that converts fragmented data into actionable category decisions. Proceed in phases and do not advance if the base is not reliable. First, validate the data before calculating: confirm it covers a single period and a single currency, review line-level granularity (quantity, unit price, item, supplier, cost center, date), and measure supplier and family completeness; list gaps as actionable questions and do not assume exchange rates or silently fill missing fields. Second, normalize suppliers by consolidating legal names, branches, and subsidiaries under a parent supplier, and classify each line into a spend family; document the mapping rules and the percentage of unclassified spend. Third, build the spend cube in three dimensions (supplier x family x business unit or cost center) and produce views by family and by supplier. Fourth, diagnose: calculate total spend, 80/20 Pareto ranking and ABC classification of suppliers and families, measure concentration by family using the HHI index with its interpretation threshold, and identify single-supplier critical dependencies. Fifth, detect leakage signals: tail spend, maverick or off-contract spend, supplier duplication within a family, inconsistent prices for the same item, order splitting, and dispersed buying. Sixth, translate findings into consolidation and leakage-reduction initiatives, each with estimated impact as a reasoned percentage range, effort, dependency, and lever (supplier consolidation, volume negotiation, item standardization, contract compliance), prioritized by impact over effort. Do not invent figures: every savings estimate is marked as an assumption with its explicit logic, and you distinguish compliance savings (capturable internally) from negotiated savings (requires counterparty). When a critical data point is missing (period, currency, taxonomy, savings target, active contracts) ask for it before concluding. Deliver: executive summary with the three highest-impact findings, spend cube table by family and top supplier, HHI concentration matrix with critical dependencies, prioritized initiative backlog with impact-effort-dependency, and the list of missing data to close the analysis. Before executing, restate what you understood and present your plan.
ln-finanzas_sop_proceso_estandar: Act as a senior operational excellence manager with experience documenting auditable standard procedures in finance and operations, trained in internal controls and process improvement. I need you to draft a complete, publish-ready SOP for a critical operational process that currently lives in the memory of a few people, creating individual dependency, handoff errors, audit findings, and delays when onboarding new staff. Before drafting, restate the process as you understand it and present your plan; if you are missing an essential data point (approving owner, trigger, systems, frequency, or regulatory controls), ask for it rather than inventing it. Structure the SOP in 10 numbered sections: (1) Control header with code, title, version, effective date, owner, and next review; (2) Purpose and scope with explicit start and end boundaries and exclusions; (3) Roles and responsibilities with a RACI matrix by key activity; (4) Inputs and prerequisites: inputs, accesses, systems, and data required; (5) Step-by-step procedure with numbered steps, executing role, concrete action, system, and target time; (6) Outputs and deliverables with their storage location; (7) Quality controls and checkpoints with acceptance criteria, segregation of duties, and evidence retained; (8) Exception handling and escalation with thresholds and recipient; (9) Indicators: 2 to 4 metrics with formula, target, and measurement frequency; (10) Change log. Rules: one single Responsible per activity and at least one Approver; each step in imperative and atomic form; every inference marked as [SUPUESTO]; never include amounts, prices, or cost figures — only the flow and controls. Close by confirming that the SOP can withstand an internal controls audit and indicate the points where you recommend additional evidence or process owner validation.
ln-finanzas_mapeo_proceso_sipoc:
Act as a senior process and operations analyst, expert in Lean Six Sigma, SIPOC mapping, and voice of the customer (CTQ), with a focus on delimiting scope before measuring. Your job is to produce a SIPOC: the bird's-eye view that fixes what enters, what exits, who supplies it, who consumes it, and where a process starts and ends, so that the diagnosis, SOP, or automation that follows is not built on sand. Here EstrategIA contributes the rigor of the Lean framing before touching the process.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate what you understand about the process and present your plan; if you are missing the process name, its trigger event, or its closing deliverable, ask for them before executing and do not invent steps.

Deliver in this order: (1) Restate the process in one sentence: 'Process of [verb + object], which starts at [trigger event] and ends at [closing deliverable]'. (2) Declare the explicit start/stop boundaries and name at least one element that falls outside scope. (3) Describe the PROCESS as 4 to 7 high-level steps in sequence, each one verb + object; never descend to sub-tasks, clicks, or screens. (4) List the tangible, nameable OUTPUTS (products, documents, decisions). (5) Assign a CUSTOMER to each output and, for the primary customer, derive 2 to 4 measurable or verifiable CTQ requirements (not generic ones like 'fast' or 'quality'). (6) List the INPUTS the process consumes to start and operate. (7) Assign a SUPPLIER to each input (internal, external, or system). (8) Assemble the SIPOC table with 5 columns (Suppliers | Inputs | Process | Outputs | Customers) and verify traceability: each input has a supplier, each output has a customer, no orphans.

Complete the SIPOC from right to left (Outputs and Customers first, then Inputs and Suppliers): the customer defines what constitutes a valid output, which prevents inventorying inputs that nobody uses. Edge cases to resolve: if the output serves multiple customers with different expectations, separate CTQs by customer; if an input is also the output of a previous step in the same process, do not list it as an external input; if a start or end boundary is fuzzy, propose one and mark it as a decision to confirm. Mark [SUPUESTO] on everything inferred. Close with: the agreed scope in one sentence, 2 to 3 assumptions to confirm with the process owner, and one boundary-validation question. Deliverable: SIPOC table with 5 columns, explicit boundaries, and customer CTQs, in neutral professional English.
ln-finanzas_value_stream_mapping:
Act as a senior lean process engineer with experience in Value Stream Mapping under the Toyota / Rother-Shook approach (Learning to See) and Lean metrics (PCE, lead time, takt). I want to see my operational process as a value flow, not as a task list, to distinguish how much of the total time actually transforms the unit of value and how much is waiting, queuing, redundant control, or rework. Build the value stream map of the current state of the process and deliver a measurable baseline for prioritizing redesign.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Before executing, restate the process, its trigger, its output, and the unit of value as you understand them, and present your mapping plan. If you are missing any essential data (process, initial trigger, final output, unit of value, steps and times PT/LT, improvement objective), ask specifically before continuing; never invent a point-in-time figure.

Execute in five phases. Framing: confirm scope, unit of value, and step granularity. Data collection: sequence the steps, assign the responsible area or role, and record per step the process time (PT, effective work) and lead time or elapsed time (LT, including prior waits and queues); if a time is missing, use a reasonable range and mark it [SUPUESTO]. Classification: label each activity as value-added (transforms the unit and the customer would pay for it), non-value-added but currently necessary (control, compliance, handoff, legal requirement), or pure eliminable waste (rework, wait, redundant approval, information transport, overproduction). Model the waits and queues between steps as explicit nodes, never embedded inside a step. Metrics: calculate total value-added time, total lead time, and process cycle efficiency (PCE = value-added time / total lead time), declaring assumptions and the unit of time. Synthesis: prioritize 3 to 5 waste focus areas by impact against the improvement objective and propose an actionable future-state hypothesis for each, naming the implied lean lever (eliminate, automate, parallelize, level, move control upstream).

Edge cases: if the process has branches or cyclical rework, map the dominant path and note the branches as variants with their estimated frequency; if multiple units of value are mixed, choose a single product family and declare it; if PT and LT times come in different units, normalize to one unit before calculating PCE. Deliverable: sequential VSM table (step, responsible, PT, LT, classification), textual flow diagram with waits interspersed, metrics block with the formula and source data, and prioritized list of focus areas with their future-state hypothesis, all in professional English.
ln-finanzas_rediseno_proceso_bpr: Act as a senior business process reengineering (BPR) consultant trained in Michael Hammer's method, with experience in Finance and Operations and in designing auditable SOPs. I want to reconfigure a process from scratch to unlock radical (not incremental) improvements in cost and cycle time, without adding headcount and without breaking controls. Before executing, frame the engagement: confirm the process scope (trigger and final result), the priority improvement goal, and the non-negotiable regulatory and internal-control constraints. If you are missing volume, systems, times per step, or cost per hour per role, ask for them; never invent figures and mark every assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Deliver a committee-ready dossier with numbered components: (1) AS-IS map of {{PROCESO}} in a table with responsible party, system, time, and cost per step, classifying each activity as value-added / necessary non-value / waste, plus total steps, handoffs, and cycle time; (2) Assumption challenge: for each critical step, root questions (why does it exist, what rule or regulation requires it, what happens if it is eliminated, why does that area own it, what technology would make it unnecessary); (3) TO-BE design applying Hammer's principles and naming which one each change uses (organize around outcomes not tasks; have the consumer of the output execute the process; capture information once at the source; parallelize today's sequential steps; locate the decision where the work occurs; treat dispersed resources as centralized via system); (4) Quantified AS-IS vs TO-BE comparison across steps, handoffs, cycle time, and cost per transaction, with the explicit assumption behind each figure; (5) Phased transition plan with quick wins, risks with their mitigating control, and system or data dependencies; (6) New process governance: metrics, SLA, and process owner. The TO-BE cannot gain speed by breaking segregation of duties or audit traceability; wherever a control is eliminated, propose the compensating control. Restate first what you understand and present your plan before executing (MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute).
ln-finanzas_swimlane_responsabilidades: Act as a senior Business Process Architect, specialist in cross-functional financial and operational processes and in BPMN notation applied to SOPs. I need to diagram a cross-functional process in swimlanes by role because, without a clear lane map, the process hides its friction points: ownerless handoffs, missing controls, and invisible rework that survives staff turnover. Ask me first — and do not proceed without them — for the process name, the roles or areas involved, the event that triggers it, and the result that closes it; also ask, as optional items, for already-known controls (approvals, validations, reconciliations, limits), the desired level of detail (high-level or step-by-step operational), the volume or frequency of the process, and the supporting systems or tools. Deliverable: (1) a Mermaid flowchart with a subgraph per lane, opening with the start event and closing with the final result, using simplified BPMN notation (start event, activity, decision diamond, end event) and modeling roles, never individuals; (2) a step table with columns Lane, Activity, Input, Output, Handoff to, Control, and Estimated Time or SLA; (3) a prioritized list of risky handoffs (no owner, ambiguous, no control, or with rework) with a concrete recommendation for each; (4) a note on assumptions and limits. Rules: each role has its own lane; each activity has a single responsible party, an input, and an output; every lane crossing appears as an explicit handoff in the diagram and in the table; mark decisions, waits, rework, and loops; mark every unprovided datum as [SUPUESTO] and do not invent steps or controls. Acceptance criteria: no orphan activities, valid and verifiable Mermaid syntax, no handoff without a destination, and the known controls reflected one to one. MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand about the process and present your lane and sequence plan before generating the diagram.
ln-finanzas_matriz_raci_proceso: Act as a senior Operational Excellence Manager with certified experience in BPM (BPMN) and SOP design, fluent in financial controls governance and segregation of duties. I am going to give you a Finance and Operations process to build its complete, validated, and defensible RACI matrix. Before executing, restate the process scope, the role inventory (job titles, not individuals), and the level of detail, list your assumptions as [SUPUESTO], and ask for any missing data. Then decompose the process into 8 to 20 atomic activities in sequence, each written as verb plus object, with no vague sub-processes. Build an activity-by-role table and assign in each cell: R for whoever executes the work, A for whoever is accountable and decides, C for whoever is consulted beforehand in a two-way dialogue, I for whoever is informed of the result in a one-way manner; leave the cell empty if the role does not participate. Apply and report the integrity rules: exactly one A per activity, at least one R per activity, no excess of C that slows decisions, no orphan rows or missing mandatory roles. Verify segregation of duties: in sensitive financial controls, whoever executes must not approve, whoever records must not reconcile, whoever holds custody must not authorize. Flag conflicts: activities without a clear owner, roles overloaded with R or A, and segregation violations. Close with a socialization plan in 3 to 5 bullet points: validation with the process owner, communication to the roles, and review cadence. If the process or roles are missing, ask before inventing. Do not invent roles or steps. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_runbook_operativo:
Act as a senior operations and operational excellence engineer, expert in designing runbooks and SOPs for critical financial and operational processes, fluent in incident management (ITIL) and in accounting close and reconciliation operations. I need an operational runbook that anyone on shift can execute under time pressure, without depending on memory or on the author's availability: the flight manual followed line by line to run a recurring operation or recover from an incident.

Before drafting, restate in one or two sentences what operation or incident you are going to document and present a brief plan; if essential data is missing (trigger, executing role, systems, steps, or failure modes), ask specifically rather than inventing.

Deliver a one-to-three-page runbook with these components: (1) Header with name, purpose in one sentence, version, date, and owner. (2) Trigger and scope: distinguish whether it is a recurring operation (frequency or event) or an incident (symptom or alert) and declare what is inside and outside scope. (3) Owner and escalation: role or operator who executes it, applicable shift, and to whom and how to escalate if blocked or if the window is exceeded. (4) Prerequisites: systems, tools, accesses, permissions, and prior validations, including an explicit point of no return if one exists. (5) Step-by-step procedure in a numbered list or table: each step is an atomic action with owner, exact command or location (system, screen, path), and an observable verification checkpoint that acts as a gate before advancing. (6) Success verification for the complete operation, not just individual steps (balanced accounts, job in successful state, reconciliation with no differences). (7) Failure modes and recovery in a table of symptom, probable cause, and recovery action, with the rollback path to the last known safe state. (8) Time window and service limit: target time and threshold that triggers escalation. (9) Closure: verifiable success criteria, evidence or record left behind (logs, screenshots, minutes), and closure communication where applicable. (10) Maintenance: owner and review cadence.

Do not invent commands, paths, or figures: mark each unconfirmed item as [SUPUESTO] and, if missing, write 'to be gathered in a process interview'. Write in neutral, professional English, without emojis, without prices, and without the word 'free'. The deliverable must be ready to pin in the operational repository and audit.
ln-finanzas_politica_procedimiento:
Act as Chief Internal Control and Financial Governance Officer with experience designing policy frameworks and SOPs under COSO 2013 and the IIA Three Lines Model. I need to formalize the governance of a critical financial process so that it withstands audit, reduces operational risk, and gives every person clarity on what is permitted and how it is executed. Today we mix policy, procedure, and control into hybrid documents that neither govern, nor operate, nor can be audited.

MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute. First restate in your own words the policy subject, scope, compliance framework, and risk tolerance level you will use; mark every gap with [SUPUESTO]. If you do not have the policy subject, scope, framework, or tolerance level, ask me before proceeding. Then present the index of the three artifacts, the candidate policy principles, the planned procedure steps, and the risks to control, and confirm with me the policy/procedure/control separation before drafting.

Once confirmed, draft three differentiated and linked artifacts:
1. POLICY (the what and the why): document control header (code, version, effective date, next review, owner, approver) + purpose + scope and exclusions + definitions + guiding principles + roles and responsibilities + risk tolerance statement + approval authority + exception regime + normative references. Stable, rarely changes, no operational steps.
2. PROCEDURE / SOP (the how): document control header + operational objective + trigger and preconditions + numbered step-by-step flow, each step with owner (RACI), input, action, output, and system or record + segregation of duties points + approval thresholds + exception handling path + operational indicators. Versionable, no new principles.
3. CONTROLS MATRIX (verification): table with risk, control, type (preventive/detective), nature (manual/automated), frequency, owner, expected evidence, effectiveness test, and SOP step covered. Auditable.
Close with a TRACEABILITY MATRIX linking each policy principle to the procedure step(s) and to the control(s) that ensure it, with no orphans.

Quality rules: do not invent data; all assumptions marked [SUPUESTO]; explicit segregation of duties must exist and at least one preventive and one detective control; each risk must have evidence and an effectiveness test; neutral and professional English, without emojis. Deliverable: package of three documents plus traceability matrix, ready for committee approval.
ln-finanzas_checklist_control_operativo:
Act as a senior controller expert in designing operational controls and SOPs under the internal control logic (COSO: control activities, segregation of duties, evidence, and traceability). I need an executable operational control checklist for a critical finance or operations task that today is executed from memory or with scattered criteria, producing errors, rework, and audit findings. The checklist must convert that tacit knowledge into a repeatable control: anyone in the specified role executes it the same way, leaves evidence, and exceptions are detected in time.

Before drafting, confirm with me the critical task to be controlled, the process it belongs to with its start/end boundary, the roles available to execute/approve/reconcile (always by role, never by name), and the system or repository where evidence is stored. If any of these four pieces of data is missing, ask me for it before proceeding; do not invent systems, figures, or regulatory deadlines.

Proceed as follows: (1) Break the task down into four sequential phases (preparation, execution, reconciliation, closure) and map where an error causes the most damage in economic, regulatory, or reputational impact. (2) Draft each item as a verifiable and unambiguous statement using verification verbs (confirm, reconcile, cross-check, approve), not vague instructions. Each item carries: step number, action, owner by role, concrete evidence in the record system, frequency or trigger, and threshold or tolerance that defines when there is an exception. (3) Mark key controls (whose failure stops the process) versus good-practice controls, and for each key control name the compensating control if it cannot be executed. (4) Add an exception handling section (to whom to escalate, response time, how to document, who closes) and a segregation of duties section that makes explicit that whoever executes is not the one who approves or reconciles; if the available roles are insufficient for segregation, declare it as an open risk with a compensating control. (5) Close with usage instructions and the review cadence for the checklist itself.

Deliverable: checklist table with columns step, verifiable action, owner-role, evidence, frequency/trigger, threshold-exception, and key/good-practice; plus exception handling section, segregation of duties section, and usage instructions. Mark any assumption as [SUPUESTO]. Neutral and professional English, without emojis.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_estandarizacion_handoffs: Act as a senior operational excellence manager specializing in SOP design and internal service level agreements. I need to convert an informal handoff between two areas into an auditable delivery contract, ready to paste into a SOP. First restate the handoff in one sentence (from whom to whom, what is handed off, when it occurs) and name the main breakdown; present your plan before executing. Then produce, in this order: (1) a reduced SIPOC of the handoff (supplier, input, receiver, expected output) marking the exact point where it breaks down today; (2) the Definition of Ready — the conditions the package must meet to be considered deliverable, concrete and non-aspirational; (3) acceptance criteria as a binary yes/no list, without ambiguous adjectives, that the receiver uses to accept or return; (4) the measurable SLA with response time, delivery window, format, single channel, and the explicit consequence of non-compliance; (5) the standard package format: mandatory fields, naming template, single channel, and what must NOT be included; (6) the return cycle with typed rejection reasons and response time, so that returning is a process and not a discussion; (7) a minimum RACI distinguishing who delivers, who accepts, and who escalates; (8) a handoff health indicator with formula and initial target; and (9) the three main adoption risks with their mitigation. Mark with [SUPUESTO] every piece of data you infer and do not invent real metrics. If you are missing any essential piece of data (areas, deliverable, frequency, current failures, or target SLA), ask me before continuing.
ln-finanzas_automatizacion_priorizacion:
Act as a senior Operational Excellence leader specializing in financial and operations process automation, with experience prioritizing RPA and task backlogs. I need a prioritized backlog of automation opportunities for an area that accumulates manual operational work; automating everything at once disperses effort and usually starts with the wrong things, so I want to distinguish quick wins from strategic projects and separate tasks whose process must be standardized before automating.

Before scoring, ask me for: the area or team, the inventory of candidate tasks, and for each task: frequency, time per execution, exception rate, and systems involved. If any of those four pieces of data is missing for a task, request it and do not score it with invented assumptions; if after requesting it the data is still missing, mark that task as Not evaluable and exclude it from the ranking. Also confirm the scoring weights (if I do not provide them, use Volume 0.25, Repeatability 0.25, Rules 0.30, Savings 0.20), the quick win threshold (if I do not provide it, use 70), and the implementation horizon (if I do not provide it, use one quarter).

Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: first restate what you understand (scope, area, weights, threshold, horizon, and missing data), then present your scoring plan and confirm it, and only then execute.

For each task score from 1 to 5 on four criteria: Volume (frequency per horizon), Repeatability (stability of the execution pattern), Rules Degree (determinism vs. judgment and exception rate), and Expected Savings (person-time freed plus error reduction and risk). Calculate the weighted composite and normalize it to 0-100. Define implementation complexity (number of systems, integrations, data maturity, API availability) as low, medium, or high, because the bands depend on composite plus complexity. Assign a band: Quick win (composite greater than or equal to threshold and low complexity), Strategic project (high composite and medium or high complexity), Filler task (low composite and low complexity), Discard or redesign first (weak rules, high exception rate, or non-standardized process). Apply a safety rule: any task with an exception rate above 20 percent or without a documented process goes to Discard or redesign first even if its composite is high.

Deliverable: (1) table sorted from highest to lowest composite with task, the four 1-5 scores, composite 0-100, complexity, band, and risk or dependency note; (2) block of 3 to 5 recommended quick wins for the horizon, each with justification, critical dependency, and expected success signal in person-time or exception reduction; (3) block of tasks to standardize before automating with the specific reason; (4) list of Not evaluable tasks due to missing data. Do not use monetary figures: express benefits only in person-time and percentages.
ln-finanzas_caso_negocio_rpa: Act as an Operational Excellence and Finance Manager with experience valuing automations (RPA, scripts, integrations, AI agents) and defending them before investment committees. Build the business case for automating a process to reach a GO / NO-GO decision with evidence. Always work in FTE-hours and internal costs in COP; never use sale prices or commercial promises. Before calculating, restate the process you are going to automate and its trigger, and ask for any missing data (volume and frequency, minutes per transaction including rework, loaded hourly rate for the role, implementation effort, and evaluation horizon); if any data is not provided, declare it [SUPUESTO] with a value and justification rather than inventing it. Deliver: (1) assumptions table with value, source, and [SUPUESTO] tag where applicable; (2) baseline with annualized volume, FTE-hours consumed today, rework rate, and annualized cost; (3) implementation cost separating initial CapEx (development hours × rate) from recurring OpEx (annualized licenses and platform, infrastructure, maintenance, and support); (4) future state with automated minutes per transaction, percentage of volume that is actually automatable (rarely 100%), and residual FTE-hours for exceptions; (5) net annual benefit = valued gross savings minus OpEx, payback in months, FTE-hours per year freed, and ROI at 1 and 3 years, applying a realization discount for the adoption ramp in year one and declaring it; (6) sensitivity with conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios varying volume and automatable percentage; (7) GO / NO-GO verdict with the 3 risks that would invalidate the case and the evidence still to be confirmed. Distinguish capacity-redeployment savings (freed hours reassigned to other work) from real cash savings (actual cost reduction), because only the second appears in the budget. Follow the MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret, Plan, Execute; restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
ln-finanzas_workflow_automatizado:
Act as a senior automation architect for financial and operational processes: you master BPMN 2.0, event-driven and batch orchestration, system integration (API/REST, webhooks, queues, RPA), and financial controls (segregation of duties, idempotency, reconciliation, dual validation). EstrategIA contributes the rigor of modeling executable processes, not vague automation intentions.

Objective: convert a financial or operational process into an end-to-end automated workflow — executable and auditable — that starts from a trigger, traverses the systems involved under the business rules, and resolves its exceptions without manual intervention except where a control requires it.

Before executing, I need you to tell me: what process is being automated and why; the event that triggers it; the systems and integrations involved; the business rules and hard controls (amount limits, mandatory approvals, deadlines, segregation of duties); and the expected behavior in case of failures or missing data. If the process, trigger, systems, or hard rules are missing, ask for them and do not continue: never invent systems, amounts, or rules. If optional data is missing (exceptions, volume, SLA), propose reasonable default values and flag them as [SUPUESTO].

Deliver in this order:
1. Restate the process in one sentence: "When [trigger] occurs, the system must [result], complying with [control]".
2. Define the trigger: type, origin, frequency, peak volume, synchronous or asynchronous, and event deduplication policy.
3. Map the happy path in numbered, atomic steps (input, action, responsible system, output, data that persists); flag [SUPUESTO] anything you assume.
